en: May there be prosperity.
Here begins the first chapter of the *Nāṭyaśāstra* composed by the sage Bharata.
Having bowed my head to the two gods, Pitāmaha and Maheśvara,
I shall proclaim the Nāṭyaśāstra as it was uttered by Brahmā.
Once, during a period when study was forbidden, Bharata— who was skilled in dramatic arts— was surrounded by his sons after completing his recitation as one observing a vow.
In former times, the great-souled sages, led by Ātreya and possessing restrained senses and intellects, attended upon him and questioned him.
O Brahmin, how did this Nāṭyaveda, which was correctly composed by the Blessed One and is equal in authority to the Vedas, arise, and for whose sake was it created?
How many limbs does it have, what is its measure, and what is the nature of its application?
O Blessed One, you should explain all of this according to reality.
Having heard those words of the sages, the sage Bharata then replied with these words concerning the discourse on the science of drama (nāṭyaveda).
Having become pure and with attentive minds,
you should hear the origin of the Nāṭya Veda as created by Brahmā.
Formerly, O Brahmins, when the Kṛta Yuga had passed during the Svāyambhuva interval,
and the Tretā Yuga of Manu Vaivasvata had arrived.
But when the world is engaged in vulgar practices, fallen under the sway of desire and greed, deluded by envy, anger, and the like, and [thus] experiencing pleasure and pain; BhN 1.9.
When Jambudvīpa was overrun by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and mahoragas, it was brought under the protection of the world-guardians.
It is said that the Grandfather was addressed by the gods, headed by Mahendra:
"We desire a spectacle for our amusement that may be both seen and heard."
"This Vedic practice must not be proclaimed among the Śūdra castes;
therefore, create another fifth Veda intended for all social classes."
Having said "So be it" to them and dismissed the king of the gods, he,
the knower of reality, resorted to yoga and recalled the four Vedas.
"These Vedas are not to be heard by those born among the classes of women, Śūdras, and others;
therefore, I shall create another fifth Veda that may be heard by everyone."
It is consistent with the Dharma, meaningful, conducive to fame, instructive, and inclusive;
it reveals all actions for the sake of the world to come.
I shall compose the fifth Veda, known as Nāṭya, which is endowed with the meaning of all the Śāstras, which initiates all arts, and which includes the Itihāsas. (BhN 1.15)
Having thus resolved and recollecting all the Vedas, the Blessed One then created the Nāṭya-veda, which arose from the limbs of the four Vedas.
He took up the recitation from the Ṛgveda, the singing from the Sāmans,
the dramatic gestures from the Yajurveda, and even the aesthetic sentiments from the Atharvaveda.
Thus was the Nāṭyaveda, connected with the Vedas and Upavedas,
created by the blessed, all-knowing, and high-souled Brahmā.
Having created the Nāṭyaveda, Brahmā said to the Lord of the Gods:
"This Itihāsa has been created by me; let it be assigned to the gods."
"Let this Veda known as Nāṭya be transmitted by you to those who are virtuous, discerning, bold, and have overcome all fatigue. (BhN 1.20)
Having heard those words uttered by Brahmā, Śakra,
bowing with palms joined in reverence, replied to the Grandfather.
O Best of Beings, O Blessed One, the gods are incapable and unfit for its grasping, retention, understanding, and application, as it pertains to the art of drama. (BhN 1.22)
Those sages who know the secret knowledge of the Vedas and are firm in their vows—they alone are capable of grasping this [knowledge], as well as applying and retaining it. (BhN 1.23)
Having heard the words of Śakra, the Lotus-born One said to me:
"O sinless one, you, accompanied by a hundred sons, shall be the performer of this [sacrifice]."
Having understood that I had been commanded by my grandfather, I taught the sons the science of drama (nāṭyaveda) and its practical application according to the truth.
Śāṇḍilya, Vātsya, Kohala, and likewise Dattila; Jaṭila and Ambaṣṭaka, as well as Taṇḍu and Agniśikha. BhN 1.26.
Saindhava, Sapulomā, Śāḍvali, Vipula,
as well as Kapiñjali, Vādira, and Yamadhūmrāyaṇa.
Jambudhvaja, Kākajaṅgha, Svarṇaka, Tāpasa, as well as Kaidārin, Śālikarṇa, Dīrghagātra, and Śālika.
Kautsa, Tāṇḍāyani, Piṅgala, Citraka, Bandhula, Bhallaka, Muṣṭhika, and Saindhavāyana; BhN 1.29.
Taitila, Bhārgava, Śuci, Bahula,
Abudha, Budhasena, Pāṇḍukarṇa, and Sukerala.
Ṛjuka, Maṇḍaka, Śambara, Vañjula, as well as Māgadha, Sarala, Kartāra, and Ugra. BhN 1.31.
Tuṣāra, Pārṣada, Gautama, Bādarāyaṇa,
Viśāla, Śabala, Sunāman, and Meṣa.
Kāliya, Bhramara, as well as the sage Pīṭhamukha, Nakhakuṭṭa, Aśmakuṭṭa, and likewise Ṣaṭpada, who is the most excellent. BhN 1.33.
Pāduka and Upānaha, Śruti and Aṣasvara, Agnikuṇḍa and Ājyakuṇḍa, Vitaṇḍya and Tāṇḍya. BhN 1.34.
Kartarākṣa, Hiraṇyākṣa, Kuśala, Dussaha, as well as Lāja, Bhayānaka, Bībhatsa, and Savicakṣaṇa. BhN 1.35.
Puṇḍrākṣa, Puṇḍranāsa, Asita, and Sitaka, Vidyujjihva, Mahājihva, and Śālaṅkāyana.
Śyāmāyana, Māṭhara, and likewise Lohitāṅga;
Saṃvartaka, Pañcaśikha, Triśikha, and Śikha as well. BhN 1.37.
Śaṇḍa, whose face is the color of a conch shell, as well as Śaṅkukarṇa, Śakranemi, Gabhasti, Aṃśumālin, and likewise Śaṭha; BhN 1.38.
By the command of the Grandfather and out of a desire for the welfare of the world, we [created] Vidyuta, Śātajaṅgha, Raudra, and also Vīra. (BhN 1.39)
A hundred sons were appointed according to the division of their respective domains;
each was assigned to that specific task for which he was suitable, and in the manner appropriate to him.
"O twice-born ones, this performance has indeed been employed by me, relying upon the Bhāratī, Sātvatī, and likewise the Ārabhaṭī styles. (BhN 1.41)
Having accepted [the work] and paid homage, Brahmā was then addressed by me;
thereupon the Teacher of the Gods said to me, "Employ the Kaiśikī style as well."
"O best of the twice-born, tell me what wealth is suitable for her.
Thus was I addressed by him, and I replied to the lord.
"O Blessed One, let the materials for Kaiśikī be provided;
she is perfected by the movements of dance and gestures, and consists of the functions of rasa and bhāva. (BhN 1.44)
I have seen the *kaiśikī* style of the Lord Nīlakaṇṭha as he danced—a style characterized by delicate attire and arising from the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*). (BhN 1.45)
But she could not be employed by men except through women;
therefore, the all-pervading Lord of great splendor created the Apsarases by means of his mind.
Skilled in the ornaments of drama, they bestowed upon me through practical application [the teachings of] Mañjukeśī, Sukeśī, Miśrakeśī, and Sulocanā. (BhN 1.47)
Saudāminī, Devadattā, Devasenā, Manoramā, Sudatī, Sundarī, Vidagdhā, and likewise Vipulā. (BhN 1.48)
Sumālā, Santati, Sunandā, and likewise Sumukhī;
Māgadhī, Arjunī, Saralā, Keralā, and Dhṛti. BhN 1.49.
Svāti, who was appointed to the management of the vessels by Svayambhū along with his disciples, gave me Nandā, Sapuṣkalā, and Kalamā.
And the Gandharvas, headed by Nārada, were appointed to the art of singing; thus, having thoroughly understood this drama, he [Bharata] together with all his sons— BhN 1.51.
Accompanied by Svāti and Nārada, the cause of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
I approached Brahmā with palms joined in reverence for the purpose of ritual application.
"The mastery of the drama has been attained; tell me, what shall I do?
Having heard these words, the Grandfather replied:
This great occasion for ritual practice has arrived;
this glorious festival of Indra’s banner is now underway.
Now, let this Veda known as the Nāṭya be employed here; then, during that festival of the banner, the Asuras and Dānavas shall be slain. (BhN 1.55)
During the festival celebrating the victory of Mahendra, which was crowded with joyful immortals,
I first performed a *nāndī* consisting of words of benediction.
Consisting of eight parts, variegated, and fashioned according to the Vedas,
at its conclusion a mimicry was performed, just as the Daityas were defeated by the gods.
Causing confusion and flight, consisting of battles involving cutting and piercing, and [acts of] digging,
the gods beginning with Brahmā were then gratified by his practice.
They indeed bestowed all kinds of implements upon the sons of Mṛta;
Śakra, being pleased, first gave his own auspicious banner.
Brahmā [bears] the *kuṭilaka*, Varuṇa the auspicious water-pot (*bhṛṅgāra*),
Sūrya the parasol, Śiva success (*siddhi*), and Vāyu the fan.
Viṣṇu gave him the lion-throne, Kubera likewise the crown,
and the goddess Sarasvatī granted him the quality of being worthy of hearing and seeing.
The remaining gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas,
who were intended as members of that assembly, were based on various species and qualities.
With portions of their own portions, those delighted denizens of heaven bestowed dispositions, sentiments, forms, and likewise strength upon my sons. (BhN 1.63)
When this undertaking for the destruction of the Daityas and Dānavas had thus begun,
all the Daityas who were assembled there became agitated.
Having incited the obstacles led by Virūpākṣa, they said:
"We will not tolerate this dance; come here! (BhN 1.65)
Then, together with those asuras, the obstructors resorted to their illusory powers and paralyzed the speech, gestures, and memory of those who were dancing.
Having seen such destruction by the architect, the king of the gods said, "Why this discrepancy in the application? and entered into meditation.
Then he saw the sacrificial hall surrounded on all sides by obstacles;
there he found the architect, together with others, rendered senseless and deprived of consciousness.
Rising up quickly, he seized Śakra’s supreme banner;
his body was radiant with every kind of jewel, and his eyes were slightly rolled back.
Then the King of the Gods, with his thunderbolt, rendered those obstacles and asuras who had taken their places upon the stage of the arena into beings with shattered bodies.
When all the obstacles along with the Dānavas had been slain, all the inhabitants of heaven rejoiced and then spoke these words: ||| BhN_1.71 |||
"Aha! This divine weapon has been obtained by you, by which these Dānavas have had all their limbs shattered to pieces."
"Since those obstacles, along with the asuras, have been shattered by him,
therefore he shall be known by the name Jarjara."
And those other assailants who shall approach for the purpose of violence,
upon seeing him thus decayed, they too will likewise depart in the same manner.
"So be it," Śakra then said to those gods;
"and this Jarjara shall become the protector of them all."
For while this vast festival of Śakra was thus underway, other obstacles caused terror to arise among those who were dancing. (BhN 1.76)
Having seen the resolve of those Daityas born of their hostile intent,
I approached Brahmā accompanied by all my sons.
"O Blessed One, the obstacles to the destruction of this drama are certain;
O Lord of the Gods, please duly command the method for its protection. (BhN 1.78)
Then Brahmā spoke with diligence to Viśvakarman:
"O high-minded one, construct a theater hall endowed with all auspicious characteristics."
Then, after a short time, Viśvakarman, having constructed a magnificent and auspicious theater hall endowed with every excellent characteristic, [presented it].
Having gone to the assembly hall with palms joined in reverence, he said to Brahmā:
"O Lord, the theater is ready; you should inspect it."
Then, together with Mahendra and all the gods, both those [allied] and others,
Druhiṇa arrived in haste to behold the dance pavilion.
Having seen the theater hall, Brahmā then said to all the gods:
"This theater pavilion must be protected by you through your respective portions."
Then the Moon was appointed to the protection of the pavilion;
likewise, the world-protectors were stationed in the cardinal directions and the Maruts in the intermediate directions.
Mitra was stationed on the stage for the dressing room, Varuṇa in the sky, Vahni at the protection of the altar, and all the gods in the vessel. (BhN 1.85)
Furthermore, the four castes are assigned to the pillars,
while the Ādityas and Rudras are stationed within the intervals between the pillars.
Then the Dhāraṇīs, the Bhūtas, and likewise the Apsarases in the halls; the Yakṣiṇīs in all dwellings, and the Great Ocean upon the surface of the earth.
Kṛtānta and Kāla were appointed to the gate-hall,
while two mighty chief Nāgas were stationed at the door-panels.
At the threshold stands the staff of Yama, and upon it is fixed a trident;
both Niyati and Mṛtyu stand there as the two gatekeepers.
And on the side of the stage platform, Mahendra himself stood;
there, the goddess Vidyut, the slayer of the Daityas, was stationed within a *mattavāraṇī* pavilion.
Upon the pillars of the intoxicated female elephant, for the purpose of protection,
were stationed spirits, yakṣas, piśācas, and mighty guhyakas.
The thunderbolt that destroys the Daityas was placed within the joints;
indeed, the lords of the gods of immeasurable power were placed within its segments.
Brahmā resides in the first joint of the head; likewise, Śaṅkara is in the second;
Viṣṇu is situated in the third, and Skanda indeed in the fourth.
And on the fifth [pillar], the great nāgas Śeṣa, Vāsuki, and Takṣaka—
thus were the gods established upon Jarjara for the destruction of obstacles.
Brahmā himself is established in the center of the stage;
for the sake of the sacrifice, the scattering of flowers is performed in the middle of the stage.
And those yakṣas, guhyakas, and pannagas who dwell in the netherworld (pātāla) have been appointed to guard the base of the stage from below.
Indra protects the hero, Sarasvatī the heroine, and Oṃkāra the jester; the remaining [deities] are Prakṛti, while Hara is the [final] one.
He said, "Those deities who have been appointed here for protection shall themselves become the presiding deities (adhidaiva) over these."
In the meantime, the Grandfather was addressed by all the gods:
"For now, let these obstacles be pacified by you with conciliatory words."
First, conciliation should be employed, and secondly, indeed, bribery;
after those two, sowing dissension, and then punishment is applied.
Having heard the words of the gods, Brahmā spoke to the obstacles: "Why have you risen up for the destruction of the dance? (BhN 1.101)
Having heard the words of Brahmā, Virūpākṣa then spoke these words, preceded by conciliation, together with the Daityas and the hosts of obstacles: BhN 1.102.
"This science of drama which has been created by the Blessed One through the will of the gods is a repudiation of us, made by you for the sake of the gods. (BhN 1.103)
Therefore, O Grandfather of the World, you should not act in this way;
for as are the gods, so are the Daityas, all of whom have emerged from you.
Having heard the words of the obstacles, Brahmā spoke these words:
"Enough of your anger, O Daityas; cast away your despondency, O sinless ones."
I have composed the Nāṭya-veda for you and for the gods, which distinguishes between the auspicious and the inauspicious and depends upon the sequence of the nature of one's karma.
In this regard, there is no absolute experience of yours or of the gods;
rather, this drama of the entire triple world is a representation of the nature of things.
In one place there is Dharma, in another sport; in one place wealth, in another tranquility; in one place laughter, in another battle; in one place desire, and in another slaughter.
Dharma is for those who practice dharma; desire is for those who indulge in desire;
restraint is for the ill-behaved; and the act of taming is for the disciplined.
It generates audacity in the weak-willed, enthusiasm in those who pride themselves on being heroes, awakening in the ignorant, and even erudition in the learned. (BhN 1.110)
The playfulness of the powerful, the steadfastness of those afflicted by suffering,
the wealth of those who live for the sake of profit, and the fortitude of those with agitated minds.
"Endowed with various states of being and consisting of diverse internal conditions, this drama, which imitates the conduct of the world, has been composed by me. (BhN 1.112)
It is the basis for the actions of superior, inferior, and middling men;
it generates beneficial instruction, and it produces steadfastness, play, pleasure, and so forth.
Thus, among the sentiments (rasas), the emotional states (bhāvas), and all ritual actions, drama shall become the source of all instruction in the world. (BhN 1.113)
This drama will, at the proper time, provide rest for those afflicted by suffering, those exhausted by toil, those tormented by grief, and for ascetics.
This drama will be righteous, conducive to fame and long life, beneficial, increasing the intellect, and generating instruction for the world.
There is no such knowledge, no such craft, no such science, no such art,
no such yoga, and no such action that is not seen in this drama.
Therefore, you should not harbor resentment toward the immortals;
this will be a dance that imitates the seven continents.
That by which this dramatic representation is imitated is that which has been performed by me.
Drama, which reveals various narratives, is to be understood as pertaining to the gods, the asuras, kings, householders, and celestial sages. (BhN 1.118)
This very nature of the world, endowed with pleasure and pain,
when combined with the gestures of the limbs and other elements, is designated as "drama" (nāṭya).
This drama shall be the creation of narratives from the Vedas, the sciences, and the histories,
serving as a source of diversion for the world.

This drama will become a source of diversion in the world, providing a means of imagining the meaning of what remains after the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the conduct of the virtuous have been considered. 1.119**
In the meantime, the Grandfather said to all the gods:
"Let a sacrifice be performed today according to the rules in the theater pavilion."
Let the sacrificial offering (bali) be prepared with gifts, oblations accompanied by mantras and medicinal herbs, as well as with foods to be eaten, chewed, and drunk. BhN 1.121.
All those who have come to the world of mortals shall receive auspicious honor;
however, one should never engage in a performance without first honoring the stage.
But he who, without having honored the stage, shall arrange for a performance, his knowledge will be fruitless and he will go to the womb of an animal. (BhN 1.123)
For this worship of the deities of the stage is indeed equal to a sacrifice;
therefore, it must be performed with every effort by those who employ dramatic performance.
Whether he be a dancer or even a lord of wealth, whoever does not perform worship himself,
nor causes others to do so, incurs only decline.
Whoever performs the worship according to the prescribed rule and as it has been seen [in tradition],
shall obtain auspicious benefits and go to the heavenly world.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Druhiṇa, together with the gods, exhorted me in this way: "Perform the worship of the arena! (BhN 1.127).
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Origin of Drama," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
Now begins the second chapter of the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*:
having heard the words of Bharata, the sages then questioned him.
O Blessed One, we wish to hear about the ritual performance that takes place upon the stage.
Alternatively, how should the ritual actions and the worship that constitute its characteristics be performed by future men in a theater? (BhN 2.2)
For here, the theater itself is indeed the starting point of the application of drama;
therefore, you should first state its definition.
Having heard those words of the sages, Bharata said:
"Listen now to the characteristics and the worship of the theater hall."

The mental creation of the divine occurs in their houses and groves; whereas all human states are brought about by [external] conditions, the ritual actions prescribed according to their characteristics must be performed by men with effort. (BhN 2.5)
Listen to how the theater pavilion should be constructed,
and how its site and worship should be diligently applied.
Having observed the dwellings here on earth, the wise Viśvakarman devised three types of architectural layout according to the scriptures.
The pavilion may be elongated, square, or triangular;
for these, there are three measurements: the superior, the middling, and the inferior.
Their measurement is specified as being based on the hand and the cubit:
one hundred, eight, sixty-four, and thirty-two cubits.
The largest [temple] is one hundred and eight cubits, the medium is sixty-four,
and the smallest is desired to be thirty-two cubits.
For the gods, it shall be the highest; for kings, it shall be middling;
but for the remaining constituents, the lowest is ordained.
Among all types of theaters, the middle one is considered the most excellent;
therein, both recited and sung performances will be most pleasant and easy to hear. (BhN 2.11*)
For all theaters, a threefold method is prescribed by practitioners:
the elongated, the square, and the triangular.
The smallest is known to be triangular, the medium-sized is square, and the largest is to be understood as elongated by those who practice the Nāṭya-veda. (BhN 2.11)
And listen now to that very measurement and characteristic which was prescribed by Viśvakarman for all types of assembly halls.

The atom (aṇu), the speck of dust (rajas), the hair-tip (vāla), the nit (likṣā), the louse-egg (yūkā), the barley-corn (yava), as well as the finger-breadth (aṅgula), the cubit (hasta), and the staff (daṇḍa) have thus been proclaimed. BhN 2.13.
Eight *aṇu*s are said to be one *rajas*; eight of those are called a *vāla*.
Eight *vāla*s constitute a *likṣā*, and eight *likṣā*s make one *yūkā*. (BhN 2.14)
Eight lice are known as one barley-corn (*yava*), and likewise eight barley-corns are one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
Twenty-four such finger-breadths are said to constitute one cubit (*hasta*).
The staff is specified as being four cubits in length according to its measurement;
by this very measurement, I shall explain their determination.
One should construct a pavilion for mortals here that is sixty-four cubits in length and thirty-two cubits in width. (BhN 2.17)
From this point forward, the theater pavilion (nāṭyamaṇḍapa) should not be constructed by the performers, because therein the performance would indeed fall into a state of indistinctness. (BhN 2.18)
But in a distant pavilion, the recitation must be performed with a raised tone;
because it cannot escape [the space], it will very easily fall into a discordant pitch. (BhN 2.19)
Furthermore, whatever state has entered this mouth, endowed with various views,
shall attain the supreme state of unmanifestness due to the excellence of the abode.
Therefore, among all assembly halls, a middle-sized one is desired, so that both what is to be recited and what is to be sung may be heard most clearly therein. (BhN 2.21)
For all assembly halls, a threefold rule is prescribed by practitioners:
the elongated, the square, and the triangular.
The smallest is recorded as triangular, the medium as square, and the largest is to be understood as elongated by those who practice the Nāṭya-veda. (BhN 2.21)
The creation of the gods occurs through the power of mind within their celestial abodes and groves;
for all human states are produced through the application of effort.
Therefore, a human being should not strive against things created by the gods;
however, I shall now fully describe the characteristics of a human dwelling.
First, the person undertaking the work should examine the classification of the ground;
thereafter, with a desire for auspiciousness, he should begin the construction according to the proper measurements of the site.
Where the ground is level, firm, hard, and either black or white,
there alone should the performers construct the dance pavilion.
Having first performed the purification, one should plow it with a plough;
one should clear away bones, stakes, potsherds, grass, and shrubs. (BhN 2.26)
Having purified the ground, one should then specify the astrological measure:
"The three Uttarās, Saumya (Mṛgaśirā), Viśākhā, Revatī, Hasta, Tiṣya (Puṣya), and Anurādhā are recommended for the performance of dance."
In conjunction with the Puṣya asterism, one should stretch out a white thread.
The wise should prepare a thread made of cotton, or *bālbaja* grass, or *muñja* grass, or even from bark, provided that it is not subject to breaking. (BhN 2.28)
If the cord is cut in half, the death of the master is certain;
if the rope is cut into three parts, national upheaval is ordained.
If [the thread] is cut at the fourth part, the destruction of the practitioner is said to occur;
or even if it slips from the hand, some diminution will take place. (BhN 2.30)
Therefore, one should always strive diligently to secure the rope, and likewise, one must take great care to measure the theater building. BhN 2.31.
Then, during a favorable moment, on an auspicious lunar day and with an excellent karana,
having gratified the brahmins, he should cause them to pronounce the declaration of a meritorious day (puṇyāha).
Then, having offered the water of pacification, one should extend the thread;
having made it sixty-four cubits long, one should again divide those [lengths] into two.
Of that [area] which has been divided into two, one should arrange the *raṅgaśīrṣa* (stage-front) by dividing the rear portion equally into two halves. (BhN 2.34)
And in the western section, one should designate the dressing room,
having divided the sections according to rule, correctly, and in proper sequence.
And during an auspicious conjunction of the lunar mansions, the installation of the pavilion should take place amidst the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, mṛdaṅgas, paṇavas, and other instruments.
The installation must indeed be performed with all musical instruments being played;
however, those who are undesirable, as well as heretics and those belonging to other stages of life (āśramas), should be removed.
And for those men who wear saffron robes and those who are physically impaired,
an offering (bali) consisting of various kinds of food should be made at night.
Possessing fragrances, flowers, and fruits, it extends throughout the ten directions;
in the east it is joined with white food, and in the south with blue food.
The offering in the west is yellow, while that in the north is red;
in whatever direction a deity is assigned, it should be of the corresponding color.
Such an offering (bali), preceded by mantras, should be presented there;
and for the installation ceremony, ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa) should be given to the Brahmins.
Likewise, the honey-mixture (madhuparka) should be offered to the king, and rice with jaggery (guḍaudana) to the performers;
furthermore, the wise should perform the installation under the asterism Mūla.
Having thus performed the installation during a favorable moment, on an auspicious lunar day, and under a good karana, one should proceed with the work of plastering the walls.

Once the work of the walls is completed, the erection of the pillars should then take place on an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable constellation, and with a propitious conjunction and division.
The erection of the pillars should be performed by a well-disciplined preceptor who has fasted for three nights, under either the asterism Rohiṇī or Śravaṇa.
The installation of the pillars should be performed at the auspicious time when the sun has risen;
on the first pillar, which belongs to the Brāhmaṇas, [an offering] prepared with ghee and mustard seeds should be made.
An entirely white ritual procedure should be performed, and one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) alone;
thereafter, upon the pillar of the Kṣatriya, one should place cloth, garlands, and ointments.
Everything should be given in red, and molasses with rice (guḍaudana) should be offered to the twice-born;
this rite is to be performed at the pillar of the Vaiśya in the northwestern direction.
Everything should be given with joy, including ghee-rice to the twice-born;
and the ritual for the Śūdra pillar should be performed properly, based on the preceding and subsequent rules.

One should diligently prepare a *kūsara* porridge that is predominantly blue for the twice-born to eat, while the previously mentioned pillar for the Brahmins is adorned with white garlands and unguents. (BhN 2.50)
One should deposit gold at the base, serving as an ornament for the ear, and copper should be placed below on the pillar designated for a Kṣatriya. (BhN 2.51)
At the base of the Vaiśya pillar, one should cause silver to be given;
at the base of the Śūdra pillar, however, one should give iron. BhN 2.52.
However, gold should indeed be deposited at the bases of all the pillars amidst the sounding of auspicious and meritorious proclamations and the cry of "Victory! (BhN 2.53).
The erection of the pillars should be performed preceded by offerings of flower garlands,
along with abundant gifts of jewels, gifts of cows, and gifts of garments.
Having gratified the Brahmins, one should then raise the pillars—
those that are immovable, unshakable, and likewise not leaning.
These are indeed declared to be the faults when the pillar rises correctly;
lack of rain is said to occur upon its swaying, and there is fear of death from its tilting.
From an earthquake, there arises a terrible fear from an enemy army;
however, if it is free from these defects, one should erect an auspicious pillar.
In the case of the *pavitra* rite and the *brāhmaṇastambha*, a cow should be given as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
For the remaining rites, a meal should be provided for the performers associated with the installation.
That [food] should be given, purified by mantras, by the wise dance-teacher;
he should also feed the royal priest and the king with honeyed milk-rice.
Likewise, one should provide all the cooks with *kṛsarā* mixed with an abundance of salt;
having thus performed the entire rite, one should play all kinds of musical instruments.
Having consecrated them according to the rule, the pure practitioner should raise up the pillars, [reciting]:
"Just as the mountain Meru is immovable, and the Himavat is of great strength... (BhN 2.61).
"Be thus immovable for the victory of the lord of men;
[protect] the pillar, the door, the wall, and the dressing room. (BhN 2.62)
One who knows this should thus erect it through the ritual procedure prescribed by rule;
moreover, a *mattavāraṇī* (elephant-enclosure) should be constructed at the side of the stage-platform.
The *mattavāraṇī* (the elephant-enclosure) should be constructed with four pillars, equal in measurement to the stage-platform (*raṅgapīṭha*),
and one and a half cubits in height.
The performance hall should be made equal to those two in height;
therein one should provide garlands, incense, perfume, and likewise clothing.
Offerings of various colors should be given, as well as a bali-oblation dear to the bhūtas;
there, iron should be placed beneath the pillars by those skilled in the craft.
At the meal, rice mixed with sesame (kṛsara) should be given as food for the Brahmins;
thus, the Mattavāraṇī rite should be performed according to the prescribed rules.
Then the stage-platform (raṅgapīṭha) should be constructed according to the rites prescribed by rule;
the stage-front (raṅgaśīrṣa), moreover, should be made provided with six wooden beams (ṣaḍdāruka).
In this case, there should be two doorways for the dressing room;
furthermore, black earth should be diligently applied here for filling.
Having ploughed with the plough and cleared away the clods, grass,
and gravel, one should diligently yoke two oxen of pure color to the plough.
In this rite, those who are the performers— being free from defects of limb and possessing all their members intact—
should carry the clay in new baskets.
The stage-front (raṅgaśīrṣa) should be constructed with such [materials] with great care;
it must not be made like the back of a tortoise, nor likewise like the back of a fish.
The painting surface is praised when it has the appearance of a polished mirror;
and here, jewels should be offered by the wise, with a diamond in the east.
Lapis lazuli is on the right side, crystal likewise on the west,
coral on the north, and gold should be in the center.
Having thus established the primary proportions, one should apply the work of woodcraft, employing various crafts joined with both direct and indirect methods. (BhN 2.75)
It was endowed with various pleasure groves, graced by many beasts of prey,
and beautifully adorned on all sides with statues of women.
It was provided with turrets and recesses, with variously constructed altars,
arranged in diverse layouts, and featuring latticed windows of variegated design.
It was provided with excellent seats, filled with flocks of doves,
and further adorned with pillars set upon various mosaic floors.
Having thus performed the procedure for the wooden framework, one should apply the work of the walls,
or the pillars, or the brackets, or even the windows.
One should not construct a corner that has an opposing door or one where a door is pierced;
rather, a two-storied theater pavilion should be made in the shape of a mountain cave.
Provided with gentle windows, free from drafts, and possessing a steady sound;
therefore, the dance pavilion should be made windless by its builders.
By means of which there will be a deep resonance for the drum;
having performed the rite for the wall-work, one should cause the plastering of the wall to be applied. BhN 2.82.
Once the walls have been plastered and polished on all sides, the application of whitewash (sudhākarma) should be diligently performed upon them. (BhN 2.83)
One should employ the art of painting on surfaces that are even and naturally beautiful;
and in the art of painting, both men and women are to be depicted.
Creeper-tying gestures (latābandha) and actions arising from self-enjoyment should be performed;
thus should the theater space be arranged by the performers. (BhN 2.85)
Furthermore, I shall again describe the characteristics of the square:
it must be made with exactly thirty-two cubits on all sides.

The theater pavilion, situated on an auspicious site and according to the rules of those skilled in drama, follows the procedure previously described, as well as its defining characteristics and auspicious rites. (BhN 2.87)
One should cause all those [lines] to be drawn even in a square that is extended;
having made the square equal and having divided it with a cord.
On the outside, a firm wall should be constructed on all sides using closely joined bricks;
therein, on the inside, [the pillars] should be placed upon the stage-platform (raṅgapīṭha).
Ten pillars are capable of supporting the pavilion for the practitioners;
furthermore, outside the pillars, there should be a pedestal in the form of a staircase.
The dwellings for the spectators should be constructed with bricks and wood,
rising from the ground to a height measured by the span of a hand.
Having surveyed the stage-platform, one should perform the ritual pertaining to the seat;
then, at a distance of six [units], one should again erect pillars in their respective directions.
The knower, according to the prescribed rite, should firmly establish eight pillars for the support of the pavilion, and furthermore, he should arrange [beams] above them.
Then, a pedestal measuring eight cubits in size should be established;
having pierced the face [of the image] to a depth of eight cubits, one should then place [the image] upon those pedestals.
In that [maṇḍapa], pillars should be provided by those who know it for the support of the pavilion;
they are the upholders of the *dhāraṇīs*, and they are adorned with *śāla* trees and women.
Then, the dressing room (nepathyagṛhaka) should be constructed with great care;
there shall be a single door for entry into the stage area (raṅgapīṭha). (BhN 2.96)
Furthermore, one should cause the entry of the people to take place facing another direction;
however, the second door itself must be made to face the stage.
The colored platform (raṅgapīṭha) should be made eight cubits in measurement;
it should be square, level, and beautifully adorned with a pedestal (vedikā).
The *mattavāraṇī* should be constructed as previously specified by the authoritative measures;
it should be provided with four pillars on the side of the altar (*vedikā*).
One should cause the front of the stage (raṅgaśīrṣa) to be made either elevated or level;
however, in a rectangular space it should be elevated, and likewise level in a square one.
In this manner, by this procedure, the house shall be square.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of a triangular house.
A triangle, a three-cornered space, should be constructed by those who employ the theater;
in its center, one should have a triangular stage-platform made. (BhN 2.102)
The door of that house should be made at that very corner,
and a second one should be made behind the stage-platform (raṅgapīṭha).
Whatever rule applies to a square [altar] based on its walls and pillars,
all of that should also be employed by practitioners for a triangular one.
In this manner, theaters should be constructed by the wise according to this rule;
furthermore, I shall explain their worship according to the prescribed ritual.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Construction of the Maṇḍapa," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
Now begins the third chapter:
When an auspicious theater (*nāṭyagṛha*), endowed with all the required characteristics, has been constructed;
The cows should remain for seven days together with twice-born men engaged in the recitation of prayers.
Then, at the arrival of night, having sprinkled his limbs with water purified by mantras, he should consecrate the house and likewise the painted mandala platform.
Having entered another place as prescribed, the consecrated teacher of dance, being restrained, pure, having fasted for three nights, and wearing unwashed garments; BhN 3.3.
Having paid homage to Mahādeva, the source of all worlds, to Bhava, as well as to the Grandfather of the universe, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Guha; BhN 3.4.
And Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Siddhi, Medhā, Dhṛti, and Smṛti;
Soma, Sūrya, the Maruts, the world-protectors, and likewise the two Aśvins.
Mitra, Agni, the divine castes, the Rudras, as well as Kāla and Kali;
and likewise Mṛtyu, Niyati, and the Staff of Time (Kāladaṇḍa).
As well as Viṣṇu’s weapon, the serpent king Vāsuki,
the thunderbolt, lightning, oceans, gandharvas, apsarases, and sages.
[He saw] spirits, piśācas, yakṣas, guhyakas, and great lords;
asuras, those who cause obstacles to dance, and likewise other daityas and rākṣasas.
Likewise, he saw the Nāṭya-kumāris, the Mahāgrāmaṇyas,
as well as the Yakṣas, the Guhyakas, and the hosts of Bhūtas.

Having prostrated to these and other celestial sages (devarṣis) with palms joined in reverence, and having invoked them as they occupy their respective places, one should then speak as follows: BhN 3.10.
"You must take us under your protection during the night, and you, along with your followers, must provide assistance in this drama. (BhN 3.11)
Having worshipped all [the deities] together in one place and having provided the *kutapa* garment,
one should offer worship to Jarjarā for the sake of success in dance (*nāṭya*).
You are the weapon of Mahendra, the destroyer of all Dānavas,
created by all the gods, and the eradicator of all obstacles.
Proclaim the victory of the king and the defeat of his enemies;
likewise, proclaim the welfare of cows, Brahmins, and Śiva, as well as the flourishing of the drama.
Having done this according to the rule and having worshipped in the dance hall, one should commence the worship here at the break of dawn.

The worship of the stage (raṅgapūjana) should be performed under the asterisms of Ārdrā, Maghā, those of Yama (Bharaṇī), the three preceding [asterisms] (Pūrvaphalgunī, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Pūrvabhādrapadā), or also under Āśleṣā and Mūla. (BhN 3.16)
The preceptor, being disciplined, pure, and initiated,
must perform the illumination of the ritual arena and the worship of the deities.
At the end of the day, during the terrible and fierce hour presided over by Yama,
having performed the ritual sipping of water according to the rule, he should indeed install the deities.
Red protective amulets, red thread, and red perfumes are to be honored;
likewise, red *sumanas* flowers and whatever fruit may be red.
With barley, white mustard seeds, parched grain, unbroken grains of rice,
powder of *nāgapuṣpa*, and husked *priyaṅgu* seeds.
One should prepare the dwelling for the deities endowed with these materials;
first, one should draw the maṇḍala in its proper place according to the prescribed rule. (BhN 3.21)
A mandala measuring sixteen cubits should be constructed all around;
one should also fashion doors here in the four directions according to the prescribed rule.
And in the center, two lines—one horizontal and one vertical—should be drawn; within the divisions of their enclosures, one should install the deities.
One should place Brahmā seated upon a lotus in the center of that;
first, the Blessed Lord Śiva should be placed together with his hosts of spirits.
Nārāyaṇa, Mahendra, Skanda, Sūrya, the two Aśvins, and Śaśin, as well as Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Śraddhā, and Medhā, are in the east. BhN 3.25.
In the southeast, Vahni (Agni) should be established together with Svāhā;
likewise the Viśvedevas along with the Gandharvas, and the Rudras together with the hosts of serpents.
To the south, Yama and Mitra, along with their followers, should be established;
he should also establish the ancestors, the piśācas, the uragas, and the guhyakas.
In the southwest, he established the Rākṣasas and the spirits;
and in the west, the oceans and Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures.
Likewise, one should establish the seven winds in the northwestern direction;
and right there, Garuḍa should be established together with the birds.
Likewise, one should place the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada) in the northern direction,
as well as the Mothers of Dance, the Yakṣas, and the Guhyakas.
In the same manner, in the northeast, he should station the lords of the Gaṇas, such as Nandin and others,
as well as the hosts of Brahmanical sages and spirits, each in their respective places.
One should install Sanatkumāra on the pillar, Dakṣa on the southern one, and Grāmaṇī on the northern pillar for the purpose of worship. (BhN 3.32)
By this very procedure, according to the proper place and according to the rule,
he should install all the deities who are well-pleased.
Having installed the deities in their respective places according to the rule,
one should then perform their worship as is appropriate.
White garlands and unguents should be offered to the deities;
red garlands and unguents to the Gandharvas, Agni, and Sūrya.
Having offered perfume, garlands, and incense in due order and according to the rules,
one should then perform the bali offering and worship according to the prescribed ritual.
One should worship Brahmā with honey-cakes (*madukarpa*), Sarasvatī with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and then Śiva, Viṣṇu, Mahendra, and the other deities with sweetmeat balls (*modaka*).

The Fire-god and the Moon are [satisfied] by offerings of rice cooked with ghee; the Viśvedevas along with the Gandharvas and the sages, by offerings of rice with jaggery; and [the ancestors] by offerings of honeyed milk-rice.
Having worshipped Yama and Mitra with cakes and sweetmeats,
one should satisfy the ancestors, the piśācas, and the serpents with clarified butter and milk.
One should worship the hosts of spirits with cooked meat, liquor, *sīthu*, fruit-ferments, and chickpeas soaked in minced meat.
By this very procedure, Mattavāraṇī is to be worshipped;
the hosts of Rākṣasas are to be worshipped with cooked and raw meat.
One who knows the proper rites should honor the Dānavas with offerings of liquor and meat; the remaining hosts of gods, he should worship with cakes, fried pastries, and boiled rice.
Having worshipped Varuṇa with fish, flour-based foods, and offerings from the ocean and rivers, one should also give ghee and milk-rice as a gift.
One should also honor the sages with various flowers and fruits,
and likewise the winds and birds with diverse kinds of food and edibles.
One should worship all those Mothers of the dance, as well as Dhanada along with his followers, with cakes mixed with parched grain and various kinds of foods and edibles.
In this way, their bali offering should be performed, consisting of various kinds of food;
furthermore, the ritual of the bali offering will be described again according to the rules of the mantra.
O God of gods, O highly fortunate one, O Grandfather of all the worlds,
please accept this entire offering from me, purified by mantras.
O God of gods, O illustrious one, O Gaṇeśa, O destroyer of Tripura!
O Lord, please accept this offering (bali), purified by mantra, which has been presented by me.
O Nārāyaṇa of immeasurable gait, O Padmanābha, best of gods,
accept this Bali, O Lord, which has been purified by mantra and offered by me.
O Purandara, Lord of the Immortals, wielder of the thunderbolt, performer of a hundred sacrifices!
O God, let Bali be seized, preceded by the prescribed rites and mantras.
O Skanda, commander of the divine army, O Blessed One, beloved of Śaṅkara!
O Six-faced One, may this offering be accepted with a pleased mind.
O Mahādeva, O Mahāyogin, O God of gods, O Supreme among Gods!
Accepting this offering, O Lord, protect us from the obstacles that constantly arise.
O Goddess, O highly fortunate one, O Sarasvatī, beloved of Hari!
O Mother, please accept this bali offering presented by me with devotion.
"Arising from various signs, all these lords of the Rākṣasas, descendants of Pulastya and possessed of great strength, accept my offering! (BhN 3.53)
O Goddesses— Lakṣmī, Siddhi, Mati, and Medhā, who are honored by all the worlds— may you accept this bali offering purified by mantra from me.
O Knower of the power of all beings, O Life of the World, O Wind-god!
O Lord, please accept this offering presented by me, purified by mantra.
O mouth of the gods, best of deities, smoke-bannered consumer of oblations!
O Lord, this Bali is now offered; please accept it with devotion.
O Sun, most excellent among all planetary deities, mass of splendor!
O Lord, please now accept this offering prepared by me with devotion.
O Soma, lord of all grahas, king of the twice-born, beloved of the world:
please accept this offering, purified by mantras, which has been presented by me.
All the great lords of the Gaṇas, led by Nandīśvara,
have now been urged by me and are offering Bali with devotion.
Homage to all the ancestors; may they accept this offering.
Homage always to the spirits (*bhūtas*) for whom this offering is dear.
O Kāmapāla, homage to you always, for whom this ritual has been performed.
"May Nārada, Tumburu, and all the Gandharvas led by Viśvāvasu accept this offering presented by me."
Yama and the blessed Mitra, the lords worshipped by the world, may they both accept this offering of mine accompanied by this mantra. BhN 3.62.
And salutations again and again to the serpents who have gone to the subterranean realm;
being honored, may they, the destroyers of evil, grant success to the drama.
The god Varuṇa, lord of all waters, whose vehicle is a swan,
being worshipped, became pleased along with the oceans, rivers, and streams.
O Vainateya, great being, lord of all birds, omnipresent one!
O God, please accept this Bali, purified by mantra, which has been offered by me.
May the Lord of Wealth, the King of Yakṣas, the Guardian of the World, the Master of Riches—
along with the Guhyakas and the Yakṣas— accept my offering.
Homage be to the Mothers of Dance, to Brāhmī and the others; salutations again and again! O fair-faced and gracious ones, may this offering be accepted today.
May Rudra accept all my offerings,
as well as the weapon of Viṣṇu which has been raised by me with devotion to Viṣṇu.
Likewise, let Kṛtānta and Kāla, the lords over the slaughter of all living beings,
as well as Mṛtyu and Niyati, accept my offering.
And whatever local deities reside in this intoxicated grove,
may they properly accept this my offering, purified by mantra.
To those other gods and gandharvas who dwell throughout the ten directions—
whether celestial, atmospheric, or terrestrial— this offering is made.
One should place a jar filled with water and adorned with a garland of flowers in the center of the arena, and one should cause gold to be offered there.
Having covered all the musical instruments with cloths,
one should worship them with perfumes, garlands, incense, and various kinds of food and edibles.
Having worshipped all the deities in their proper order,
one should then worship Jarjara and, after that, Vighnajarjara.
On the head there should be a white cloth on the Raudra festival, a blue one on the Viṣṇu festival, and a red one on the Skanda festival. (BhN 3.74)
On the Mṛḍaparvan, one who seeks his own welfare should give a variegated garment;
likewise, incense, garlands, and ointments of similar quality should be offered.
One should cover all musical instruments with cloths and worship them with perfumes, garlands, incense, and various kinds of food and edibles.
Having performed this entire rite with perfumes, garlands,
and ointments, one should consecrate the *jarjara* (the ritual effigy) for the purpose of crushing obstacles.
In this matter, for the purpose of destroying obstacles, you were created by the gods headed by Pitāmaha—
possessing great heroism, the essence of a diamond, and a massive body.
May Brahmā protect your head with all divine qualities;
may Hara protect the second joint, and Janārdana the third.
May your fourth [son] and the fifth, the best of serpents, protect you always; and for the sake of the gods, may you be auspicious.
O destroyer of enemies, for you were indeed born under the constellation Abhijit;
therefore, bring about both victory and prosperity for the king.
Having worshipped the jarjara and offered all the sacrificial oblations (bali),
one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa) preceded by the recitation of mantras and the offering of oblations.
Fire itself, by means of blazing meteors, performs the polishing of a king and increases the radiance of dancers. (BhN 3.83)
Having illuminated the king and likewise the dancers with musical instruments,
and having sprinkled them again with water purified by mantras, he should speak to them as follows.
"You are born into great families and adorned with a multitude of virtues;
may that which is endowed with the qualities of your birth be yours forever. (BhN 3.85)
Having thus spoken these words for the welfare of the king, the wise one should then offer benedictions for the sake of attaining success in the application of dance.
May Sarasvatī, Dhṛti, Medhā, Hrī, Śrī, Lakṣmī, Smṛti, and Mati—
these gentle Mothers— protect you and grant you the attainment of all perfections.
Having performed the fire sacrifice according to the rule, preceded by the oblation and the mantra,
the dance instructor should then diligently break the jar.
If the jar remains unbroken, there will be fear for the master from his enemies;
but if it is broken, the destruction of the master's enemies should be known to occur.
Then, once the jar has been broken, the dance master should diligently take up a blazing lamp and illuminate the entire stage.
With shouts, bursts of laughter, leaps, and gallops,
one should employ that blazing and resonant [performance] in the center of the arena.
One should cause battles to be enacted on the stage with the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, as well as mṛdaṅgas and paṇavas, and all musical instruments resounding together.
In that regard, being cut, pierced, torn, or covered in blood;
being wounded, inflamed, or distressed—these are the signs that indicate success.
A theater properly consecrated indeed brings auspiciousness to the master, as well as to the city from the children to the elderly, and likewise to the countryside. (BhN 3.94)
Furthermore, a stage that is ill-constructed or poorly presided over by the deities will cause the destruction of the drama and bring misfortune to the king. (BhN 3.95)
Whoever abandons this rule and applies [the practices] according to their own whim will quickly incur decline and go to the womb of an animal.
For this worship of the deities of the theater is equal to a sacrifice;
indeed, one should not hold a performance without having first worshipped the theater.
When honored, these [deities] honor in return; when respected, they show respect.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the worship of the stage (raṅga-pūjana).
Fire, even when fanned by a gale, does not burn as intensely as a wrongly applied [mantra],
when properly employed, consumes [the enemy] in an instant.
The worship of the stage (raṅgapūjana) should be performed by a peaceful dance master who is learned in the treatises, disciplined, pure, and initiated. (BhN 3.100)
But he who, with an agitated mind, offers the bali-oblation at the wrong place,
being like a priest devoid of mantra, shall be subject to an expiation.
Thus, this procedure which has been observed for the worship of the deities of the stage should be performed by practitioners in a new theater hall and during a performance.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Worship of the Deities of the Stage," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
Now begins the fourth chapter:
"Having performed the worship in this manner, I addressed the Grandfather (Brahmā):"
Command us quickly, O Lord: what practice should be undertaken?
Then, being thus urged by the Blessed One, I undertook the churning of the nectar;
this [work] generates enthusiasm and likewise brings joy to the gods.
O learned one, let this dramatic composition (*samavakāra*), which accomplishes the goals of Dharma, Kāma, and Artha, which was previously composed by me, now be performed. (BhN 4.3)
When that samavakāra was performed, all the gods and dānavas became joyful upon observing the manifestation of the action.
Then, after some time, the lotus-born Brahmā said to me:
"Today we shall show a dance to the great-souled Three-eyed One."
Then, having gone together with the gods to the abode of the bull-bannered one and having worshipped Śiva, the Grandfather spoke as follows.
O best of gods, you ought to show favor toward this Samavākara which has been created by me, both in its hearing and its sight.
"Let us see," the Lord of Gods said to Druhiṇa;
then the Blessed One said to me, "Be ready, O high-minded one."
Then, on the slopes of the Himalayas, which were crowded with various serpents, teeming with many hosts of spirits, and possessed of delightful caves and waterfalls; BhN 4.9.
O best of the twice-born, the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga) was performed there first;
likewise, the burning of Tripura, known as a *ḍima*, was then enacted.
Then the hosts of spirits were delighted by the recitation of Karṇa’s deeds,
and Mahādeva, being well-pleased, spoke to the Grandfather.
"Oh, this drama has been perfectly created by you, O high-minded one! It brings fame, leads to auspicious results, generates merit, and increases the intellect. (BhN 4.12)
I too remember this dance, performed by me during the periods of twilight,
adorned with various movements of the limbs and complex choreographic sequences.
In this preliminary ritual performance, you must apply yourself correctly to the *vardhamānaka* compositions, the songs, and the *āsārita* melodies.
And you shall correctly interpret the meanings within the great songs;
furthermore, this introductory ritual (*pūrvaraṅga*) which has been performed by you in its pure form—BhN 4.15.
"And this [tantra], being mixed with these, shall be known by the name Citra.
Having heard the words of Maheśvara, the Self-born One replied: (BhN 4.16)
"O best of gods, tell me of the applications of the *maṅgahāra*s.
Then the Lord of the World, having summoned Taṇḍu, spoke to him. (BhN 4.17)
"Tell Bharata indeed the application of the *aṅgahāras*, as well as those *aṅgahāras* which were proclaimed by the high-souled Taṇḍu. (BhN 4.18)
I shall explain to you those [postures] joined with the organs and accompanied by exhalation (sarecaka):
namely, the firm-handed (sthirahasta), the movement of limbs (aṅgahāra), and likewise the overturned (paryastaka) is recorded.
Likewise, the *sūcividdha* (needle-pierced), the *apaviddha* (cast-off),
the *ākṣiptaka* (thrown-out) should be known, and the *uddhaṭṭita* (uplifted) is likewise recorded.
Viṣkambha is indeed proclaimed, as well as Aparājita;
and Viṣkambhāpasṛta, and likewise Mattākrīḍa.
The Svastika, the Recita, and the Pārśvasvastika;
the Vṛścikāpasṛta is proclaimed, and likewise another, the Bhramara.
The stumbling gait of one intoxicated, as well as the playful gait from intoxication,
should be known as the circular gait, and likewise the restricted gait.
Then there may be the *parivṛttacita*, as well as the *vaiśākharecita*;
furthermore, the *parāvṛtta* is to be known, as well as the *alātaka*.
Then the pārśvaccheda is proclaimed, as well as the vidyudbhrānta;
likewise there is the ūrūdvṛtta, and similarly the ālīḍha.
Recita is to be understood in the same way, as is acchurita;
likewise, ākṣiptarecita and sambhrānta are further [varieties]. (BhN 4.26)
The *apasarpa* and likewise the *ardhanikuṭṭaka* should be known;
these thirty-two are proclaimed by name as the *aṅgahāras*.
I shall now explain the application of these based on their execution, as well as how the movement of hands and feet should be employed by practitioners. (BhN 4.28)
O twice-born ones, I shall now describe the *aṅgahāras* and the *karaṇas*,
for the accomplishment of all *aṅgahāras* is derived from the *karaṇas*.
I shall now explain those [elements] by name and by their function:
the coordination of hands and feet constitutes the *karaṇa* of dance. (BhN 4.30)
There are two dance-movements (nṛttakaraṇa) that constitute the matrix of dance (nṛttamātṛkā);
however, a full sequence of movements (aṅgahāra) consists of two, three, or four such matrices.
With three [verses] there is a *kalāpaka*, and with four it becomes a *ṣaṇḍaka*;
with five there are the *karaṇas*, which is known as a *saṅghātaka*.
Aṅgahāras are proclaimed here as being joined with six, seven, eight, or likewise nine karaṇas. (BhN 4.33)
I shall now describe the formation of hands and feet for these very [deities]:
first, the palms joined like a flower-bowl, and the thighs bent.
The *apaviddha*, the *samanakha*, the *līna*, the *svastikarecita*,
the *maṇḍalasvastika*, and also the *nikuṭṭaka*.
Likewise, there is the half-stamped (ardhanikuṭṭa) and similarly the severed-waist (kaṭicchinna),
as well as the half-retracted (ardharecitaka) and the chest-cross (vakṣaḥsvastika).
The Unmatta, the Svastika, the Pṛṣṭhasvastika, the Diksvastika, the Alāta, and likewise the Kaṭīsama.
Ākṣiptarecita, as well as Vikṣiptākṣiptaka;
Ardhasvastika is taught, and likewise another, Añcita.
The *bhujaṅgatrasita* (the serpent-frightened) has been described, as well as the *ūrdhvajānu* (raised-knee), the *nikuñcita* (contracted), the *mattalli*, and indeed the *ardhamattalli*. BhN 4.39.
There may be the recaka-nikkuṭṭa, as well as the pādāpaviddhaka;
likewise the valita, the ghūrṇita, and another called the lalita.
Likewise, the *daṇḍapakṣa*, the *bhujaṅgatrasta-recita*,
the *nūpura*, and the *vaiśākharecita* have been fully described.
The *bhramara*, the *catura*, the *bhujaṅgāñcita*,
the *daṇḍarecitaka*, and likewise the *vṛścikakuṭṭita*.
Likewise, the hip-whirl (*kaṭibhrānta*), the vine-and-scorpion (*latāvṛścika*),
the severed (*chinna*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the scorpion-recoil (*vṛścikarecita*) are thus declared.
The scorpion, the deceptive, likewise the side-stamping,
the forehead-mark, the traversing, the contracted, and the wheel-circle.
The shoulder-circle (uromaṇḍala), the drawn-back (ākṣipta), likewise the floor-playful (talavilāsita),
the bolt (argala), the cast-forth (vikṣipta), the turned-back (āvṛtta), and the swing-foot (dolapādaka).
The turned-back, the retreated, the side-step, the struck-down, the lightning-twirl, the over-stepped, and the whirled-around; BhN 4.46.
The elephant’s play (*gajakrīḍitaka*), likewise the clapping of the palms (*talasaṃsphoṭita*), the eagle’s leap (*garuḍaplutaka*), and furthermore the cheek-needle (*gaṇḍasūci*). BhN 4.47.
The *parivṛtta*, the *samuddiṣṭa*, likewise the *pārśvajānu*, the *gṛdhrāvalīnaka*, the *sannata*, and also the *sūcī*. BhN 4.48.
The *ardhasūcī* (half-needle) technique, as well as the *sūcividdha* (needle-pierced),
the *apakrānta* (withdrawn), and likewise the *mayūralalita* (peacock’s grace) have been fully described.
The serpent-like gait, the staff-like step, and likewise the leap of the deer; the swaying, the broad-hipped, the stumbling, and the trunk of an elephant.

The *prasarpitaka* (the gliding step) has been described, as well as the *siṃhavikrīḍita* (lion’s play), the *siṃhākarṣita* (lion’s draw), the *udvṛtta* (the raised step), and likewise the *upasṛta* (the approaching step).
The *talasaṃghaṭṭita*, the *janita*,
the *āvahitthaka*, the *niveśa*, the *melakākrīḍa*, and likewise the *ūrūdvṛtta*.
The *madaskhalitaka*, the *viṣṇukrānta*, the *sambhrānta*, the *viṣkambha*, and also the *udghaṭṭita*. (BhN 4.53)
The Bull’s Play, the Swinging, and likewise another,
the Serpent’s Recoil, and similarly the Cart-Mouth.
And "the descent of the Gaṅgā" has been mentioned; thus, one hundred and eight [sections] have been declared by me as these constituent parts. (BhN 4.55)
Regarding dance, combat, wrestling, as well as movement and progression,
and the various modes of locomotion, I shall now describe the various applications of martial movements.
In whatever [context], the teachers who possess the power of dramatic performance should generally join the left hand, placed upon the chest, to the *karaṇa* gesture.
The right hand should also follow the foot;
the movement of the hands and feet should be in coordination with the hips, sides, and thighs.
Understand now that which concerns the chest, back, and abdomen, as well as the positions and the noble dance-hands that are about to be described. (BhN 4.59)
That should be known as the *mātṛkā*; through its application, it becomes the instrument (*karaṇa*).
It is that in which the hips are level with the ears, and likewise the elbows, shoulders, and head.
With the chest well-elevated, that is indeed called *sauṣṭhava*;
with a flower-basket on the left side, the foot moves along the surface of the ground.
Likewise, the side [of the hand] should be bent, with the palm forming a hollow like a flower-vessel;
the wrists, however, should be contracted, turned away, and rotated.
When the two hands fall upon the thighs, that is the *karaṇa* called *vartita*;
when the two hands are shaped like a parrot’s beak (*śukatuṇḍa*) and are turned outward and inward, [that is another].
When the two thighs are contracted, it is called *valitoruka*;
having rotated the [hand] known as *śukatuṇḍa*, one should strike it upon the back of the thigh.
And when the left hand is placed upon the chest, it becomes the *apaviddha* [mudrā].
Furthermore, when the two feet are joined with the nails touching and the two hands are also extended downward, [it is the *śliṣṭa* mudrā].
The natural posture (*svābhāvika*) is that in which the body, including the nails, is held together;
the arms are in the *añjali* gesture at the chest, and the neck is extended. (BhN 4.66)
When the shoulders are lowered and pressed together, that is known as the *tallina* hand-gesture (*karaṇa*).
When the hands are in the *svastika*, *recita*, or *āviddha* positions, they are separated and placed upon the hips.
Where that instrument is to be known by the wise as *svastikarecita*:
having made the two hands into *svastika* gestures, with palms facing upward, equal, and directed toward the front of the body. (BhN 4.68)
And likewise, when the two hands are pressed together between one's own arms and head, that is the *maṇḍala* position, which is indeed the *maṇḍalasvastika*.
When the feet are likewise stamped down, that should be known as the *nikuṭṭaka*;
the hands, with fingers directed forward, are bent toward the head of the arms.
By means of the half-contracted union, there arises the *arthanikuṭṭaka*;
with the hips severed in turn, the two hands [rest] upon the head like sprouts.
Performing it again and again, that becomes the "cut waist" (kaṭicchinna); likewise, there are the "hand cast aside" (apaviddhakara) with the needle (sūcī), and the "stamped foot" (nikuṭṭitapāda).
Where one side of the body is bent, that becomes the *ardharecita*;
where the feet are in the *svastika* position and the hands are extended toward the chest, [that is another]. (BhN 4.73)
When the chest is contracted, that is the Vakṣassvastika;
it is the same when the feet are extended and the hands are held in the recita position.
That should be known as the *unmatta* (intoxicated) movement by those skilled in dance,
when both the hands and the feet form the *svastika* position.
This is declared by those seeking mastery in technique to be the *svastika* posture (*karaṇa*), when both feet are in the *svastika* position with the arms cast out and drawn back. (BhN 4.76)
When the two hands, with their middle fingers slightly withdrawn, form a svastika on their backs at the sides and in front, and the hands are joined together, that is [the posture]. (BhN 4.77)
When the hands and feet form the *svastika* posture, it is called the *astika* in that direction;
having placed the foot in the *alāta* position, one should move the right hand.
One should perform the sequence with the knees raised; this is known as the *alātaka*.
With the feet drawn back in the *svastika* posture, the hands are placed at the navel and the hips. (BhN 4.79)
That *karaṇa* is called *pārśvamudvāhita*, which is level with the hips;
the left hand should be at the heart, while the right is thrown out and extended.
When the *recita* and *apaviddha* are performed together, it is called *ākṣiptarecita*;
likewise, when the hand and foot are thrown out (*vikṣipta*) and then again cast forth (*ākṣepaṇa*), that too is [the same].
O twice-born ones, that instrument [of dance] should be known as *vikṣiptākṣiptaka*;
it is performed by placing the feet in the *svastika* position and making the right hand into the *karihasta* gesture. (BhN 4.82)
Likewise, one should indicate the left half-svastika at the region of the chest;
however, when that same hand is rotated and turned back, it is [the other].
When the nose-tip is bent, that is declared the añcita [mudrā];
having lifted the foot, one should rotate the thigh in a triangular fashion—this is the kuñcita [mudrā].
From the rotation of the hips and knees, the *bhujaṅgatrāsita* (the serpent-frightened) posture arises;
having lifted the bent foot, one should place it level with the knee or the breast.
The two hands, under the influence of the preparatory application, are proclaimed as being with the knees raised;
having placed the foot in the scorpion posture, one should contract the hand against the side.
The right [hand] should be known as being at the tip of the nose and slightly bent;
with the left and right feet, one should move forward while whirling.
With hands that are twisted and cast aside, it is called the *mattalli*;
the feet are moved with a stumbling and withdrawing motion, and the left hand is *recita*.
The left hand should rest on the hip; this is known as *ardhamattalli*.
The right hand is extended, and the left foot is stamped down (*nikuṭṭita*). (BhN 4.89)
The *dolā* (swing) gesture should likewise be performed with the left hand; it is a *nikuṭṭita* (stamping) movement executed while releasing that [hand].
Both hands, facing forward and in the *khaṭakāmukha* (sword-blade) position, should be placed upon the region of the navel.
In the *sūcīviddha* and *apakrānta*, the feet are [joined] with the feet; in the *pādāpaviddhaka*, the hand is extended, and likewise in the *sūcīpāda*. (BhN 4.91)
Likewise, that which is turned back and twisted is called *valita*;
the right hand is rotated and whirled, while the left is swung. (BhN 4.92)
When the foot is withdrawn in the *svastika* position, that is the *ghūrṇita* (whirling) *karaṇa*;
the left hand should be in the *karihasta* (elephant-trunk) position, and the right hand should be *vivartita* (twisted).
When the foot is repeatedly pressed down, that should be known as *lalita* by the wise;
having then placed the knee upward, one should place the vine upon it. (BhN 4.94)
That is called the *daṇḍapakṣa* ear by those learned in the science of dance,
wherein both [hands] are made into the *bhujaṅgatrāsita* and then *recita*.
Having placed the two hands on the left side upon a bed of serpents,
and having made the triple-joint well-flexed, the two hands perform the *latā-recita* gesture.
Likewise, one should place the *nūpura* and *pāda* hand gestures upon the *nūpura*;
both the hands and feet are extended (*recita*), as are the hips and neck.
In this very birth, this [dance] is performed with the Vaiśākha stance;
the foot is cast into the Svastika position, and the two hands are likewise rotated outward.
And from the turning of the triad, that indeed should be known as the *bhramaraka*;
the left hand should be bent (*añcita*), while the right is simply *catura*. (BhN 4.99)
The right foot is stamped; that is proclaimed as the *catura* [stance].
The right foot is in the *bhujaṅgatrāsita* [position] and the hand is extended (*recita*).
The left hand, known as *latākhyā*, should be curved like a serpent;
meanwhile, the hands and feet are cast out in all directions like a staff. (BhN 4.101)
That indeed is to be known as the *karaṇa* called *daṇḍakarecita*.
Having made both feet into *vṛścika*, they are then both *nikuṭṭita*.
The two hands should be positioned as such; that is to be known as the *vṛścikakuṭṭita* [posture].
Having formed a needle [with the hands], one should cast it aside and place the right foot down.
When the waist is bent backward, that is called *kaṭibhrānta*;
the foot is drawn back with its toes curled upward. (BhN 4.104)
The left hand is called *latā*; when it forms a scorpion, it becomes the *latāvṛścika*.
When the *alapaḍma* is at the region of the waist, it is called *chinnā*, with the waist [moving] alternately.
By means of the Vaiśākha stance here, that severed posture (karaṇa) is formed;
having placed the feet in the scorpion position (vṛścika), both hands are made into the svastika.
The two hands are extended apart in the *viprakīrṇa* gesture, while the arms are bent at the shoulders in the *vṛścikarecita*;
likewise, the feet are bent backward at the backs.
That is proclaimed as the *vṛścika* (scorpion) posture, characterized by a back that is drawn far back;
it is the *ālīḍha* stance where the two hands are extended at the chest.

When the hands are scattered upwards and downwards, that is the *vyaṃsita* movement; likewise, when the hands are in the *svastika* position at the sides and the foot is stamped down (*nikuṭṭita*), it is the same. (BhN 4.109)
Where that instrument is employed, it should be known by the wise as *pārśvanikuṭṭita*;
having placed the foot in the *vṛścika* position, one strikes with the big toe of the foot. (BhN 4.110)
One should apply a tilaka on the forehead; that is indeed the "forehead-tilaka. Then, having made it curved at the back, one proceeds with the sequence of movements.
O twice-born ones, in the Krāntaka Karaṇa, the two hands should be thrown out;
the first foot should be bent, and the left hand should be contracted.
When one lies on the left side with the face upward, it is called *tatkuñcita*;
this is done with the arms hanging down and the body bent. (BhN 4.113)

When the feet are cast inward during the *svastika* and *apasṛta* movements, that should be known as the *cakramaṇḍala* (wheel-circle) gait. When the feet are cast outward, it is the *apaviddha* (cast-off) gait. (BhN 4.114)
The two hands are in the chest-circle (uromaṇḍalaka) position;
that [dance] is called *ākṣipta* where the hands and feet are moved with great speed. (BhN 4.115)
O best of the twice-born, that instrument known as *ākṣiptaka* should be understood as follows:
the foot with its toes and sole pointing upward is extended sideways and upwards.
In the *talavilāsita* gesture, one should perform the hands with their palms arched;
the two feet are extended behind by one and a half *tāla*s.
And his hand follows right after it, while that bolt remains in front;
likewise, the hands and feet are cast out behind, or even to the sides. (BhN 4.118)
When one foot has gone onto a single path, that is declared to be *vikṣipta*; having extended the bent foot, one should quickly bring it back again. BhN 4.119.
When the two hands are under the control of the *prayoga* movement, that is called *āvarta*;
having lifted a bent foot, one should swing it from side to side. (BhN 4.120)
When the two hands are under the control of the preparatory movement, it is called *ḍolāpāda*;
one should then cause the hands, feet, and the triple-joint (*trika*) to be thrown back (*ākṣipta*) and turned (*vivartita*). (BhN 4.121)
O twice-born ones, having likewise performed the recitation and the hand-movements in the *vivṛtta* manner,
one should then execute the *sūcīviddha* and turn the three [parts] back.
O best of the twice-born, when [the movement] has ceased, the two hands should be made to exhale (recita);
having performed the step across the sides, one should then cast them down in front.
When the two hands are under the control of the preparatory movement (prayoga), it is called pārśvakrānta;
the feet are bent backward and the chest is held high. BhN 4.124.
The hand should be placed on the forehead; this is called *nistambhita*.
One should extend the foot, which has been drawn back and turned, so that it rubs against the head. (BhN 4.125)
When it is pierced from all sides by the mandala and whirled like lightning, that is called "the whirl of lightning.
Having performed the *atikrāntakrama*, one should extend [the hands] forward.
The two hands are proclaimed to be under the control of the preparatory movement (prayoga) when they have transcended [the previous position];
likewise, the hand and foot are thrown forward (ākṣipta), and the triple-joint (trika) is indeed turned back (vivartita).
The second hand is extended, performed as a *vivartitaka*;
the left hand is bent at the ear, and the right hand is a *latāhasta*.
Likewise, there is the dolāpāda (swinging-foot) and the gajakrīḍitaka (elephant-play).
Having quickly lifted the foot forward, one should then let it fall.
The two hands clapped against the palms are considered *talasaṃsphoṭita*;
the foot extended behind and the two hands in the *latārecita* position [constitute another]. (BhN 4.130)
With the head held high, it becomes the *garuḍaplutaka* (the Garuḍa-leap);
with the feet like needles, the side bent, and one hand placed upon the chest.
When the second hand is bent at the cheek, it is called *gaṇḍasūcī*.
When the hands are turned upward and entwined, and the foot is rotated, it is *sūcīpāda*.
When the three [parts] have been rotated, it is called *parivṛtta* (the rotated);
one foot remains standing upright while the other rests upon the back of the thigh.
With the fist placed on the chest and the knee against the side, it is called *pārśvajānu*;
with the foot extended behind and the knee slightly bent, it is [the next].
Where the arms are extended, that is the *gṛdhrāvalīnaka*;
having leaped up, the two feet should be placed in front in the *svastika* position.
When both hands are likewise bent, that is described as *sannata*.
Having raised a contracted foot, one should place it forward upon the ground.
The two hands, brought under the control of the *prayoga* [mudrā], are proclaimed as the *sūcī*;
the head-hand is the *alapaḍma*, and the right foot is the *sūcī*. (BhN 4.137)
The instrument used therein should be known by the name *ardhasūcī* (half-needle),
when the second foot is pierced by means of the *pādasūcī*.
When the hands are positioned at the waist and chest, that is called the Needle (sūcī).
Having rotated the leg across the thigh, one should place it in the apakrānta step.
That which is under the influence of the preparatory movement (prayoga) is called *hastavapakrānta*.
Having placed the feet in the *vṛścika* posture, the hands are likewise extended (*recita*). (BhN 4.140)
Likewise, when the three [parts] are turned outward, it becomes the *mayūralalita* (peacock-playful) posture;
the feet are bent and drawn back, and the head is whirled around.
When the hands are likewise extended, it is called *tatsarpita*;
having placed the foot in the *nūpura* position, one should extend the leg in the *daṇḍapāda* posture.
That which quickly pierces [the opponent] is called the Staff-foot (daṇḍapāda);
having performed the transgressing step (atikrāntakrama), one should leap up and strike down.
When the raised leg is cast over the bent one, one should know that to be the *hariṇapluta* (leaping deer);
having performed the *ḍolāpādakrama* (swinging-step movement), one should leap up and land. (BhN 4.144)
When the three [parts] are rotated, it is called *preṅkholita*;
the two arms are extended upward, and the hands have their fingers facing forward.
Likewise, the bound movement (baddhācārī) occurs in the navel region;
having performed the step of the swing's foot, both hands follow accordingly. BhN 4.146.
Whether recited or even whirled, the *karaṇa* may become faltering;
one hand is placed on the chest, while the other has its palm turned upward.
In the *karihastaka* gesture, one hand should be performed as *añcita* and the other as *caraṇa*;
furthermore, one hand should be *recita* while the other is called *latā*.
The two feet, with their soles extended forward, constitute the *prasarpitaka* movement;
then, placing a firebrand (*alāta*) before one, one performs the second [movement] with rapid steps.
In the *siṃhavikrīḍita* [gesture], both hands are also known to follow the feet;
likewise, one foot is extended backward while the two hands are contracted.
Furthermore, O twice-born ones, the two [mudrās] for the Lion’s Attraction should be performed in the same manner:
with the hand drawn back, the body drawn back, and the feet drawn back. (BhN 4.151)
The term *advṛttagātra* is known as the means for producing the *udvṛtta* [hand];
in this [movement], one foot is thrown forward (*ākṣiptacaraṇa*), and the two hands follow that very foot.
The body should likewise be bent, and it should be drawn close;
having positioned the feet in the manner of a swing, the hands should be joined with their palms together.
One should always raise the left hand with the palms joined together;
one hand should rest upon the chest, while the second hangs down.
When the feet are placed on the tips of the palms, it becomes the *janita* posture;
having performed the *janita* posture, the two hands have their fingers directed toward each other. (BhN 4.155)
When the hands fall slowly and the chest is held steady while the thighs are bent, that should be known as *avahitthaka* (the gesture of concealment). BhN 4.156.
