The mandala-sthānaka is indeed its placement and its formation;
it consists of jumping up with both feet moving on the ground and then landing. BhN 4.157.
That which is bent, curved, and playful with the joining of the limbs is the *melakākrīḍita*; one should place the hand, having performed a circular movement, bent upon the back of the thigh.
The calves are bent and likewise the thighs are turned upward;
the hands should be made to hang down and the head should be tilted back.
O twice-born ones, in the *madaskhalita* [dance], the feet are turned and struck;
the foot extended forward is bent and directed upward toward the sky.
When both hands are extended [outward], that is called Viṣṇukrānta. Having rotated the hand, one should indeed contract it against the back of the thigh. (BhN 4.161)
The thigh is likewise pierced; that is the *sambhrānta* movement. The hand is cast aside with the needle (*sūcī*), and the foot is likewise trampled (*nikuṭṭita*). (BhN 4.162)
The left hand should rest upon the chest in the Viṣkambha and Karaṇa [mudrās];
the feet should be raised, and the palms of the hands should be joined together.
When the *uddhaṭṭita* [hand] is performed, the wise should always bend the side;
first one should employ the *alātaka* [movement] and also release the two hands. (BhN 4.164)
In the *vṛṣabhakrīḍita* [gesture], the hands are always contracted and bent downward;
the hands are *recita* and bent downward, while the head is shaken and turned.
When the feet are extended in a svastika and withdrawn from both sides, and the head is turned around, that is called the *lollita* posture. (BhN 4.166)
The two hands should likewise be extended like a crawling serpent,
while the body is seated with one leg stretched out, moving along the surface of the palm.
Having raised the chest and assumed the cart-mouth posture (*śakaṭāsya*),
one should employ the feet with the soles turned upward and the fingers extended, while the hands are in the triple-bannered gesture (*tripatāka*) facing downward.
The two hands, the head-bending, and the descent of the Gaṅgā—
these are the postures which the Noble One has described in the context of physical exercise.
This, however, shall be the movement of the feet for these [hands],
as well as those dance-hands which have been described for the performance of dance.
Their application in the instruments is briefly explained:
generally, when an instrument is to be played, the left hand is placed upon the chest.
The foot and the following right hand should likewise be moved;
and those which have been described as *cārīs* as well as *nṛttahastas* [should be employed]. (BhN 4.172)
That should be known as the *mātṛkā*; from its divisions arise the instruments (*karaṇas*).
Indeed, these one hundred and eight instruments have been declared by me. (BhN 4.173)
Hereafter, I shall explain the various formations of *aṅgahāra*:
having extended and raised both hands, one should employ the *samapāda* stance. (BhN 4.174)
Having executed the *apasṛta* with the left hand, one should extend it upward;
then one should perform the *pratyālīḍha* and likewise the *nikuṭṭaka*.
Then one should perform ūrūdvṛtta, followed by akṣipta and svastika; then nitamba, karihasta, and kaṭicchinna in their proper sequence.
He shall have a steady hand, possessing graceful movements dear to Hara;
there are the two [gestures] talapuṣpa and apaviddha, as well as vartita and saṃnikuṭṭika.
The *ūrūdvṛtta*, the *ākṣipta*, the *uraḥmaṇḍala*, the *nitamba*, the *karihasta*, and likewise the *kaṭicchinna*.
This is indeed the *paryastaka* limb-movement (*aṅgahāra*) originating from Śiva;
it is performed by making the *alapallava* and *sūcī* gestures, followed by the *vikṣipta*.
Then one should perform the *āvartita*, as well as the *nikuṭṭaka*,
the *ūrūdvṛtta*, the *ākṣipta*, and the *uraḥmaṇḍala*.
The *karihasta*, the *kaṭicchinna*, and this *sūcīviddha*;
likewise, the *apaviddha* and the *sūcīviddha* [are] *karaṇas*. (BhN 4.181)
One should rotate the triple-joint with the hand wrapped around it;
likewise, one performs the chest-circle (*ura-maṇḍalaka*) and the hip-cut (*kaṭi-cchinna*) with both hands.
This [movement] should be understood by performers as the *apaviddha* (cast-off) *aṅgahāra*,
having performed the *nūpura* *karaṇa* and then the *vikṣiptālātaka*.
Furthermore, one should perform the *ākṣiptaka*, as well as the *uromaṇḍalaka*,
the *nitamba*, the *karihasta*, and likewise the *kaṭicchinna*.
Performers should know that this *aṅgahāra* is to be understood as the *ākṣiptaka*;
it consists of the hand being whirled and cast aside, while the foot is stamped down. (BhN 4.185)
Again, by that same yoga, the two hands should then be on the left side,
forming the circle of the chest and the "elephant-trunk" gesture at the hip.
In the *uddhaṭṭita* dance, one should always perform the *kaṭicchinna* movement;
the hands are alternately twisted and the feet are likewise stamped.
Having formed the hand in the *kuñcita*, *avañcita*, *ūrūdvṛtta*, and likewise the *caturaśra* positions, one performs the *nikuṭṭaka* with the foot.
Furthermore, the hand should be made to appear as if terrified by a serpent, then again extended upward, and finally severed; this triad of gestures is performed with the *bhramaraka* [hand].
The *karihasta* and *kaṭicchinna* are proclaimed as being in the *viṣkambha* [posture], having indeed cast out and drawn back the staff-like foot and the hand. (BhN 4.190)
One should cause the left hand, which has been withdrawn, to glide along with the foot;
the two *nikuṭṭaka* movements should be performed, and the *ākṣipta* movement executed at the chest within the *maṇḍala*.
In the Aparājita posture, one should perform the elephant-hand (karihasta) and the waist-cut (kaṭicchinna);
likewise, having performed the beaten (kuṭṭita) movement, one should execute the serpent-frightened (bhujaṅgatrāsita).
With the recited hand, one should indicate the banner-hand;
likewise, one should employ the *ākṣiptaka* and the chest-circle (*ura-maṇḍalaka*). BhN 4.193.
The *latākhya* [hand-gesture] is formed when the *sakatākṣipta* is cut off; it occurs when the *viṣkambha* is drawn away.
Having performed the *trika* with a beautiful twist, one likewise forms the *nūpura* gesture.
Having performed the *bhujaṅgatrāsita* on the left, as well as the *vaiśākharecita*,
then the *ākṣiptaka*, and likewise the *paricchinna*.
One should perform the *bāhyabhramaraka*, as well as the *uromaṇḍala*,
the *nitamba*, the *karihasta*, and likewise the *kaṭicchinna*.
This indeed is the *mattākrīḍa*, a sequence of gestures (*aṅgahāra*) beloved by Hara;
it is performed by executing the *recita* movement of the hands and feet, as well as the *vṛścika*.
Again, by that very same yoga, one should apply the scorpion posture,
as well as the *nikuṭṭaka*, performed alternately on the left and right in succession.
The *sakatīccheda* known as *latā* occurs in the *svastikarecita*;
having formed a *svastika* on the side, one should then perform the *nikuṭṭaka*.
The procedure for the second side should indeed be exactly the same;
then, having rotated the hand, one should cause it to fall upon the back of the thigh.
Then one should perform the ūrūdvṛtta, and likewise the ākṣipta;
then the nitamba, the karihasta, and similarly the kaṭicchinna.
This is proclaimed as the *pārśvasvastika* (side-cross) *aṅgahāra*;
it is performed by assuming the *vṛścika* posture and the hand gesture known as *latā*.
One should again contract that very same hand at the tip of the nose;
having made that same [hand] encircled, one should rotate the hip.
The *karihasta* (elephant-trunk hand) and the *kaṭicchinna* (waist-cut) should be employed in the *vṛścikāpasṛta* (scorpion-recoil);
likewise, one should perform the *nūpurapāda* (anklet-foot) and the *ākṣiptaka* (thrown).
And the *paricchinna*, as well as the *sūcīpāda*, the *nitamba*, the *karihasta*, and likewise the *uromaṇḍalaka* should be performed. BhN 4.205.
Then, having severed the waist, that is designated as the *bhramara*;
having performed the *matallikaraṇa* and having rotated the right hand.
In the region of the cheek, however, the movement should be properly contracted,
cast aside, and swift, combined with the clapping of the palms.
The *karihasta* (elephant-trunk hand) and the *kaṭicchinna* (waist-broken) movements should be performed with the gait of one intoxicated and stumbling,
using swinging hands that move about and feet that step back in the *svastika* position.
With hands bent, turned, and likewise struck together at the palms,
one should perform the *nikuṭṭita* and similarly the *ūrūdvṛta*.
The *karihasta* and *kaṭicchinna* gestures should be performed with playful movements out of intoxication;
having assumed the *maṇḍala* stance, the two hands should likewise be extended in the *recita* position.
With the foot extended, there should be the *mattallikaraṇa*;
likewise, the *ākṣiptakaraṇa* and the *uromaṇḍala*. (BhN 4.211)
Likewise, there should be the *kaṭicchinna* (waist-cut) in the circle of movement;
then one should employ the *samapāda* (even-footed), and immediately after that, the *paricchinna* (severed).
With the foot cast aside, there is likewise the *bāhyabhramaraka*;
with the left foot as a needle, there is the *atikrānta*, and likewise the *bhujaṅgatrāsita*.
The *karihasta* and *kaṭicchinna* [hand gestures] are prescribed for the *paricchinna* [dance];
the two hands, having moved away, are placed above the head in the *svastika* position.
Then, having bent the left hand and the body, one should exhale;
then, having raised the body and lifted it up, one should exhale there once more.
Having formed the hands known as *latā*, one should employ the *vṛścika* (scorpion),
the *recita* (retracted), the *karihasta* (elephant-trunk hand), and likewise the *bhujaṅgatrāsita* (terrified serpent).
One should employ the *ākṣiptaka* and the *svastika-pāda*;
furthermore, the procedure for the *parāṅmukha* [movement] should likewise be performed here.

When the hands are in the *karihasta* and *kaṭicchinna* positions, and then moved in the *parivṛttakaracita* manner, the two hands are cast aside along with the body in the *recita* movement. (BhN 4.218)
Again, raising the body with that same side, one should perform the *recaka* (exhalation);
likewise, one should perform the *nūpurapāda* and the *bhujaṅgatrāsita*.
One should likewise perform the recited maṇḍala, contract the upper arms at the shoulders,
rotate the thighs, cast [the limbs] aside, and [perform] the chest-maṇḍala as well.
In the Vaiśākha recitation, one should perform the *karihasta* and *kaṭicchinna*;
having first performed the *janita*, one should extend one foot.
In the same manner, one should perform the *alātaka* movement, but rotate the three [parts of the body];
the left hand, being bent, should be struck against the region of the cheek.
Likewise, when the waist is severed, one should employ the *parāvṛtta* [turning] movement;
having performed the *svastika* formation, the two hands are then again made to be *vyaṃsita*.
One should employ the *alātaka* (firebrand) movement with the knees raised and tucked;
likewise, the *ardhasūcī*, the *vikṣipta*, and the *udvṛtta-ākṣiptaka*.
In the *aṅgahāra* known as *alātaka*, one should perform the *karihasta* and *kaṭicchinnaka* gestures;
having drawn the two hands toward the chest, one should then extend them with the knees raised.
Having performed the *ākṣiptasvastika*, one should rotate the three [parts of the body];
the hands form the *uraḥmaṇḍala* and the hips form the *karihastaka*.
Likewise, in the case of a severed waist or a severed side,
one should apply the *sūcīvāmapada* (needle-left-foot) and the *vidyudbhrānta* (wandering lightning) [mudrās] on the right.
Furthermore, with the right [hand] there is the needle, and with the left, the whirling lightning;
likewise, there is the severed and the one that has overstepped on the left.
That which is called *latā* (the creeper) is known as *kaṭicchinna* (waist-broken) and *vidyudbhrānta* (lightning-twirl);
having performed the *nūpura* (anklet) step, the left and right feet are then suspended.
Then, with those two hands at the sides, one should perform the *vikṣipta*;
likewise, with those two, the *sūcī*, and one should rotate the *trika*.
The *latā* (creeper) hand, severed at the hip, should always be raised from the *kūrpara*;
with the hands in *ālīḍha* and *vyasita*, one should strike at the head of the arm.
The left foot is in the *nūpura* position and the right is in the *alāta*;
with that same [posture], one should perform the *ākṣiptaka*, with both hands in the *uro-maṇḍala* position.
One should employ the *karihasta* hand in the *kaṭicchinna* posture during the *ālīḍha* stance;
having made the hand *recita*, one should extend it toward the side. (BhN 4.233)
Again, by that same yoga, one should exhale the measure of the body;
the exhalation (recita) is to be performed upon the circle of the chest itself.
When the *aṅgahāra* is recited, however, one should perform the *kaṭicchinna*;
having placed the foot upon the anklet (*nūpura*), one should rotate the triple-joint (*trika*).
With the hand thus extended, one should rotate the very triad;
having made the left [hand] like a whirling firebrand, one should apply the needle right there.
In the *ācchurita* [dance], one should always perform the *karihasta* and the *kaṭicchinna*;
the feet are extended in the *svastika* position, and the hands are extended in the *svastika* position. (BhN 4.237)
Having thus effected the separation by that very same method, one should again perform the upward lifting by means of the *recaka* breaths alone. (BhN 4.238)
The *udvṛtta*, the *ākṣiptaka*, the *uromaṇḍala*, the *nitamba*, the *karihasta*, and likewise the *kaṭicchinna*. (BhN 4.239)
For this procedure of the *karaṇas* is traditionally taught as being performed with the limbs drawn back and then extended;
having executed the *vikṣipta-karaṇa*, one brings the hands, feet, and face together.
One should throw the left hand forward, assisted by the left index finger;
the right [hand] should be at the region of the chest, and the three [parts of the body] should be turned.
The *nūpurākṣiptaka*, the *ardhasvastika*, the *nitamba*, the *karihasta*, and likewise the *uraḥmaṇḍalaka*. (BhN 4.242)
When one is bewildered, the dancers should perform the "severed waist" (kaṭicchinna),
having executed the sequence of the "withdrawn" (apakrānta) and the "shoulder-turned" (vyaṃsita) hand.
One should likewise perform the *udveṣṭita*, the *ardhasūcī*,
the *vikṣipta*, the *kaṭicchinnam*, as well as the *udvṛtta* and the *ākṣiptaka*.
The *karihasta* and *kaṭicchinna* gestures should be performed during the *apasarpaṇa*;
having executed the *nūpurapāda*, one should quickly withdraw the step.
One should rotate the hands following the feet and the triple-joint region;
then, having contracted the hands and feet, one performs the breast-circle again.
O best of the twice-born, these thirty-two aṅgahāras have been proclaimed: the karihasta, the kaṭicchinna, and the kārya performed in the ardhaniikuṭṭaka posture.
Understand also the four types of exhalations (*recaka*) as I describe them:
one is the exhalation of the feet, and the second is the exhalation of the hips.
The third is the *kararecaka*, while the fourth is the *kaṇṭharecaka*. It is designated as *recita* when occurring separately,
and it is also called *recaka* because of its lifting (*udvāhana*), separation (*pṛthagbhāva*), and movement (*calana*).
Moving from side to side with faltering and shifting steps,
as well as various movements of the feet, is called *pādarecaka*.
The upward turning of the triple [bandha], the sixth being the lateral movement,
as well as the backward withdrawal— this is called kaṭirecaka.
Lifting up, throwing around, throwing out, turning over, and gliding—these movements of the hand are called *hastarecaka*. (BhN 4.249ab)
Elevation, bending forward, as well as the bending of the side and whirling— these should be known by the wise as the extensions of the neck.
Having beheld Śaṅkara dancing with exhalations and graceful bodily movements, [the gods were amazed].
And Pārvatī was dancing with graceful movements,
accompanied by the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, bherīs, paṭahas, bhāṇḍas, ḍiṇḍimas, and gomukhas.
When Dakṣa’s sacrifice had been destroyed, at the time of twilight, Maheśvara [was accompanied] by the sounding of paṇavas, ḍamarus, and all kinds of musical instruments.
Then, following the dictates of rhythm and tempo, the hosts headed by Nandin and Bhadramukha danced with various graceful movements of the limbs, having observed the formal group formations.
They gave names to these lumps according to their characteristics:
the lump of Īśvara is the Īśvarī, and that of Nandin is the Paṭṭasī.
The piṇḍī of Caṇḍikā is likewise that of the Lion-vehicled Goddess;
the piṇḍī of Viṣṇu is that of Tārkṣya, and the piṇḍī of Svayaṃbhū is that of the Lotus.
The *airāvatī* ball belongs to Śakra; the *jhaṣapiṇḍī* belongs to Mānmatha;
the *śikhipiṇḍī* belongs to Kumāra; and the *rūpapiṇḍī* belongs to Śrī.
The *dhārāpiṇḍī* belongs to Jāhnavī; the *pāśapiṇḍī* belongs to Yama;
the *nadīpiṇḍī* belongs to Vāruṇī; and the *yākṣī* belongs to Dhanada. (BhN 4.256)
The *halapiṇḍī* belongs to Bala, while the *sarpapiṇḍī* belongs to the serpents;
the *mahāpiṇḍī* belongs to Gaṇeśvara and is the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Raudrī, belonging to the enemy of Andhaka (Śiva), has the configuration of a trident;
likewise, it should be understood for the other deities as well, in their respective order.
The *piṇḍībandhas*, well-marked by signs, should be employed as banners;
likewise, the *recakas* and *aṅgahāras* are situated within the *piṇḍībandhas*.
Having created them, they were then given by the Blessed One to the Sage during the dance;
and by him, in turn, they were properly provided with musical instruments.

The application of dance that was created is known as *tāṇḍava*. The sages said: "When the experts in that [dance] performed the dramatic representation (*abhinaya*) for the sake of attaining wealth," BhN 4.261.
Why has this dancing been performed? To what intrinsic nature does it refer? It is not connected with the meaning of the song, nor does it bring that meaning to life. (BhN 4.262)
"Why was this dance performed amidst songs and musical recitations?
Bharata replies:
"In this regard, it is said that dance does not depend upon any particular meaning."
However, dance was introduced so as to produce beauty;
for, by its very nature, dance is generally desired by all the world.
And considering it to be auspicious, this dance has been proclaimed for use on occasions such as weddings, births, arrivals, festivals, and times of prosperity. (BhN 4.265)
And this dance was introduced as a means of diversion;
furthermore, because of its rejection, it was introduced by the hosts of spirits.
Those who are properly employed at the beginning of songs and so forth as dividers of the dance were also proclaimed by the God, preceded by the Tāṇḍava, as being Tāṇḍu.
"Let this dance be performed by relying on the application of song;
for the ritual of *tāṇḍava* generally takes the form of praise to the gods. (BhN 4.268)

And the performance of the *tāṇḍava* dance, which is delicate in its execution and arises from the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), when performed by Taṇḍu—the ritual procedure for that—[is now described]. (BhN 4.269)
Having reached the *vardhamānaka* [scale], I shall explain its characteristics,
for it is so called because of the increase of the *kalās* and the augmentation of the syllables.
Because it increases from the base (*laya*), it is called *vardhamānaka*;
having properly arranged the placement of the *kutapa* notes, O best of the twice-born. (BhN 4.271)
Thereafter, the practitioners should perform the *āsārita* application;
in that case, having performed the *upohana* accompanied by stringed instruments and singing.
The entrance of the dancer should be performed accompanied by the *bhāṇḍa* drum;
however, in the case of the *jāti* known as *viśuddhakaraṇā*, one should employ instrumental music.
One should employ the *cārī* of that [movement] with a gait following the instrumental music;
here, by means of the *vaiśākha* stance, there is the movement characterized by all the *recakas*.
Having taken up a handful of flowers, she should enter the performance pavilion;
then, having cast down the handful of flowers and circumambulated the stage-altar, she should proceed.
Having prostrated before the deities, one should then perform the dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*);
where there is singing to be enacted, one should not employ instrumental music there.
In the performance of the *aṅgahāras*, however, the *bhāṇḍavādya* (percussive instrumental music) is prescribed;
it should be even, resonant, well-distributed, clear, and produced by pure strokes.
In the *tāṇḍava*, the instrumental music should be coordinated by those skilled in musical instruments so as to follow the movements of the dance;
having thus employed song and instrumental accompaniment, the dancer should then exit.
By this very same procedure, others enter separately;
and then other women, in due order, form the *piṇḍī*.
The overturning of the vessels should be performed as long as the *piṇḍī* has not been tied;
once the *piṇḍī* has been tied, all those women should then depart.
In this context, the instrumentalists should perform music during the *piṇḍībandhas*, according to the measure of the *paryastaka*, accompanied by the execution of various musical sequences.
In that regard, the invocation (upavāhana) should again be performed exactly as before;
thereafter, one should further employ the singing of the āsārita.
The dancer should also enter according to the very same procedure as before,
and she should perform the meaning of the song for the second *sārita*.
Furthermore, one should demonstrate that very same subject matter through dance as well;
then, when the *āsārita* is completed, the dancer shall exit from there.
As before, others enter; for that indeed is the same procedure.
Thus, at every step, the rule for the āsārita must be performed.
For the purpose of playing musical instruments and likewise for singing, one [finger] should first be employed, and two [fingers] in the same way for the second [note]. BhN 4.286.
The first [piṇḍī] consists of three items, the third of four, and the fourth likewise of four;
thus, the four rules for the piṇḍīs have been fully proclaimed. (BhN 4.287)
The *piṇḍī*, the *śṛṅkhalikā*, the *latābandha*, and then the *bhedyaka*;
the *piṇḍībandha* is so called because of its massiveness (*piṇḍatva*), while the *gulma* becomes the *śṛṅkhalikā*.
The *jālopanaddhā* creeper is known as the *sanṛtta-bhedyaka*;
the *piṇḍībandha* occurs at the *kaniṣṭhā*, while the *śṛṅkhalā* occurs within the *laya*.
In the middle [scale] there is the *latābandha*, and in the highest (*jyeṣṭha*) there is the *bhedyaka*;
likewise, there are the various *yonis* of the *piṇḍīs*, as well as the *yantra* and the *bhadrāsana*.
Likewise, practitioners should apply themselves to the yoga of training;
O you whose wealth is austerity, such is the practice to be performed during the increasing fortnight.
I shall further explain the rules for songs and meters—
those which are based on specific subjects as well as those that are composed according to fixed limbs.
I shall describe their songs, as well as the application of dance and instrumental music;
therein, the entry of the dancer with her full array of musical instruments must be performed.

That which is produced through casting and counter-casting, refined by the striking together of vessels, should be the first type of dramatic performance (*abhineya*); it consists of all types of musical subjects (*vastu*) set to song.
And furthermore, one should demonstrate that very same object through dance as well;
for the method previously described regarding dance, dramatic gesture, and instrumental music [applies here too]. (BhN 4.295)
That [method] should also apply to the *vastukas* of songs in the procedure for *āsārita*;
thus is the rule for songs composed upon a subject matter (*vastu*) traditionally taught.
Listen also to the characteristics of songs composed with gestures;
for the very same method that applies to the subject matter applies to dance, dramatic gesture, and instrumental music.
One should likewise apply that same [method] to the chandakas bound to the limbs, as well as to instrumental music produced with long syllables and those with short syllables. (BhN 4.298)
One should apply the *sopohana* at the beginning of the syllables when, by the force of the melody, a limb [of the body] returns again and again. (BhN 4.299)
Among these, the first should be performed as a dramatic representation (abhinaya), while the remainder should be joined with dance (nṛtta).
This occurs when, by the power of the song, the limbs are repeated again and again.
One should employ instrumental music there in conjunction with the three tempos (laya);
the performers here must play the music in accordance with the tempo.
The extended, the followed, the flood, and that which is endowed with the instruments—
these should be applied to the stable reality, and the followed should be situated in the middle.
Furthermore, this procedure pertaining to the instruments should be applied repeatedly;
having reached the *chandogīta*, one should transpose the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).

This rule must always be observed regarding dance, gesture, and instrumental music: for those [performances] that are based on a specific subject matter, the conclusion (graha) should occur at the end;
however, in the case of the bodily movements (aṅga), the conclusion is considered to occur at the very beginning.
In this same manner, this rule should be applied to songs and also to āsāritas;
for this [performance] based on the praise of the deity is delicate—understand it thus.
Furthermore, that conversation between a man and a woman which arises from desire should be known as *sukumāra* (delicate), for it originates from the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*). (BhN 4.303)
In whichever particular state the dance is to be employed by performers, I shall explain all of that; listen to it from me, O twice-born ones. (BhN 4.304)
When the limbs and the objects [of expression] have ceased, as well as when the colors have ceased, and likewise in a place of non-arising, the knower of that [dance] should employ the dance.
Whatever is observed as a basis for passion between a husband and wife,
there the dance should be performed, arising from the quality of the purpose of great joy.
Wherever a lover is present, the sight of the menses and so forth,
as well as dance connected with the meaning of songs, is also desired there.
A young woman who has been rejected, deceived, or separated by a quarrel should not be employed in that part of the dance where she resides.
When a conversation has been initiated by her friends and the beloved is not present,
she for whom the beloved has not gone abroad should certainly not perform a dance.
But when there is a vision of the messenger (dūtī) based on her physical form, such as the appearance of her menses and so forth,
which is connected with longing and anxiety, one should not employ dance in that situation.
In whichever limb the heroine gradually gains confidence,
from that point onward one should apply the dance to the remaining limbs.
Furthermore, whatever limb [of the dance] is performed based on the praise of the gods,
one should employ that with bold *aṅgahāras* belonging to the followers of Maheśvara.
As for the song connected with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), which concerns men and women,
one should employ it accompanied by the graceful *aṅgahāras* performed by the Goddess.
I shall now fully explain the procedure regarding the four-footed *narkuṭaka*, the *khañjaka*, and the *parigītaka*, as well as the rules for the sounding of musical instruments.
When a quadruped is joined with a Khañjana and an Arkuṭa, it should be smeared with ashes;
if there is a conjunction at the end of its foot, there will be the seizing of its vessel.
That which is fixed, joined with meters, having equal feet and equal syllables—
at the conclusion of its feet, there should be the grasping of the forefinger.
Having performed one complete cycle of both singing and gesturing,
one should again conclude with a foot-step and join it with the *bhāṇḍa* drum.
But when the limbs and the objects have ceased, and when the other colors have ceased,
one should likewise employ musical instruments for the purpose of providing support.
Furthermore, whatever intermediate paths may exist, which are fashioned by the instruments of speech and tantra,
the needle should be applied to them along with the vessel during the *tāṇḍava* dance.
Whoever applies this account of Maheśvara’s deeds,
having his soul purified of all sins, goes to the world of Śiva.
Thus has this rule for the performance of the tāṇḍava been described;
what else regarding the rules of the Nāṭya-veda should be told further?
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Tāṇḍava," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
Now begins the fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Pūrvaraṅga.
Having heard the words of Bharata regarding the cause for the continuity of the dramatic art, [the sages asked:]
Once again, the sages, with joyful minds, spoke these words.
Just as there is this origin of drama and the production of the *jarjara* mask, so too there is the pacification of obstacles and the worship of the deities. (BhN 5.2)
All of that has been heard by us and grasped;
we wish to know it once again in its entirety, according to its true nature.
O Brahmin, you should explain that great splendor, which is endowed with all auspicious marks and serves as the preliminary rite, exactly as we understand it.
Having heard those words of the sages, the sage Bharata replied again with these words concerning the preliminary ritual of the performance.
O noble ones, understand from my speaking the preliminary rite (*pūrvaraṅga*), as well as the divisions of the quarters (*pādabhāga*), the *kalās*, and likewise the *parivartas*. BhN 5.6.
O best of the twice-born, because this performance is first employed on the stage, it should therefore be known as the *pūrvaraṅga* (the preliminary rite).
Its constituent parts, however, should be performed in due order and according to rule,
through the combination of strings and instruments, as well as through the application of recitation.
Withdrawal, as well as descent, and likewise the very beginning; the sounding, the hand upon the mouth, and the rubbing together. BhN 5.9.
Then the *saṅghoṭanā* should be performed, as well as the *mārgāsārita*;
likewise, the *jyeṣṭha*, *madhya*, and *kaniṣṭha* [melodies], as well as the *asāra* [melodies].
These songs, however, which are sung externally, should be performed by performers situated behind the curtain, as well as those produced by stringed instruments.
Then, having removed the curtain, one should have all the Kutapas joined together here with the various performances of dance and recitation. (BhN 5.12)
One song from among the *gītas* such as the *madraka* and others should be employed; likewise, the *vardhamāna* or the *tāṇḍava* may also be used here where appropriate. (BhN 5.13)
Then the raising [of the curtain] should be performed, as well as the change of scene;
likewise the *nāndī*, the *śuṣkāvakṛṣṭā*, and the stage entrance (*raṅgadvāra*).
Furthermore, the *cāri*, the *mahācāri*, the *trika*, and the *prarocanā* indeed constitute the *pūrvaraṅga*. (BhN 5.15)
O twice-born ones, these are the constituent parts to be performed in the ritual of the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga);
I shall explain their characteristics in due order. (BhN 5.16)
The arrangement of the *kutapa* is known as *pratyāhāra*;
likewise, the settling of the singers is declared to be the *avataraṇa*.
The commencement of the performance that is celebrated by all is proclaimed as the *ārambha*;
however, for the purpose of tuning the instruments, there should be the procedure of the *āśrāvaṇā*.
The hand is positioned at the mouth of the instrument for the purpose of distinguishing the playing technique;
however, friction [of the bow] is employed for the purpose of imparting strength to the strings. (BhN 5.19)
Likewise, for the purpose of distinguishing the hands, there is the method of rhythmic clapping;
through the combination of strings and instruments, it is intended as the *mārgāsārita*.

The performance of the *āsārita* should take place for the purpose of distinguishing the clarity of the musical measures (*kalā*), as well as for the glorification of the deities; thus should the procedure for song be understood.
Henceforth, I shall indeed explain the ritual procedure for the rite of raising up.
Because the reciters of the *nāndī* initiate the performance here on this stage even beforehand, it is therefore known as "the commencement" (*utthāpana*). (BhN 5.22)
And because the world-protectors circumambulate it in the four directions and offer salutations, it is therefore called "the circumambulation. (BhN 5.23)
Because it is always employed, joined with words of benediction for gods, the twice-born, kings, and others, it is therefore designated as *nāndī*.
Since the *dhruvā* here is indeed drawn out by means of dry syllables alone,
it is therefore called "dry-drawn" (*śuṣkāvakṛṣṭā*), as demonstrated in this worn-out verse.
Since the dramatic representation (abhinaya) is introduced here first,
it should therefore be known as the "Entrance to the Stage" (raṅgadvāra), consisting of vocal and physical representation (vāgaṅgābhinaya).
It is proclaimed as *cārī* because it proceeds from the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), and it is also proclaimed as *mahācārī* because it proceeds from the furious sentiment (*raudra*). (BhN 5.27)
Where the Vidūṣaka, the Sūtradhāra, and likewise the Pāripārśvaka engage in conversation, that too is considered a Trigata.
When there is an address by means of a proven fact, based on a reason or a logical argument for the sake of introducing a poetic work, that should be known as *prarocanā* (persuasion). BhN 5.29.
Hereafter, I shall explain the ritual procedure for the *āśrāvaṇa*,
as well as the correct origin and the cause of the external singing rite.
But when the sevenfold form, accompanied by various offerings and fees, has been set in motion—
along with the *apohana*, the *nirghoṣa*, and the celebration of the praise of the deity— BhN 5.31.
In the assembly hall, the gods and dānavas were made to hear the song perfectly sung by Nārada and other gandharvas, accompanied by proper rhythm and tempo.
Having heard that pleasant singing, which was accompanied by the praise of the gods,
all the Daityas and Rākṣasas became agitated out of envy.
Having deliberated with one another, they stood there and said:
"We shall take up this [sacrifice] which has been proclaimed along with its musical instruments."
The gods are satisfied with seven forms through the recitation of one's deeds; we accept what is sung and are always pleased right here. (BhN 5.35)
There those Daityas were satisfied and performed [the rites] again and again;
then the gods, becoming enraged, addressed Nārada.
These Dānavas, together with the Rākṣasas, are satisfied when there is no singing;
let this ritual practice perish—what do you think? (BhN 5.37)
Having heard the words of the gods, Nārada spoke these words: "Let this song, composed as a support for the alchemy of the elements, not perish."
However, this song, though devoid of vocal singing, will be accompanied by instrumental introductions and adorned with the playing of musical instruments,
according to the arrangement of the seven notes.
And the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas, bound by this song,
being thus gratified, shall cause neither agitation nor obstruction here.
Thus, O twice-born ones, this [Veda] was sung internally out of rivalry with the Daityas;
it is remembered as having been sung externally out of great respect for the gods.
Then, wise men should employ [the music] on a multi-toned lute (citravīṇā), accompanied by long and short syllables and joined with phonetic ornaments (varṇālaṅkāra). BhN 5.42.
Because it is sung as a song without words through the arrangement of phonemes,
and because of the gods' envy, this is known as the "Outward Song" (Bahirgīta).
That which has been proclaimed by me as the Nirgīta, endowed with its seven forms,
and that which consists of the Utthāpana and so forth— the cause of that is now being stated.
When the *āśrāvaṇā* is properly performed, the Daityas are constantly satisfied;
and when the *vaktrapāṇi* is likewise performed, the Dānavas are always satisfied.
The hosts of Rākṣasas are pleased by clashing together,
while the Guhyakas also find satisfaction in the act of grinding one another.
Indeed, the yakṣas become joyful upon encountering that which is performed according to the path;
and when songs are employed, the gods are always pleased.
When the *vardhamāna* is employed, Rudra, together with his followers, is pleased;
likewise, when the *utthāpana* is employed, Brahmā becomes gratified here in this world.
The world-protectors are pleased when the *parivartana* is performed;
moreover, when the *nāndī* application is made, the Moon becomes delighted.
For when the *yuktā* [oblation] is drawn out, the Nāgas indeed become pleased;
likewise, when the *śuṣkā* is drawn out, the host of Pitṛs becomes pleased. (BhN 5.50)
When the *raṅgadvāra* is employed, Viṣṇu becomes pleased here;
when the *jarjara* is employed, the Vighnas and Vināyakas are satisfied. (BhN 5.51)
Likewise, when the Āryā is employed here, Umā becomes pleased;
but when the Mahācāryā is employed, the host of spirits (bhūtagaṇa) becomes pleased. (BhN 5.52)

This worship of the deities, beginning with the invocation (āśrāvaṇā) and ending with the dismissal (cāryanta), as well as the arrangement of the ritual limbs, has been declared by me in the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga). BhN 5.53.
"O best of the twice-born, I have previously explained that the gods are pleased by whatever is dear to the mind of each individual; such is the preliminary rite."
Worthy of worship by all the deities and itself the worship of all the deities,
this commencement of the preliminary rite brings merit, fame, and long life.
For the sake of pleasing the Daityas, Dānavas, and all the inhabitants of heaven,
the preliminary rites were performed with both instrumental music and vocal song.
Whatever knowledge, whatever crafts, whatever destiny, and whatever activity there is for the world that illuminates the world— all that is contained within this drama.
I shall indeed explain the characteristics and the ritual application for *dhruvās* that are without song, those with song, and likewise for the *vardhamāna*. BhN 5.57.
Having performed the ritual for the *gītaka* and likewise the *vardhamāna*,
then at the conclusion of the *gītaka*, the *dhruvā* known as the *utthāpanī* should indeed be performed.
One should know that the first two syllables, as well as the fourth, eighth, and eleventh, are heavy syllables in the foot; likewise, in the eleventh [foot], it is so.
It should consist of four quarters and likewise be square;
it possesses four junctions, three tempos, and three meters.
There are four *parivartas* and exactly three *pāṇis*;
indeed, they are distinguished by their *jāti*, and one should apply them according to the *tāla*.
The *śamyā* should be made of two *kalās*, and the *tala* likewise of two *kalās*;
again, the *śamyā* is one *kalā*, while the *sannipāta* consists of three *kalās*.
In this way, the combination (sannipāta) consisting of eight parts should be constructed by the wise;
and four such combinations are called a "parivarta."
First, the dissolution of the stationary state should be performed by the wise;
however, upon the third conjunction, there occurs her grasping of the vessel.
When one revolution has passed and the second has arrived,
the experts should perform the entry of the master builder (sūtradhāra) into the middle layer.
Having taken up a handful of flowers, consecrated by protective and auspicious rites,
wearing pure garments and with joyful minds, they likewise possessed wondrous vision.
Having prepared the Vaiṣṇava site, adorned with excellence and its constituent parts,
the three initiated and pure individuals should enter together.
The two attendants (pāripārśvika) should carry water-pitchers with frayed handles;
meanwhile, the director (sūtradhṛt), surrounded by them, should walk five steps in the center.
Five steps may be taken by a Brahmin with the desire to perform a sacrifice;
I shall now explain the measurement of those steps in their proper sequence.
One should slowly lift the foot, spanning the distance of three tālas, and having raised it from the side, one should then bring it down again into its middle position.
Having thus stepped five paces, the master weaver and his companion should place a needle in the left foot and make a mark with the right.
Furthermore, the offering of a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) should be performed within the Brahma-maṇḍala;
for Brahmā himself is established in the center of the colored pedestal.
Then, having paid homage to the Grandfather with graceful hand gestures,
one should perform three salutations with the hand upon the ground.
And due to the length of time, it consists of the division of the quarters, beginning with the entry of the Sūtradhāra and ending with the performance of salutation. (BhN 5.74)
The second chapter, however, should be performed with a medium tempo;
thereafter, in the third, there is the circumambulation of the mandala.
There should be sipping of water (ācamana) as well as the grasping of a worn-out rag;
then, rising quickly from the mandala, one should lift up the right foot.
One should perform the piercing with that [same foot] and the shifting with the left;
then one should again lift up the right foot, keeping it positioned at the side.
Then, having performed the circumambulation correctly according to this rule— "the piercing with the left and the casting away of the right"— BhN 5.78.
Having summoned one who holds a water-pitcher, he should also perform purification;
indeed, the rite of sipping water (ācamana) must be performed by him according to the prescribed rule.
The self-sprinkling with water must indeed be performed in the proper sequence by the Sūtradhāra, who has diligently maintained his purity with great effort. (BhN 5.80)
It should be understood as being equal to the conjunction [of the planets], worn out, and shattered by obstacles;
it is to be known as beginning with circumambulation and ending with the grasping of the worn-out state.
The third chapter, however, should be understood as being performed at a rapid tempo;
having taken up the *jarjara* [rhythm], one should apply the recitation for eight *kalās*. (BhN 5.82)
Then one should perform the piercing with the left and the scattering of the right;
thereafter, one should proceed toward the Kutapa fire at a distance of five steps.
In that case as well, there is the piercing from the left, while the distraction belongs to the right;
this [piercing] which begins with the seizing of the jarjara ends facing toward the kutapa.
The fourth section, however, should be performed again at a fast tempo;
here, there are sixteen strokes of the hands and feet.
In the triangular [mudrā], there are twelve prostrations for the hands and feet;
then, three salutations with the hand should be performed upon the ground.
Sprinkling oneself with water in a triangular manner is not prescribed at all;
in this way, the rite of raising [the vessel] should be performed, followed by the turning around.
It is square in its middle cadence due to eight pauses;
it consists entirely of short syllables, with only the final syllable being long.
In the *atijagatī* meter, that *dhruvā* should be performed with variation,
following the path of the *vārtika* and accompanied by instrumental music.
The gods are to be worshipped with graceful placements of the feet according to their respective directions;
the falling of the foot for two *kalās* constitutes the movement known as *pādacārī*.
The piercing with the left foot should be performed by those who employ the dance;
the throwing out of the right [foot] occurs at an interval of two *tālas* and a distance of one *viṣkambha*.
Then one should walk five steps beyond the chariot tracks;
thereafter, one should perform salutations to the deities according to their respective directions.
One should first pay homage to the eastern direction, of which Śakra is the presiding deity;
one should pay homage to the second, the southern quarter, of which Yama is the deity.
One should salute the western direction, whose presiding deity is Varuṇa;
then one should salute the fourth, the northern direction, which has Kubera as its refuge.
Having performed the salutation to the directions, one should employ the leftward piercing;
the shifting of the gaze should be performed with the right.
Then, facing eastward, the man should perform the salutation to Rudra, Brahmā, and Upendra with three verses, using the masculine, feminine, and neuter forms respectively. BhN 5.96.
The right foot is proclaimed for men, while the left is for women;
for a neuter, it should be the right foot again, neither raised too high.
One should worship the Lord with the masculine form, Janārdana with the feminine form,
and likewise the Lotus-born One with the neuter form.
The exchange should be performed in this manner; at its conclusion, one should then enter, with the fourth person holding flowers according to the prescribed rite.
One should perform the worship of the worn-out [image], of the *kutapa* blanket, of everything else, and indeed of the architect (*sūtradhāra*) according to the prescribed rule.
The movement and progression of that [drum] should be made by experts equal to those of a musical instrument;
singing should not be performed there, but rather the practice of *stobha* should occur.
Having performed the fourth type of worship, he becomes invisible;
then, drawn forth by song, she stands firm and motionless in a square formation.
It should be composed mostly of *guru* syllables, likewise with an *avapāṇika* cadence,
endowed with a stable metrical pattern (*sthāyivarṇa*), and constructed from eight *kalās*.
When the fourth, fifth, seventh,
and likewise the eighth syllables in the foot of a *paṅkti* are short, it is known as the *sāvakṛṣṭā dhruvā*.
There, the director (sūtradhāra), relying on a medium pitch,
should recite the *nāndī*, adorned with either twelve or eight metrical feet.
Homage be to all the gods and likewise auspiciousness to the twice-born;
victory indeed belongs to King Soma, and may there be well-being for cows and brahmins.
"May there likewise be a preeminence of Brahman, and may those who hate Brahman be slain;
may the great king rule this earth together with its oceans."
May the kingdom indeed flourish, and may the hopes of the theater company be fulfilled; may great merit, as spoken by Brahmā, accrue to the patron of the performance.
"May the fame of the author of this poem endure, may his merit also increase, and may the deities be perpetually pleased by this sacrifice. BhN 5.108.
In these intervals between the *nāndī* verses, those two attendants (*pāripārśvika*) should always address the Noble Lady thus with well-spoken words: BhN 5.109.
In this manner, the *nāndī* should be composed, endowed with its proper characteristics;
thereafter, it should be recited in a dry and drawn-out style, indicating the *jarjara* verse.
Nine syllables beginning with heavy ones, followed by six light and three heavy syllables—
this is indeed the *śuṣkāvakṛṣṭā* kalā, measuring eight [mātrās] in duration.

Just so, O best of the twice-born: having performed the *digle* [ritual] four times for the sake of the *jambukapalitaka* [rite], one should duly perform the drying and extraction [of the substance]. (BhN 5.112)
Then, having placed the hymn of praise for the deity whose worship is being performed at the forefront, one should recite a single verse with a deep tone. (BhN 5.113)
Or where there is devotion to the king, or else by reciting a hymn to Brahmā consisting of worn-out verses, and that which is remembered at the entrance to the theater. BhN 5.114.
One should then recite another verse for the destruction of the jarjara;
having bent the jarjara, one should thereafter employ the cārī.
The two attendants should withdraw behind [the stage],
and here the *dhruvā* song, marked with its characteristic signs, should be performed in a medium tempo.
It is square in measure due to the combination of four [units], and likewise, the first, the last, the fourth, and the fifth [syllables] are heavy. (BhN 5.117)
That [meter] in which the remaining [syllables] are short should be known by the wise as *tvaṅkitā*.
I shall describe its application just as Maheśvara did previously.
He sported with Umā through various playful gestures,
assuming a pose of feigned indifference while keeping his left arm bent and turned downward.
The chest should be made square and the head slightly inclined;
having placed the worn-out [cloth] upon the region of the navel, it is held up by a balance.
With the hand [held like] a left sprout and with feet rising at intervals of a *tāla*,
she should walk five steps with graceful movements of her limbs.
The piercing with the left hand should be performed, as well as the diversion of the right;
the wise one should recite an Āryā verse imbued with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa).
Having recited the *cārī* verse and performed the turning,
one should effect the withdrawal toward the west by means of those very same steps.
Having placed the excellent *jarjara* in the hand of the *pāripārśvika*, one should then employ the *mahācārī* according to the prescribed rule. (BhN 5.124)
In that [context], the *dhruvā* is square-shaped and likewise possesses a fast tempo (*drutalaya*);
it consists of four *sannipātas*, and its duration is eight *kalās*.

In the first quarter of the *dhruvā* consisting of twenty-four syllables, the first, fourth, last (twenty-fourth), seventh, and tenth syllables shall be heavy, while the remaining syllables shall be light. (BhN 5.126)

May this Tandava dance of Hara, which at the end of the cosmic dissolution strikes down mountains with the tread of his soles and agitates the entire ocean along with its beings, protect the world and bestow happiness upon it. (BhN 5.127)
Then, with the face turned toward the vessel, one should perform the movement of the feet;
having formed the needle position, one should again perform the turning of the movements.
Then, with feet that are gracefully extended and endowed with a quick tempo,
one should proceed through five steps with upward tosses occurring at intervals of three tālas.
In that case as well, there is the piercing with the left and the diversion of the right;
by those very steps, one should perform the withdrawal while facing the east.
Furthermore, he should take exactly three steps facing east;
then there shall be a leftward piercing and a displacement to the right.
Then one should recite a verse of the *raudra* (fierce) sentiment with the feet drawn together;
at its conclusion, however, one should cause the two attendants (*pāripārśvika*) to utter three verses.
Upon their arrival, the wise should employ the *narkuṭaka* song;
likewise, in the various divisions of the *bhāratī* style, one should apply the *trigata*.
Then the Vidūṣaka should deliver a monologue (kathanikā) consisting mostly of incoherent talk, which elicits a smile from the Sūtradhāra and lasts for only a single moment. BhN 5.134.

One should employ the *vitaṇḍā* (destructive criticism), the *gaṇḍa* (the "swelling" or complex argument), and the *tālikā* (the "linking" or clincher), which describe such things as "Who remains? and "By whom has victory been won? (BhN 5.134).
The dialogue of the attendants, embellished by the *vidūṣaka*, established by the director (*sūtradhāra*), is employed as the *tri-gata*. (BhN 5.134*2)
An incitement should be made, and an invitation by one who has attained success;
furthermore, once the stage is prepared, the determination of the subject matter of the poem should be performed. (BhN 5.135)
Then, having performed the entire ritual procedure, the three should exit together with steps that have not been pierced by needle-punctures and which move evenly.
O best of the twice-born, this preliminary ritual (pūrvaraṅga) should be performed according to the rules as a square; now learn also of the triangular form.
This indeed shall be the practice, and these very [elements] are its limbs;
the palm-tree measure is abbreviated, but it alone is what produces the distinction.
The *śamyā* should be made of two *kalās*, while the *tāla* is likewise one *kalā*;
again, the *śamyā* is one *kalā*, and the *sannipāta* consists of two *kalās*.

For by this means, the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga)—which consists of the three acts beginning with the *utthāpana*—should be performed, accompanied by rhythmic divisions (*kalā*), tempo (*tāla*), and musical timing (*laya*). (BhN 5.140)
That *jagatī* meter in which the first, fourth, eighth, tenth,
and final syllables are heavy is the *tryaśrotthāpinī* *dhruvā*.

Musical instruments, the movement of the gait, the *dhruvā* verses, and likewise the rhythmic beats (*tāla*)— these actions should be performed in a concise manner by those skilled in the triangular dance (*tryaśra-nṛtta*).
One should perform the movements of the limbs according to the measure of instrumental music and song,
whether they are extensive or concise, fashioned according to two measures.
The movement of the hands and feet is proclaimed to take two *kalās*;
when moving in a square formation, there should be exactly sixteen steps.
In the triangular [hand position], there are twelve beats for both the hands and the feet;
this measurement should be understood to apply to both of the preliminary sequences (pūrvaraṅga).
In the case of a simple circumambulation, there should be three steps;
for the salutation of the directions, five steps are prescribed in a square formation.
It should be made with the intention of honoring the Teacher, triangular in shape and according to the measure of a *tāla*;
therefore, no further characteristic is taught here, lest it become redundant.
O best of the twice-born, this introductory ritual (pūrvaraṅga) is to be performed in this manner:
it may be triangular or square, pure, and based upon the Bhāratī style.
Thus far, I have described this pure *pūrvaraṅga*;
I shall now explain its variegated nature as it should be employed by performers according to the requirements of the work.

When the rite of raising [the image] has been performed, O Brahmins, and the turning around has been completed, and it has been adorned with flowers offered by those who have uttered the fourth formula; BhN 5.150.
The Gandharvas sang with resonant melodies according to the prescribed measures,
and the divine drums resounded loudly from every side.
The Siddhas should scatter flower garlands all around,
and those goddesses should dance before him with graceful movements of their limbs.
The procedure for the *tāṇḍava* dance that has been taught, which is accompanied by the *piṇḍī*,
joined with breath-exhalations (*recaka*), bodily movements (*aṅgahāra*), and the placement and re-placement [of gestures] (*nyāsopanyāsa*).
Among the various types of *nāndī* verses, each one should be employed separately by the wise who desire to achieve a variety of aesthetic effects.
Having thus prepared the pure and variegated [stage] with effort according to the rule,
thereafter one should employ a drama endowed with the proper characteristics.
Then all those divine women would vanish;
and after all the female dancers have departed, thereafter—
Thereafter, the collection of subsidiary elements (aṅga) should be employed in the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga).
In this manner, according to the prescribed rule, the pure preliminary rite becomes variegated.
One should not allow excessive indulgence here regarding the rules for dancing and singing;
for when singing, instrumental music, and dancing proceed with excessive indulgence, [it leads to ruin]. BhN 5.158.
There would be weariness for both the performers and likewise for the spectators;
and for those who are weary, clarity regarding the aesthetic flavors (rasas) and emotional states (bhāvas) does not arise. (BhN 5.159)
Consequently, the remaining application would not produce passion;
[for] without a defining characteristic, it would become extensive due to external characteristics.
Therefore, drama proceeds in accordance with worldly conventions and treatises. (BhN 5.160ab)
It may be triangular or quadrangular, and it may be either plain or variegated.
Having performed [the preliminaries], the stage director should exit the stage along with his followers, accompanied by benedictory verses for the gods, the king, and the audience. (BhN 5.161)
It should be endowed with the name and qualities of the poet, consisting of the presentation of the subject matter, composed of concise syllables and words, and adorned with various meters.
Then, standing behind the inner curtain, he should perform the call for attention;
and at the conclusion of that call, having performed the *nāndī*, the director (*sūtradhṛt*) shall re-enter the stage and then perform the prologue (*prastāvanā*).
Having thus performed the preliminary rite according to the prescribed rule through its application, // BhN 5.161 //
The Sthāpaka, possessing the qualities and appearance of a Sūtradhāra, should enter there;
having assumed the Vaiṣṇava posture, preceded by graceful gestures and bodily movements.
Having entered the stage, one should proceed using those very words of the *sūtradhāra*;
however, upon the entrance of the *sthāpaka*, a *dhruvā* verse conforming to the subject matter must be performed.
Whether triangular or square, provided it is endowed with a moderate tempo according to those who know it,
one should immediately perform the *cārī* that indicates the presence of Devarāhmaṇa.
Having duly propitiated the audience with verses that are sweet with excellent words and endowed with various meters and sentiments, one should proclaim the name of the poet.
The introductory sections (prastāva). Then one should perform that which serves as the basis for proclaiming the poem;
the *uddhātyaka* and other such elements should be employed as the means for introducing the subject matter of the poem. (BhN 5.166)
Having become one with a divine basis in a divine state, or with a human basis in a human state, or in the conjunction of the divine and human, he may be either divine or even human. (BhN 5.167)
The introduction to a poem may consist of introductory remarks that resemble the seed of the plot and rely upon various narrative paths. (BhN 5.168)
Having thus introduced [the performance], the introducer of the poetic work should then exit;
in this manner, the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga) is to be performed according to the rule.
Whoever performs this preliminary rite according to the prescribed rule shall not encounter anything inauspicious and shall go to the heavenly world.
Furthermore, whoever abandons the prescribed rule and acts according to his own whims incurs terrible ruin and goes to the womb of an animal.
Fire, even when fanned by a strong wind, does not burn as intensely as fire that is applied without prior effort; for the latter consumes everything in an instant.
Thus, the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga) should be performed by those from Avantī, Pañcāla, the Deccan, Oḍhra, and Magadha, constructed with two measures.
O Brahmins, this rule concerning the preliminary rite (pūrvaraṅga) has been told to you.
What more may be correctly told regarding the rules of the science of drama (nāṭyaveda)?
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Application of the Pūrvaraṅga," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
Now begins the sixth chapter:
Having heard the rules for the *pūrvaraṅga*, the most eminent authorities spoke again.
O Bharata, all the sages say: "Answer us our five questions."
Those which are recited as "rasas" in drama by those expert in dramatic art—by what means do they possess the state of being a rasa? You ought to explain this.

And how are the existents (bhāva) described? What do they bring about? [Explain] their summary, their verse-formulation (kārikā), and their etymological analysis (nirukta) according to reality. BhN 6.3.
Having heard those words of the sages, the sage Bharata replied once more with speech that was full of aesthetic flavor and emotional resonance.
O you whose wealth is asceticism, I shall relate to you in its entirety the summary,
the mnemonic verses, and the etymological explanations, in their proper order.
It is not possible to reach the end of this dramatic art in any way;
why? Because of the multiplicity of sciences and the infinity of crafts.
Indeed, it is not possible to reach the end of even this single ocean of knowledge;
how much less so for other forms of knowledge in their true meaning?
However, I shall expound the compendium of rasa, bhāva, and other elements of this drama, which establishes the meaning of the brief sūtra-text through inference.
The wise know that "Compendium" (saṅgraha) is the concise compilation of those meanings taught in detail within both the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya. BhN 6.9.

The aesthetic sentiments (rasas), the emotional states (bhāvas), the dramatic representations (abhinayas), the essential qualities (dharmī), the modes of action (vṛtti) and their applications (pravṛttis), success (siddhi), the musical scales (svaras), as well as the instruments (ātodya), singing (gāna), the stage (raṅga), and the compendium (saṅgraha). // BhN 6.10 //

That meaning which is expressed by the wise in brief through concise terminology should be understood as being established by way of a *sūtra*; it is a *kārikā* that demonstrates the intended meaning. (BhN 6.11)
It arises from various names as its basis, is endowed with glossaries and Vedic citations,
is connected with the meanings and roots of words, and is established through various philosophical systems.
Where a meaning is established that indicates the sense in brief, they call that here "nirukta" (etymological explanation) by means of stating the root-meaning. BhN 6.13.
O best of the twice-born, that compendium which has been declared by me in brief—
I shall now explain it in detail, together with its etymologies and its summary verses.

In dramatic performance, eight aesthetic sentiments (rasas) are traditionally recognized: the erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, the terrifying, the loathsome, and that known as the marvelous.
These eight rasas have indeed been proclaimed by the high-souled Druhina;
furthermore, I shall now describe the emotional states (bhāvas) born of the stable, the transitory, and the essential natures.
Love, mirth, sorrow, anger, energy, fear, as well as disgust and wonder—these are proclaimed to be the permanent emotional states (*sthāyibhāva*). (BhN 6.17)
Disgust, lassitude, doubt, as well as envy, pride, fatigue, indolence, dejection, anxiety, delusion, memory, and fortitude; BhN 6.18.
Shame, fickleness, joy, agitation, as well as dullness, pride, despondency, longing, sleep, and epilepsy. (BhN 6.19)
Awakening from sleep, indignation, dissimulation, and ferocity; discernment, disease, madness, and likewise death. (BhN 6.20)
Fear and deliberation are also to be known as transitory states;
these thirty-three emotional states have thus been fully enumerated by name.
Stupefaction, perspiration, horripilation, change of voice, trembling, change of color, tears, and fainting—these eight are known as the *sāttvika* [emotions]. (BhN 6.22)
The bodily, the vocal, the artificial (costume-based), and likewise the natural (psychophysical)—
these four modes of representation are to be understood as pertaining to drama.
The dramatic style is traditionally held to be twofold: that which conforms to worldly conventions and that which conforms to the rules of drama;
these are the Bhāratī, Sātvatī, Kaiśikī, and Ārabhaṭī.
For these are the four styles (vṛtti) upon which drama is established:
the Āvantī, the Dākṣiṇātyā, and likewise the Oḍhrī and Māgadhī. (BhN 6.25)
The *pāñcāla-madhyamā* should also be understood as types of activity;
furthermore, accomplishment (*siddhi*) is indeed twofold: divine and human. (BhN 6.26)
The seven musical notes, beginning with ṣaḍja, are both bodily and produced by the flute: niṣāda, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, madhyama, pañcama, dhaivata, and niṣāda. (BhN 6.27ab)
The stringed, the covered, the solid, and the hollow.

And musical instruments should be known as fourfold, endowed with their defining characteristics: the stringed instrument is to be known as that which consists of strings, while the percussion instrument is that which is covered with skin, such as the drum.
The solid [instrument] is to be known as the *tāla*, and the hollow one as the *vaṃśa* (flute).
Then there is the *antara*, which consists of the entry (*praveśa*), the throw (*ākṣepa*), the exit (*niṣkrāma*), and the pleasing (*prāsādika*).
Singing is to be known as fivefold, endowed with the application of the *dhruvā* [refrain].
It is proclaimed to be quadrangular, extended, angular, triangular, and circular.
Thus has this compendium of drama (nāṭyasaṃgraha), consisting of a brief exposition of the meaning of the Sūtra, been taught.
Hereafter, I shall explain the detailed analysis of the textual composition of the Sūtra.
In this regard, we shall first explain the aesthetic flavors (rasas) themselves;
for no meaning whatsoever proceeds without the flavor.
In that context, the production of flavor arises from the conjunction of the determinants (vibhāvas), the consequents (anubhāvas), and the transitory mental states (vyabhicāribhāvas).
What is the illustration?

To this it is said: Just as the production of flavor results from the combination of various condiments, medicinal herbs, and substances, so too does the production of flavor result from the attainment of various emotional states (*bhāva*).

For just as flavors such as the *ṣāḍava* are produced by means of substances like molasses, condiments, and medicinal herbs, so too do the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*), having attained various [accessory] states, reach the state of being a flavor (*rasatva*).
Here it is asked: what is the category-meaning (padārtha) of "taste" (rasa)?
It is said: because it is that which is tasted.

How is the aesthetic flavor (rasa) relished? Just as people with clear minds, while eating food prepared with various seasonings, relish its flavors and experience joy and other such states, so too do spectators with clear minds relish the stable emotions (sthāyibhāva)— which are manifested through various emotional states and dramatic gestures and endowed with speech, physical action, and internal disposition.
And they experience joy and other such states;

therefore, they are explained as the dramatic sentiments (*nāṭyarasa*). On this point, there are two traditional verses: [Verse 1] Just as the various tastes are perceived in food through the contact of the tongue, so too are the various sentiments perceived in drama through the contact of the mind. [Verse 2] Just as the various tastes are perceived in food through the contact of the palate, so too are the various sentiments perceived in drama through the contact of the intellect.
Just as those who know how to eat relish their food when it is accompanied by many side dishes prepared with numerous ingredients, so too do they experience the taste.
The wise likewise savor with their minds the stable emotions (sthāyibhāvas) connected with the enactment of the [transient] states; therefore, they are known as the dramatic sentiments (nāṭyarasa).
Regarding this, it is asked:
does the manifestation of the emotional states (bhāvas) arise from the aesthetic sentiments (rasas), or do the aesthetic sentiments arise from the emotional states?
According to the opinion of some, their manifestation occurs through mutual interdependence.
That is not so.
Why?

Because it is observed that the manifestation of aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) arises from the emotional states (*bhāva*), but the manifestation of emotional states does not arise from the aesthetic flavors.
And there are verses on this subject:

"Because they bring to being the measures of aesthetic flavor (rasa) through connection with various modes of representation (abhinaya), these are therefore to be understood as 'bhāvas' by those who employ dramatic performance. (BhN 6.34)
Just as a sauce is prepared with various and manifold ingredients,
so too do the emotional states (bhāvas) produce aesthetic flavors (rasas) in conjunction with the dramatic gestures (abhinayas).
There is no rasa devoid of bhāva, nor is there any bhāva devoid of rasa;
their perfection is achieved through their mutual interaction in dramatic performance.
Just as the combination of condiments and herbs brings sweetness to food,
so too do dispositions and flavors mutually influence one another.
Just as a tree arises from a seed, and from the tree come flowers and fruit,
so too do all tastes arise from the root, and from them all states of being are established.
Thus, we shall explain the origins, colors, deities, and characteristics of these flavors. There are four primary causes for their origin:
namely, the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), the furious (*raudra*), the heroic (*vīra*), and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*). Regarding these:
For from the erotic (śṛṅgāra) arises the comic (hāsya), and from the furious (raudra) the pathetic (karuṇa) sentiment;
from the heroic (vīra) arises the marvelous (adbhuta), and from the loathsome (bībhatsa) the terrifying (bhayānaka).
That which is an imitation of the erotic (śṛṅgāra) is proclaimed as the comic (hāsya);
and that which is the action of the furious (raudra) is to be known as the pathetic (karuṇa) sentiment.
Furthermore, whatever action belongs to a hero is proclaimed as the *adbhuta* (marvelous);
and that which has a loathsome appearance should be known as the *bhayānaka* (terrifying).
Now, regarding the colors: the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) is dark (śyāma), the comic (hāsya) is proclaimed to be white (sita);
the pathetic (karuṇa) is dove-grey (kapota), and the furious (raudra) is proclaimed to be red (rakta).
The fair-complexioned one is to be known as the Heroic; the black one is the Terrible;
the blue-colored one is the Disgusting; and the yellow one is remembered as the Marvelous.
Now, as for the presiding deities:
the erotic sentiment has Viṣṇu as its deity; the comic has the Pramathas as its deity; the furious has Rudra as its presiding deity; and the pathetic has Yama as its deity. (BhN 6.44)
For the *bībhatsa* [sentiment], Mahākāla and Kāladaiva are the presiding deities; for the *bhayānaka*, Vīra and Mahendradeva; and for the *adbhuta*, Brahmā is the deity. (BhN 6.45)
Thus have the origins, colors, and presiding deities of these rasas been fully explained.

Now we shall explain the definitions and illustrations of those [rasas] when they are conjoined with the determinants (vibhāva), the consequents (anubhāva), and the transitory states (vyabhicāribhāva). We shall also bring the stable emotions (sthāyibhāvas) to the state of rasa.
Among these, that which is called *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic) originates from the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of love (*rati*).
Its essence consists of radiant attire.
Whatever in the world is pure, sanctifying, radiant, or beautiful is compared to the *śṛṅgāra*.
That which possesses a radiant appearance is called "possessing the erotic" (*śṛṅgāravat*).

Just as men have names that arise from their lineage, family, and conduct, and are established through the instruction of authoritative teachers, so too do these *rasas*, *bhāvas*, and meanings dependent upon drama have names that arise from their conduct and are established through the instruction of authoritative teachers.

Thus, this *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment is established by its conduct (*ācāra*), consisting essentially of a charming and radiant appearance. It is caused by women and men, has as its fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) excellent youths, and possesses two bases: union (*sambhoga*) and separation (*vipralambha*).

In that regard, *sambhoga* (the erotic sentiment of union) arises from excitants (*vibhāva*) such as the experience of seasons, garlands, ointments, ornaments, beloved persons, excellent dwellings, enjoyments, excursions to pleasure groves, listening, seeing, play, and dalliance.

Its representation (*abhinaya*) should be performed through ensuants (*anubhāva*) such as skillful glances, the movement of the eyebrows, side-long looks, graceful and sweet gestures of the limbs, and speech.
Its transitory states (vyabhicāribhāvas) are all except for indolence, ferocity, and disgust.

That which is produced by separation (vipralambha), however, is to be represented through such consequent states (anubhāvas) as despondency, exhaustion, apprehension, envy, fatigue, anxiety, longing, sleep, dreaming, waking, disease, madness, intoxication, epilepsy, stupor, and death.
Regarding this, it is said:
If this *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment) originates from pleasure (*rati*), how can its emotional states (*bhāva*) be based on *karuṇā* (compassion/sorrow)?
To this it is replied:
It was already stated previously that *śṛṅgāra* is produced by both union (*sambhoga*) and separation (*vipralambha*).
The authors of the *Vaiśika-śāstra* have also described [the hero] as being in ten states;
we shall discuss those in the section on general acting (*sāmānyābhinaya*).

The pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*), however, arises from curses, afflictions, the downfall of loved ones, the loss of wealth, execution, or imprisonment, and is characterized by a state of indifference.
The state of longing arising from anxiety and accompanied by a sense of dependence is produced by *vipralambha* (separation).
Thus, one [type] is *karuṇa* (pathos) and the other is *vipralambha*.
In this way, this *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment) becomes associated with all emotional states (*bhāva*).
Moreover,
a man who is endowed with abundance amidst circumstances favorable to pleasure, who enjoys the arts of the seasons and garlands,
and who is united with a woman, is designated as "the erotic" (śṛṅgāra).

Moreover, in this case, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*) arises for noble persons who are permeated by the meaning of the Sūtras through seasonal garlands and ornaments, through service to beloved ones, music, and poetry, and through strolls and diversions in pleasure groves. (BhN 6.47)
His performance should be enacted with the clarity of his eyes and face, with smiles, sweet words, composure, and joy, as well as with graceful movements of the limbs.
Now, *hāsa* (laughter) is that which consists of the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of laughter.
It arises through determinants (*vibhāvas*) such as the sight of distorted dress and ornaments of others, audacity, fickleness, deceit, false speech, and examples illustrating physical defects.

Its performance (*abhinaya*) should be executed through consequents (*anubhāvas*) such as the quivering of the lips, nose, and cheeks; the opening and closing of the eyes; perspiration; the reddening of the face; and the clutching of the sides.

Its transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāva*) include dissimulation (*avahittha*), lassitude (*ālasya*), languor (*tandrā*), sleep (*nidrā*), dreaming (*svapna*), waking (*prabodha*), and so forth.
This [laughter] is of two kinds: residing within oneself (*ātmastha*) and residing in another (*parastha*).
When one laughs by oneself, it is then residing within oneself.
But when one causes another to laugh, then one is "standing in another's place" (*parastha*).
In this context, there are two types of noble lineages (*anuvaṃśya*):
those who are noble by nature, and those who are so through the use of contrary ornaments, distorted conduct, speech, and dress.
The aesthetic flavor known as the comic (hāsya) is remembered as that which causes one to laugh through various distorted objects.
Because it causes people to laugh through distorted behaviors, speech, contortions of the limbs, and strange costumes,
it should be known as the comic rasa (hāsya).
This sentiment is most frequently observed in women and those of lowly nature;
its six varieties should be understood, and I shall describe them again. (BhN 6.51)
Smile, laughter, chuckling, derisive laughter, mocking laughter, and excessive laughter—
these six types occur in pairs according to the superior, middling, and inferior natures of beings.
In that regard,
among the superior and the middling, there are smiling and laughing, as well as chuckling and derisive laughter; however,
among the inferior, one should recognize both scornful laughter and excessive laughter.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"The smile of the most excellent ones is characterized by cheeks slightly blossomed, side-glances endowed with grace, and a steady gaze in which the teeth are not visible. (BhN 6.54)
That smile is performed wherein the face and eyes are blossomed, the cheeks are expanded, and the teeth are slightly revealed. (BhN 6.55)

Now, regarding the middle [laughter]: that which involves the contraction of the eyes and cheeks, is accompanied by sound, is sweet, occurs at the proper time, and possesses its characteristic passion—that indeed is *vihasita* (the smile). BhN 6.56.
That which is performed with the nostrils flared, looking with a sidelong glance,
and with the limbs and head contracted, is the "mocking smile" (upahasita).
Now, regarding the lowest [types of laughter]:
that which is a laugh out of place, as well as one with tearful eyes, and with the shoulders and head trembling—that shall be known as *apahāsita* (mocking laughter). BhN 6.58.
That laughter is excessive when it is accompanied by agitation and tearful eyes, an elevated and distorted voice, and the sides of the body being pressed by the hands. BhN 6.59.
Whatever occasions for laughter may arise from the action in a drama,
one should employ them in this manner for characters of high, low, and middle status.
Thus, this comic sentiment (hāsya-rasa) should be understood as being twofold—arising from oneself and arising from another—and as consisting of three natures and existing in three states. (BhN 6.61)
Now, *karuṇa* (the pathetic sentiment) originates from the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of sorrow.

It arises through determinants (*vibhāva*) such as the falling away of loved ones, separation from those one desires, the loss of wealth, execution, imprisonment, flight, injury, the onset of calamities, and the like—caused by curses, afflictions, or misfortunes.

Its representation (*abhinaya*) should be performed through consequents (*anubhāva*) such as the shedding of tears, lamentation, parching of the mouth, change of complexion, drooping of the limbs, sighing, and loss of memory.

And the transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) of this [hero] are: despondency, languor, anxiety, longing, agitation, confusion, delusion, fatigue, fear, dejection, wretchedness, disease, numbness, madness, epilepsy, terror, lassitude, death, paralysis, trembling, change of color, tears, and broken voice.
