That gaze which has the tips of its lashes slightly contracted, with pupils raised in wonder,
gentle, and with wide-open corners, is the "wonderful" (adbhuta) gaze used for the marvelous.
In the Furious (raudra) [sentiment], the gaze is known as fierce (raudrī), with eyes rough, reddish, upturned, and fixed upon the pupils, and the brow knit into a frown. (BhN 8.51)
Blazing, blossoming, agitated, profound,
and with even pupils— the "heroic" gaze has its center fully opened and is the locus of the heroic sentiment.
With the corners of the eyes contracted, the pupils rolling and submerged, and the eyelashes closely pressed together and motionless—this is considered the loathsome gaze (bībhatsā-dṛṣṭi). BhN 8.53.
Fixed on the tip of the nose, unblinking, moving downward,
with slightly narrowed lids— such is this gaze that becomes tranquil during a state of tranquility.
For these visions born of aesthetic flavor (rasa) should be understood as endowed with their specific characteristics;
hereafter, I shall explain those based upon the stable emotional states (sthāyibhāva).
With its pupils slightly dilated and fixed in longing, this affectionate gaze—sweet, with its center blossoming and flooded with tears of joy—is born of the sentiment of love (rati). (BhN 8.56)
A gaze that is moving, filled with laughter, with pupils entering and blinking, slightly contracted, and joyful, is proclaimed as the "laughing" (hāsya) look. BhN 8.57.
With the upper eyelid drooping, the pupil slightly agitated,
and moving slowly, that wretched gaze is prescribed for sorrow.
Rough, steady, and with upturned lids, with pupils fixed and rolling,
and crooked eyebrows— the angry gaze is prescribed for anger.
When the eyebrows are fixed in that manner,
her gaze— arising from enthusiasm, proud, and emitting vitality— remains thus blossomed.
With both eyelids wide open and pupils trembling with fear, the gaze is withdrawn from the center;
such is the gaze possessed of fear in a state of terror.
In disgust, the gaze is contracted into its sockets, darkened, with the pupils closed; it is agitated by the lashes and looks loathsome. (BhN 8.62)
With pupils widely dilated and both eyelids closed, the gaze is even and wide-open;
this "astonished" gaze is prescribed for occasions of wonder.
For these glances should be understood by the wise as being based upon the stable emotions (sthāyibhāva). I shall now fully describe the characteristics of the transitory glances (saṃcāriṇī-dṛṣṭi).
Equal, with equal margins, unwavering, and seeing emptiness;
not grasping at external objects, serene, and empty—this is proclaimed as the "view of emptiness. (BhN 8.65)
With the tips of her eyelashes quivering and her lids not fully closed,
her gaze was dark at the corners, soiled, and her pupils were wide with wonder.
With eyelids withered by fatigue, emaciated, with eyes narrowed,
drooping, and the pupils sunken— such is proclaimed to be the gaze of one who is exhausted.
With the tips of its lashes slightly arched, with the upper lids drooping out of shame,
and with the pupils cast downward through bashfulness— that gaze is indeed possessed of modesty.
That gaze in which the eyelids and lashes are withered, which is slack and moves slowly,
and in which the pupils appear gradually, is known as the "glānā" (withered) gaze.
Slightly moving, steady in part, raised, and extended sideways;
with pupils hidden and startled, the gaze is considered apprehensive.
With eyelids wide with despondency, the corners turned downward, blinking, and with the pupil slightly fixed, the gaze should be made despondent. (BhN 8.71)
The *mukula* (bud-like) gaze is considered to have its eyelashes quivering and closely joined, the upper lids slightly curved like buds, and the pupils opened with ease.
With the tips of the eyelashes contracted and the eyelids likewise contracted,
and with the pupils drawn inward, the gaze is considered "contracted" (kuñcitā).
The gaze with pupils sluggish and eyelids flickering, overwhelmed by heat and scorched, is indeed afflicted with pain. (BhN 8.74)
With eyelids drooping and slightly contracted, looking askance slowly, with the pupils hidden and concealed—the gaze is described as "slanted" (jihmā). BhN 8.75.
That gaze which is sweet, with its corners slightly contracted, accompanied by a knitting of the brows and a smile, and free from other emotional disturbances, is known as *lalitā* (the graceful).
With the eyelids raised by initial thought (vitarka), with the pupils likewise dilated,
and with sustained thought (vicāra) directed downward— this is the gaze characterized by initial thought.
And the gaze has eyelashes half-unfurled, with lids that are half-closed in delight; it possesses the buds of a smile, with pupils slightly rolling. (BhN 8.78)
With pupils that do not remain steady, with a gaze that is wandering and agitated,
and with the center of the eyes wide open and rolling— this is called the "wandering" gaze.
When the two eyelids throb, become fixed, and then fall,
and the gaze has its pupils lost or rolling upward, this is the "disturbed" (viplutā) gaze.
With the corners of the eyes contracted, the lids joined and half-closed, and the pupils repeatedly rolling back,
such a gaze is known as *ākekarā*.
With both eyelids opened wide, fully blossomed, and unblinking,
with its movement unsettled— this is called the "unveiled" (vikośā) gaze.
That gaze whose eyelids are turned upward in terror, whose pupils are trembling, and whose center is dilated with alarm, is declared to be the "terrified" (trastā) look. BhN 8.83.
With a whirling waist, eyes turned toward the corners of the mouth,
and glances with blossoming outer corners, her gaze was like wine in the prime of intoxication.
With the eyelids slightly contracted, the pupils unsettled, and the lashes trembling— such is the gaze of one who is intoxicated.
The gaze that blinks and does not blink, with the pupil slightly revealed,
moving toward the lower part [of the face], is said to belong to the lowest stage of intoxication.
Thus have these thirty-six views been characterized by me; now learn their application, both those born of aesthetic flavor (rasaja) and those that are innate (sahaja). BhN 8.87.
Those born of rasa exist only within the stable [rasas], being perceived as stable;
now hear how the transitory states (vyabhicāriṇyaḥ) are situated among the moving [states]. (BhN 8.88)
The "Empty" gaze is proclaimed for use during reflection and also during paralysis; the "Sullied" gaze is prescribed for despondency and for discoloration.
Śrāntā is prescribed for exhaustion and fatigue, as well as for perspiration; Lalitā likewise for modesty; and Glānā is ordained for epilepsy, disease, and debility.
When there is doubt, the gaze should be known as "doubtful"; when there is a sense of despondency, it is "despondent";
and for the purposes of sleep, dreaming, and pleasure, the gaze is considered to be "half-closed" (mukulā).

The *kuñcita* (contracted) [gaze] is used for envy (*asūyita*), the undesirable (*aniṣṭa*), and the pain of the eyes (*duṣprekṣākṣivyathā*); the *abhitapta* (tormented) [gaze] is for despondency (*nirveda*), as well as for assault (*abhighāta*) and affliction (*abhitāpa*).
The gaze is averted in envy, as well as in dullness and laziness;
it is graced with charm in fortitude and joy; and it is considered speculative in reasoning.

In the presence of delightful things, such as the pleasure of fragrance and touch, the gaze becomes half-closed; likewise, it is wandering in cases of intense emotion, agitation, and confusion. (BhN 8.94)
It is "lost" (*viluptā*) in states such as fickleness, intoxication, suffering, affliction, and death;
it is "squinting" (*ākekarā*) when the object is difficult to perceive or when it is glimpsed at the moment of separation. (BhN 8.95)

The gaze is wide-open (*vikośitā*) in those whose minds are characterized by wakefulness, pride, contempt, and cruelty; it is terrified (*trastā*) in fear, and intoxicated (*madirā*) in states of intoxication. (BhN 8.96)
These thirty-six views have indeed been correctly set forth,
as well as those views born of taste and likewise those born of existence.
"Understand from me as I describe the action of those whose eyebrows are like the arches of a boat:
whirling, turning, falling, moving, and entering. (BhN 8.98)
Turning back, rising up, exiting, and likewise the natural state;
the rotation within the circle of the lids, and the circling of the two pupils—these are recorded as [the movements].
Turning, moving, triangular motion, falling, as well as sagging;
shaking, trembling—these are to be known [as movements]; and entry is internal penetration. (BhN 8.100)
Turning away is called *kaṭākṣa*; rising up is *samudvṛtta*;
going out is said to be *niṣkrāma* or *nirgama*; and that which is born of one's own nature is *prākṛta*.
Now, learn the application of these in the states of rasa:
whirling is for agitation and excitement; exiting is for the heroic and the furious.
In the terrifying [sentiment], both exit and entry should be performed;
likewise, in the comic and the loathsome, entry is desired here.
The *pātana* (falling) gesture should be employed for the sentiment of compassion (*karuṇa*), and the *niṣkrāmaṇa* (exit) for the marvelous (*adbhuta*);
the *prākṛta* (natural) is used for the remaining states, and the *vivartita* (turned) for the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).
This very action, which is based on worldly activity, is established by its own nature;
in this way, one should apply the actions of the stars to the tastes and the dispositions.
Now, in this very context, I shall explain the modes of vision: namely, the even gaze, the downward gaze, the forward gaze, and the side-long gaze. (BhN 8.106)
Looking ahead and looking aside, as well as looking downward, with evenness and gentleness—that which is thus seen is known as "even. (BhN 8.107)
When the pupil is positioned between the eyelashes, forming a triangle and cast askance,
it is known as *anuvṛtta*, which is employed for the contemplation of beauty.
That which is a sudden glance is called *ālokita*;
looking behind is *vilokita*, while looking from the sides is *pralokita*.
Looking upward is to be known as the "upward gaze," and looking downward is the "downward gaze";
such is the method of gazing among these, which is the basis for the aesthetic flavor (rasa) of all things.
Understand now the application of the lids following the formation of the stars:
the opening, the closing, the extended, the contracted, and the even. BhN 8.111.
That which is turned away, quivering, covered, or struck,
as well as the separation of the two lids— this is proclaimed as *unmeṣa*.
The meeting [of the fingers] is the *nimeṣa*; the extended [hand] is the *prasṛta*. The contracted [hand] is the *kuñcita*, while the even [hand] is known as the natural (*svābhāvika*). BhN 8.113.
It is said to be *vivartita* (turned), *samudvṛtta* (elevated), *sphurita* (throbbing), and likewise *spandita* (quivering);
*sthagita* (covered) and *pihita* (concealed), while *āhata* (struck) is *vitāḍita* (beaten).
Now, learn the application of these [eyes] among the sentiments (rasas) and emotional states (bhāvas):
in anger, they should be made to roll, along with the closing and opening of the eyelids.
It is taught that the *prasṛta* (extended) gaze is used for objects of wonder, joy, and the heroic sentiment;
the *kuñcita* (contracted) gaze is used upon seeing something undesirable, or when encountering unpleasant odors, tastes, or tactile sensations.

In the erotic sentiment, it should be performed with evenness; likewise, its manifestation occurs in states of jealousy, as well as in sleep, fainting, wind, heat, smoke, rain, and affliction from collyrium.
In cases of eye disease, it is covered; in the event of injury, it is struck open. Such is the procedure for the pupils and the eyelids according to the nature of the humor.
Learn now the function of this very [forehead] as it follows from its effects:
the raising, the lowering, and the knitting of the eyebrows, which is the clever movement of the brows.
The raising of the eyebrows is sevenfold: contracted, released, and natural; it may be simultaneous or performed one by one. (BhN 8.120)
In this very sequence, there should be a downward-facing descent;
by the upward lifting of the roots of the eyebrows, it is proclaimed as the *bhrukuṭī* (the frown).
When the eyebrows are slightly raised with a sweet, elongated curve through some inhalation, whether on one or both, it is called *kuñcita* due to its gentle bending. (BhN 8.122)
The *recita* arises from the upward lifting of a single eyebrow in a graceful manner;
however, that which is born simultaneously with it is known as the innate (*sahaja*), natural action.
Now I shall fully explain the application of rasa and bhāva in anger, deliberation, sportiveness, playfulness, and likewise in that which is innate. (BhN 8.124)
One should raise a single eyebrow both when hearing and when seeing;
this raising [of the brow] occurs in wonder, joy, and anger, as well as in both [of these states].
A wise person should employ the frown in cases of envy, disgust, laughter, and smelling, as well as in those instances of anger that are characterized by intensity.
One should employ the *catura* [mudrā] in such states as the erotic, the graceful, the gentle, pleasure, touch, and awakening. (BhN 8.127)
And in the conversation between a woman and a man, which consists of various changing states—namely, *moṭṭāyita*, *kuṭṭamita*, *vilāsa*, and *kilakiñcita*— [the following occurs]. (BhN 8.128)
The *nikuñcita* (contracted) gesture should be employed in dance, while the *recita* (extended) gesture is to be used;
the wise one should recognize the *svābhāvika* (natural) gesture as being applied to unmoved (*anāviddha*) emotional states.
Thus has the action of the eyebrows been described; now learn the actions of the nose:
it may be bent, slow, drawn back, accompanied by a breath, or contracted.
The wise have declared that the nose is of six kinds:
natural, bent, repeatedly touching the nostrils, slow, and restrained. BhN 8.131.

The [eye] with the lids drawn back and opened wide, the one with exhalation and inward-drawn breath, the squinted, the contracted, the even, and the natural—these are recorded as the [eight types]. BhN 8.132.
This is indeed the characteristic of the nose; learn its application in the pursuit of women who are possessed by intoxication and trembling. (BhN 8.133)
In exhalation, the nose should be bent down by those who perform the drama;
it is prescribed as bent also during interrupted or faint sobbing and when accompanied by a sigh.
One should employ the "slow" [breathing] during states of lack of dispassion, longing, and anxiety, as well as in grief;
one should employ the "distant" [breathing] during intense odors, and likewise in the Furious and Heroic sentiments.
Likewise, when smelling something desirable or exhaling, one should employ a long exhalation;
and in cases of disgust, envy, and so forth, the nose should be wrinkled.
In the case of objects to be acted upon, experts likewise recognize six natural states:
emaciated, blooming, rolling, trembling, contracted, and even. BhN 8.137.
Six types of swellings have been indicated; their characteristics are now described:
one should know that *kṣāma* is sunken, while *phulla* is fully blossomed. BhN 8.138.
Extended, whirling, and trembling have been described; there may also be throbbing.
Contracted and fully bent are called natural and even.
The characteristics of the cheeks have been declared; now learn their application:
they should be made thin during states of suffering, and indeed full during great joy.
The eyes are full in cases of enthusiasm and pride; they tremble during horripilation;
and they are contracted with bristling hair in response to cold touch, fear, or fever. (BhN 8.141)
In the remaining states, the natural function (gaṇḍakarma) occurs;
these are turning, trembling, emission, and concealment. (BhN 8.142)
The *sandaṣṭaka*, the *samudga*, and the six actions of the lower lip; the *vikūṇita*, the *vivarta*, the *vepana*, and the *kampana* are thus remembered. (BhN 8.143)
Departure is emission; entry is concealment.
The "bitten" (*sandaṣṭaka*) is that which is not bitten by the twice-born [teeth]; the "enclosed" (*samudga*) is natural elevation. (BhN 8.144)
Thus the characteristics of the lips have been declared; now learn their application:
turning away [the face] occurs in cases of envy, pain, contempt, fear, and so forth. (BhN 8.145)
*Trembling* (*kampana*) and *quivering* (*vepana*) occur due to cold, fear, anger, passion, and the like;
likewise, *emission* (*visarga*) occurs in the playful gestures of women, in a sudden startle, and in sexual arousal. (BhN 8.146)
*Vinigūhana* (concealment) is employed in acts of deceit; *sandaṣṭa* (biting) is used in acts of anger; *samudga* (clasping) is for compassion; and *cumbana* (kissing) is for rejoicing. (BhN 8.147)
Thus the actions of the lips have been described; now learn those of the chin:
*kuṭṭana* (grinding), *khaṇḍana* (breaking), *chinna* (cutting), *cukkita* (crunching), and *lehana* (licking) are the five. BhN 8.148.
And here, the chin is observed to be bitten by the action of the teeth;
"gnawing" (kuṭṭana) is the friction of the teeth, while "cracking" (saṃsphoṭa) is repeated breaking. (BhN 8.149)
When it is severed, there is a firm embrace; when it is bitten, there is a falling away at a distance.
Licking with the tongue is *leha*; a slight adhesion would be equal [to the previous]. (BhN 8.150)
When the lower lip is bitten by the teeth, the application for these [persons] is as follows:
for those seized by fear, cold, fever, or anger, there should be a crushing [massage]. (BhN 8.151)
There is an interruption [of the breath] during recitation, study, conversation, and while engaged in eating;
it is also interrupted by disease, fear, cold, physical exertion, weeping, and death. (BhN 8.152)
In yawning, the action is missed; likewise, in licking, the licking is missed.
It is equal in the states of natural disposition, but it is seized in acts of anger.
Thus, from the action of the teeth, lips, and tongue, there arises the movement of the chin:
the shaking, the turning back, the bending away, and the bending toward.
Likewise, *vivṛta* and *udvāhi* are [types of movement]; however, the actions born therein are *vyāvṛtta*, *vinivṛtta*, and *vidhuta*, which is extended obliquely. (BhN 8.155)
The downward-turned face is bent back, the distorted is slightly extended, the open-mouthed has parted lips, and the upturned is indeed raised upward. (BhN 8.156)

Performers should employ [these gestures] for women when they have turned away from malice, and from that which is caused by envy or anger, as well as in cases of contempt, exposure, and the like. (BhN 8.157)
The *vidhuta* (shaken) gesture is used in expressions such as "and indeed in warding off," "it is not so," and the like;
the *nirbhugna* (bent) gesture is likewise to be understood in contexts such as "profound gazing" and so forth. *BhN 8.158*

The *bhugna* (curved) gesture should be employed for those filled with shame; however, that which arises from the very nature of ascetics is used for despondency, longing, anxiety, guidance, and invitation. (BhN 8.159)
It should also be understood as "turned away" (vivṛtta) in cases such as laughter, grief, and fear;
it is used for women's playful gestures, pride, and in expressing disregard. (BhN 8.160)

The wise should likewise employ the particle *nāma* in expressions of anger, as well as [the use of] the same [word], witnesses, subsequent conduct, and whatever is inferred from one's gaze. (BhN 8.161)
The expert, following that [knowledge], should apply the corresponding facial expression;
now, therefore, the coloring of the face is proclaimed to be fourfold.
The natural [expression] is serene, while the passionate and the dark are based on the object [of the emotion].
The natural expression, however, should be performed by relying on the representation of innate disposition.

Performers should maintain a bright facial expression toward neutral and other such sentiments; however, it should be made radiant in the marvelous (*adbhuta*), as well as in the comic (*hāsya*) and the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).
In the sentiments of heroism, fury, and intoxication, as well as in the pathetic, the face becomes red; in the terrible and the loathsome, it becomes dark blue.
In this way, one should employ facial coloration (mukharāga) for the sake of the sentiments (bhāva) and aesthetic flavors (rasa);
for even a performance (abhinaya) that is otherwise well-executed, provided with its primary, secondary, and tertiary limbs (śākhā-aṅga-upāṅga), is rendered auspicious [only through this].
Indeed, one devoid of facial expression does not possess beauty at all;
whereas even a slight physical gesture, when endowed with facial expression, becomes truly effective.
He attains double the beauty, like the moon at night;
even his gestures with the eyes become manifest through various emotions and aesthetic sentiments.
Since drama is established here upon the coloring of the face,
it should proceed just as the eye moves, conjoined with the gaze originating from the face.
In that manner, one should employ facial expression endowed with emotion and rasa;
thus has facial expression, which rests upon emotion and rasa, been described. BhN 8.170.
Henceforth, O twice-born ones, I shall indeed explain the actions of the neck:
it may be level, elevated, depressed, triangular, extended, contracted, or bent.
The neck is bent and turned back in nine ways;
it is even and natural during the practice of meditation and recitation.
The neck is bent when forming an ornament upon the face, it hangs down when serving as a pendant, it is raised when the face is lifted up, and it is held erect when positioned above. (BhN 8.173)
The triangular [hand-gesture] directed toward the side is to be known when one is extremely distressed by a burden on the shoulder;
the *recita*, *vidhuta*, and *bhrānta* [gestures] are used in the *hāva* emotion and in the *mathana* dance.
When held at the head, whether contracted or uncontracted, it serves for protecting the throat;
when bent back and drawn away, it is used for strangling, pulling the hair, and looking upward.
The *valitā* (twisted) glance occurs when one turns the face toward the side; it is used for looking with various movements of the neck.
The *nivṛtā* (turned back) glance occurs when one has turned away from the front, while the *abhimukhī* (facing forward) occurs when one is directed toward one's own position and so forth.
Thus, for the purpose of worldly expression, all actions of the neck are performed in many ways through various movements of the neck, for they indeed follow the movements of the head. (BhN 8.177)
The action of the head proceeds from the action of the neck;
this has been declared as the characteristic based on the minor limbs (*upāṅga*) of the head.
Now, learn from me as I speak of the remaining actions of the limbs.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Rules for the Minor Limbs" (*upāṅgavidhāna*), in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
Now begins the ninth chapter:
"In this manner, [the expressions] arising from the head, eyes, eyebrows, nose, lips, and cheeks..."
I have thus declared the characteristics of the actions associated with the secondary limbs.
I shall now correctly explain the characteristics and the application [of the marks] starting from the hands, the flanks, the belly, the hips, the shanks, the thighs, and the feet. BhN 9.2.
I shall now declare the function of the hands and other limbs that impels the dance; listen as I speak of how and what is to be represented through them. BhN 9.3.
The *patāka*, the *tripatāka*, as well as the *kartarīmukha*,
the *ardhacandra*, the *arāla*, and likewise the *śukatuṇḍa*.
The fist (muṣṭi), the one called the peak (śikhara), the wood-apple (kapittha), the scissor-mouth (khaṭakāmukha),
the needle-mouth (sūcyāsya), the lotus-bud (padmakośa), and likewise the serpent-head (sarpaśīrṣaka).
The *mṛgaśīrṣa* is to be known as the last [of the hand gestures], according to those who employ the *hastābhinaya*;
likewise, there are the *kāṅgulaka*, the *alapaṃkaja*, the *catuḥ*, and the *bhramara*.
The Haṃsāsya, the Haṃsapakṣa, the Sandaṃśa, the Mukula,
the Ūrṇanābha, and the Tāmracūḍa— these twenty-four [mudrās] have been proclaimed.
"Understand from me as I speak those that are unjoined and those that are joined:
the añjali, the kapota, the karkaṭa, and likewise the svastika."
The Khaṭakā, the Vardhamāna, the Utsaṅga, and likewise the Niṣadha;
the Dola, the Puṣpapuṭa, and also the Makara.
The Gajadanta, the Avahittha, and likewise the Vardhamāna—
these thirteen types of joined hands have been described by me.
Now, listen as I describe the *nṛttahasta* hand gestures, both those directed downwards and upwards:
they are known to be the *caturasra*, the *udvṛtta*, and likewise the *talamukha*.
The *svastika*, the *viprakīrṇa*, the *arāla*, the *khaṭakāmukha*, the *āviddha*, the *vakra*, the *sūcyāsya*, the *recita*, and the *ardharecita*. (BhN 9.12)
The palms should be known as either turned upward or downward, and likewise the fingers;
the buttocks and the hair-ties should be understood in the same manner.
The *karihasta* and likewise the *latākhya*, as well as the *pakṣavañcita* and the *pakṣapradyotaka*, have been fully described. (BhN 9.14)
One should know the Garuḍa-wing and likewise the Haṃsa-wing;
also the upward-circling and the side-circling.
The two shoulder-encirclers (uromaṇḍalinau), the chest-and-side-half-encirclers (uraḥpārśvārdhamaṇḍalau),
the fist-crossed (muṣṭikasvastikau), and the lotus-bud (nalinīpadmakośakau).
The *alapa*, *padma*, *ulbaṇa*, *lalita*, and *valita*—these seventy-six hand gestures have indeed been declared by me according to their names. (BhN 9.17)
Learn now their characteristics and their functions:
when all the fingers are extended and straight, and the thumb is likewise bent inward, that is known as the *patāka* (banner) mudrā. (BhN 9.18)

When a blow is struck, when there is an impulse to strike, in joy, and even in pride, those who know [the signs] should understand that the letter "A" has arisen in the region of the forehead. (BhN 9.19)
In representing showers of fire and the falling of a rain of flowers, the hands should be joined together with the fingers slightly spread and moving. (BhN 9.20)

That which is fashioned from earth—consisting of young shoots, flowers, offerings, and grasses, by means of removing [dust] with a svastika-shaped tool—that substance is also to be described. (BhN 9.21)
Because it causes the destruction of the auspicious cross (svastika), it should instead be performed with the face turned downwards;
it should be protected as both closed and open, concealed, dense, and guarded.
And with the fingers of this very [hand], moving up and down while facing downward,
one should produce the agitation caused by the force of wind and waves at the shore, as well as a torrential flood.
One should express encouragement extensively, as well as the striking of large, long lotuses by the multitude,
and the gesture of raising the wings through the performance of the *recaka* maneuver.
But when it stands on its rubbed base, it is washed, crushed, and wiped; one should likewise represent the holding of the stone and the opening [of the vessel]. (BhN 9.25)
In this manner, this hand-gesture should be employed in the dramatic representation of men and women;
it is to be performed by the actors using both hands in the *patākā* (flag) position.
There are those called the ten-fold, the hundred-fold, and likewise the thousand-fold;
hereafter I shall explain the characteristics of the *tripatāka* [hand gesture].
When, however, the ring finger of the *patāka* [mudrā] is bent, it should be known as the *tripatāka*; now learn its ritual application.
Invocation, descent, dismissal, restraint, and entry;
raising up, prostration, demonstration, and various utterances.
The touching of auspicious objects, as well as placing them upon the head, the wearing of turbans and crowns, and the covering of the nose, mouth, and ears. BhN 9.30.
And with this very [hand], by means of two fingers moving downward, upward, and shaking, one should produce the illusions of a swift wind, a stream, a serpent, a bee, and so forth. (BhN 9.31)
Wiping away tears, applying a forehead mark with yellow pigment (*rocanā*), touching the three folds of the neck, and touching the *anāmikā* finger—these are the actions of an *alakā*. (BhN 9.32)
The *svastika* and *tripatāka* hand gestures are to be used when bowing at the feet of one's gurus;
however, in the case of witnessing a wedding, they should be performed in a loosened and moving position.
When appearing before a king, the two hands should be joined with their tips touching each other;
when appearing before a planet, they should be bound in a horizontal *svastika* gesture.
Upon seeing an ascetic, the two hands should be raised and turned away;
but upon seeing a giver of boons, they should be made to face one another.
When observing the submarine fire, a battle, or sea-monsters, the two [hands] should be placed facing forward at the tip of the mouth, one turned upward and the other downward.
In drama, those skilled in dramatic art employ this very [expression] for gestures, for the leaping waves of monkeys, for the wind, and for women. (BhN 9.37)
When observing the crescent moon, the thumb should be extended forward;
however, when traveling, it should be turned away from the person by those who employ it.
When the hand is in the *tripatāka* position and the index finger is behind the middle finger for the purpose of looking back, it is then called *kartarīmukha*.
On the path, one should perform the movements for arranging the feet and the stage of beautification while facing downwards;
however, one should face upwards when performing the *daṣṭa*, *śṛṅga*, and *lekhya* gestures.

One should perform the *patana*, *maraṇa*, *vyatikrama*, *parivṛtti*, and *vitarkita* [mantras], as well as the *nyasta*, using the tip of the fingers of the *kartarī* [mudrā] with its [fingers] bent and opened. BhN 9.41.
Whether joined together or separate, it is employed by those who know it upon the humps of the ruru-deer,
the yak, the buffalo, the celestial elephant, the bull, the city-gate, and the mountain peaks.
That hand whose fingers, together with the thumb, are bent like a bow is to be known as the *ardhacandra* (half-moon); its ritual application shall now be described.
By this [comparison], the young trees, the crescent moon, the water-jars, and the bracelets are described as being emaciated, distressed,
middling, and stout respectively.

The expressive application (*abhinaya-yoga*) for women’s girdles, hips, waists, faces, forehead-ornaments, earrings, and so forth, should be performed with the *ardhacandra* [hand gesture]. (BhN 9.45)
In the *arāla* hand gesture, the first finger (the index) should be bent like a bow, the thumb likewise curved, and the remaining fingers separated, turned upward, and curled. BhN 9.46.
By this [method], the qualities of courage, magnanimity, heroism, fortitude, beauty, and divine profundity,
as well as benedictions and other such states designated as "beneficial," should be cultivated.
Furthermore, by this [means], women should perform the gathering and arranging of their hair, as well as the detailed inspection of all their limbs and themselves. (BhN 9.48)
The yoga of the marriage of curiosity, the union by circumambulation alone, and the yogas of the svastika with the tips of the fingers, all performed in a circular manner. BhN 9.49.
One should perform a circumambulation in a circular path and include a great multitude of people;
furthermore, whatever objects are arranged upon the surface of the ground should be represented there.

This [breath] is auspicious for summoning, for warding off and creating, for speaking in many voices, for removing sweat, and for smelling fragrances, whether they be auspicious or inauspicious. (BhN 9.51)
However, those actions previously described as being performed with the *tripatāka* hand may be correctly employed by women when there is a need for haste.
When the ring finger of the *arāla* hand is curved, that hand is called the *śukatuṇḍa*; now learn its function.
By this [method], O Noble Lady, one should address the actor with "Neither I, nor you, nor the task exists," and with a contemptuous "Shame! during the invocation and the dismissal. (BhN 9.54)
That hand whose fingers are positioned with their tips toward the center of the palm,
and over which the thumb is placed, is designated as a "fist" (muṣṭi).
This [knowledge] is for striking, exertion, exiting, and likewise for pressing; as well as for massaging, and for grasping swords, clubs, spears, and staffs.
But when the thumb is raised from this very fist, that hand should then be known by practitioners as the *śikhara* (peak) mudrā. (BhN 9.57)

[The ability to perform] the discharge of rays, goads, hooks, bows, spears, and javelins; as well as the coloring of the lower lip and feet, and the lifting up of the forehead-mark (tilaka). BhN 9.58.
When the index finger of this very same [mudrā] called Śikhara is bent and pressed by the thumb,
it is then known as Kapittha.
The sword, bow, discus, tomara-weapon, spear, mace, javelin, thunderbolt, and arrow—these weapons are to be represented through gesture; however, truth and what is beneficial must be practiced.
But when the ring finger and the little finger are raised and bent,
this very same *kapittha* [mudrā] then becomes the *khaṭakāmukha*.
Sacrificial offering, oblation, an umbrella, drawing [a chariot], fanning, holding a mirror, cutting, and likewise grinding; BhN 9.62.
Holding a long staff, wearing pearl necklaces,
garlands of flowers, and likewise trailing the ends of one's garments.
The gathering of black flowers like the arrows of Manmatha serves as the goad;
and the mere sight of women, with their drawing of ropes and hooks, is the task to be performed.
When the index finger is extended upon the hand known as *khaṭaka*,
it should then be recognized by practitioners as the hand called *sūcīmukha*.
I shall describe its various applications in brief:
when the forefinger is directed upward, turned downward, moved, shaken, yawned, raised, or wavered.
The wheel, the lightning-banner, the clusters of blossoms, the ear-ornaments,
those with crooked movements— all these, as well as the words of praise, are to be described.
The young snakes, the strength of the bridegroom, the lamps, the creepers,
and the crests of the peacocks are to be represented by the upward-swinging movement of the *paripatana* and *navakramaṇḍala*.
In the practice of facial expressions, the face should be contracted and yawned when forming speech;
furthermore, it should be raised upward for the eyes, the nose, and the single-staffed pole;
and again, it should be bent down for fanged creatures, in accordance with the configuration of the mouth.
Furthermore, the grasping of all [planets] situated within the mandala is likewise for the world;
it occurs when the end of the day has arrived, during the first part of the night, during a long day, and during the day itself.

During the practice of listening, when there is a distortion or a yawning during the occasion of forming sentences, one should apply the "meti" and "vadeti" [gestures], which are extended, trembling, and turned upward. BhN 9.71.

The enactment [of this] should be performed through trembling, the appearance of tears, and the manifestation of perspiration, as well as by means of the hair, earrings, armlets, and the region of the cheeks. BhN 9.72.
In pride, at the thought "I am," likewise upon seeing an enemy, in anger, in the inquiry "Who is this?", and also when there is an itch in the ear or an eye; BhN 9.73.
In conjunction, they should be joined; in separation, they should be detached.
In a quarrel, they should be positioned as a svastika with one pressing upon the other; in binding, they should be mutually compressed.

But with two [hands], on one's own side to the right, one should employ the *ninada* and *niśāvasāna* [techniques] using the hands facing each other and turned away from each other, with the fingers separated.
Furthermore, its tip should be whirled upon stone wheels and mechanical rocks;
likewise, during the act of grinding, it must always be held with the face turned downwards.
In the form of Śambhu, she should be made with her face downward, clinging to the surface of the forehead;
even for Śakra, she should be made face-upward by those who know [the tradition], and positioned obliquely.
One should always display the full orb of the moon with two [fingers]; it should be joined at the forehead of Śakra and placed in a supine position. BhN 9.78.
By being rotated in a circular manner, one should display the mandala of the moon;
and on the forehead of Śakra, there is also the fierce, upward-facing [eye] of Hara.
When the fingers are extended and the thumbs are bent, with their tips held upward and not touching, that is the *padmakośaka* [mudrā].
When seizing bilva and kapittha fruits, women show their breasts;
indeed, when seizing meat, they appear with their tips bent inward.
One should offer many citron seeds and pieces of meat during the worship of the gods and the presentation of ritual oblations (*bali*); likewise, when giving the *sāgra-piṇḍa*,
one should perform the scattering of flowers with the hand shaped like a lotus bud.
With the hands separated at the wrists, with fingers moving slightly apart,
and turned outward, one should perform the graceful gesture of blossoming lotuses and water lilies.
When all the fingers together with the thumb are joined,
and likewise the palm is concave, that is the *sarpaśiras* (serpent-head) hand.
This [mudrā] is to be employed for the offering of water, for sprinkling water upon the two arms,
for clapping, and for striking the frontal globes of elephants and similar acts.
The joining of all the fingers with their tips pointing downward,
while the little finger and the thumb are turned upward, constitutes the *mṛgaśīrṣaka* mudrā.

In this context, at the present time, today, during the arousal of power, at nightfall, during the wiping away of perspiration, and during the act of *kuṭṭamita*, one should be in a state of movement. (BhN 9.87)

When the middle finger is positioned between the fire-triad (the thumb and ring finger), the index finger is joined with the thumb, the ring finger is bent, and the little finger is pointing upward; [this is the *kāṅgula* mudrā]. (BhN 9.88)
By this [method], various kinds of light young fruits produced by anger should be made to fall through the casting of fingers at a woman's words.

One should display emeralds, lapis lazuli, and the like, as well as flowers; those skilled in the application [of such arts] should adopt the "swan's gait" (marālapada) in their performances. BhN 9.90.
Indeed, he whose fingers are curled upon the palm and then scattered toward the sides is one who possesses the *alapa* hand-gesture.
In the context of negation, to whom does "yours" apply within these statements of emptiness? Furthermore, by this [negation], women must be introduced as the subject.
Where three fingers are extended and likewise the little finger is raised,
with the thumb positioned in their midst— that hand is known as catura.
One should employ speech that is governed by policy and discipline, measured and gentle, directed toward the welfare of children, the sick, and the truthful,
and which is coherent, beneficial, true, and conducive to tranquility.
With one or two hands, having formed some kind of mudrā, he reflects upon his own conduct as it was previously examined and analyzed, and he feels ashamed. (BhN 9.95)
The comparison to the eyes, the description of the lotus-petal form, and the designation of the deer-ear—
all these one should perform by means of the *saṃyutakaraṇa* movement alone.
Playfulness, delight, desire, memory, intelligence, discernment, forbearance, nourishment, mere ideation, affection, deliberation, association, and purity; BhN 9.97.
Cleverness, sweetness, courtesy, gentleness, happiness, and good character;
inquiry, conversation, logic, dress, soft grassy ground, and a little [food]. BhN 9.98.
One who is skillful should thus employ wealth and non-wealth, pleasure and its absence, virtues and faults, youth, home, wife, and likewise various castes.
One should produce white with the head [of the hand], red and yellow with the palm,
blue with the back of the hand, and the various colors with the four fingers.
In the *bhramara* hand gesture, the middle finger and thumb form a pincer, the index finger is bent, and the other two fingers are raised and spread apart. (BhN 9.101)

The method for gathering flowers— such as the lotus (*padma*), the blue lotus (*utpala*), the white water lily (*kumuda*), and others with long stalks— and the fashioning of ear-ornaments (*karṇapūra*) should be performed.
In cases such as reprimanding, one should perform the *vicyuta* and *saśabda* types; likewise, in childish chatter, in haste, in keeping time (*tāla*), and in inspiring confidence. BhN 9.103.
The index, middle, and thumb fingers should be held close together like the three fires; these belong to Haṃsavaktra, while the remaining two fingers are extended.
In cases involving smoothness, smallness, looseness, lightness, insubstantiality, and the application of softness,
a specific mode of representation (abhinaya) should be performed with the tips of the fingers slightly trembling.
The three fingers [of the hand] are extended evenly and likewise the little finger is raised;
the thumb is also bent—this is known as the *haṃsapakṣa* (swan-wing) mudrā.

And this [water] should be used for the water-offering (nivāpa), when water is to be given at the side of the cheek, and for the purposes of receiving gifts, sipping water (ācamana), and eating for the Brahmins. (BhN 9.107)
It is to be employed for embracing, for the appearance of great firmness, for causing horripilation, for the purpose of anointing with ointments upon touch, and indeed for massaging. (BhN 9.108)
Furthermore, specific gestures of coquetry (*vibhrama*) should be performed by women with their hands placed between the breasts,
according to the sentiment (*rasa*), as well as during moments of distress or when holding the chin.

When the thumb and index finger form a pincer-like grip as they would in the *arāla* [hand gesture], situated in the middle of the hollowed palm, that is known as the *sandaṃśa* (pincer) gesture. // BhN 9.110 //

The *sandaṃśa* (tongs) should be known as threefold: namely, the *agraja* (foremost), the *mukhaja* (mouth-born), and the *pārśvagata* (situated on the side), all of which are augmented by rasa and bhāva.
The forceps with a pointed tip is used for gathering and stringing flowers, for grasping grass, leaves, hair, and thread,
and for seizing and extracting splinters or bone fragments.

Plucking a flower from its stalk, filling a wick or a probe with [substances], and the utterance of the word "Fie! in anger—these are the functions of the *mukhasandamśa* (the mouth-tongs). BhN 9.113.
In the wearing of the sacred thread, in piercing, in qualities, in fine targets for arrows,
in yoga, in meditation, and in small tasks, one should indeed employ the combined fingers.
And when speaking words that are charming, contemptuous, or characterized by the fault of envy, the *pārśvasandaṃśa* gesture is employed with the left hand,
its fingertips slightly turned away.
Women should perform the coloring of painted eyes, the fashioning of coral ornaments, and likewise the pressing of lac-dye.
When the fingers are brought together and joined so that their tips meet and point upward like the beak of a swan, that is indeed the *mukula* hand gesture.
In the worship of the gods, in making offerings, and likewise in the form of the lotus, water-lily, and night-lily,
as well as in kissing a courtesan, one should employ the *vikutsita* and the *viprakīrṇa* [mudrās].
This [mudrā] should be employed by those who know it when counting food or gold, when closing the face, when giving gifts quickly, and likewise when flowers are in bud. (BhN 9.119)
When the fingers of the lotus-bud hand are contracted,
it should be known as the Ūrṇanābha mudrā, used in cases such as the theft of hair or the seizing of spirits.
Likewise, there is mimetic representation in scratching the head, in the diagnosis of leprosy,
in encounters with lions and tigers, and similarly in the grasping of a sacrificial grass mat.
The middle finger and the thumb should form a pincer, the forefinger should be bent,
and the remaining fingers of the *tāmracūlaka* hand should be placed flat upon the palm.
It should be executed with a release and accompanied by sound in cases such as rebuking;
likewise, it is used for the *tāla* beat, for inspiring confidence, and for gestures signifying speed.
Likewise, in the case of calling out to a child, this very hand-gesture should be performed during the divisions of time known as *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, *nimeṣa*, and *kṣaṇa*.
Alternatively, when the fingers are joined, curved, with the thumbs pressing upon them from above,
and the little fingers extended, this hand gesture is known as the *tāmracūḍa*.
One may join a hundred, a thousand, or even a hundred thousand [fingers] with a single hand;
likewise, one may swiftly discharge sparks and droplets from the fingers. (BhN 9.126)
O best of the twice-born, these hands have indeed been described by me as unjoined; therefore, listen now as I speak of the hands when they are joined. BhN 9.127.
When the two hands, with their palms joined together, are brought into close contact, it is known as the añjali;
it is used for saluting deities, teachers, and friends. (BhN 9.128)
Furthermore, his [the yogin’s] three locations are the chest, the mouth, and likewise the head.
He resides in the head of the deities, in the mouth of the gurus, and in the chest of friends; for women, however, he is not fixed.
When both hands are joined together by their sides with the palms facing each other, it is called the *kapotaka* hand; now learn its application.

This [gesture], with the hands placed upon the chest and slightly trembling, should be performed by women when accepting discipline, when prostrating, when addressing a teacher, and in the presence of cold or fear. (BhN 9.131)

This very [particle] is used when something is being rubbed with a finger, in expressions of exhaustion, to indicate "only this much," and in the sense of "there is nothing more to be done now. (BhN 9.132)
That hand whose fingers are indeed interlaced with one another should be known as the *karkaṭa* (crab) hand; its application will now be described.

This [mudrā] should be employed by those who know the true meaning for crushing the limbs of Madana, for yawning upon waking from sleep, for the enlargement of the body, for holding the jaw, and for seizing the conch shell. BhN 9.134.
When the two *avarāla* hands are placed at the wrists, joined by a woman,
turned upward, and positioned on the left side, it is proclaimed as the *svastika*.

Through the manifestation of the Svastika transformation, the quarters, the clouds, the sky, the forest, the oceans, the seasons, the earth, and likewise a vast flood would be represented on stage. (BhN 9.136)
The *khaṭaka* placed upon the *khaṭaka* forms the *khaṭakāvardhamānaka*;
it should be employed for amorous gestures as well as for making salutations. Others [variations] should be used with lotus flowers, palm-leaf fans, and for holding parasols. Thus [it is said].
When the two hands are curved and inverted, they are called *vardhamānaka*; when turned upward, they are known as the *utsaṅga* hand, used for the perception of touch.
It may also arise from being squeezed, from the bristling of body hair due to indignation, from being pressed again, or from the jealousy of women. (BhN 9.140)
When one clenches the fist like a *kapittha* fruit,
that hand should then be known by the name "Niṣadha."
Gathering, grasping, and retention; the pledge, and truthful speech;
in brief, that which is condensed should be indicated by one who is pressed.
When the Śikhara hand is pressed by the Mṛgaśīrṣa [hand], it should be known as Niṣadha; it is employed when one is afflicted by fear.
Having grasped the right arm within the hollow of the left hand,
one should likewise place the left [hand] within the hollow of the right.
And that right hand should be properly formed into a fist;
this is the Niṣadha hand—now learn its ritual application.
By this [same method], steadfastness, intoxication with pride, elegance, eagerness, the arrogance of valor,
self-conceit, firmness, paralysis, stability, and so forth are to be portrayed.
One should know that the one called Niṣadha consists of two swan-wings turned away from each other;
it is to be employed for striking against lattice windows and the like.
When the two shoulders are relaxed and released, and the two flags (arms) are hanging down,
that posture in the performance is designated as the *dola*.

The application of *abhinaya* (acting) should be employed in cases of agitation, despondency, fainting, or the impact of intoxication; likewise in states of non-excitement, when overwhelmed by disease, or when wounded by a weapon. (BhN 9.149)
That which is called *sarpaśiras* has its fingers held close together;
when the second [hand] is joined to its side, it is known as *puṣpapuṭa*.
By means of this [instrument], various things resembling grain, fruit, and flowers are prepared;
they are to be grasped and brought forward, as well as for the drawing in and removal of water.
When the two hands are like banners, with the thumbs pointing upward and the palms facing downward, placed one above the other, then that is the *makara* hand-gesture.
The depiction of lions, tigers, elephants, crocodiles, makaras, and fish,
as well as other flesh-eating creatures, should be represented according to their respective characteristics.
When the two hands, resembling the heads of serpents, rest upon the elbows, that is to be known as the Gajadanta (Elephant-tusk) mudrā; now learn its ritual application.
And likewise during the wedding of a bride and groom, during an extremely heavy exertion, when grasping a pillar, and also when uprooting a mountain rock. BhN 9.155.
Having placed the hands like parrot-beaks, slightly bent toward the chest,
and slowly turned downward with the palms facing inward, that is known as the avahittha [mudrā].
When there is weakness, sighing, the appearance of emaciation in the limbs,
and longing, those who know [the art] should employ the application of dramatic representation (abhinaya).
When the hand is closed like a bud and encircled by the thumb like a wood-apple, it should be known as the *vardhamāna*; now learn its application.
Gathering, grasping, retention, the pledge, and truthful speech—
in brief, when one is pressed, one should act with conciseness.

The *haṃsapakṣa* (swan-wing) should indeed be known as the *vardhamāna* (increasing); with its two outer ends facing away from each other, it is to be employed for opening lattices, windows, and the like.
For these have been described in brief as being of two kinds: those that are unconnected and those that are connected.
However, those which serve as models for performance here must also be established according to their meaning in other contexts.
Having recognized [the object] again by its shape, movement, marks, and genus,
the wise should themselves perform hand gestures after due deliberation.
In drama, there is no meaning regarding the representation that is not conveyed by the hand;
whatever form is seen [in it], it has been repeatedly practiced as being composed of that very thing.
Furthermore, whatever other worldly gestures (karas) are connected with meaning in this world should be employed at will, according to the movements of rasa and bhāva.
Having considered the place, the time, the application, and the appropriateness of the meaning,
these hand gestures (hasta) should indeed be employed, especially for men and women.
Indeed, I shall fully describe all the actions belonging to every hand, which are produced by rasa and bhāva.
Elevation, as well as attraction and likewise depression, encompassing, restraint, summoning, and even impelling; BhN 9.167.
Union and separation, as well as protection and liberation; likewise, distraction and shaking, as well as emission and threatening. (BhN 9.168)
Cutting, splitting, bursting, crushing, and likewise beating—these are to be understood by those who know as the actions directed against the hands. (BhN 9.169)
The palm-sweep (hastapracāra) is of three kinds, based on the principles of dramatic art (nāṭyatattva): the upward-facing, the sideways-facing, and likewise the downward-facing.
All movements of the hands and the expressions of the eyes, eyebrows, and face should be made manifest by the wise according to the rules during their performance.
Having carefully considered the instrument, the action, the position, the logic of the movement, and the execution,
one should perform [the dance] through hand gestures by those who know them, in accordance with worldly convention.
For the superior [type of person], the lines should extend to the forehead;
for the middling, they should reach the chest; and for the inferior, they should go downward.

In the superior [mudrās], the hands should have very little movement; in the middling ones, they move moderately; and in the inferior ones, they should be scattered about by the performers. (BhN 9.174)

The hands of those who are superior or middling should be depicted as characterized by the [auspicious] marks; even those of the lowest status may be shown with hands that rely on worldly activities for their livelihood.
Alternatively, having encountered a different application and a different time,
the hands should either be employed by the wise with their positions reversed, or not at all.
When one is despondent, fainted, terrified, afflicted by loathing or grief, weary, dreaming, agitated, motionless, drowsy, or dull-witted; BhN 9.177.
When one is seized by disease, afflicted by old age, tormented by fear, overwhelmed by cold, intoxicated, heedless, insane, or established in contemplation and austerity; BhN 9.178.
When struck by a rain of snow, when bound, when floating upon water, when dreaming, when bewildered, and likewise when the nose-tip is pressed; BhN 9.179.

One should not employ gesticulation with the hands; rather, one should practice the gathering of sentient beings, as well as various modulations of voice endowed with the flavors of diverse existences.
Where both hands are separated, one should perform the expressive indication (*abhinaya*) of the speaker through various glances and looks, using pauses that reveal the meaning.
The movement of the limbs, which serves as the basis for both dramatic dance (nāṭya) and pure dance (nṛtta), is threefold: upward-facing, lateral, and downward-facing. (BhN 9.182)
Upright, circular, triangular, stationary, and facing downwards:
these are the five types of hand gestures employed in dramatic dance (nāṭya) and classical dance (nṛtta).
Thus should these hands be understood when they do not rely on dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*);
hereafter, I shall explain the hands based on dance (*nṛtta*).
Positioned eight finger-breadths from the chest, facing forward with palms turned outward,
and having equal elbows and shoulders, these are proclaimed as the *caturasra* (square) hands.
The two hands, formed like the wings of a swan and turned outward like a palm-leaf fan, are to be known as *udvṛtta*; alternatively, they are called *tālavṛntaka*.
When the two hands are held square and formed like the wings of a swan,
positioned sideways and facing one another, they are to be known as the *tālamukha* (palm-faced) mudrā.

When those same two [hands] are positioned at the ends of the wrists in the form of a svastika, they are renowned as *svastikas*; when they are displaced and scattered apart, they are *viprakīrṇakas*.
The *padmakośa* gestures have their palms facing upward and are shaped like the buds of lotuses;
they are also known as *arāla-khaṭaka* and *arāla-khaṭakāmukha*.
Likewise, when both hands are curved and extended as far as the wrists, they should always be known by practitioners as the *arāla-khaṭaka* and the *khaṭaka*. (BhN 9.190)
When the hands are curved and rotated by means of the forearms, shoulders, and elbows,
with the palms turned away from the other limb, they are to be known as *āviddhavakra* (twisted-curved).
When both hands have the fingers and thumbs shaped like the heads of serpents and their mouths are extended sideways, they are then known as the "needle-mouthed" (sūcīmukha) mudrās.
When the two hands are positioned like the heads of serpents in the svastika posture,
with the thumbs extended toward the center, they are then to be known as the *sūcīmukha* (needle-mouth) mudrās.
The *recita* hands should also be understood as being like the wings of a swan, moving rapidly;
when they are extended with their palms turned upward, they are designated as *recita*.
The left [hand] should be square-shaped and the right hand extended;
these two are to be known by those who know the reality of dance as the *dhara* and *recita* gestures.
When the elbows and shoulders are bent and the hands are formed into the *tripatāka* gesture, these two, when turned slightly sideways, are known as the *uttanavañcita*.
The two *patāka* hands released from the wrist-joint are known as the *pallava*;
those emerging from the tops of the arms are celebrated as the *nitamba*.
When the two [hands] emerge from the region of the hair and rise up at the sides,
these should be known as the *keśabandha* (hair-binding) gestures, according to the consensus of Karavīra and Ācārya.
When the two hands are extended horizontally and likewise positioned at the sides,
they are to be known as the *latā* (creeper) hands in the context of dramatic gesture (*nṛttābhinaya*).
When the *latāhasta* is raised and moved from side to side,
while the other hand is a *tripatāka* at the ear, it is proclaimed as the *karihasta*.
When the two hands have their tips resting on the hips and form the *tripatāka* gesture, they are then to be known by practitioners as *pakṣavañcita*.

When those same two are turned over, they are known as the "illuminators of the wings" (pakṣapradyotaka); when their palms face downward and are thrust upward, they are to be understood as the "garuḍa-wings" (garuḍapakṣaka).
The hands formed into the shape of swan’s wings, rotated and turned outward,
with the arms likewise extended, are known as the *daṇḍapakṣa* (staff-wing) gesture.
The two hands are called *ūrdhvamaṇḍalinau* because they are turned toward the upper region;
those same two, when placed at the sides, are known as *pārśvamaṇḍalinau*.
One [hand] should be wrapped around and the second unwrapped;
when rotated in the region of the chest, they are known as the *uraḥmaṇḍalī* gestures.
From the sequence of whirling the chest, which is made formidable by the movement of the forearms,
the *pārśvāvarta*, the *urastaḥ*, and the *pārśvārdhamaṇḍala* are to be understood.
When the two hands, from the wrist down, are both bent and extended, they are known as *khaṭaka*; when they are likewise positioned, they are then called *muṣṭika-svastika*.
When the two hands are turned away and then turned back again like the buds of a lotus, they should be known by practitioners as the *nalini-padma-kośa* (lotus-bud) mudrās.
Having formed the tips of the hands so that they are entwined like young shoots,
the two [hands] should be extended upwards, turned, and made prominent.
When the two graceful sprouts reach the region of the head, they are known as *lalita*;
when they extend to the *karpūra* and *svastika* positions, they are called *latākhya* and *valita*.

However, the *nṛttahasta* (dancing hand) should be employed specifically for the instrument, as well as by performers in the expressive representation (*abhinaya*) of objects using the *patākā* (banner) hand. (BhN 9.211)
Furthermore, there may be a confusion among them due to their application according to the requirements of the meaning;
however, in this context of dance (nṛtta) within drama (nāṭya), the designations are determined by the predominance of the hand movements (karas).
Dancing hand gestures (nṛttahasta) are proclaimed to be both separated and joined;
hereafter, I shall explain the hands based on their technical application (karaṇa).
Those who instruct on dramatic hand gestures (nāṭyahasta) must diligently apply all hands according to the fourfold system of execution (karaṇa). BhN 9.214.
One [type] is unwound, another is wound upward;
the third is turned away, and the fourth is turned around. (BhN 9.215)
When the fingers, beginning with the index finger,
are wrapped around in sequence by the interior [of the hand], that is called the *āveṣṭita* (encircled) formation.
O Brahmins, when the fingers beginning with the index finger are uncoiled outwardly in succession, that mudrā is called *udveṣṭita*.
When the fingers, beginning with the little finger, are rotated inwardly in their proper sequence,
that mudrā is called Vyāvartita.
O Brahmins, when the fingers, beginning with the little finger, are rotated outward in sequence, that mudrā is called *parivartita*. BhN 9.219.

In dance, in the application of dramatic gesture, or in the use of hand movements based on circular motions, one should employ the *karaṇas* (hand postures) in conjunction with the face, eyebrows, and eyes. BhN 9.220.
For it may be positioned horizontally, upwards, or downwards; it may be bent, cast away, moving in a circle, in the form of a svastika, or following behind.

"Twisted" and "extended"—these are indeed remembered as the varieties belonging to the arms; they should always be understood by practitioners of dance as being included within the *karaṇas*. (BhN 9.222)
O brahmins, the procedure for the formation of the hands has been declared by me in brief;
hereafter, I shall explain the operations of the heart, the abdomen, and the sides.
Bent, then straightened, as well as trembling,
raised up, and level— thus the chest is said to be of five kinds.
One should recognize that chest as being sunken, with a raised back, shoulders drooping, slack in some places, and bent; now learn of its medical treatment.
In cases of agitation, despair, fainting, grief, fear, disease, or a heart-thorn,
the rite should be performed with cold-scented water mixed with parched grain (lāja), as required by the purpose.
It is stiff, with a sunken back, drooping shoulders, and a protruding chest; indeed, this is its nature—now learn of its function as well. (BhN 9.227)
One should apply [the practice] toward arrogance, grasping at pride, looking with wonder, and speaking words of truth;
and toward the conceited speech "I am," as well as the swelling of pride.
[In the case of long sighing, yawning, stretching, and likewise in the *bibboka* of women, that should be recognized by practitioners. // BhN 9.229 //
When the chest is made to vibrate by means of upward thrusts performed without interruption,
that is to be recognized as the *ura* (chest) movement by practitioners of drama.

In the applications of dramatic performance (nāṭya-yoga), the chest is employed for various emotional states occurring in objects afflicted by laughter, weeping, agitation, fear, exhaustion, disease, and pain.
In laughter and weeping, in action, in fatigue, in fear,
and likewise in sighing and gasping, as well as in hiccup and pain, those skilled in drama [should employ it] according to the requirements of the meaning.
The chest should be known by practitioners as being raised and directed upwards;
its state of long exhalation is observed in the world during actions such as yawning.
When all the limbs are performed with grace and formed into a square posture,
it is known as the *saman* chest, which is healthy and endowed with elegance.
Thus has the correct differentiation of the tastes been explained by me;
hereafter, I shall describe the characteristics of the two sides.
Bent, raised, extended, turned,
and likewise drawn back— thus, the action of the sides is fivefold.
The waist becomes bent, as does the side;
likewise, with the shoulder drawn back, it is known as slightly inclined to one side. (BhN 9.237)
And its other side is the reverse, according to the proper method;
it should be described as having the hips, sides, arms, and shoulders raised upward.
When extended from both sides by stretching it out, it is called *āyāmana*;
when turned over even three times, it is here considered *vivartita*.
By removing the turned [hand], it becomes *apasṛta*;
this is called the characteristic of the side (*pārśva*). Now, learn its application.
The *upasarpa* (approaching) hand-gesture is used for what is low; the *apasarpaṇa* (withdrawing) for what is high;
the *prasārita* (extended) for joy and the like; and the *parivṛtta* (revolved) for turning around.
When [the abdomen] has receded, it may bulge at the sides due to the influence of the contents;
understand these to be the actions of the sides of the abdomen. (BhN 9.242)
The abdomen is said to be of three types: emaciated (kṣāma), sunken (khālva), and full (pūrṇa).
A thin, emaciated, and sunken abdomen is called *kṣāma*, while a full and distended one is called *ādhmāta*.
A thin smile may occur during laughter, weeping, sighing, or yawning;
it is indeed desired when one is ill, engaged in austerity, exhausted, or afflicted by hunger. (BhN 9.244)
The abdomen is said to be full during deep inhalation, in cases of corpulence, illness, overeating, and so forth; now learn of the functions of the waist. BhN 9.245.
Others, however, say that the abdomen may be of four types: emaciated, thin, even, and full;
and likewise, it may be severed, withdrawn, emptied, or trembling.
And the raised hip is likewise fivefold in both dramatic dance and pure dance.
The *chinnā* is proclaimed as the bending of the middle of the waist;
when facing away, turning toward [the front] is the *nivṛttā*. BhN 9.247.
The waist is to be known as *recitā* from revolving in every direction;
it is to be known as *kṣiptā* when moving sideways back and forth, and as *prakampitā* when trembling.
Because it supports the hips and the sides, the waist is called "udvāhitā" (the bearer).
I have explained the function of the waist; now learn its application. BhN 9.249.
The *chinnā* (severed) occurs in cases such as looking about while agitated by exertion;
the *nivṛttā* (returned) likewise in turning back; and the *recitā* (released) in whirling and similar movements.
For hunchbacks, dwarfs, and those of low stature, the gait should be made tremulous;
for those who are stout, it should be raised upward, and it should be employed for women in their graceful, playful movements.
One should perform these five actions of the thighs: trembling, bending, stiffening, turning upward, and likewise turning back. (BhN 9.252)
When there is repeated sinking and rising of the heel accompanied by trembling of the thighs,
and the knee moves inward, that is known as *valana*.
Stambhana (stiffening) should also be understood as consisting of the action of apaviddha;
udvartana (twisting upward) is recorded as arising from the karaṇas valita and āviddha of the thighs.
When the heel moves inward, that is called *nivartana*;
for those of inferior vessels, there is also trembling during movements and in times of fear.
Indeed, a turning away (valana) should be performed by women during their independent movements;
however, one should employ a paralyzing gesture (stambhana) in cases of terror and despair.
In physical exercise and in the tāṇḍava dance, the wise should perform *udvartana*; however, *nivartana* should be performed during the whirling movements of the *saṃbhrānta* and other such dances.
Furthermore, other [details] should be adopted by practitioners according to what is observed in the world;
thus has the definition of the thighs been declared—now learn that of the shanks.
Twisted, bent, cast forward, raised upward,
and likewise turned back— these are the five types of movements of the shanks.
O Brahmins, when the left foot moves along the right side and the right foot likewise along the left, that is called *āvartita*.

One should lead [the leg] in a gradual rotation by means of the *jaṅghāsvastika* (crossing of the shanks); it is known as *nata* (bent) by practitioners due to the contraction of the knee, and it is designated as *kṣipta* (thrown) due to the outward projection of the shank. // BhN 9.261 //
It is *nata* (bent) from the bending of the knee; *kṣipta* (thrown out) from being cast outward;
*udvāhita* (raised up) is to be known from raising it upward;
and that which is the turning back [of the gaze] is called *parivṛtta* (revolved). (BhN 9.262)
The *āvartita* [turn] should be employed during the movements of the *vidūṣaka*,
and the *nata* [bend] should also be performed during standing, sitting, walking, and other such actions.
The *kṣipta* [hand] is employed in athletic exercises and in the *tāṇḍava* dance;
likewise, one should perform the *udvāhita* [hand] in movements such as the *āviddha* gait.
In the *tāṇḍava* dances, the performers should employ the *parivṛtta* (turning) movement;
thus has been described the action of the shanks. Now, learn of that of the feet.
The foot is said to be of five kinds: the extended (udghaṭṭita), the level (sama), likewise the one moving on the tip (agratalasañcara), the bent (añcita), and the contracted (kuñcita).
Standing on the tip of the forefoot, the heel is brought down to the ground;
when this is performed with the foot, it is known as the *udghaṭṭita*.
In this case of the *udveṣṭita* movement, having employed the performance for the sake of imitation,
it should be applied once or repeatedly with a fast or medium tempo (*drutamadhyamapracāra*).
When the ground is naturally level and the position is even, that foot which remains level should be known as the *svabhāvābhinaya* (natural gesture). BhN 9.269.
In the representation of a stable nature, when relying on various gestures,
the movement should again be performed by those who know the rules during the rhythmic foot-steps.
When the heel is indeed level and situated on the inside of the foot,
while the big toe is positioned on the outside edge, that is known as the triangular foot (tryaśrapāda).
Having abandoned (or having formed) a position with feet level, as well as the *aśvakrānta* [position],
one should form a triangular foot-step according to the rule when dealing with matters such as agitation and the like.
If the heel of this very same even-footed stance should be positioned toward the inside,
it is to be known as the triangular foot (tryaśrapāda), which is employed in various standing postures and the like.
The heel should be raised, the big toe extended, and all the other toes bent; this is the movement of the foot on its forepart.

By this [practice], there occurs striking, pounding, the steady suppression [of breath], trampling the ground, whirling, tossing about, various types of *recaka* exhalation, and the movement of the heels. BhN 9.275.
That foot whose heel is pressed against the ground, as is the forepart of the sole,
and all the toes are likewise bent, is known as the *añcita* (bent) foot.
Likewise, in the movements of the tips of the feet, in the rolling and turning [of the feet],
as well as in the striking with the feet and in various *bhramaraka* (swarming) movements, it should be performed in this manner.
When the heel is raised and the toes are likewise contracted,
and the middle part [of the foot] is also bent, that foot is known as *kuñcita* (contracted).
In the *udāttagamana* (raised gait) as well as in the *vartita* and *udvartita* gaits,
the heel (*pārṣṇi*) should be lifted, while the foot remains balanced on the tip of the big toe (*aṅguṣṭhāgra*).
The left foot, remaining in its natural position, is proclaimed as the *sūcīpāda*;
its application is described in the dance (*nṛtta*) for the execution of the anklet gesture (*nūpurakaraṇa*).
And in the *atikrāntakrama* [gait], one should employ this same foot-step;
the practitioners should perform the action consisting of the movements of the feet, shanks, and thighs.
The entire action of the foot is considered to be performed by the shank and the thigh;
just as the foot moves, so too does the thigh move.
Because these two share the same instrument, one should employ the foot-stroke;
thus has been declared the definition and the action pertaining to the limbs. (BhN 9.283)
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of movement and physical exercise.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "Gestures of the Limbs," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
Now begins the tenth chapter:
In this manner, [the gestures] of the foot, the shank, the thighs, and likewise of the hips [have been described].
When there is a single instrument of action, that movement is designated as *cārī*.
The noble ones, having entered upon the method, strive with one another;
because they are endowed with the constituent factors, it is therefore called "exertion. (BhN 10.2)
That which is the movement of a single foot is designated as *cārī*;
however, that which is the stepping of both feet shall be known as *karaṇa*.
The conjunction of the constituent parts is called a *khaṇḍa*;
a *maṇḍala* consists of three or four such *khaṇḍas* joined together. BhN 10.4.
Dance is extended by means of *cārīs*, and likewise movement is performed by means of *cārīs*;
the discharge of weapons is also performed by means of *cārīs*, and thus *cārīs* are proclaimed in battle.
This drama that has been introduced here is designated precisely by means of the *cārīs*;
for without the *cārīs*, no part of the dramatic performance proceeds at all. (BhN 10.6)
Therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the rules for movement—
how and in what manner each [movement] is to be applied in dance, combat, and likewise in walking.
Samapādā, sthitāvartā, śakaṭāsyā, likewise adhyardhikā, cāṣagati, and another, vicyavā. (BhN 10.8)
The *eḍakākrīḍitā*, the *baddhā*, the *uruvṛttā*, and likewise the *āḍḍitā*;
the *utspanditā*, the *janitā*, the *syanditā*, and the *apasyanditā*.
Samotsarita, Mattallī, and Mattallī—these sixteen are remembered as the noble (ārya) *bhaumya* [melodic ornaments]. Now listen again to those belonging to the ether (*ākāśika*). BhN 10.10.
For there are the *atikrāntā*, the *apakrāntā*, and likewise the *pārśvakrāntā*;
as well as the *ūrdhvajānu*, the *sūcī*, and the *nūpurapādikā*.
The swinging-footed, the likewise thrown, those known as the whirled and the upturned, the lightning-twirling, the fire-brand circle, and likewise the terrifying serpent. BhN 10.12.
The *mṛgaplutā*, the *daṇḍā*, and the *bhramarī*—these sixteen are known as the *ākāśikya* gaits; now learn their characteristics. BhN 10.13.
When the feet are placed without any interval, even including the nails, this is known as the *samapādā* stance; it should be understood as a *cārī* based on a fixed position (*sthāna*).
Having made the inner circle with the foot rubbed upon the ground, one should again sweep away another; that is known as the *sthitāvarta*.
Seated with the limbs relaxed, having extended the foot so that the sole moves along the ground,
and having raised the chest, one should employ the śakaṭāsya posture.
When the left foot is behind the right,
that movement should be known by the wise as *sādhyardhikā*.
The left foot is extended and then drawn back again;
the right foot likewise draws back as the left moves forward—this is prescribed for the *cāṣagati* (the gait of a blue jay).
From the *vicyava* position with feet together, one should perform the *vicyava*; striking the surface of the earth with the tips of the palms of the feet. BhN 10.19.
When one leaps up with both feet moving on the surface and then descends,
performing this in alternating succession, that is the *eḍakākrīḍitā* (the sheep’s play).
Having formed the *svastika* by the mutual pressure of the calves, there is a twisting with the thighs;
because of this, it is declared the *baddha* posture.
When the heel of the foot moving on the surface is turned outward,
and the shank is likewise bent and rotated, that is known as the *ūrudvṛtta* (thigh-rotated) position.
Whether in front or behind, when one foot moves on the sole while the second foot is rubbed against it, that is called *aḍḍitā*. (BhN 10.23)
The foot should be withdrawn slowly, both externally and internally;
that which follows the exhaling breath is known as the *utsyanditā* [breathing technique].
With the fist held at the chest and another hand extended,
with the feet moving across the palms, this is declared to be the *janitā* cārī.
Extending the foot five tālas away, one should place it in the *syandita* position;
with the second foot, one should likewise place it in the *apasyandita* position.
When the feet move with a rolling gait as they advance,
and the *mattallī* step is executed evenly, this is declared to be the *samutsarita* in the *vyāyāma* style.
With whirling approaches on both feet,
and with hands that are entwined and cast aside, this is declared to be the *mattallī*.
These noble movements (cārīs) pertaining to the ground have been described as being based on the techniques of wrestling;
now I shall fully explain the characteristics of those movements pertaining to the sky.
Having lifted the contracted foot, one should extend it forward;
having lifted it, one should let it fall—that is known as the *atikrāntā*.
Having performed a twisting motion with the thighs, one should lift the bent foot and cast it to the side; this is known as the *apakrāntā*.
Lifting the contracted foot, one should place it by leaping sideways;
with the foot extended, the *pārśvakrāntā* (sideways-step) is performed.
Lifting the bent foot, one should place it level with the knee or the breast;
the second [leg] is likewise held steady in succession—this is proclaimed as *ūrdhvajānu*.
Lifting the contracted foot and extending it above the knee, one should let it fall by means of the tip;
that is proclaimed as the *sūcī* posture.
Having bent the foot behind, one should swiftly extend it to the ground with the sole facing upward; this is the *nūpurapādikā* carriage (*cārī*).
Lifting the bent foot and swinging it from side to side, one should likewise let it fall while flexed; this is known as the *dolapādā*.
Having lifted the contracted foot and drawn it back, one should place it with the ankles crossed;
that is known as the *ākṣiptā* posture.
When the foot in front of the *svastika* is bent and then extended, falling with a circular motion,
that is known as the *āviddhā*.
Having twisted the foot, having encircled it, and having lifted it up, one should cast it down;
turning it around a second time—this is declared to be the *sodvṛttā* gait.
One should extend the foot, which was turned backward and rubbed against the head, in all directions in a circular motion; that is known as the *vidyudbhrāntā*.
With the foot extended backward, bent inward,
and the heel dropped down, it is indeed proclaimed as the *alātā* posture.
Lifting the bent foot and turning the thigh into a triangle,
and by the turning of the hip and knee, it becomes the *bhujaṅgatrāsitā* (the "terrifying serpent").
