Having performed the *atikrāntakrama* and leaping up, one should let [the foot] fall;
with the calf drawn up and cast over, that is to be known as the *hariṇaplutā*.
Having placed the *nūpura* foot forward and extending it, one quickly performs the *āviddha* movement; that is known as the *daṇḍapādā*.
Having performed the transposition of the sequence, one should rotate the triad;
from the circling of the second foot with the sole [of the hand], it is known as the *bhramarī*.
For these are known as aerial movements, consisting of graceful bodily actions;
they should be employed by practitioners when using weapons such as the bow, the thunderbolt, and the sword.

Whether positioned in front, behind, or even as attendants according to the requirements of the yoga, the hands must be placed at the feet by those who perform the dance, O twice-born ones. (BhN 10.47)
Where the foot is, there the hand is; where the hand is, there the triangle is. Having understood the emergence of the foot, one should likewise apply the subsidiary limbs.
Just as the foot moves toward the ground during walking,
so too, after the hand has moved, it should rest upon the region of the waist.
These noble ones, whose nature consists of graceful bodily movements, have been described by me;
I shall now declare their positions for the discharge of all weapons.
The Vaiṣṇava, the Samapāda, the Vaiśākha, the Maṇḍala,
as well as the Pratyālīḍha and the Ālīḍha— these are the six standing postures (sthāna) for men.
The distance between the two feet should be two *tālas* and a half-*tāla*;
one [foot] should be positioned evenly, while the other, triangular [in shape], is situated on the side.
With the shanks slightly bent and the limbs held with graceful poise, this is indeed the Vaiṣṇava posture;
Viṣṇu is the presiding deity here.
In this situation,
one should engage in conversation that arises naturally with men of superior or middling status who are occupied with various other affairs.
One should employ [the *mudrā*] in the releasing of the discus as well as in the holding of the bow, in acts of bestowing courage and playful gestures, and likewise in anger. (BhN 10.55)
This very same [state], when inverted, is considered to be anger born of affection;
it likewise occurs when one is intent on reproaching, as well as when there is agitation caused by affection.
Indeed, [these are found] in fear, envy, ferocity, thought, intelligence, and memory; as well as in dejection, fickleness, pride, desired objects, and powers. (BhN 10.57)
It is joined with the predominance of the erotic, the marvelous, the loathsome, and the heroic sentiments;
when the feet are equal, both feet are placed at an interval of one *tāla*. (BhN 10.58)
Endowed with natural excellence, Brahmā is the presiding deity here; by means of this position, one should perform the auspicious rite for the Brahmin.
In the matter of transforming forms, birds possess excellence and even curiosity;
this applies both to those situated on chariots and to those dwelling in celestial palaces.
One should construct this station for those established in the liṅga and those established in their vows;
the distance between the two feet should be three tālas and half a tāla.
One should form the seated thigh with three *tālas* and one and a half *tālas*;
the two feet, situated at the chest, should be triangular in shape and applied there.
This is indeed the Vaiśākha station, and Skanda is its presiding deity;
by means of this station, the wise should perform the mounting of horses.
The exit from the practice area, the examination of large birds, and likewise the lifting of arrows during the performance of the exercises. BhN 10.64.
This very same [procedure] should be performed by practitioners during the *recakas*;
however, in the *aindra* mandala, the two feet should be positioned four *tālas* apart.
The two shoulders should be triangular and the hips and knees should be level;
one should employ the bow, the thunderbolt, and the sword weapons with circular movements.
The mount for elephants is characterized by thick-feathered birds;
its right leg, moreover, is extended five tālas.
One should assume the *ālīḍha* stance; Rudra is the presiding deity here.
Whatever is performed with heroism or ferocity should be done in this posture. (BhN 10.68)
Furthermore, there is mutual verbal exchange arising from anger and resentment, as well as the wrestling match of boxers and the sizing up of enemies. (BhN 10.69)
Likewise, there is charging forward and the discharging of weapons;
having bent the right leg and extended the left foot.
The turning from the *ālīḍha* stance is known as *pratyālīḍha*.
One should release a weapon held in the *ālīḍha* stance by means of the *pratyālīḍha*. (BhN 10.71)
Indeed, the discharge of various weapons must be performed by the practitioners; furthermore, four principles regarding the discharge of weapons are to be understood. BhN 10.72.
The Bhārata, the Sātvata, the Vārṣagaṇya, and the Kaiśika;
among these, the cutting of the waist is for the Bhārata, while the cutting of the feet is for the Sātvata.
In the Vārṣagaṇya style, however, the chest is emphasized, while in the Kaiśika style, the head is to be severed.
By these methods employed by practitioners, various movements (ācarī) arise.
Having deliberated, one should apply various discharges of weapons with *aṅgahāras* that rely on correct principles and arise from those very principles. (BhN 10.75)
Because battles take place, therefore these rules of conduct have been proclaimed;
[one should act] having placed the shield that wards off weapons in the left hand. (BhN 10.76)
Then, taking up a weapon with his hand, he should perform a thorough examination;
having properly extended both hands, he should indeed withdraw them once again.
The shield should then be whirled from side to side,
and the wielders of the weapon must also perform a circumambulation around the head.
Or likewise, the unwrapping of the weapon within the hollow of the cheek,
and again with the sword in hand, gracefully unwrapped.
The wise should perform a circumambulation of the head with the shield;
such is the manner of movement to be practiced in the land of Bhārata during the discharge of weapons.
And I shall explain the detailed analysis of the *sātvata* [weapon] according to the rule;
that same detailed analysis is prescribed for the sword (*khaḍga*) and the shield (*kheṭaka*).
O Sātvata, one must indeed keep the weapon behind one's back;
and even when moving toward the Vārṣagaṇya [position], one should do so according to the Sātvata method.
The whirling of the sword and the shield is also performed;
likewise, in this case, there should be the circumambulation of the head with the sword.
The binding of the chest should be performed, or alternatively, the binding of the weapon;
this deliberation is prescribed for the *bhārata* style, but it should be applied in the *kaiśika* style as well. (BhN 10.84)
Having thus caused the weapon to whirl, one should cause it to fall solely upon the head;
for these movements are to be employed in this manner through the play of the fingers.
Bows, vajras, swords, and weapons should be employed for the purpose of liberation;
there is nothing to be pierced, nor anything to be cut, nor even the shedding of blood.
In battle, one should employ weapons, yet not engage in the slaughter of those who are clearly visible;
the wise should discharge their arms merely for the sake of signaling.

Alternatively, one should perform the *chedya* (cutting) movements according to the prescribed rules, accompanied by dramatic gestures (*abhinaya*) and adorned with *aṅgahāras* that possess graceful articulation of the limbs.

One should perform physical exercise properly, accompanied by the *laya* and *tāla* rhythms; indeed, those who practice exercise must exert effort toward aesthetic perfection (*sauṣṭhava*). (BhN 10.89)
The definition of *sauṣṭhava* (excellence) has been declared as that which is joined with the sequence of execution;
for all beauty indeed always depends upon excellence.
One should employ a posture that is steady, not hunched, with the limbs drawn close together, neither too high nor with moving feet, and characterized by the grace of well-proportioned limbs.
Where the hips are level with the ears, as are the elbows, shoulders, and head,
and the chest is well-elevated— that is called *sauṣṭhava* (symmetry).
One whose limbs lack gracefulness does not shine in dramatic dance or pure dance; therefore, those of middling and superior ability must always apply diligent effort in this regard. (BhN 10.93)
Indeed, all drama and dance are established upon gracefulness;
the hands are positioned for the pelvic movements, and the chest is held well-raised.
The Vaiṣṇava position, O dear one, is declared to be the square posture;

One should cause a person to perform exercises by stretching the limbs against a wall;
for the sake of strength, one should likewise employ nasal therapy (nasya) and the procedure of enemas (basti).
Likewise, there are other unctuous substances, as well as syrups and drinks;
the vital breaths are established in food, and the yogas are established in the vital breath.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining fitness, one should be diligent regarding food;
[for] the body becomes impure, exhausted, and excessively afflicted by hunger and thirst.

One should not engage in physical exercise after drinking excessively or eating to excess; rather, one should possess limbs that are steady and sweet, and a chest that is well-proportioned and square.
The wise man should cause a person to perform physical exercise consisting of bodily movements;
thus, in conjunction with physical exercise, the method of *cārī* should be practiced.
Henceforth, I shall explain the classification of the mandalas.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Rules for the Cārīs," in the Bharatīya Nāṭyaśāstra.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.

The *atikrānta*, the *vicitra*, and likewise the *lalitasañcara*;

likewise, they say there is the *eḍakākrīḍita*.

the *piṣṭakuṭṭa* should be known, and also the *cāṣagata*. (BhN 11.5)
These ten [types of marriages] have also been declared here by name as pertaining to the [respective] social classes;
having first performed the rite that produces the offspring, one should then perform the rite of marriage.
The *alāta* (firebrand) and the left *pārśvakrānta*, the right *pārśvakrānta* and the left *sūcī*, and again the right *pārśvakrānta*. BhN 11.7.
One should apply the needle-step with the left foot, and the *apakrānta* with the right;

Having first performed the *janita* with that very same [leg], one should perform the *nikuṭṭaka*;

then the left performs a side-step, followed by the needle-step with the left. BhN 11.13.

as well as the cut-off (paricchinna), should indeed be performed with the outward circling (bāhyabhramaṇaka).
This practice of movement should be performed with graceful steps;
one should apply the "needle" step on the left foot and rotate the triple-joint.
Then there is the side-step (pārśvakrānta), first with the right and then with the left, as well as the crossing-over (atikrānta);
one should again perform the first pointing-step (sūcī) and the left crossing-over.
Furthermore, when the first [movement] is performed as a lateral step (pārśvakrānta) within a maṇḍala pierced by a needle,
that first [movement], having been produced, becomes the staff-step (daṇḍakrama).
One should again apply the left needle and rotate the triple-joint;
the right [joint] becomes elevated, while the left becomes like a firebrand.

the first is the "terrified serpent," while the left is both the "transgressed" and the "exceeded."
This is the application of the *cārī* movement when the mandala has been traversed:
having performed the sequence beginning with the needle-step (*sūcī*), one performs the *apakrānta* step with the left foot.
Then, having whirled through the maṇḍala in succession by means of these *cārīs*—namely, *pārśvakrānta*, *ādya*, *alāta*, and *vāmaka*— [the dance proceeds]. (BhN 11.29)

In the mandala of the left-binding, the *alāta* step is performed on the left side, the *pārśvakrānta* on the right, and the *atikrānta* again on the left. (BhN 11.35)
Having performed the sequence beginning with the needle-step (*sūcī*), one then performs the leftward step (*apakrānta*);
then again the first side-step (*pārśvakrānta*), and that *bhujaṅgatrāsita*. (BhN 11.36)
Again, the left [foot] is extended and the right is likewise drawn back; again, the left is extended and the thighs are likewise rotated. (BhN 11.37)
Furthermore, the left [foot] is in the *alāta* position and the right is in the *pārśvakrānta*;
then one should place the left in the *sūcī* position while the right is in the *apakrānta*.
Furthermore, the left [foot] should be extended and made known as *lalita*;
this extension of the foot occurs in the *lalita* mandala. (BhN 11.39)
Having performed the needle-like movement, one indeed steps away to the left;
then again, the first side-step and likewise the step to the left side.
Having performed these movements in rotation around the mandala,
one should then apply the left-pointing needle (vāmasūcī) and the rightward withdrawal (apakrānta).

For this maṇḍala is arranged for the purpose of moving according to one's own nature; however, it should be understood by those who perform the dance that this [movement] is designated by the name "krānta" (the stride). BhN 11.42.
These ten should be known as moving through the sky;
hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of those who move upon the earth.
The first [hand] is generated as the effect and should be extended to the left;
the second is again the first [hand], with the mouth like a cart, and also extended to the left.

then the left is the *āskandita* (leaping) and the right is the *śakaṭāsya* (cart-mouth).
Moving to the left and gliding backward, one should likewise perform the *bhramaraka*; that same movement, when performed without trembling, constitutes the *bhramaramaṇḍala*.
The first [hand] should be made into a *bhramaraka*; the left one should be bent (*āḍhita*);
the right one should be made into a *trikavivarta* and a *śakaṭāsya*.
That same [hand] should be rotated outward and turned to the left while drawn back; the right [hand] should be formed by turning the three joints and made to vibrate.
When the left [hand] becomes like a cart-mouth, that indeed is the "slapping" (āsphoṭana);
this is called "throbbing" (āspandita) in the context of exertion on the battlefield. BhN 11.49.
The first, however, having performed the *janita*, and the left [foot] likewise the *nikuṭṭaka*;
then again the first [foot] becomes the *śakaṭāsya*, while that very same [foot] is the *ūrudvṛtta*.
The left [hand] moves backward and has the gait of a blue jay;
furthermore, the right hand quivers and the left one has the mouth of a cart.
One should rotate the first, the *bhramaraka*, and the *trika*;
with the *pṛṣṭhāpasarpī* and the left [hand], there shall be the *āvarta-maṇḍala*.
Having made his feet even, the wise one should extend his hands,
wrapping them around so that their upper surfaces are close together and facing upward, repeatedly encircling and releasing.
Having placed it on the surface of the hip, one should rotate it first in sequence;
then, in due order, one should extend it to the left by means of a counter-rotation.
Having wandered through this and that [track] in succession around the mandala, this entire circuit of the exercise-mandala has been completed. BhN 11.55.
With feet joined to the ground, likewise with the needle-pierced [step], with the "goat's play," and with the swift triple-turning; BhN 11.56.
Having pierced and cast aside [the opponent] with needle-like thrusts, and having circled the mandala in sequence,
one should know this as the "ram's play" (eḍakākrīḍita), which is designated as the "fragmented mandala" (khaṇḍamaṇḍala).
Having performed the *udghaṭṭita* with the right [hand], one should perform the *āvarta* with that same [hand];
likewise, the *āskandita*, the *śakaṭāsya*, and the *vāmaka* should be performed with that same [hand].
The first [step] is one that recedes from the back, and it should have the gait of a blue jay;
then there is the *aḍḍita* [step], followed by the left, and the first [step] again is drawn back.
The left foot should be placed in the *bhramaraka* position, while the right is in the initial *āskandita*;
one should perform the slapping with that very [foot]—this is the *aḍḍitamaṇḍala*.
Having first performed the *janita* and then the *nikuṭṭaka* with that same [foot],
that very foot becomes the *śakaṭāsya*, while the left foot performs the *āskandita*.
The cart-mouth (śakaṭāsya) formation is to be understood as a circular battle array used in exertion;
furthermore, the circular array is formed by the feet positioned in the cart-mouth formation in successive turns.
But that which is first produced, having been generated, remains unassailed;
moreover, the left [wind] moves backward, while the right is shaped like the mouth of a cart.
Having moved through these various gaits in turn within the circle,
one should know that this same circle, measuring one and a half [units], applies also to wrestling.
Having first performed the needle-step (sūcī), one then steps backward with the left foot;
likewise, the left foot alone performs the "terrified serpent" (bhujaṅgatrāsita).
Having moved about with feet that terrify serpents and having performed the *maṇḍala* with the *piṣṭakuṭṭa*, the wise should recognize the *maṇḍala* by means of these *cārīs*.
Having circled the mandala with all the steps of the blue jay (cāṣagata), one should know this to be the cāṣagata; it is also a mandala used in hand-to-hand combat.
The mandalas arising from various modes of conduct have been explained in brief; hereafter, one should apply those belonging to the uniform mode of conduct.
The application of the conduct of equality is that which is called the Maṇḍala of Equality;
those [practices] should be performed here by practitioners with the thought that they are the Master (ācārya). BhN 11.69.

These sections, together with their circular movements, should be performed by experts in battle, wrestling, and rhythmic paces; they should be preceded by the sweetness of graceful limbs and accompanied by instrumental music.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Maṇḍala," in the Bharatanāṭyaśāstra.
Now begins the twelfth chapter: "The Movement of Gait.
In this manner, the formation of the maṇḍala should be performed in conjunction with physical exercise (*vyāyāma*).
Hereafter, I shall explain the destinies that abide within primordial nature.
Having performed the ceremonial procession there, preceded by musical instruments and the sounding of vessels,
he should enter among the subjects with flavors suited to the path.
When the *dhruvā* has been joined and the cloth has been removed,
the entrance of the actors (*pātra*) should be performed, which gives rise to various purposes and aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*).
Having established the Vaiṣṇava posture, whether in the highest or the middle [position],
the chest should be well-raised, level, and square.
One should have the shoulders made smooth and neither excessively raised;
the region of the neck should be fashioned with the head bent like that of a peacock.
One should apply [the gaze] to the top of the arm when it is eight finger-breadths from the ear,
and the chin should likewise be positioned four finger-breadths from the chest.
The hands should likewise be positioned at the hips and the navel;
the right hand should rest at the navel, while the left hand is placed upon the hip.
The distance between the two feet should be made to be two and a half tālas;
the lifting of the foot, moreover, should be performed according to its own prescribed measure.
It may be four tālas, two tālas, or likewise one tāla;
however, for deities as well as for kings, it should be four tālas.
The *dvitāla* is the tempo for middle [voices], as well as for women and those of low gender;
it is likewise recorded as being four beats (*catuṣkala*), two beats (*dvikala*), and one beat (*ekakala*).
For the highest [class], a foot consists of four beats; for the middling, it should consist of two beats;
and likewise, a foot of one beat is proclaimed for the lowest class. (BhN 12.11)
Having observed the three tempos— slow, medium, and fast— as well as the three pauses,
one who knows the nature of dramatic performance should employ the movement accordingly.
The movement endowed with steadfastness is for the highest beings; the medium movement is for those esteemed as middling;
and the rapid movement is for the most base. These three tempos (layas) should be applied according to the nature of the being.
This indeed is the rule to be understood regarding the measures (kalā), time-units (tāla), and rhythmic pauses (laya);
now listen, O sinless ones, to the application of the movement of the return [of the breath]. BhN 12.14.
In the supreme gait, however, the movement should be performed with the knees level with the hips;
in the application of martial movements, one should place the knee level with the breast.
Then, with side-steps that are graceful and accompanied by instrumental music,
he should proceed toward the corner of the stage for exactly five steps.
Then one should perform the leftward piercing with the left hand, while the right hand performs the scattering;
having turned around for the second time, one should then proceed to the next corner.
There too, piercing with the left is distraction, as is [piercing] with the right;
therefore, one should proceed facing the vessel, taking those very same steps.
Having thus performed twenty steps by means of going and returning,
one should then perform the left piercing and the displacement of the right.
On a long (rectangular) stage, Bharata should perform the movement of the feet through coming and going;
on a triangular or trapezoidal stage, the movement is likewise [diagonal]; and on a square stage, the movement of the feet is indeed square.
When one proceeds with equal [beats] joined together, there the support of *laya* (tempo) should be applied;
namely, as four-beat (*catuṣkala*), then two-beat (*dvikalā*), and likewise again as one-beat (*ekakala*).
Now, he who proceeds surrounded by those of middling and low status should likewise move for four beats, then half a beat, and again for one beat.
Furthermore, for Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, kings, Pannagas, and Rākṣasas,
the wise should determine their gait with a measurement of four tālas.
The intermediate state is desired for all those who dwell in heaven;
even among them, however, those who are arrogant have a destiny equal to that of the gods.
The sages said:
"When men become kings, how can they attain the state of the gods? To this it is replied: how is it that this state will not belong to kings? (BhN 12.25)
In this context, regarding the performance of dramatic dance (*nāṭya-nṛtta*), the *prakṛtis* (types of characters) are to be understood as divine, celestial-human, and human. (BhN 12.26)
The nature of the gods is divine; that of kings is indeed divine-human;
but any other which is known in the world is proclaimed as purely human.
But kings are declared in the Vedas and the Upanishads to be born from portions of the gods;
thus, there is indeed no fault here in imitating the gods.
This rule, however, must be observed regarding going according to one's own will;
in cases of emergency, sudden calamity, or anger, no such restriction is prescribed.
However, performers must effect the movement of all characters— whether superior, inferior, or middling— by resorting to different internal states.
It may consist of four and a half kalās, or even half of that;
having reached another state, it performs its various movements.
In the superior [form], there are four beats; here, in the middling, there should be two beats;
and where the superior has two beats, the middling should have one beat.
Where there is one *kalā* in the middle [of the sequence], there shall be half a *kalā* for the lower ones;
in this manner, one should apply [the proportions] to the dull-witted, reducing them by half and half again.
To one afflicted by fever, one afflicted by hunger, one exhausted by austerity, one possessed by fear, one who is astonished, one who is indifferent, and likewise one endowed with longing; BhN 12.34.
In the erotic sentiment, in sorrow, and likewise in unrestrained movement,
the gait should be performed with a steady tempo, falling within the intervals of the additional *kalās*.
Furthermore, when accompanied by anxiety, one should employ a movement of four beats;
likewise when there is a desire for something unwholesome, or when one is terrified or frightened.
In moments of agitation or joy, in matters requiring haste, upon hearing something undesirable, in the face of reproach, or at the sight of a marvel; BhN 12.37.
Moreover, in matters of extreme urgency, when one is suffering, when searching for an enemy, when pursuing one who has committed an offense, or likewise when following after wild beasts; BhN 12.38.
A wise person should thus apply these modes of movement according to their specific deficiencies;
however, one should not employ the mode of movement intended for the superior among them in the case of those who are middling.
One should not apply to those of low status that same disposition which belongs to those of middle rank;
rather, a graceful disposition should be adopted, arising from the natural desires of one who is well-situated.
Having been shown the way by the female messenger, he should enter the performance arena;
and with the *sūcī* gesture, he should perform the representation based on the meaning of the subject matter.
Adorned with pleasing fragrances, garments,
and ornaments, he was further embellished with garlands possessing the sweet scent of various flowers.
One should walk with graceful steps, moving and pausing with such elegance, in accordance with the rhythm and tempo.
The hands should always be made subordinate to the feet by performers;
[this is done] by raising the hand while the foot descends, and by the reverse.
Now learn further of the conduct toward one who desires in secret:
he has dismissed his attendants, is relaxed, and is accompanied by a female messenger.
The lamp of Nirvāṇa is not excessively adorned with ornaments;
its garment is like the shore, and thus it moves slowly together with the messenger.
One whose desire is concealed should proceed with silent and slow steps;
apprehensive of noise, he should remain alert and intent on observation.
With a trembling body and filled with apprehension, tripping repeatedly,
I shall describe the Furious Sentiment (raudra-rasa) as directed toward the hosts of Daityas and Rakshasas.
O best of the twice-born, their single, stable rasa is the Furious (raudra);
it should be understood as both the Furious in costume (nepathyaraudra) and likewise the Furious in action (aṅgaraudra).
Likewise, the fierce [form] arising from its own nature is likewise conceived as threefold:
he whose body is drenched in blood, whose face is moist with blood, and likewise he who has flesh in his hand;
that is the fierce form born of costume.
Having many arms and many faces, he is crowded with various weapons.
He is proclaimed to have a massive body, to be tall, and to have a fierce appearance;
he has red eyes, tawny hair, is dark-complexioned, and possesses a distorted voice.
This [gait] is harsh, intent on reviling, and fierce; it is innate to him.
He moves with feet lifted four tālas apart and dropped down with force.
The path should be prepared in this manner for them and for those of their kind,
where the earth is unpleasant, defiled by cremation grounds and battlefields.
In that context, one should employ the appropriate movement for the representation of disgust (*bībhatsa*);
in some cases with movements as if about to fall, and in others with movements already fallen far away. (BhN 12.55)
With feet placed one upon another in the *elakākrīḍita* style,
and with their own following hands [held in a similar manner], such a gait is desired for the *bībhatse* (loathsome) dance.
Now, in the *vīra* [rhythm], it should be performed with the shifting of the feet,
established upon rapid movement, and filled with various *cārīs*.
One should employ movement with speed through side-steps, swift thrusts, and likewise needle-piercing steps,
using feet that move according to the subtle divisions of time during the performance of *āvega* (agitation).
The course of the highest beings has for the most part been described;
I shall now further explain the course of those who are middling and inferior.
Having encountered the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of laughter, one should employ this and other [flavors] characterized by the striding of scattered steps in both wonder and joy. (BhN 12.60)
Furthermore, one should proceed with compassion in firm steps,
with eyes obstructed by tears and the body likewise [stiff].
With his hands raised and then dropped, and likewise weeping with a loud cry,
he should go with excessive haste toward the embrace of a fresh lover.
This [mode of weeping] should be employed by women toward those of low character;
however, for those of noble character, it should be performed with fortitude and accompanied by tears.
By means of long-drawn sighs and likewise by upward glances,
one should not display elegance there, nor should such a manner be considered a standard of measure.
The course of those of middling strength should also be applied according to the prescribed method;
their enthusiasm is struck down by a fall upon the chest, and their consciousness is agitated by grief.
One should not walk with excessively lifted steps when there is the falling of a beloved kinsman;
and when a severe blow has been struck, one should adopt a posture with relaxed limbs and arms.
Furthermore, the gait is characterized by a trembling body and shuffling steps, as if one were overcome by cold and drenched by rain. (BhN 12.67)
Furthermore, for women and those of low character, the performer should employ a movement in which the limbs are drawn together and then shaken. (BhN 12.68)
Placing both hands upon the chest and likewise becoming hunched over, one should also quiver the teeth and lips and tremble the chin. (BhN 12.69)
An action should be performed slowly when acting out the sentiment of the peaceful (*śānta*),
and likewise, the wise should employ a [slow] gait in the terrifying (*bhayānaka*) as well.
For women, for cowards, and for others who are devoid of courage,
the eyes are wide and flickering, and likewise the head is shaken.
With a gaze joined by fear, glancing toward both sides, with swift and mincing steps, and having formed the *kapota* hand-gesture; BhN 12.72.
With a trembling body and dry lips, one should walk with faltering steps;
this [gait] should be employed in imitation, as well as in threatening and terrifying others.
Having observed a change in their physical constitution and having heard a distorted voice, this [spell] should be performed against women and men whose prowess has been impaired. (BhN 12.74)
In some places with feet that had fallen nearby, in others with those fallen far away, and in others with feet dropped one upon another in the manner of the *elakākrīḍita* gait; BhN 12.75.
One should employ the "frightened" gait with the hands following these very same movements;
however, for merchants and ministers, the gait should be one born of their own natural disposition.
Having placed the hand on the region of the navel with the palm facing upward in the *khaṭakāmukha* position,
one should place the first [hand] curved and facing upward on the side between the breasts.
Neither sitting down, nor stiffening [the body], nor even swaying it about—
having positioned the limbs in such a manner, one should proceed by that very same method.
O Brahmins, with strides that leap over two spans (*dvitāla*),
those ascetics (*yatīnām*), mendicants (*śramaṇānām*), and others who are established in austerity [proceed].
But for those who have taken recourse to the lifelong vow (naiṣṭhika-vrata), their course of action is as follows:
his gaze should be steady, looking only a yoke’s length ahead.
With mindfulness established and having composed his entire body,
he should remain with an unshakable mind, relying upon the appropriate physical posture.
The wise one should be modestly dressed and likewise wear saffron-colored robes; first, he should indeed stand in a posture with both feet even.
Having made one hand skillful and likewise extending the other,
one should keep the face serene, following the requirements of the practice.
One should move with a steady, unslouching body; by transgressing this, one would fail the mark of those supreme ascetics who observe the great vows.
One should apply these very same perverted qualities to others;
for such is the state of those following vows and the destiny of other practitioners of outward signs.
Whether wandering, or sublime, or even wandering yet restrained, [the gait] is likewise characterized by feet placed like the mouth of a cart or by those that have stepped beyond it. (BhN 12.86)
The movement of the Pāśupatas should be performed with a haughty gait;
furthermore, practitioners should adopt this gait when traveling in the dark.
Even for one standing in a chariot, movement should be made with feet and hands trailing along the ground, showing the path, or else by means of footprints made with powdered earth.
Having placed his feet evenly, he should proceed with the gait of a chariot;
holding the bow with one hand and the pole with the other.
Likewise, his charioteer should be one who is skilled with the whip and the reins; and various kinds of vehicles should be provided according to their respective divisions.
One should move upon the stage with swift, powdered steps;
indeed, this same gliding movement should be performed for one situated in a celestial chariot.
To ascend, one should lift the body slightly while remaining with the face turned upward;
for descending, one should perform the opposite of this.
Those who perform the dance must execute downward glances, circumambulations of the mandala, and movements through the air.
One should cause this same movement to be performed by one who can descend from the sky with both feet placed evenly on the ground, or even by means of powdered footprints.
Furthermore, the movement of one falling from the sky consists of straight, extended, raised, or lowered motions, as well as crooked and whirling movements, with arms cast out and flung about.
With her garments scattered, she likewise casts her eyes upon the ground,
[seeking him] among palaces, trees, and mountains, and in rivers, valleys, and elevations.
The wise should perform the ascent and descent according to the requirements of the situation;
however, the ascent of a palace should be performed by means of steps that have been bypassed.
Having raised his body and foot, a person should place them upon the steps;
likewise, during descent, he should bend his body and release [the foot].
In the palace, that which I have described as the *pratāra* (step) should be entirely level; however, for the *pratāra* on the roof-terrace, a slight forward inclination of the body is desired.
However, movement within water depends upon the measurement of the water:
when the water is shallow, there is the drawing up of a garment; when it is deep, there is the dragging of the hands.
Stretching out each arm one after another with repeated splashing in the water, she was indeed dragged sideways by the current as she was being carried away.
A movement with the face shaken and all the limbs agitated is prescribed;
this gait, performed with rapid *cūrṇa* steps, should also be employed by one standing on a boat.
That which is performed when ascending a palace with the second foot stepped forward and gracefully bent, one should employ that very same manner on mountains.
Furthermore, one's limbs may be cast upward toward the mountains,
or one may perform the act of climbing a tree with steps that have been overstepped and then halted.

One should likewise apply this same method of descent for those who have departed by piercing with a needle, as well as for those who have passed away by the side. One should employ it even in the case of rivers.
By this very same method, the movements and activities [of the body] should be performed;
these should be carried out according to the prescribed rule, merely by means of mental designation.
When it is asked, "Why is he dead?", what should be done by those who employ [the remedy]?
[One should treat] the elephant by seizing its goad, and the horse by seizing its bit. (BhN 12.107)
Just as in the case of grasping the reins, so too in other instances;
however, in the practice of horse-riding, the movement should be performed while standing in the *vaiśākha* posture.
Just as with various colorful powder patterns cast one above the other,
the movement of serpents should be executed with steps known as the *svastika*.
One should perform a step with a lateral movement and execute the *svastika* here; furthermore, the gait of a libertine (*viṭa*) should be characterized by graceful strides.
With the feet slightly contracted and dropped inward toward the palms,
the hands, endowed with their own natural grace, follow the movement of the feet.
Having performed the *khaṭakā* and *vardhamāna* hand gestures, one should proceed with the gait of a libertine;
for a chamberlain, however, this should be done according to his specific stage of life.

One who knows the application [of movement] should employ the gait for one who has not yet grown old in this manner: with steps rising to the height of half a tāla, and with straight *viṣkambha* [steps]. BhN 12.113.
One should walk as if carrying one's limbs, like one stuck in mud;
indeed, for an old man, the gait should be with a trembling body.
With their vital breaths suppressed by the *viṣkambhana* [breathing technique], and with their steps raised slowly,
the gait of one who is emaciated should indeed be represented as having a slow progression.
When one is seized by disease, afflicted by fever, exhausted by ascetic toil, or overcome by hunger;
when one's life-force is constrained, and one is emaciated with a thin belly. (BhN 12.116)
With a feeble voice and hollow cheeks, and likewise with downcast eyes,
one should move the hands and feet only slowly.
There is trembling of the limbs as well as distress, and even when traveling a long distance, one's gait consists of slow steps. (BhN 12.118)
One should perform the contraction of the limbs and the pressing together of the knees;
even for a large person, the movement should be such that it draws the body along.
One should mostly carry [the body] in a balanced manner, with steps raised slowly,
moving with a steady stride, and likewise breathing deeply and frequently.

And when overcome by the sweat of fatigue, one should likewise move with short steps; furthermore, the gait of those who are intoxicated should be performed according to the degree of intoxication, whether it be fresh or middling.
With her left and right feet whirling and retreating, and with her steps drawn back, she indeed has unsteady feet.
With her body reeling and her hands faltering,
her gait should be performed like that of a madman, lacking any fixed order.
She is constantly engaged in much wandering, relying on imitation of the ways of the world;
her hair is coarse and split, and her body is likewise covered in dust. BhN 12.124.

One who speaks of the signless yet talks excessively, one who is subject to mental fluctuations, who sings suddenly and laughs, and who does not remain attached even in social company—[such a person is possessed by a spirit]. (BhN 12.125)
He dances with great joy, or again he plays musical instruments;
sometimes he runs with speed, and sometimes he stands still.
Sometimes he may be seated, and sometimes he may be lying down;
wearing various garments, he has no fixed abode on the streets.
For one thus becomes intoxicated; one should cause him to perform this gait:
standing with the foot in the *nūpura* position, one should extend the foot in the *daṇḍapāda* position.
Having likewise performed the bound movement (baddhā-cārī) and the svastika,
one should traverse the mandala by means of this application of movements.
One should extend the *bāhyabhramaraka* at the corner of the stage,
having formed the very graceful *trika* and the hand known as *latā*.
With hands turned in the opposite direction, there should be movement by means of the feet;
indeed, three types of movement should be performed as if one were lame, paralyzed, or a dwarf.
Regarding the deceptive performance involving the use of impaired limbs:
one [type] always has a foot that is stiff during a limping gait. BhN 12.132.
Likewise, the second foot should be placed on the ground with the toes;
then, the limb must be raised by means of the stiffened foot.
He may be seated with one foot advanced while the other remains behind;
he may sit with the other foot likewise, and indeed he should walk in this very sequence.
This "lame gait" (khañjagati) should be performed when there is a wound from a splinter in the sole;
for one should walk with the foot placed on its forepart and slightly drawn up.
The gait of a cripple is one where the body is hunched and the shanks are bent;
likewise, the gait of a dwarf is desired to be with all the limbs contracted.
One should not display prowess nor any shuffling of the feet;
she should be carried along with her feet covered in powder, acting with a deceptive nature.
The gait of the *vidūṣaka* is also accompanied by three types of laughter;
laughter produced by gesture and speech, and laughter arising from costume, is thus remembered.
One who has protruding teeth, is bald, hunchbacked, lame, or has a deformed face—if such a person should enter, that would constitute "bodily laughter" (aṅgahāsya). BhN 12.139.
But when one walks like a crane, looking here and there, and because of the improper placement of the feet, that person becomes an object of ridicule for his gait. (BhN 12.140)
One should recognize forced laughter through incoherent speech, meaningless gestures, and likewise through the utterance of vulgar words. (BhN 12.141)
O Brahmins, he who is adorned with rags, skins, ashes, red ochre, and so forth— such a person is merely ridiculous, for his [appearance] is born of mere dress.
Therefore, having understood primordial nature (prakṛti), one should act according to reality;
one should discern the movement of the states of existence, which consists of various internal conditions.
Having placed the *svabhāva* [mudrā] on the left hand, one should then form the *kuṭila* [mudrā] on the left hand and again form the *caturaka* [mudrā] on the right hand.
One should gradually bend one side of the body, as well as the head, hand, and foot,
following the rhythm and tempo of the laya.
This movement of his arises from his own nature, while another arises from transformation;
for one who is liberated from gain and loss, his movement becomes steady.
Indeed, it should be performed by low-born individuals such as servants and the like; furthermore, those who are known as "inferior" are of various characters.

The side-sprinkling (pārśvaseka), the head, the hand, and likewise the foot—these should be performed for the syllable Śa; and the movement should be that of a flickering body. In the movement, one should bow down like a servant, and the gaze should wander half-wardly.
By the touch of her garments and ornaments, by her repeated glances, by her limbs agitated with emotional changes, and likewise by her dangling garments and garlands; BhN 12.149.
The gait of Śakāra should be haughty and characterized by a stamping of the feet with powder;
it should be employed for those of low birth, while his gaze should be fixed upon looking around.
And because of their lack of contact with the world, they conceal their own limbs; as for the various tribes of Mlecchas, such as the Pulindas, Śabaras, and others— BhN_12.151.
O best of the twice-born, the actions, movements, and behavior of those birds, beasts of prey, and domestic animals must be observed according to their respective regions.
The gait should be performed by practitioners according to the nature arising from each respective species; thus, the gait of lions, bears, and monkeys must be executed.
That which was performed by Narasiṃha, the powerful Viṣṇu,
having assumed the *ālīḍha* stance, with his body following that very posture.
Placing one hand above the knee and the other on the chest, looking toward the directions, and resting the chin upon the head of the arm; BhN 12.155.
O Brahmins, one should move with strides rising at intervals of five tālas during the time of wrestling as well as when entering the arena.
This movement of the lion and others should be employed by performers; for the remaining [beasts], one should apply the movement and posture according to their respective characteristics.
In the employment of vehicles for purposes, and in entering the stage,
wise men should employ these human gaits in this manner.
Whatever [topics] have not been mentioned by me here, those should be understood from the world;
beyond this, I shall now declare the movements and gestures of women.
The postures, activities, and gaits of women, as well as their ornaments, and also the *āyatam*, the *avahittham*, and the *aśvakrāntam* [are described].
These are the positions for women; now their characteristic is described:
that in which the left foot is naturally placed flat.
With another [arm] placed at a distance of one palm-span, forming a triangle and positioned like a wing,
where the face is serene and the chest is level and well-elevated.
When the two hands rest upon the hips of a creeper-like posture, that stance is to be known as *āyata* (extended).
The right foot is even, while the other is triangular and situated on the side.
The left hip should be raised and the stance should be extended during invocation,
dismissal, and likewise during visualizations.
One should employ this position during moments of reflection and feigned indifference; it is used at the beginning of entering the stage and when casting the handful of flowers.
The anger arising from jealousy toward me, the snapping of fingers and the clenching of fists,
the silence of forbidding pride and depth, and the maintenance of self-respect.
In this place, one should determine the directions such that the left side is level where it stands, while the other side situated at the flank is triangular.
When the left hip is raised, that is the *avahittha* (the "concealed" gesture);
when it moves forward, it is the *tryaśra* (the "triangular"); and when it is moved toward the other side, it is the *sama* (the "even").
When one foot is placed between the beats (tāla), the three [parts of the body] are slightly raised;
where one hand is called "the creeper" (latā) and the other is placed on the hip, that is the [gesture]. (BhN 12.169)
This posture is called *avahittha* by those who adorn the traditions of the scriptures; it is considered the natural stance of women during conversation arising from their own disposition.

It is used in the sense of certainty and satisfaction, as well as in deliberation and reflection; likewise, it denotes playful charm, sportiveness, coquetry, erotic sentiment, and self-representation.
This position should be employed when observing the path for one's master:
one foot is placed flat on the ground, and the other is slightly raised with its forepart.
Whether pierced by a needle or not pierced at all, that is called "trodden by a horse";
as well as stumbling, reeling, and the wearing of garments that have slipped down.
Plucking clusters of flowers, guarding them, charmingly startling [the deer], and hanging from the branches of trees. (BhN 12.174)
In this place, the following should be arranged by those who employ women:
they should perform the act of hanging from branches as well as gathering clusters of blossoms.
Furthermore, during the rest periods of gods and humans, according to their respective purposes,
the state of standing still lasts only as long as physical activity continues.
If the standing posture is broken during a dance and a *cārī* (step) is about to be performed, this rule for the postures should be applied for both women and men. BhN 12.177.
Furthermore, I shall explain their movement as it exists in its natural state:
having assumed a posture of concealment (*āvahitthā*), one should place the left hand facing downwards.
Having placed the left hand in the *khaṭakāmukha* position at the region of the navel,
one should then raise the gracefully moving foot to the height of a *tāla*.
One should place the right foot on the outer side of the left foot;
at that very same moment, the left arm is called the "creeper" (latā).
One should bend the right side and place it upon the surface of the navel;
then, having placed the right hand on the hip, one should twist the left arm upward.
Then one should place the left foot forward and the right hand extended like a creeper,
with the head gracefully tilted upward and turned slightly toward it.
Then, with his body slightly bent, he should walk five steps;
such is the rule for men when circumambulating the stage-platform.
That very [measure] indeed should be employed for women by those who perform the drama;
however, the six-mora and likewise the eight-mora [measures] should not be used.
Falling at her feet is known by the experts as "causing distress" for a woman;
this is how the wise should conduct themselves toward women in the prime of their youth.
I shall now fully describe the movement of these more substantial [vows]:
having cast aside the [right] position and placing the left hand upon the hip.
One should make the first [hand] open-palmed and turned upward between the navel and the breasts;
it should not be resting, nor stiff, nor should it be rotated.
Having thus prepared her body, she should proceed by that very same sequence;
even for female servants, the gait should be performed with a graceful, swaying motion.
In some places, with her limbs raised and her arms extended in a display of prowess,
she assumes a pose of feigned indifference, while her left arm is bent downward.
Having placed the left hand in the *khaṭakāmukha* position at the region of the navel,
the movement of the Half-Woman (*ardhanārī*) should be performed, which is a mixture of both female and male gestures.
With limbs raised and graceful, and feet endowed with playful charm— this, indeed, is what was previously described by me as the gait of the most excellent beings.
One should apply half and half again of that [measure] for women and for cowards; likewise, one should apply it according to the gait and behavior of men who are middling, superior, or inferior.
That same [gait] should be performed by women with graceful strides;
it should also be performed by children with steps taken according to their own will.
Its excellence need not be considered, nor its measurement, by those who employ it;
it should be treated as a third gender and designated by the name "neuter. (BhN 12.194)
Having abandoned the male nature, one should apply the female state there;
the reverse should be applied in the case of male, female, and neuter.
Having abandoned one's own nature and attained the state of that [other] here in this world—
whether by means of a pretext, through play, or likewise by further deception— BhN 12.196.
A woman may adopt the nature of a man, and a man likewise the state of a woman,
through fortitude, generosity, goodness, intelligence, and similarly through action.
A woman, however, should represent a man through her dress, speech, and gestures,
as well as by adopting female attire and speech, and by acting as if she were sent or not sent.
A man with a gentle and steady gait may assume the state of a woman;
likewise, those women of low birth, such as the wives of Pulindas and Śabaras.

Furthermore, for those women who are established in vows, established in asceticism, or likewise established in sectarian marks, their destiny shall be one corresponding to that [of their respective] class.
For women who are standing, one should employ the *samapāda* stance; this applies to those *aṅgahāras* that are elevated, as well as to the noble *maṇḍalas*.
These [gestures] should not be performed by women by those skilled in the practice of drama;
likewise, the rules for posture should be observed by men, and especially by women.
Joined with various movements, resting upon a bed, with the feet extended and slightly bent, and the sacrum slightly raised. (BhN 12.203)
When sitting in a composed posture, both hands should be placed on the hips or thighs;
one leg may be slightly extended while the other rests upon the seat.
When sitting with anxiety, the head is bent to one side;
the hands rest upon the chin, and the head rests upon the shoulders.
With his senses and mind utterly lost in the sitting of grief and longing,
he stretched out his limp arms and leaned against a pillow.
In cases of delusion, fainting, intoxication, exhaustion, and despondency,
one should cause the patient to sit down with all the limbs drawn together and the feet joined with the knees.
A person should sit in meditation when afflicted by disease or overcome by shame, or when sleepiness arises;
likewise, one may adopt the *utkaṭika* posture, which is the bringing together of the buttocks and the heels.
During the ancestral offering (pitrya), the pouring of water (nivāpa), the recitation of prayers (japya), at the twilights (saṃdhyā), and even during the ritual sipping of water (ācamana),
one should likewise lower the knee to the ground once it has been drawn back.
In order to appease one's beloved and when performing oblations and other such rites,
one should remain with knees touching the ground and face turned downwards.
And likewise when approaching deities, when pacifying those who are enraged, in grief, during intense lamentation, and upon seeing the dead; BhN 12.211.
One should cause it to be performed for the purpose of terrifying base beings, for the begging of those who are lowly,
for the performance of fire-offerings and sacrifices, and for the sake of servants.
This rule regarding the arising of postures (āsana) shall apply to the observances of the sages;
likewise, various rules for postures based on dramatic performance should be performed.
For both women and men, there is that which is external and internal;
for a king, it is internal, whereas for one who has gone abroad, it is external.
A twice-born man should offer a lion-throne to the gods and to kings;
likewise, there should be a cane-seat for domestic priests and ministers.
A seat with a shaven head-pattern should be given to the commander-in-chief and the crown prince;
a wooden seat for the twice-born, and a rug seat for the princes.
Having thus entered the royal assembly, one should perform the ritual pertaining to taking one's seat;
furthermore, I shall now fully explain the rules for the seating of women.
A lion-throne should be given to the queens and princesses, a shaven-seat to the wives of the domestic priest and the ministers, and likewise a cane-seat to others.
Likewise, for the women who enjoy pleasures, there is clothing, skins, or even rugs;
and for Brahmin women and female ascetics, there is likewise a seat of woven cloth.
O twice-born ones, a peacock-feather seat should be provided for courtesans,
while for all other women there should be a seat made of the ground.

Thus should be known the internal procedure for the postures, as well as the external one; likewise, regarding the conduct within one's own home, the posture is prescribed according to one's inclination.

The rule concerning the posture of sages established in their observances shall apply; for those bearing sectarian marks, the procedure for posture should be performed in reliance upon their specific vows.
One should employ a seat consisting mostly of a grass mat, a shaven-seat, or even a cane seat for the performance of fire offerings, sacrificial rites, and ancestral ceremonies. (BhN 12.223)
And those local men who are endowed with noble lineage and learning—honors and seats should be provided for them here by kings. (BhN 12.224)

One should provide a seat of equal status; for one of middle rank, a middle seat; for one who is superior, a superior seat; and for one who is inferior, there should be a seat on the bare ground. (BhN 12.225)
In the presence of the preceptor, the king, and elders,
the wise should likewise use a seat made of earth or a wooden seat.
In boats, elephants, chariots, and vehicles, as well as on wooden seats upon the ground,
one does not incur fault by sitting together with one's preceptor, teacher, or a king.
Contracted, even, extended, and turned; raised up and bent—these are proclaimed as the movements for the act of lying down.
When both knees are pressed against the bed with all the limbs contracted,
one should employ this posture called *ākuñcita* for those afflicted by cold.
With the face turned upward and the hands likewise relaxed and released,
this posture of one who is sleeping soundly is designated as "sama" (even).
Placing one arm as a pillow with the knees fully extended, one should assume the posture named *prasārita*, suitable for sleeping comfortably. (BhN 12.231)
That which is situated face-down is known as "inverted" (vivartita);
one should employ it in cases of wounds from weapons, death, being cast down, intoxication, or insanity.
Placing the head upon the shoulder and even the agitation caused by camphor—
this is to be understood as the "raised" (udvāhita) gesture of the Lord during playful entry.
When both hands are allowed to hang down while the shanks are slightly extended, this posture, known as *nata*,
is prescribed for states of indolence, fatigue, and exhaustion.
This movement and conduct has been described by me; that which has not been stated should be accomplished according to the requirements of the situation.
Hereafter, I shall describe the division of the stages for the performance on the stage, complete with its distinct sections.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Movement of Gait," in the *Bharatīya Nāṭyaśāstra*.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter:
Regarding those three types of theatrical pavilions (*nāṭyamaṇḍapa*) which were previously described by me—
Having understood their classification, one should then apply the appropriate enclosure.
The performers should place the musical instruments between those two [doors] which were previously described by me as being at the door of the dressing room (nepathyagṛha). BhN 13.2.
The division of the zones (kakṣyā) should be indicated by moving around the stage platform;
for indeed, another zone is established by the movement across the stage.
Houses and cities are to be known according to the division of their enclosures;
likewise are gardens, groves, rivers, hermitages, and forests.
The earth and the oceans, the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving, the seven continents for years, and likewise various mountains.
The light and the world, as well as the netherworld (rasātala),
the abodes of the Daityas and Nāgas, and their houses and palaces.
Whether in a city or a forest, in a year or even on a mountain—
wherever news circulates, there one should establish the enclosure.
One should likewise imagine a location that is either external, intermediate, or internal; whether it be distant or near. BhN 13.8.
Those who have entered the arena first should be known by the wise as the insiders;
those who enter later should be understood as being on the outer part of the enclosure.
But he who, desiring to see them, enters the performance hall,
should then offer himself while facing the south.
That direction from which the vessel and the entrance to the dressing room (nepathya) are situated should be considered as the East in the application of drama; it is not fixed eternally.
And whoever should depart from that [place], he should likewise proceed by that very same path,
because the announcement was made for him by that person.
If he has already departed but should enter that house for the sake of some purpose,
the man from whom he received [the gift] should exit by the same path by which he arrived.
Or else, for the sake of a specific purpose, he may go along with that very person;
likewise, he may enter a house either alone or accompanied.
And as those two enter, one should designate another enclosure;
however, by means of circumambulating the stage, another enclosure is prescribed.
One should travel accompanied by those who are equal and surrounded by those who are lower;
furthermore, those who are merely onlookers should be known as being in the vanguard.
That very same ground may be distant due to many circumambulations;
one should thus distinguish whether it is middling or near for those [circumambulators]. (BhN 13.17)
Whether in a city or a forest, in the ocean or even on a mountain,
one should effect the travel of divine beings, or again, to islands and regions.
Whether by means of a celestial chariot traveling through the sky, or again through illusion, or by various activities performed for diverse purposes through application; BhN 13.19.
In a drama, the movement on earth of divine beings in disguised forms occurs so that they may be seen by humans for a specific purpose. (BhN 13.20)
Whether in Bhārata, or in Haimavata, or in Harivarṣa, Ilāvṛta, Ramya, Kimpuruṣa, or even in the Northern Kurus; BhN 13.21.
The movement of the divine [beings] at will among all the continents is celebrated; however, for humans, movement is ordained only within Bhārata.
If, however, due to the constraints of place and time, a man must go to a distant location, he should have his mark cut on another part during the introductory scene (*praveśaka*). BhN 13.23.
Having determined the duration of the day, one should predict the attainment of the task;
however, if the task is not attained, the cutting of the mark (aṅkaccheda) is prescribed.

In a one-act play (*ekāṅka*), the duration—whether a moment (*kṣaṇa*), a muhūrta, a watch (*yāma*), or even a day—should be determined according to the requirements of the plot’s seed (*bīja*). (BhN 13.25)
Once the marking has been completed, whether it be after a month or even a year, no further work involving the marks should be performed beyond that year.
Thus, in the land of Bhārata, the classification should be made according to practice;
now learn of the destiny of humans as well as that of the divine beings. BhN 13.27.
But on Kailāsa, the best of mountains, situated upon the back of the Himavat,
there were yakṣas, guhyakas, and those who are followers of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada).
The Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and Bhūtas are all known to dwell on Himavat;
and on Hemakūṭa, the Gandharvas together with the hosts of Apsarases are to be found.
All the Nāgas—Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and the rest—are on Niṣadha;
the wise should know that the thirty-three classes of gods reside on Mahāmeru.
On the blue mountain made of lapis lazuli dwell the Siddhas and the Brahman-sages; the Śveta mountain is said to belong to the Daityas and the Dānavas.
The Pitṛs are also to be known as residing upon Śṛṅgavan;
thus these excellent mountains are proclaimed to be divine abodes.
And this shall be the division of their zones within Jambūdvīpa;
nor is there any activity or purpose for them other than through their own respective karmic powers.
However, the distinction regarding their dimensions is like that in the world of humans; furthermore,
all divine entities must be conceived as having recourse to human forms.
However, that which constitutes their state of being unblinking need not be intentionally produced by performers;
for in this world, both the dramatic states (*bhāvas*) and the aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*) are established solely upon what is seen.
For a state of being indicated by the gaze is further manifested by the limbs;
thus, O best of the twice-born, have I described the division of the stages.
Furthermore, I shall explain the characteristics of the modes of performance (*pravṛtti*);
for four types of performance are proclaimed according to the application of drama:
the *Āvantī*, the *Dākṣiṇātyā*, the *Pāñcālī*, and the *Oḍhramāgadhī*. (BhN 13.37)

Here it is asked: why is it called "activity" (*pravṛtti*)? It is said: it is called "functioning" (*vṛtti*) because it makes known upon the earth various regions, costumes, languages, customs, and news.
And there is activity in the act of reporting.
Here he says: just as there are many regions on the earth, [so it is here].
How is it that these four types are established, given that their application is said to have identical characteristics?
This is true.
The application of these [vṛttis] possesses identical characteristics; however,
since the world consists of diverse regions, costumes, languages, and customs, I have [described] the vṛttis of drama— which relies on conduct— in accordance with worldly convention.
The fourfold nature has been declared as Sāttvatī, Kaiśikī, Ārabhaṭī, and Bhāratī.

And the regions have been declared by means of the applications based on these modes (vṛtti), since the fourfold activity has been brought forth and the performance (prayoga) has been produced. In that regard:

The [dramas] of the South, moreover, abound in dance, song, and instrumental music; they are characterized by the *kaiśikī* style and feature clever, sweet, and graceful bodily gestures and acting. For example: Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Mekala, and Pālamañjara.
The regions situated within these [mountains] should be known as the Deccan (Dakṣiṇāpatha).
The Kosalas, Agastas, Uśalas, Kaliṅgas, Yavanas, Khasas, Draviḍas, Āndhras, Mahārāṣṭras, Vaiṣṇas, and those born in Vanavāsa; BhN 13.39.
One should always employ the southern [mantras] in those countries that lie between the southern ocean and the Vindhya mountains.
The people of Āvantika, Vaidiśika, Saurāṣṭra, and Mālava;
likewise the Saindhavas, Sauvīras, Āvartas, and the inhabitants of Arbuda.
The Dāśārṇas, the Aitupuras, and likewise the Mārtikāvatas—
these always carry out the affairs of Avanti.
The performance in this drama should rely upon both the Sāttvatī and Kaiśikī styles; it is these that must be employed by the performers.
The Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, Vatsas, Uḍras, Māgadhas,
Pauṇḍras, and Nepālakas— those dwelling both within the mountains and beyond the mountains.
Likewise, the Plavaṅgamas, Maladas, Mallavartakas, those beginning with the Brahmottaras, the Bhārgavas, and the Mārgavas are to be known [as belonging to the same group]. BhN 13.45.
The Prājyotiṣas, Pulindas, Vaidehas, Tāmraliptakas,
Prāṅgas, and Prāvṛtas employ here the Uḍra-Māgadhī woman.
Furthermore, those other eastern regions which are celebrated in the Purāṇas—in them, this Uḍramāgadhī usage is indeed employed. (BhN 13.47)
The Pañcālas, the Saurasenās, the Kāśmīras, those from Hastināpura, the Bāhlīkas, the Śalyakas, as well as the Madras and the Kauśīnaras; BhN 13.48.
Those who dwell in the Himalayas and in the northern direction of the Gaṅgā,
among those inhabited regions, the Pāñcālas are considered the most central.
In the Pāñcālamadhyamā style, however, the Sāttvatī and Ārabhaṭī are prescribed;
its performance involves little singing and is characterized by agitated movements and valor.
Their movement across the stage is of two kinds:
clockwise and likewise counter-clockwise. (BhN 13.51)
The Āvantī and Dākṣiṇātyā follow a clockwise movement;
however, the Pāñcālī, Oḍhrī, and Māgadhī follow a counter-clockwise direction.
In the case of the Āvantī and Dākṣiṇātyā [styles], the north side-door is used;
however, in the Pāñcālī, Oḍhra, and Māgadhī [styles], the south door should be employed.
Furthermore, these [qualities] should be employed by practitioners as a unified whole,
having considered the assembly, the place and time, and the logic of the purpose.
In whatever regions whatever conduct has been proclaimed as appropriate,
a knower of that [conduct] should employ forms corresponding to that conduct in those places.
Furthermore, these [emotions] indeed become unified in dramas and similar works;
having observed the abundance of the *vṛttis*, one should perform each respective action accordingly. (BhN 13.56)
In a caravan, the wise man should ensure the majority of one [type of animal] while keeping the others in the minority;
he should then fulfill the requirements of activity for whichever group is most numerous.
Furthermore, the application (prayoga) based on drama should be understood as being of two kinds:
the delicate (sukumāra) and the piercing (viddha), both of which rely on the principles of dramatic performance (nāṭyayukti).
That which consists of pierced limbs and necklaces, characterized by cutting and piercing in combat, abounding in illusions and sorcery, and joined with puppets and costumes; BhN 13.59.
The dramatic performance known as Āviddha is characterized by many male actors and few female ones, and it likewise employs the Sāttvatī and Ārabhaṭī styles.
The *ḍima*, the *samavakāra*, the *vyāyoga*, and likewise the *īhāmṛga*—
these should be known by practitioners as having the designation "āviddha" (the mixed).
This application should be employed by Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas, as well as by those arrogant men who are endowed with heroism, valor, and strength. (BhN 13.62)
The drama (*nāṭaka*), along with the *prakaraṇa*, the *bhāṇa*, the *vīthī*, the *aṅka*, and the *nāṭikā*—these are compositions of delicate performance that rely upon human characters. (BhN 13.63)
Now, regarding external applications, the performance area may sometimes be located even in the intermediate directions, provided it is free from an audience hall and by the command of the Master.

Since the Bharatas maintain that the face [of the stage] is toward the west during a performance, those who know the art of drama should consider that direction as the east at the time of the performance. BhN 13.65.
And there are six doors for this stage, determined according to the cardinal directions,
indeed for the purpose of entering during the performance of a drama.
There is entry in the eastern and western directions.
And just as in a theatrical performance one may deviate from the prescribed rule and act in various directions without authority,
because the door is the source from which the musical instruments and vessels emerge.
One should mentally resolve upon that eastern direction.
First, the costume should be appropriate to the age; the movement and gait should be appropriate to the costume;
the recitation should follow the movement and gait, and the acting should be performed in accordance with the recitation.
O best of the twice-born, I have previously described the two-fold nature of the subject (dharmī);
I shall now state the characteristics of the worldly and the dramatic.
It has attained the state of being the intrinsic nature of existence; it is pure, unchanging, engaged in worldly discourse and activity, yet devoid of playful dalliance.
If a drama should consist of various male and female characters endowed with natural gestures and expressions, it is known as *lokadharmī*. (BhN 13.71)
It was endowed with the performance of excellent speech and actions, possessed of supreme courage and intense emotion,
characterized by graceful gestures, movements of the limbs, and dramatic expression, and marked by the defining features of the art of dance.
When a dramatic performance is endowed with vocal ornaments and based on characters who are not in their natural state, such a form is known as *nāṭyadharmī*.
When a substance well-known in the world is employed in drama as having a physical form and possessing desire, that is remembered as *nāṭyadharmin* (the dramatic convention). BhN 13.74.
When a sentence spoken nearby is not heard by one another, yet that unspoken sentence is nevertheless heard, this is known as *nāṭyadharmin*. (BhN 13.75)
Mountains, vehicles, celestial chariots, shields, armor, weapons, and banners are employed in embodied forms; that is traditionally known as the dramatic convention (*nāṭyadharma*).
When one performs another stage after having completed one,
either due to skill or because of its singleness, that is known as *nāṭyadharmī*.
A woman who, having been a permissible partner, is joined with permissible stages,
yet becomes impermissible on those same permissible stages— that is known as the dramatic convention (*nāṭyadharmin*).
That which is danced and that which is walked with graceful arrangements of the limbs as well as with raised steps is known as *nāṭyadharmin*.
This very nature of the world, consisting of the performance of pleasure and pain,
when joined with the representation of limbs and gestures, is known as the dramatic art (nāṭyadharmī).
That which is the meaning of the Itihāsas and Vedas as proclaimed by Brahmā for the sake of divine and human delight is known as the dramatic art (nāṭyadharmī).
And this division of the zones, which relies on various rules and is described as pertaining to the stage platform, shall indeed constitute the dramatic convention (nāṭyadharmin).
One should always employ drama that is engaged in dramatic convention (*nāṭyadharmī*);
for no passion (*rāga*) arises apart from the representation of the limbs (*aṅgābhinaya*). (BhN 13.83)
Every state of being is innate, for every gesture is inherently meaningful;
thus, the dramatic art is proclaimed to consist of the movements of limbs and ornaments.
Thus, the classification of the sections (kakṣyā-vibhāga), as well as the subject matter (dharmin) and the logical arguments (yukti),
should be understood by those who know the true principles of drama and applied according to their essential nature.
I have duly explained here the enactment performed through the *śākhās* and that which is performed by means of *aṅgahāras*;
furthermore, I shall now describe the enactment of speech (*vākyābhinaya*) as it truly is, joined with vowels, consonants, and phonemes.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Nature of Hand-Gestures," in the *Bharatīya Nāṭyaśāstra*.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter:
"O best of the twice-born, that which was previously described by me as the dramatic representation of speech (*vāgabhinaya*)," [is now to be explained].
I shall explain its characteristics, which arise from vowels and consonants.
Effort must be exerted in speech, for this is considered the body of drama; indeed, it is the limbs, costume, and internal state that manifest the meaning of the words.
In this world, the scriptures consist of speech and are likewise established upon speech;
therefore, there is nothing higher than speech, for speech is indeed the cause of everything.

Vocal acting (vācikābhinaya) consists of that which is joined with verbs, nouns, particles, prefixes, compounds, and secondary derivatives; and it is further characterized by euphonic combination (sandhi), verbal forms, case endings, and voice (upagraha). (BhN 14.4)
For recitation is traditionally held to be of two kinds: Sanskrit and likewise Prākṛta.
I shall explain their distinction correctly and in due order.
Consonants and vowels, as well as euphonic combinations, case endings,
nouns, verbs, prefixes, particles, and likewise secondary derivatives.
Through these components and combinations, the refined speech (saṃskṛta) based on various phonemes is to be understood; now learn its recitation and its practical application. BhN 14.7.
The fourteen vowels are to be known as beginning with *a* and ending with *au*;
the wise know the consonants to be those beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*.
In that regard, there are fourteen vowels: a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, e, ai, o, and au; these are to be known as the vowels.
The consonants beginning with *ka*, as follows: *ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa; ca, cha, ja, jha, ña; ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa; ta, tha, da, dha, na; pa, pha, ba, bha, ma; ya, ra, la, va;
śa, ṣa, sa, ha*. This is the class of consonants (*vyañjanavarga*).
In each group, two letters are declared to have been situated previously;
those others which are unvoiced (aghoṣa) are proclaimed to be voiced (saghoṣa).
There are eight places for the articulation of phonemes: the chest, the throat, and likewise the head; the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate. BhN 14.10.

The letters *a*, *ku* (the gutturals), and the *visarjanīya* are guttural (*kaṇṭhya*). The letters *i*, *cu* (the palatals), *ya*, and *śa* are palatal (*tālavya*). The letters *ṛ*, *ṭu* (the retroflexes), *ra*, and *ṣa* are retroflex (*mūrdhanya*).
The sounds *ḷ*, *la*, and *sā* are dental; *u* and the *upadhmānīya* are labial;
and the sounds *-pa* and *-pha* are those preceding *p* and *ph*.
The *upadhmānīya* resembles half a *visarga*.
The *jihvāmūlīya* resembles half a *visarga* and occurs before the letters *ka* and *kha*.
E and ai are guttural-palatal; o and au are guttural-labial;
the letter va is dental-labial.
The letters ṅa, ña, ṇa, na, and ma are nasalized (anunāsika).
Some say that the *visarjanīya* is produced from the chest (*aurasya*).
Others say that [the letter *s*] is the mouth and the place of articulation for all the consonants (*varṇa*).

However, the first two letters of each group (*varga*), as well as the three others—*ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*—are proclaimed to be voiceless (*aghoṣa*), while the remaining ones are voiced (*ghoṣavat*). (BhN 14.11)
These sounds—both voiced and voiceless, guttural, labial, dental, and nasalized, as well as the sibilants (*ūṣman*) and the *visarjanīya*—should be understood as palatal. (BhN 14.12)
The sounds *ga, gha, ṅa; ja, jha, ña; ḍa, ḍha, ṇa; da, dha, na; ba, bha, ma*; as well as *ya, ra, la, va*, are considered voiced (*ghoṣa*).
*Ka, kha; ca, cha; ṭa, ṭha; ta, tha; pa, pha*—these in their respective classes (*varga*) are unvoiced (*aghoṣa*). (BhN 14.13)
Ka, kha, ga, gha, and ṅa are located in the throat; ca, cha, ja, jha, and ña are located in the palate; ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, and ṇa are retroflex (mūrdhan); and ta, tha, da, dha, and na are dental.
The letters *pa*, *pha*, *ba*, *bha*, and *ma* are labials (*oṣṭhya*); *ḷ*, *la*, *sa*, *ha*, and *aḥ* are dentals (*dantya*); *ka* and *ha* are gutturals (*kaṇṭhastha*);
*i*, *ca*, *ya*, and *śa* are palatals (*tālavya*); and *ṛ*, *ṭa*, *ra*, and *ṣa* are known to be retroflex (*mūrdhasthita*). (BhN 14.15)
Ḷ and ḹ are dental; o and au are labio-velar; e and ai are velar-palatal;
the visarga is velar; and the jihvāmūlīya arises at the root of the tongue before the sounds k and kh. (BhN 14.16)
The letter *u* is the vowel produced at the position of the lips, which are spread apart (*vivṛta*).
The consonants from *ka* to *ma* are produced by contact (*spṛṣṭa*), while *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, *ha*, and *kara* (the semivowels) are likewise spread apart (*vivṛta*).

The semi-vowels (antasthā) are born from the closed [lips], while ṅa, ña, ṇa, na, and ma are known to arise from the nose; likewise, the sibilants (ūṣman)—śa, ṣa, sa, and ha—and the letters ya, ra, la, and va are also semi-vowels.
The jihvāmūlīya (the *k* sound) and the upadhmānīya (the *p* sound) are to be known by their respective technical names.
The sounds *k, c, ṭ, t,* and *p* are svarita; *kh, ch, ṭh, th,* and *ph* are always to be pronounced with a krama-utterance.
