One should know that the sounds g, j, ḍ, d, b, and bh are produced from the throat and the chest when applied in recitation; however, the letter *visarjanīya* is to be known as a sound situated in the position of the tongue.
These consonants have been briefly described by me according to their designations;
I shall now further explain the vowels in their application within the domain of speech.
That place [of articulation] should be known as "sama" (even), which is designated by the term *savarṇa* (homogeneous).
Of these fourteen vowels that have been specified, ten indeed are *samāna* (similar).
Among them, the former is to be understood as short (*hrasva*), and the latter as long (*dīrgha*).

In this way, through the conjunctions of consonants and vowels, as well as by means of verbs, nouns, and established words—including roots, particles, and prefixes—there arise compositions of poetry. (BhN 14.23)
A word is said to be that which is governed by these classes of phonemes— nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles— as well as secondary derivatives, euphonic combinations, and case endings.
The definition of words has been stated by the former teachers through the application of compound formations;
however, I shall explain it again in detail according to the requirements of the present treatise.
A noun is primarily concerned with meaning, whereas a verb is formed by action;
however, prefixes (upasargas) illuminate the specific distinction inherent in the state of being.
They say that this [object] is of seven kinds, associated with the six factors of action (kārakas), and is well-known as that which is to be accomplished (sādhya),
under such designations as "specification" (nirdeśa), "recipient" (saṃpradāna), "removal" (apādāna), and so forth.
They indicate a distinction regarding the meaning of nouns and verbs;
therein, in the unchanging rule, particles are distinct from prefixes.

Now, a statement that is joined with past actions and so forth, whose probandum is well-known, and which is not connected to the future, is distinguished by its highly similar conjunctions. (BhN 14.29)
This [grammar] consists of five hundred topics, possesses five qualities, and is of five kinds;
it is an arrangement adorned with specific meanings through the qualities of the functions of the suffixes (*svādya-adhikāra-guṇa*) and the particularities of meaning.
It should be known as being of five kinds when joined with the meanings of nominal stems (*prātipadika-artha*) and gender (*liṅga*). (BhN 14.30)
That which is known as the verb (ākhyāta) is produced by verbal roots; it is characterized by various meanings and specific grammatical distinctions.
A statement accompanied by nouns and divided according to persons—that is the verb.

For it has been taught in this treatise on grammatical refinement that prefixes (*upasarga*) are those which, by means of their own meanings, add to the meanings of verbal roots (*dhātu*) already joined with the meanings of nominal stems (*prātipadika*). (BhN 14.32)
Because they fall upon a word through their connection with the meaning of a nominal stem (prātipadika), and by virtue of their application as verbal roots, meters, or etymologies,
they are therefore called *nipātas*.

Because it fulfills the objects [of cognition] through the distinctions of conditions (*pratyaya*), as well as through excellence, conjunction, and the expression of existence, it is therefore called "condition" (*pratyaya*). (BhN 14.34)

In the world, by means of words consisting of the combination and union of bases and suffixes, as well as those expressing existence, he fulfills various meanings; therefore, that which pertains to them is called *taddhita*.
Because they divide the meaning of a single stem, or of many stems, or of many words, or of a gender,
they are therefore called *vibhaktis* (case-endings).
Because vowels that are modified, or even consonants,
are joined together within a word through grammatical application, it is therefore proclaimed as *sandhi*.
Because it is established through the sequence of letters and words, and because it arises from the conjunction of words as well as the conjunction of letters,
and because it is joined together (*sandhīyate*), it is therefore designated as *saṃdhi*.
O Brahmins, a compound (*samāsa*), which merges the single meaning of nouns whose case-endings have been elided, is designated by the names *tatpuruṣa* and so forth, and is of six kinds.
By means of these prescribed words, which are joined with extensive phonetic embellishments and meanings,
compositions of phrases should be made, whether they be fixed compositions or prose (cūrṇa).

A word should be understood as that which ends in a case-ending, whether it be composed or even a mere fragment (cūrṇa). In this regard, learn here the definition of a "fragment-word" (cūrṇapada). BhN 14.41.
The wise should know that *cūrṇapada* consists of unbound words, with syllables not fixed by the rules of prosody, where the syllables are strung together in accordance with the sense. (BhN 14.42)

That which is joined with fixed syllables and endowed with the proper pauses (yati), being composed of words whose nature is determined by specific measures, should be known as "composed" (nibaddha) verse. BhN 14.43.
Thus, a meter endowed with four feet, joined with various meanings and adorned with phonemes, shall be designated by the name *vṛtta*. BhN 14.44.
By these feet, twenty-six types are traditionally recorded in terms of numerical count within prosody:
the even, the half-even, and likewise the uneven.
In brief, it is held that there are three types of *vṛtta* (prosodic meters) joined with *chandas* (metre);
this body of sound is known to be produced from various *vṛttis*.
There is no word devoid of *chandas* (prosodic meter), nor is there *chandas* devoid of words;
therefore, the union of these two is traditionally held to be the illuminator of drama (*nāṭya*).

That which consists of one syllable is said to be *uktam*; that which consists of two syllables is *atyuktam*. They say that which consists of three syllables is *madhyam*, and that which consists of four syllables is *pratiṣṭhā*.
The *supratiṣṭhā* consists of five syllables; here, the *gāyatrī* consists of six.
The *uṣṇih* consists of seven syllables, and that which has eight syllables is called the *anuṣṭubh*.
The *bṛhatī* has nine syllables, the *paṅkti* has ten syllables,
the *triṣṭubh* has eleven syllables, and the *jagatī* has twelve syllables.
The *atijagatī* has thirteen syllables, while the *śakvarī* has fourteen;
the *atiśakvarī* has fifteen, and the *aṣṭi* is proclaimed to have sixteen. (BhN 14.51)
The *atyaṣṭi* consists of seventeen syllables; the *dhṛti* has eighteen syllables;
the *kṛti* has nineteen syllables, and likewise twenty.
The twenty-first is Prakṛti; likewise, the twenty-second is Akṛti;
the twenty-third would be Vikṛti, and the twenty-fourth is Saṃkṛti.
An *atikṛti* consists of twenty-five syllables, while an *utkṛti* consists of twenty-six; a meter with more syllables than that is considered a *mālāvṛtta*.
For likewise, due to the application of expansion (prastāra), these varieties of meters are said by the wise to be of an incalculable measure. BhN 14.55.
The measure of these [meters] is established as beginning with the *gāyatrī*;
for almost all those born of formal application do not exist. (BhN 14.56)
Sixty-four meters are proclaimed in the Gāyatrī [section],
while one hundred and twenty-eight meters are now described for the Uṣṇih.
There are two hundred and fifty-six verses in the Anuṣṭubh meter; there are five hundred and twelve verses in the Bṛhatī meter. BhN 14.58.
In the Paṅkti meter there are one thousand and twenty-four verses;
in the Triṣṭubh meter there are two thousand and forty-eight. (BhN 14.59)
There are four thousand, ninety-six in total,
of all the even-syllabled meters in this world.
In the Jagatī meter, when preceded by [the prefix] *ati*, the total number of metrical feet (*vṛtta*) is eight thousand, one hundred and ninety-two.
The total number of verses in the Śakvarī metre is sixteen thousand three hundred and eighty-four.
Thirty-two thousand,
seven hundred and sixty-eight syllables indeed constitute the *atiśakvarī* metre.
In number, sixty-five thousand and five hundred verses,
as well as thirty-six chapters, have been proclaimed in this [work].
In the section known as Atyaṣṭi, there are one hundred thousand, thirty-one thousand, and seventy-two verses.
For even within Dhṛti, the modes of conduct (vṛtta) are fashioned as aggregates by those who know them:
two hundred thousand, and likewise one hundred.
Sixty-two thousand and forty [verses] are derived from yoga;
and four [additional] verses are based on equal numerical proportions.
In *atidhṛti*, there are twenty-four thousand,
as well as five hundred thousand and two hundred and seventy-six syllables.
And eighty-eight meters have been described by those who know meters;
in the Kṛta age, they are said to number one million in total.
In terms of the number of verses, it consists of forty-eight thousand,
one hundred and seventy-six.
Likewise, in the case of hundreds of thousands, there would be twenty;
here, seven are indeed declared by way of number, as well as ninety.
One hundred and fifty-two thousand verses have been declared by those who know the meters according to their metrical measure.
In number, there are forty-one hundred thousand,
as well as ninety-four thousand here.
It is declared that there are three hundred and four [verses] in the Ākṛti;
the wise should know that there are eighty-three thousand [verses] in total.
Eighty-eight thousand, six hundred,
and eight verses have been declared in the Vikṛti.
Likewise, there are one hundred and sixty-seven thousand, seven thousand, and two hundred [years]. (BhN 14.76)
Indeed, ten million verses were spoken here in the *Saṃhitā*, and thirty-five million in the *Ābhikṛtī*. (BhN 14.77)
And likewise, with fifty-four thousand,
four hundred, and thirty-two [additional units].
Sixty million, seventy-one hundred thousand, eight hundred and sixty-four, and eight thousand [years] indeed. (BhN 14.79)
The wise one should indicate the number of possible variations for these meters, from the stated minimum up to the maximum, by means of this calculation.
Thus, indeed, the meters for all the Vedic chants have been described:
three crores, ten thousand, and one hundred [verses].
Forty-two thousand, ten, seven hundred, and seven [years]. BhN 14.82.
Twenty-six other [types] have been explained here in brief;
indeed, they are described as being equal by relying on the logic of enumeration. (BhN 14.83)
In this manner, one should employ the meter for all poetic feet (chandas) by means of triplets;
there, eight triplets are to be known by their names as *sthāna* and *acchara*.
Three syllables are to be understood as the threefold constituent part (aṃśa) conceived [as a foot],
produced by heavy and light syllables, which is constant in all meters.
The syllable *bha* has a heavy vowel preceding it; in the case of *ma*, there are three heavy syllables;
*ja* has a heavy syllable in the middle; and likewise, *sa* has a heavy syllable at the end.

The letter *ra* situated between two light syllables, followed by a *ta* that is a final light syllable, and a *ya* preceded by a light syllable—whereas in the case of *na*, there are three light syllables. (BhN 14.87)
For these eight triads should be understood by the wise as originating from Brahman;
furthermore, they are presented thus for the sake of brevity and with regard to the knowledge of prosody.
From these [mātrās], other types such as the *samā* and so forth—
both those without vowels and those with vowels— are described by means of the characteristics of their metrical feet (*vṛtta*).
A single *g* is to be known as heavy (*guru*), and likewise a single *l* is remembered as light (*laghu*).
The fixed pause in the division of words is designated as *yati*.

A syllable is heavy if it is long (guru), protracted (pluta), or followed by a conjunct consonant; likewise, it is heavy if it is accompanied by an anusvāra or a visarga, or if it is final. However, in some cases, even such a syllable may be light.
In the *gāyatrī*, two triplets (*trika*) are to be known; the *uṣṇik* has one additional syllable;
the *anuṣṭubh* has two more; and in the *bṛhatī*, there are three triplets. (BhN 14.92)
A *paṅkti* has one more syllable [than a *gāyatrī*], and a *triṣṭubh* has two more;
a *jagatī* consists of four *tripads*, while an *ati-jagatī* has one more [syllable] than that. (BhN 14.93)
A *śakvarī* is known to have two [syllables] in excess [of thirty-two]; an *atiśakvarī* has three [in excess].
An *aṣṭi* has one syllable in excess [of forty], and an *aty-aṣṭi* is said to have two [in excess].
Six times three is said to be *dhṛti*; likewise, one more than that is *atidhṛti*;
and two more than that is said to be *kṛti*. Indeed, there are seven groups of three in *prakṛti*.
Ākṛti has one additional [syllable], and likewise vikṛti has two;
in saṃkṛti there would be three times eight, and abhikṛti again has one more.
The *utkṛti* meter should be known as having two more [syllables] than the *gaṇa* count.

A single heavy syllable is called "ga," and two heavy syllables are traditionally known as "gāu. A single light syllable is to be known as "la," and two light syllables are traditionally known as "lāu. (BhN 14.97)

Prosody (chandas) consists of the rules regarding *saṃpad*, *virāma*, and *pāda*; the syllable (*akṣara*) as the locus of the deity; and the phoneme (*varṇa*), the vowel (*svara*), the rule (*vidhi*), and the meter (*vṛtta*). BhN 14.98.
Wherein the sequence is neither excessive nor deficient in its arrangement of meters, this is designated as "sampad" (perfection). BhN 14.99.
That point where the sense of a passage is completed is known as a *virāma* (pause);
and a *pāda* (quarter-verse) is known as a fourth part of the verbal root *pad*.
The deities beginning with Agni are proclaimed; their abode is said to be twofold:
that which arises based on the body and that which is based on the directions.
The bodily [mantra] born of mantra, known as the Gāyatrī metre, is declared to be at midday during the *kruṣṭa* [period]; it is celebrated as being of the *traiṣṭubha* [nature].
The third pressing (tṛtīyasavana) is indeed the head, characterized by the Jagatī meter;
moreover, the syllable is traditionally held to be of three kinds: short, long, and protracted.
Likewise, the colors of the meters (chandas) here should be understood as white and so forth;
furthermore, the threefold musical tone consists of the high (tāra), the low (mandra), and the middle (madhyama).
I shall also fully explain the characteristics of its placement on the *dhruvā* ladle;
the procedure shall be performed by the group of priests as well as for the sake of the ritual purpose.
O best of the twice-born, if according to one’s preference a syllable should be deficient or even redundant in a quarter-verse, it is declared to be *nicṛt* or *bhūri*, respectively.
That which is always two syllables more or less than [the standard] should be known by name as *svarāṭ* or also as *virāṭ*. (BhN 14.107)
The experts in these meters should know that for all types of *vṛtta*, there are three classes:
the divine (*divya*), the non-divine (*divyetara*), and the divine-human (*divyamānuṣa*).
Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti,
Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī— this is the first, divine group.
Likewise, there are the *atijagatī*, the *śakvarī*, the *atiśakvarī*,
the *aṣṭi*, the *atyaṣṭi*, the *dhṛti*, and the class known as *atidhṛti*.
Kṛti and Prakṛti, as well as Ākṛti and Vikṛti, Saṃkṛti and Abhikṛti, and Utkṛti, who is both divine and human. BhN 14.111.
I shall further explain the characteristics of these meters based on the rules for their expansion (prastāra), as well as the methods for determining lost (naṣṭa) and indicated (uddiṣṭa) verses.
The *prastāra* is indeed specified by syllables (*akṣara*) and likewise by morae (*mātra*).
When two [shorts] are denoted as "ga" and "la," it is called "specified by syllables"; when mixed, it is also called "specified by morae. (BhN 14.113)
Below the first [syllable] in the initial arrangement (prastāra), one should place a short (laghu) syllable;
however, long (guru) syllables are to be taken from the front as well as from behind.
In all meters, the method of expansion (*prastāra*) indeed consists of [identifying] the first [syllable] by its heavy syllables (*guru*), while those at the end are light (*laghu*). (BhN 14.115)
Having placed a light syllable beneath a heavy one, and likewise two by two as prescribed, one should place them;
this is the method for the *prastāra* (metrical expansion) always taught according to the syllables.
A *gaṇa* is defined by its number of morae (*mātrā*) and is composed of various combinations of morae;
it should be understood that the *gaṇas* *ga*, *la*, and *miśra* (the mixed *gaṇa*) are distinct according to their specific characteristics.
When the group of morae is characterized as heavy (guru) and light (laghu),
the expansion of four-mora units for the Āryā meters is thus conceived.
For the *gītaka* and other such forms, a group of five morae (*mātrā*) is prescribed;
likewise, for the *vaitālīya*, there are six morae and so forth.
The three-syllable [feet] are to be known as trikas, consisting of light and heavy syllables;
the division of the groups of morae (mātrās), however, depends upon heavy and light syllables.
From the last form, having doubled it, one [unit] shall become the heavy syllable;
having doubled the light syllables, one should add that number to the total sum.
The first [meter] should be known as having all heavy syllables, while that which is called *sama* consists of equal [heavy and light syllables].
The *kośa* has all light syllables at the end, while those of mixed form exist everywhere.

Having combined the number of those meters that are equal in their metrical feet, one should designate as many [meters] as there are from the total, provided they are deficient in quantity by half and are uneven. (BhN 14.123)
Having established a numerical sequence beginning with one according to the meter,
one should fill each subsequent group with the preceding number until it is complete.
Having clearly multiplied both the even and the odd [quantities],
one should likewise understand the sums of the odd numbers that are less than a given number, in brief.
Having thus completed the prior filling for all the others,
one should release each [element] in reverse order, ending with the dissolution.
Thus, understand the determination of light syllables for all meters, as well as the enumeration of even meters (samavṛtta) in brief.
Having halved the measure of the established [meter] in due order, one should place a light syllable such that it is preceded by one, and likewise a heavy syllable. BhN 14.128.
Having thus arranged the circles according to the division of the lost and the indicated,
one should demonstrate the heavy and light syllables here in all meters.
"O best of the twice-born, understand those meters which I have mentioned here that are to be employed in their respective prosodic forms within this drama. (BhN 14.130)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Prescription of Metres," in the Bharata Śāstra on Dramaturgy, concerning the enactment of speech.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter:
"O best of the twice-born, those very metres which have thus been described by me here..."
Learn now those *vṛttas* which are to be employed in this drama. (BhN 15.1)
If, however, in the first [foot] there are two [syllables], and in the last two [feet] there are two heavy syllables each,
that would be the Tanumadhyā, arising from the Gāyatrī.
For example:
"O slender-waisted one, why are you with your ornaments cast off, your eyes devoid of collyrium, and your cheek resting upon your hand? (BhN 15.3)
In the beginning there is a group of four light syllables;
at the end is a pair of heavy syllables: this is Makarakaśīrṣā.
For example:
"O Makarakaśīrṣā, you who cause fear, why do you not accept a lover who approaches you of his own accord? (BhN 15.5)
If there is one [short] syllable in the sixth [foot] and a second [short syllable] in the foot,
that meter, whose form is well-known, is by name called Mālinī.
When a foot consists of six syllables and the second one is short while the remaining ones are long, that is considered to be *mālinī*, as for example: [BhN 15.7].
By your excellence in bathing, perfumes, garments, and ornaments,
it is evident that you are known as Mālinī.
Where the second and fifth syllables are established as light,
and the remaining syllables are heavy, that is named Mālatī, as follows.
The proud woman shines with playful grace, adorned with a garland of jasmine flowers strung together and threaded by bees.
When the second, fourth,
and fifth syllables of its seven-syllable foot are short, that [meter] should be known as Uddhatā, as follows.
If there are three *tri*s in each quarter and the final syllable is indeed the letter *ga*,
it is called by the name *Uddhatā*, arising from the *uṣṇih* meter.
Your face, with its teeth-bites and disheveled locks of hair,
seems to proclaim your merciless battle of love.
Wherein the first two syllables and the final one are always heavy in a seven-syllable foot, that should be known by the name *Bhramaramālikā*.
If, at every foot, the *tsa* and *sa* are properly placed and arranged,
and there is a *ga* at the end, that is the *bhramaramālā*.
For example:
"When the fragrant month has arrived, variegated with various flowers, this intoxicated swarm of bees wanders about, O beloved. (BhN 15.16)
The first, third, last, fifth, and likewise the seventh syllables are heavy in an eight-syllable foot; that is the *siṃhalekhā*, as follows: [BhN 15.17].
When a *ga* never occurs in its foot, which otherwise consists of equal syllables,
they call that *anuṣṭubh* residing in that form the *siṃhalekhā*.
O fair-limbed one, those deeds performed by you in secret through many guises have entered my mind today, like a letter written in the Siṃhala script.
Where the fourth, second, sixth,
and eighth syllables of the eight-syllable foot are heavy, that is called *mattaceṣṭita*.
But when the letters *ra* and *la* follow the *ja*-type [opening], and the letter *ga* alone stands [at the end],
they call that the *mattaceṣṭita*, which arises from the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
For example:
"With eyes rolling in her gait, with her hair disheveled and hanging down, and with unsteady steps, my beloved performs the gestures of one intoxicated. (BhN 15.22)
When all the syllables in a foot of eight syllables are indeed heavy,
that [meter] is celebrated by the name Vidyunmālā.
That *anuṣṭubh* meter in which the last two syllables of each quarter-verse are short (*mau gau*) and there is a pause at the end of the verse, is always called *vidyunmālā* by the wise.
While the sky is pervaded by dark clouds that roar with their burden of water,
this garland of lightning wanders through the quarters, vying with the rays of the sun.
In an eight-syllable foot, the fifth, seventh, and last syllables are heavy; this meter is known by those who understand prosody as *cittavilāsita*.
O fair-limbed one, these marks of your teeth, radiant with the power of your smile, eclipse the full moon of your face.
When a foot consists of nine syllables and has three heavy syllables at the end,
that [meter] is to be known by the name Madhukarī.
If there are six short syllables here, and if the letter *a* occurs at the end of the *nidhana*,
it is the *madhukarī* by name, which has the structure of the *budhajanabṛhatī*.
Beholding the forest covered with various clusters of blossoming trees and exceedingly rich in fragrance, the female bee wanders about delighted.
In a verse consisting of ten syllables per quarter, where there are three heavy syllables at the beginning and three at the end,
that *paṅkti* meter is known as the *utpalamālikā*.
If there are three heavy syllables at the beginning, four light syllables in the middle,
and the letter 'a' at the end of the line, it should be known as the meter called *Kuvalayamālā*.
For example:

"Upon this head of yours, which is so lovely and enriched with lapis lazuli, crystal, and gold, this garland of blue water-lilies, though beautifully and tightly bound, does not bear its own natural splendor. (BhN 15.33)
Where the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth syllables are short in a foot of ten syllables, that is Śikhisāriṇī.
If the first three feet are identical and the fourth foot has *ga* and *sa* [as its opening] with the same *ta* and *sa* following,
that meter, having well-established limbs through the combination of *paṅkti*, is known by the name *mayūrasāriṇī*.
"Just as you have no union with men, nor any other sign of enjoying sensual pleasures,
yet you appear like one pregnant, O ignoble woman— why are you acting like a peahen? (BhN 15.36)
That [meter] in which the first, fourth, last (twelfth), seventh,
and tenth syllables of the Triṣṭubh foot are heavy is indeed the Dodhaka.

If the ganas of a verse consist of "bha," "au," and "bha-ga-va" (bha-au-bha-ga-va), and there is a pause after three or four syllables, that is indeed the Traiṣṭubha meter; they call it by the name Dodhaka-vṛtta. (BhN 15.38)
For example:

"Behold, O graceful woman, this elephant, with its stumbling gait that does not reach the forepart of the feet, and the playful movement of its intoxicated, reeling limbs; it performs the *dodhaka* meter. (BhN 15.39)
Where the first two syllables, as well as the fifth, eighth,
and likewise the final (twelfth) syllable of the foot are long, and the eleventh is also long, that is the *moṭaka* metre, as follows.
This elephant, roaring with a sound like a thundercloud, intoxicated and with a stumbling, slow gait,
hears the roar of the clouds on the mountain slope and crushes the trees.
The ninth, seventh, sixth, and third syllables shall be short;
in all circumstances, you are fit for the Kāma-tantra—what need is there for much more? You are indeed Indravajrā.

But when those same [syllables] are joined with light syllables in the *traiṣṭubha* meter, it is to be known as *upendravajrā*, provided that here [the first syllable] is exclusively a light syllable. (BhN 15.44)

"O beloved, through your splendor, your specific complexion, your smile, your radiance, and your delicate qualities—these virtues are indeed worthy of your beauty; yet, are you Upendravajrā? (BhN 15.45)
Where the first, third, fifth, seventh, and likewise the ninth syllables,
as well as the eleventh, are heavy in the foot, that is indeed *rathoddhatā*.

O brave warrior, what have you avoided from afar that was not dear to yourself or to your friends, such that now, as you are intent on flight, the dust raised by your chariot passes over you? (BhN 15.47)
For example:

"Why, O woman of evil intent, have you never done what is pleasing to your friends at their command? That an unprotected woman, trembling with anger at your words, should depart so swiftly from the house like a *rathoddhatā* meter! (BhN 15.48).
That [verse] in which the first, third, fifth, seventh, and tenth syllables of the *triṣṭubh* foot are heavy is to be known as *svāgatā*. (BhN 15.49)
For example:

"O lady with beautiful eyes, today my life has become fruitful through its state of being the refuge of love, since you have come to my abode; welcome to you, O fair-thighed one, please be seated. (BhN 15.50)
If the sixth and ninth syllables are light in a pāda of the Triṣṭubh meter, while the others are heavy, that is to be known as Śālinī. (BhN 15.51)
Whether toward one who is immoral, devoid of virtue, or even another in this world, you do not speak unpleasantly out of fortitude;
therefore, for the sake of the virtuous, may you always be graced with excellent conduct and sweetness through your moral discipline.
Where the third, sixth, ninth, and likewise the twelfth syllables in a foot of the Jagaṭī meter are heavy, that is the Toṭaka.

If it consists here of three *samudra* gaṇas and likewise a *yati* (caesura) after the third [syllable], and is thus constantly extended throughout the world, this is indeed declared to be the *toṭaka* meter. (BhN 15.54)
For example:

"Why do you employ this *toṭaka* meter, which is so difficult to endure due to its reliance on artifice, full of deceit, and characterized by harsh and excessive speech; for it surely causes division between one's own kin and virtuous friends? (BhN 15.55)
If the first, third, last, fifth, sixth,
and likewise the penultimate syllable are long in the Jagatī meter, it is Kumudaprabhā.
If there are two *trika* [groups] as well as two *nya* [groups], and if indeed the pause occurs after exactly six syllables in the foot,
that which is eternally established in the arrangement of the *jagatī* meter is known by the name *kumudanibhā*.
Just as:

"Pierced by the god of love, full of graceful gestures, engaged in dance and song, with eyes wide open—why are you so blameworthy today, devoid of splendor, like a night-lotus pond joined with the rays of the moon? (BhN 15.58)
According to another opinion:

If indeed, in the *jagatī* meter, the *nyau* (na, ya) occur in the first foot and the *trika* (ta, ta, ga) in the second, with the caesura likewise occurring at the sixth syllable, that which is eternally established in the arrangement of *jagatī* is renowned by the name *kumudanibhā*. (BhN 15.59)
For example:
"O lady with arched brows, you who resemble a night-lily, have you been pierced by the arrows of Love, or are you scorched by the cold wind?
For your face, pale like a tender lotus, has somehow appeared before your friends. (BhN 15.60)
In a foot of twelve syllables, the seventh and tenth are short;
with a pause at the beginning after five syllables, that is indeed Candralekhā, as follows: BhN 15.61.
Your gentle face, with eyes as broad as lotus petals, is the abode of Love, possessing beautiful nose and a lofty smile;
O lovely one, you shine like a crescent moon with such radiance, desiring to bring about even the desire of Kāma himself.
When the third, the last (twelfth), the ninth, and the fifth syllable are heavy in a foot consisting of twelve syllables, that is *pramitākṣarā*.
For example:

"A young woman who speaks with a smile, who is not fickle or harsh, who is modest and always averse to slander—even if she is someone else's wife—is pleasant; indeed, he is a man who conquers. (BhN 15.64)
When the second, the last (twelfth), the tenth, the fourth, the fifth,
and the eighth syllables are long in the twelfth foot, that Jagatī meter is called Vaṃśasthā.
If the third and fourth feet likewise consist of *tri*, *ka*, and *ja*, and *ra* and *va* are situated at the end,
then they call that metre established in the *jagatī* class by the name *vaṃśastha*.
"You are no longer dear to me, for you have abandoned respect; though you are my beloved, you speak harsh words to me.
And thus I see this conflict today; it will surely bring about the end of our lineage."
When the fourth, the last (eighth), the tenth, and the seventh syllable are long in a pāda of the Jāgata metre, it is then called Hariṇaplutā.
Struck by the whip of your harsh words, this woman of beautiful form, looking fearfully toward you from the side,
imitates the leap of a deer with her long, darting glides.
When the seventh, ninth, penultimate, and final syllables are long in a foot of twelve syllables, it is called *kāmadattā*, as follows: [BhN 15.70].

O lady with beautiful teeth, just as you are adorned with the marks of fingernails and have your lower lip bitten by teeth, so too is your gait slow due to the weight of your feet; O fawn-eyed one, you are the giver of desire.

When the first, fourth, tenth, and seventh syllables are short in a Jāgata foot, that [meter] is called Aprameyā, as follows: [O Vīra, you are] immeasurable, O Lord of the world, whose power is boundless; You are the supreme refuge for those who have fallen into the ocean of existence. May you grant me the highest peace, O Protector of the world, through your compassion. May the Blessed One, the Great Sage, bestow upon me the fruit of liberation. May all my sins be destroyed by the sight of your face. May I attain the state of a Buddha through your grace. May I never be separated from the True Dharma. May I always be born in the presence of the Victorious Ones. May I quickly realize the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. May I become a protector for all sentient beings. May I be able to lead them across the great ocean of saṃsāra. May I always practice the six perfections with diligence. May I never fall into the three evil realms. May I always be reborn in the pure lands of the Buddhas. May I always hear the sublime Dharma from the mouths of the Buddhas. May I always be surrounded by a retinue of Bodhisattvas. May I always be free from all afflictions and obstacles. May I always be endowed with the five supernatural powers. May I always be able to manifest various transformations. May I always be able to subdue all Māras and heretics. May I always be able to turn the wheel of the Dharma. May I always be able to liberate all sentient beings. May I always be able to establish them in the state of Buddhahood. May I always be able to uphold the teachings of the Buddha. May I always be able to protect the True Dharma. May I always be able to cause the light of the Dharma to shine. May I always be able to cause the world to rejoice. May I always be able to cause all beings to be at peace. May I always be able to cause all beings to be happy. May I always be able to cause all beings to be liberated. May I always be able to cause all beings to attain nirvāṇa. May I always be able to cause all beings to enter the Mahāyāna. May I always be able to cause all beings to understand emptiness. May I always be able to cause all beings to realize the non-self. May I always be able to cause all beings to abandon attachment. May I always be able to cause all beings to abandon aversion. May I always be able to cause all beings to abandon delusion. May I always be able to cause all beings to abandon the three poisons. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the four immeasurables. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the six perfections. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the eightfold noble path. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the ten powers. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the four fearlessnesses. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the great compassion. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the great love. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the great joy. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the great equanimity. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the four right efforts. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the four bases of psychic power. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the five faculties. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the five powers. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the eightfold noble path. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the eightfold noble path. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the ten powers. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the four fearlessnesses. May I always be able to cause all beings to cultivate the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. May I
No other woman equal to you is seen in the world of men, distinguished by peerless virtues;
having gathered all those possessing virtue and wisdom from the three worlds, you were created by the Creator as one immeasurable in this world.
Where the second, fifth, eighth, and eleventh syllables in a quarter-verse are light, that is called *padminī*, as follows: [BhN 15.74].
When the *rāstrikā* known as *sāgara* is established such that the pause (*yati*) occurs appropriately at every third foot,
and is thus well-settled within the *jagatī* meter, it is then proclaimed by the wise by the name *padminī*.

O beloved, you always appear to me like a lotus pond: your body is the reservoir of water, your radiant lotus-face is filled with bees that are your eyes, your smile is the white swans of your teeth, and your breasts are the ruddy geese beneath the cover of your tresses of hair. BhN 15.76.
O beloved, with a face like a full-blown lotus, eyes like bees, hair like petals, breasts like ruddy geese,
and a girdle-string like a line of yellow water-lilies, you shine like a lotus plant standing in the water.
In a *jāgata* meter, where the first six syllables, as well as the tenth, are short in the quarter-verse,
while the remaining syllables are long, it is known by the name *puṭa*.
If both feet contain the sequence *na*, *u*, *ta*, *tha*, and *ma*, *ya*, and if the rule for the pause is also appropriately applied with eight syllables,
and this [meter] always resides in the *jagatī* [class], it is indeed known here by the name *puṭavṛtta*.

The month of flowers proclaims the circular dance of the passionate women through the young lotuses of the grove waters, through the throat-songs of bees and cuckoos, and through their amorous dalliances intoxicated by passion.
In the second and last [feet], the fourth and ninth syllables are heavy; there is a pause at the eleventh.
But in Atijagatī, when there is a pause after four [syllables], it is Prabhāvatī.

O lotus-eyed one, how is it that you have come here—this house where the sun’s rays are shrouded by clouds—to the brilliance of fresh rain-showers, appearing like the goddess Prabhāvatī herself, O slender-limbed one? BhN 15.82.
In the Atijagatī meter, the first three syllables, as well as the eighth, the tenth, and the two at the end, are heavy; this [meter] with three pauses is called Prahārṣiṇī.

With your sweet speech full of meaning, your well-spoken words, and your gait—dignified, faltering, and slow—you steal away the hearts of lovers; for you are clearly both *atijagatī* and *praharṣiṇī* in your splendor. BhN 15.84.
In a foot of thirteen syllables, the sixth and seventh as well as the tenth and eleventh should be known as short; this is the *mattamayūraka*. (BhN 15.85)
Bound with lightning, their bodies adorned by Indra’s bow, tossed by the wind and graced by white cranes,
these clouds— whose brilliant signs are the roar of thunder— proclaim the rainy season to the intoxicated peacocks.
In the Śakvarī meter, the first two syllables, as well as the fourth, eighth, eleventh, and the last two (the penultimate and final), are heavy;
it is like the Vasantatilakā.
With her hair-locks fashioned from variegated spring flowers, her limbs beautifully adorned with arrangements of garlands and wreaths,
and her ears decorated with various spring ornaments, this woman shines like the goddess Vasantatilakā herself.
In the first quarter of the Śakvarī meter, there are five syllables at the beginning, followed by three heavy (long) syllables in the Naidhana;
furthermore, when there is a pause after the first five syllables, that is the Asambādhā, as for example: [BhN 15.89].
For example:
"One who knows the light of honor, who is rich in sons, strength, lineage, and virtue, should see that no equal honor exists in this place;
leaving it with swift pace, he should go to another land, for this earth is strewn with various riches and is free from crowding. (BhN 15.90)
In the Śakvarī meter, there are four heavy syllables at the beginning, as well as in the tenth and eleventh positions, and in the penultimate and final positions;
however, in its pāda, it is like the Śarabha.

"Here goes my beloved, graceful and trembling, through the forest thick with fresh shrubs; 'Alas, alas, what is this? I am bewildered and do not know!'—O dear one, it is clear that you are performing the *śarabha-lalita* dance. (BhN 15.92)
In the *atiśakvarī* meter, that [verse] in which the sixth, the tenth, and the thirteenth syllables are short is to be known as *nāndīmukhī*. (BhN 15.93)
For instance: "Indeed, never before have I seen your face with its eyes wide and copper-red with anger, its brow furrowed by a frown.
What is the use of many words here? You, who dwell within my heart, are my desire; O sweet-spoken Queen, you are like Nāndīmukhī herself. (BhN 15.94)
When the first, fourth, sixth,
and last syllables of the sixteen-syllable foot are heavy, that is the *ibhalalita* meter.
If *bha*, *ra*, *ya*, and *na* are always arranged here as the feet, and likewise *ga* occurs when the cadence (*nidhana*) has arrived,
and furthermore, if *aṣṭi* constantly follows, that indeed is the meter called *agravṛṣabhagajavilasita*.

Beholding the surface of the earth covered with sprouts and *sendragopa* insects, fragrant with the blossoms of *sarja*, *kadamba*, *nīpa*, and *kuṭaja* trees, and filled with the deep, resonant, and sharp sound of thunderclouds like the beat of drums, he performs the *vṛṣabhagajavilasita* gait.
The five syllables following the first, the twelfth, and the thirteenth, as well as the penultimate and final syllables, are long; that indeed is the most excellent Lalita.
When these two [feet] are established here as *pāda-sthau*, with *sta* and *gau* likewise, and there is a pause (*yati*) after six other syllables,
that is always said by others who know the application of meters to be the *vṛtta* named *Pravaralalita*, consisting of eight syllables.
For example: "The body is licked by the nails, the lips and cheeks are marked with tooth-prints, the head is strewn with flowers and its hair and locks are disheveled;
this gait is weary and the face has wandering eyes—oh, how praiseworthy is this conduct, so excellent, playful, and full of amorous gestures! (BhN 15.100)
In the Śikhariṇī meter, the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, and seventeenth syllables of the first foot are heavy (guru). BhN 15.101.

When that very *pravaralalita* consists of three groups of four [mātrās] each, and there is a *lau-ga* (one light and two heavy syllables) at the end of the quarter-verse in what is called *aty-aṣṭi*, and when the caesura occurs after six [mātrās] as prescribed by the path, then among meters this is indeed declared to be named *śikhariṇī*. (BhN 15.102)
Just as the hip of a great river shines like a sandbank, so does your face, rich with eyes, resemble a lotus accompanied by bees;
this gait of yours is slow, O fair-limbed one, and your movement is most graceful; with those two breasts, O lady, you are well-rounded, O mountain-like woman! (BhN 15.103)
Where there are five light syllables at the beginning, and likewise in the thirteenth, fourteenth,
sixteenth, and eleventh [syllables], that is the Vṛṣabhaceṣṭita metre.
If indeed *na*, *sa*, *la*, *sa*, and *ga* are placed in sequence in each quarter, and if the caesura occurs after six syllables and then again after ten,
and if this is prescribed as an *atyaṣṭi* meter that rests comfortably in usage, it should be known as either the *vṛṣabhalalita* or the *hariṇī* metre.
For example:

Having heard the roar of the rain-clouds again and again, the bull, arrogant with the pride of rutting, having bellowed back and tossed his horns which have scraped the earth, proceeds from one pen to another accompanied by his own young females; and, free from fear, he performs the wonderful gait of a bull upon the grassy meadow. (BhN 15.106)
In this [meter], the fourth, tenth, thirteenth, fourteenth, the last two, and also the eleventh syllables are long. BhN 15.107.
When the seventeenth foot consists of the remaining [syllables] as light syllables,
that meter is to be known by the name Śrīdharī.

If there are two *mo*s (ma-gaṇas) and a *bha* (bha-gaṇa), followed by two *na*s (na-gaṇas), and then two *ga*s (ga-gaṇas), and if the remaining portion consists of ten [syllables] and likewise four others,
and it is clearly defined by its syllabic count as an *atyaṣṭi*, it should be known by the hosts of twice-born sages as being called *Śrīdharī*.
With baths, powders, pleasant and fragrant scents, perfumes, incense, and other flowers arranged upon your head, with various garments,
and with diverse jewels set in gold that grace your limbs, O beloved, you shine intensely like Śrīdhara’s own Lakṣmī, whose abode is the lotus.
The first, fourth, sixth, tenth, and final syllables are long;
it is called *vaṃśapatrapatita*, with pauses after the tenth and seventh syllables.
Just as this elephant, surrounded by its young, plays upon the slopes of the mountain peaks amidst thickets of trees and shrubs bent with blossoms;
and hearing the roar of the clouds, O beautiful one, he rejoices and, possessing the speed of the wind, once again performs the "falling of bamboo leaves. (BhN 15.112)
In a foot of seventeen syllables, the second, last (seventeenth), sixth, eighth, twelfth, fourteenth, and fifteenth syllables [should be short]. BhN 15.113.
Wherein the long syllables and the remaining short ones occur [in such a manner],
that should be known by name as *vilambitagati*, according to its designation.
When the *jsau* (ja-sa) twice appear occupying the feet, and likewise the *trikaus* (ta-ra-ga) [twice], and furthermore the *yau lagau* (ya-la-ga) occupy the *nidhana* (concluding position),
then it is called by the twice-born the name *vilambitagati*, which is characterized by a slow pace and possesses a natural pause (*yatir*) preceded by eight syllables.
For example:

"With eyes rolling, her necklace widely scattered, her lower garment hanging loose again, and moving with slow, faltering steps due to exhaustion—O beloved, it was not for my pleasure that you, rendered helpless by intoxication, made your gait so languid out of a passion for public esteem. (BhN 15.116)

The fifth at the beginning, the fifteenth, the twelfth and eleventh, the fourteenth, and likewise the last two syllables are long; this is remembered as the Citralekhā metre when it is held [in its proper form]. BhN 15.117.

Just as you appear, O lovely one, like a painted picture—briefly speaking, what need is there for much here?—with many abundant ornaments set upon your limbs rich with various jewels; with various colorful body-pastes rich in fragrance that arouse passion; with hair enriched by bathing and laden with flowers; and with those various colors of garments. BhN 15.118.
The last [syllable] and the seventeenth, the sixteenth and the fourteenth, the thirteenth and the twelfth, as well as the sixth and the eighth. BhN 15.119.
That [meter] in which the first three syllables and the nineteenth syllable of the foot are heavy,
while the remaining syllables are light, is indeed Śārdūlakrīḍita.

In that [meter] where the gaṇas *ma*, *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, *ta*, and *ga* are fixed in application, and the three-footed [verse] has a pause at the beginning and another at the end, it is known as the "other" [variety]; when joined with four sets of three [syllables], it is known as the *parā* [variety] consisting of seven [syllables per foot].

That meter which poets always resort to, which possesses an exceedingly firm structure, and which is ever dear to them—indeed, that should be known by those skilled in meters and prosody as *śārdūlavikrīḍita*.
Just as enemies struck by various weapons, *śataghnīs*, and lances, their all arms fallen away, their bellies, feet, arms, and faces pierced through and destroyed—
so does your conduct, O slayer of foes, shine in battle like the *śārdūlavikrīḍita* [tiger’s sport], through those various diverse qualities such as fortitude, energy, and prowess. (BhN 15.122)

Therefore, O one of auspicious mind, having conquered your senses, apply your entire being every day to the practice of generosity and ethical discipline, which bring about both heaven and liberation—
before death, with its fierce claws of disease and old age and its thick mane of exertion, performs its lion’s sport upon the deer of your life.
The fourth, the sixth, the seventh along with the fourteenth, as well as the fifteenth, the sixteenth, and likewise the final one. BhN 15.124.
These [syllables] are heavy, while the remaining ones are light;
when these are arranged in a quarter-verse, it should be known by the name Suvadanā.

If the syllables *ma*, *ra*, *u*, *na*, *ya*, *bha*, *la*, and *ga* are properly arranged in the quarter-verse according to their sequence, and there is a pause (*viccheda*) after seven syllables, with a further pause (*yati*) likewise made at the seventh syllable;
and if this [meter] is composed with cleverly joined syllables and words, it is called by the name *suvadanā* among the varieties of meters by the learned. (BhN 15.126)
For instance:
"With eyes whose corners are languid with playfulness, resembling lotus petals; with eyebrows curved like a bow; with red lips, a full waist, and teeth that are even, well-aligned, dense, and glossy;

with ears hanging down to the shoulders and a well-sloped chin; with a most beautiful nose—you, O fair-limbed one, are clearly the one woman of beautiful countenance ordained in the world of mortals. (BhN 15.127)
The fourth, as well as the sixth, seventh, fourteenth, eighteenth, seventeenth, and again the fifteenth. BhN 15.128.
In this [meter], the syllables at the end and the penultimate position are heavy, while all others are always light;
when there are twenty-one syllables in a quarter-verse, it is named *sragdharā*, as follows: [BhN 15.129].

If the *mra*, *mnau*, *yau*, and *ya* are properly arranged in triplets within the metrical feet according to the syllables previously taught, and if there is a pause (*yati*) again at every seven syllables,

and if the meter is perfectly in accordance with its natural form as prescribed by the knowers of truth, it should be recognized in the class of meters as that which is beloved by poets, known by the name *sragdharā*.
For instance:

"O best of men, today the earth shines like a woman wearing a garland, strewn with various kinds of springtime flower-clusters—mangoes, *aśoka*, *aravinda*, *kuravaka*, *tilaka*, *karṇikāra*, *śirīṣa*, *punnāga*, *pārijāta*, *vakula*, *kuvalaya*, *kiṃśuka*, and *atimukta*—all abundant, fragrant, and scattered about. (BhN 15.131)
Furthermore, the fourth, first, sixth, tenth, twelfth, sixteenth, eighteenth, and the final [syllable] are heavy. (BhN 15.132)
When there are twenty-two syllables in a quarter-verse and the remaining syllables are short, that should be known by the name Bhadraka, as follows.

When the *bhra* syllables are fixed at the feet, then by the rule of succession, the *tri* syllables in the subsequent construction, and then the *nra* syllables followed by the *ru* and *ci* syllables in the next construction, and again the *na* and *ga* syllables;

and when that is composed of ten and eight syllables with pauses (*yati*) likewise applied across all four quarters, it is indeed called the *Bhadraka* metre by the wise who are skilled in the application of prosody. (BhN 15.134)

O moon-faced one, today you dance this auspicious and manifold performance, leaping with one hand and foot while the second hand plays the sweet melodies of the flute and drum; it follows various intricate gestures, O fortunate lady, performed with the graceful movements of the skilled, its steps agitated by charm and cultivated with refined aesthetic sentiments.
Now, the final [syllable], the nineteenth, the seventh, the thirteenth, the eleventh, the seventeenth, and the fifth are heavy. (BhN 15.136)
And when the remaining syllables are light in the quarter of a *vikṛti*, that metre should be known by name as *Aśvalalita*, according to its designation. (BhN 15.137)

If the syllable *na* is placed at the beginning of the foot, and the syllable *la* is placed at the very end; if the syllables *na* and *bha* are likewise arranged three times in succession, and the middle sections are also thus;
and if it indeed resorts to a variation in structure with a pause (*yati*) occurring after ten syllables plus one—that is proclaimed here by the sages of pure conduct as *Aśvalalita*.

Beholding that vast army—crowded with various horses, elephants, chariots, and warriors; risen up and spread wide with hundreds of arrows, spears, lances, iron clubs, and maces, and equipped with many weapons;

its soldiers terrified and anxious by the sound of weapons discharged by hundreds of enemies, and having thrown the quarters of the sky into a state of fear—you displayed your mastery of horsemanship at the front of the battle, having applied your full skill.
The sixth, the eighth, the eleventh, the fourteenth, the twentieth, the seventeenth, and likewise the twenty-third. (BhN 15.140)
And these [syllables] may be light, while the remaining ones are heavy;
that is the *meghamālā* in a quarter of twenty-four syllables, as follows: [BhN 15.141].
If, indeed, in the feet there are two *trikas* (groups of three) beginning with *kṛti* (the syllables ka, ra, ta, ga) and likewise *rāḥ* (ra, ra, ra),

and if the pause (*yati*) occurs respectively after seven and seven [syllables] in the first three feet, then one should know that another [meter] exists, with a pause after five [syllables] in the same way.
Drawn forth by the power of the wind, with a fierce and deep roar, girdled by rows of cranes, possessing a lofty form like a mountain, born from the womb of waters dark as great blue collyrium,

bound with the bright girth-straps of Indra’s bow, its armor-plates flashing with the brilliance of lightning, this cloud-mass of the rainy season spreads across the expanse of the sky and shines exceedingly.
The first, the fourth, the fifth, the sixth,
the ninth, the tenth, and the final syllable shall be heavy.
When the remaining other [syllables] in the quarter-verse are light, numbering twenty-five,
that should be known by those who know the meters by the name *Krauñcapādī*.

If there is *pāda* and *sbhāva* in the *bhmāu* [meter], and if indeed *ceṣṭā* and *abhikṛti* are prescribed, and if there are oceans (*samudra*) arranged therein, and if indeed a heavy syllable (*guru*) occurs at the end (*nidhana*), and if it is further endowed with a pause (*cheda*) at the beginning by five [mātrās], and if indeed the pause here is by ten [mātrās]—this is the *krauñcapada* meter, ordained in the rules of prosody by the hosts of gods, the hosts of ancestors, and the hosts of sages. (BhN 15.146)

May that eternal enemy of the hosts of Daityas burn away your entire host of enemies, as if he were burning a sacrifice— just as he once did with an arrow released from his bow, which swiftly rendered Dakṣa’s excellent rite devoid of Soma, without ladles, lacking sacrificial jars, with its stakes fallen, its *caṣāla* rings cast aside, without grass-bundles, without fuel, without animals, and without the *caru* oblation, leaving it bereft of both the hosts of gods and the hosts of ancestors.
A woman with reddish-brown eyes and tawny hair, who is daily harsh in her entreaties, whose body is covered with very long and thick veins, whose gait is exceedingly crooked,
who has long shanks, sunken cheeks, and a heart possessed by a pair of very small breasts— such a woman with the gait of a curlew must certainly be avoided here by one desiring unending happiness.
The first eight syllables should be heavy, as should the nineteenth, the twenty-first, and the twenty-fourth, along with the final syllable. (BhN 15.149)
In a quarter of twenty-six syllables, these [syllables] are heavy in number, while the remaining ones are light; this is the *bhujaṅgavijṛmbhita* meter.
In that [scale] where there are two *ma* notes,
two *gau*, and two *strīs* (notes), and if the *gaditakās* are indeed stated in successive order within the twenty-five [syllables] minus one; |||
Indeed, when the name *yatir* occurs with four or eight [syllables],
and subsequently the last two syllables are joined as *laghu-guru*, it becomes the *utkṛti* meter, which is cherished by men.
Known in the world by the name *Bhujaṅgavijṛmbhita*, it is celebrated for its conduct and is intent upon blossoming the faces of poets.
For example:
having beheld Tilottamā, endowed with beauty, created by the gods, and possessing the graceful gait of an elephant in rut;
As she approached from the right, Hari turned his head with its many faces and wide eyes to see her;
sighing deeply, he concealed within himself the longing for her breasts and face.
Having likewise beheld her beautiful hips, he saw the excellent jewel and golden bracelet placed upon her back by the Lord of the Gods, which resembled the coiled posture of a serpent.
That which exceeds the *utkṛti* meter is to be known as *daṇḍaka*;
it consists of the *meghamālā* and other such types, beginning with the syllables "nau," followed by the syllables "kā" and "guhā," and ending with three *tri*s. (BhN 15.153)
For example:
"The earth, filled with joyful people and abounding in mines of grain, honors you;
and the Vindhya and other mountains, whose forests of hintāla and tālī trees are lopped off by the trunks of elephants, bow down to you."

The oceans, filled with joyful aquatic creatures and their impurities cast away, worship you with wave-hands that offer pearls swallowed from burst shells and oyster beds; the great rivers seem to proclaim your fame.
O best of the twice-born, these even meters have been described by me;
now I shall further state the characteristics of the uneven and half-even meters.
Where the quarters are unequal, arising from various meters and composed through the joining of feet, that is known as an uneven meter (viṣamavṛtta).
In a *vṛtta* with two even and two uneven [feet], it is likewise called *ardhasama*; when all the feet are uneven, it is called an *viṣama-vṛtta*.

A *vṛtta* with even feet may consist of short syllables first and long syllables second, or long syllables first and short syllables second; likewise, it may have even feet consisting of long syllables and odd feet consisting of short syllables, or vice versa. Such a meter is called *ardhasama*. (BhN 15.158)
When the first quarter is established, the even [meter] is established; the uneven [meter] is that which applies to all quarters.
One should know that the half-even [meter] occurs when two [quarters] are equal; this division, however, is according to the quarter.
The *chedas* that I have described are those composed in even meters;
now I shall fully explain the characteristics of those composed in uneven meters by means of triplets (*trikas*).
In the *naidhana* [concluding syllable], it is optionally desired in either the first or the second foot; such is the *anuṣṭubh* in brief. (BhN 15.161)

If the first quarter consists of *sa*, *au*, *ga*, and the second consists of *sra*, *u*, *la*, and *ga*, while the even and odd quarters are identical, that [meter] is known as *pathyā* by those who know the three [feet]. (BhN 15.162)
"You are dear to the gods and to friends; you are dear to kinsmen and relatives;
you delight in giving what is beneficial; O beloved, you are dear to me."
In the first quarter there are *mra*, *au*, and *g*; in the second, *ysa*, *u*, *l*, and *g*; in the third, *bha*, *u*, *l*, and *g*; and in the fourth, *ta*, *sa*, *l*, and *g*. (BhN 15.164)
Neither conduct, nor a friend, nor one who cherishes the virtues of their kin;
in every way, O beloved, you are entirely inconsistent and not wholesome.
For this is the definition of the Ayuji [meter], whereas that in which it is reversed is known by name as the Pathyā; for example, as follows.

O friend, what is the use of your anger toward your lover for what has already been done? You have become perverse; you are not acting for your own benefit. O foolish woman, by whom have you been deluded?
Where there are three short syllables from the beginning of the fourth foot, occurring unevenly,
that *anuṣṭubh* should be known by the name *capalā*, as follows.
"Indeed, her beloved does not wish to hear what has been spoken by her friend; this fickle woman is merely describing an image of Nārada. (BhN 15.169)
The *vipulā* meter, however, should be known to occur in the even [pādas] due to the lightness of the seventh syllable;
for some, the *vipulā* occurs everywhere, just as it does for the seventh syllable alone.
For you are slender at the waist, with breasts like golden jars;
O beloved, you are broad of hip, O lady with a face like the full moon.
Like the Ganges when the clouds arrive,
flooding the earth and forcefully sweeping away the trees on its banks, she flowed forth with great might.
O timid woman born of a family of cowards, you have come to another's house at the time of the clouds; as a thief, you deserve to be bound for one night.
Thus, indeed, there are various types of *yogas* that have even-numbered quarters; while others have odd-numbered quarters, and the remaining ones have three [quarters] as appropriate.
A triad consisting entirely of light syllables is always considered heavy;
however, where the fourth syllable from the beginning is light, it is traditionally remembered as light.
Having established three light syllables at the end of the first quarter, while the other quarters always consist of heavy syllables, that is designated as *vaktra* by the wise. (BhN 15.176)
O fair-browed one, your face— its lower lip marked by tooth-bites and its eyes weary from staying awake— is all the more beautiful to behold, though exhausted by the enjoyment of love.
Thus, this [meter] is called Sarvaviṣamā by name; it is an Anuṣṭubh according to the differing opinions of those who know it, both in terms of its triplets and its syllables.
In each quarter, there are sixteen morae, arranged in four parts; those who know the meters recognize this as the Vānavāsikā.

With unsteady steps and limbs trembling, charming with gestures faltering from passion—"Where will you go, O fair-thighed one, at the time of love-making? Are you perhaps a woman from the forest, unskilled in this? (BhN 15.180)

In the first and likewise in the third quarter of the *ketumatī* meter, the groups of syllables are always declared by the wise to be *sa*, *ja*, *ga*, *ca*, followed by *bha*, *ra*, *na*, *ga*, and *ga*.
With quivering lips, startled eyes, and flushed cheeks, your lotus-petal-eyed face has its beauty stolen away by anger; tell me, what is this? It resembles that of Ketumatī.
In the first [pāda] of Vaktra, which has no prior [meter], there are two *na*s, a *ra*, and two *la*s;
in the second, there are a *na*, a *ja*, a *ra*, and a *ja*; and the remainder is exactly as before. (BhN 15.183)
In the first and third feet, the gaṇas are proclaimed to be ra, la, and ga;
whereas in the second and fourth feet of the Aparavaktra, they are na, ja, ja, and ra.

O you of delicate limbs, why is it that your face today—its eyes clouded by tears like the orb of the moon obscured by a rain-cloud—is turned away from me, appearing like an *aparavaktra* verse? O moon-faced one! BhN_15.185 //
Where there are nine *ya*s in the first quarter, and likewise *na*, *ja*, *ja*, *ra*, and *ga* in the other [the second], that is *puṣpitāgrā*, provided the remainder is as before. (BhN 15.186)

O fair-limbed one, behold this forest in full bloom, its lovely branches shaken by the power of the wind, delightful with the warbling of joyful cuckoos, and filled with the humming of bees. BhN 15.187.
Sja, sla, and cāda; likewise nsau, jgau, bhnau, jlau, and ga;
and again sjau, sjau, and ga—these nine triplets (trikās) are proclaimed as belonging to the *udgatā* meter.
O fair-limbed one, the line of hair upon your body shines most brilliantly like a cluster of blossoms on the tree of Love,
appearing like a swarm of bees emerging from the flower that is the cavity of your navel-lotus.
In the third [meter], the ganas are remembered as *sjau*, *slau*, *ca*, *tato nsau*, *jgau*, *nau*, and *sau*;
while in the fourth, they are *sjau*, *sjau*, and *ga*. These are the ganas of Lalitā.
With her beautiful garments and lovely hands moving gracefully like blossoms,
her face possessing the splendor of a fully opened lotus, the goddess shines forth, overcome by the fatigue of amorous play.
In this manner, these meters, both even and uneven,
should be employed by the wise in dramas and other poetic compositions.
There are other meters as well that have been mentioned here in groups;
however, they should not be employed [in this context], for they certainly do not produce beauty.
One should employ those songs which have been prohibited elsewhere;
however, I shall explain their application and their various alternatives in connection with the *dhruvā*.
Thus, the characteristics of metrical feet have been declared by me in brief;
hereafter, I shall indeed explain the characteristics of the Āryā meters as well.
Pathyā, Vipulā, Capalā at the beginning, another Capalā at the end, and Capalā at the end—these five types of Āryā are proclaimed. (BhN 15.196)
I shall now fully explain for these [vowels] the determination of their duration and quantity,
as well as their characteristics and rules, which depend upon the qualities of their various modifications.
The *yati* (caesura) should be known as occurring at the fourth *mātrā*, which is recorded as a *gaṇa*;
the second and last [feet] are even (*yuj*), while the other two are recorded as odd (*ayuj*).
Devoid of the syllables *gu* and *ru*, it should be endowed with four groups;
an odd number of groups is to be prescribed, while an even number may be used as desired.
The sixth [vowel] indeed has two variations; it is destructive and established as one.
In the latter half, however, the sixth would consist of a single measure alone.
But the sixth, which consists of two *vikalpas*, is the medium-heavy (*gurumadhya*); likewise, that which is entirely light (*sarvalaghu*) is designated as a *yati*. (BhN 15.201)
The second syllable and so forth are to be known as light; the pause (yati) occurs at the seventh and fifth [syllables].
Alternatively, it is prescribed at the first syllable and so forth, or at the end, or at the fifth.
That [verse] in which the *pathyā* occurs in all three groups of eight syllables is the *pathyā*;
furthermore, the other [type], characterized by its caesura, is to be known as *vipulā*.

That [meter] in which the odd-numbered *gaṇas* consist entirely of heavy syllables (*guru*), while the even-numbered *gaṇas* have a heavy syllable in their middle, should be known as *capalā*. (BhN 15.204)

In the first half, thirty [mātrās] are to be known, and in the other [half], twenty-seven; thus the total aggregate of mātrās for both halves should be understood according to their respective divisions.
And if these thirty [units] of his were doubled,
one should assign three other syllables according to the division of the count.
These have been briefly indicated as having the designation "light," according to the sequence of all such syllables of the noble ones.
The *savavāryā* is proclaimed to consist of seven and a half *gaṇas*;
furthermore, the sixth [foot] has two variations, being established as one in the *naidhana*.
Alternatively, that group which follows is said to be the sixth, consisting of a single mātrā;
however, that sixth which has two variations would have a heavy syllable in its middle.
Just as the first [meter] consists entirely of light syllables and is based on numerical count,
the second has two light syllables and its pause occurs at the seventh [syllable].
Devoid of the middle guru and endowed with four gaṇas, it should be made an odd-numbered gaṇa;
yet that very same [gaṇa] may also be an even-numbered gaṇa.
If the first and third feet consist of twelve mātrās, that is the Pathyā;
the other, Vipulā, is indeed said to be endowed with the characteristics previously mentioned.
An example of a wholesome [woman]:
"She whose eyes are red and soft like lotuses, whose hair is white, long, thick, and soft, and whose broad hips are soft—whose sister is she, with her slender arms? BhN 15.213.
Regarding the *vipulā* [meter]:
"With broad hips, face, breasts, and eyes; with copper-colored lips, hands, and feet; with a long nose, cheeks, forehead, and ears—the maiden is auspicious. (BhN 15.214)
When the second and the fourth [syllables] fall in the middle of a heavy syllable,
it should be known as *capalā*, occurring where there is a break at both halves.
Moving with haughty strides, speaking harshly, and dressing herself in the signs of passion, she knows how to mix meat with liquor; fond of wine, she is fickle in every way.
For this [gait] has its characteristic in the first half by means of the face, while in the second half it is *capalā* by means of the hips. (BhN 15.217)
An example of one who is talkative in the presence of her husband:
"Even though she is talkative in the presence of my noble husband, she is nevertheless not dear to me;
for although she is skillful in household chores, she becomes afflicted with grief when faced with sorrow. (BhN 15.218)
An example of the *jaghanacapalā* meter is as follows:

"O deer-eyed one, you are fickle; O fair-thighed one, you are fickle; O you whose face resembles the mirror of the moon, you are fickle—yet not before, O essence of desire, were you so with your beautiful hips. (BhN 15.219)
O friend, if this characteristic is seen in both halves [of the verse],
it should be known by those who know prosody as *sarvataścapalā*.
The first and third feet should each consist of twelve mātrās;
the second foot should have eighteen, and the last foot likewise fifteen. (BhN 15.221)
Having attained the method of expansion for the four groups consisting specifically of four and five types, one should demonstrate their abundance.

The first [variety] consists of fifty-five syllables, and likewise the second consists of thirty; these Āryās are to be recognized here by practitioners according to the total number of their syllables.
Furthermore, out of thirty syllables, there may be three light syllables; the remaining ones are counted as heavy. One should indicate this in all cases.
And for all the syllables of the noble ones, according to their sequence,
and for all the *jāti* and *vṛtta* meters, [the calculation] is preceded by the number of the subsequent one.
Having performed the calculation of the metrical feet, one should indicate it by means of the total sum;
the Āryāgīti is likewise truly an Āryā, consisting solely of eight gaṇas.
In other cases, the sixth syllable is *ja*, while the *na-laghu-gaṇa* (n, l, g) is desired;
thus, by means of these various meters arising from different prosodic patterns,
poetic compositions should be fashioned, endowed with the thirty-six characteristics.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Investigation of Prosody," in the Bharatanāṭyaśāstra.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter:
Ornamentation, the Combination of Syllables, Splendor, Pride, and the Proclamation of Qualities.
In the case of encouragement and examples, the definition is that the mention of qualities and the statement of excellence are the causes.
Similarity, false determination, establishment, a collection of words, lamentation, desire, narration, begging, non-prohibition, questioning, illustration, appearance, and doubt. (BhN 16.2)

Blessings, pleasant speech, deceit, forbearance, and likewise the attainment [of one's goal], repentance, compliance with one's interests, reasoning accompanied by justification, conciliation, and lamentation—these are the means to be employed. (BhN 16.3)
Indeed, these thirty-six characteristics have been declared to be equivalent to ornaments;
they pertain to the aesthetic sentiments and meanings within poetic works and should be properly employed by those who know them, according to the specific rasa.
That which is adorned with many ornaments and qualities, like various decorations arranged upon it, is known as "ornament" (bhūṣaṇa). BhN 16.5.
One should know that even a collection of syllables wherein a variety is described through few, yet interconnected, letters is designated by the term "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa).
When an unestablished point is proven by means of established points,
and where the meaning is smooth and varied, that is called "beauty" (śobhā).
But that which, even when being sustained by many words and logical arguments,
does not remain stable, is designated as *abhimāna* (conceit).
When virtues arising from various purposes are being proclaimed, and no faults are mentioned therein, that should be known as "proclamation of virtues" (guṇakīrtana). BhN 16.9.
When, in the world, one person who possesses many qualities beyond measure is designated by those very names, that should be understood as the praise of qualities (guṇakīrtana). BhN 16.10.
The wise should understand that encouragement is characterized by clear meanings that generate enthusiasm, by means of comparisons, and by being embraced by well-known [examples]. BhN 16.11.
Where, by the observation of even a single word, many others that have not been explicitly stated also attain their established meaning, that is known as an "illustration" (udāharaṇa).
Etymology is said to be of two kinds: that which is true and that which is untrue.
That which is established by proof is true; that which is not so established is untrue.
The description of qualities (*guṇānuvāda*) is that which consists of a comparison of inferior things with superior ones;
and that which is a distinction of a superior object is also known as *atiśaya* (hyperbole).
When many things are being spoken, that which establishes the determination of the meaning of one among them is designated as the "reason" (hetu), being a statement of a proven analogy.
An indirect designation (*apadeśa*), however, arises from a representation of that which is beyond the senses;
its similarity [to the object] is to be defined by virtue of having the same grammatical function as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). (BhN 16.16)
Where a determination of an object is made through objects that have never existed before,
that is called "false determination" (mithyādhyavasāya) in the definition of poetry.
When, among many principal [deities], the name of one is proclaimed for the sake of accomplishing a single purpose, that is proclaimed as *siddhi*.

That which is highly praised by means of many words possessing a single meaning, one should know as *padoccaya*; however, that which consists of a composition of various meanings is [also] *padoccaya*. (BhN 16.19)
When, having presented one's own person, there is an intense verbal expression of meaning through arguments based on similarity with another, that is proclaimed as *ākranda* (lamentation).
The clear manifestation of the meaning of a state of being residing within the heart, through the telling of stories involving others, is known as *manoratha*. (BhN 16.21)
Whether asked or unasked, that which provides a definitive conclusion should be known as *ākhyāna* (narrative); this is the characteristic based on drama (*nāṭaka*). (BhN 16.22)
That speech which initially arouses anger but later increases joy, yet remains agreeable, is proclaimed as *yāñcā*. (BhN 16.23)
If something proceeds in a manner contrary to what ought to be done, and it is then restrained by those who understand the task, that is proclaimed as "prohibition" (pratiṣedha). BhN 16.24.
When one expresses a meaning through sentences arising from a particular mode of expression, as if questioning oneself or another, that is designated as *pṛcchā* (the interrogative).
That which a learned person establishes as a state of equality with what was previously perceived,
and which is employed by those who provide illustrations, is known by the wise as an *udāharaṇa* (example).
That which consists of sentences endowed with numerous reasonings, which establishes multiple meanings,
and which is joined with many sentences, is called "manifestation" (nirbhāsana).
Where a sentence concludes without the true meaning being fully understood, that is proclaimed as "doubt" (saṃśaya), due to the multiplicity of possible investigations. (BhN 16.28)
The wise know that blessing to be one which is endowed with the meaning of the scriptures, born of the heart's desire, and not to be sought after— or indeed, any other.
That speech which generates anger at first but increases joy in the end should be known as pleasant speech endowed with a blessing. BhN 16.30.
Deceit is that which overcomes the intentions of others through trickery;
it should be understood as a collection of deceptions employed in two or three applications. (BhN 16.31)
When one is severely struck in the midst of an assembly by the harsh words uttered by wicked people,
yet remains free from anger toward those words intended to provoke it— that indeed is patience.
Upon seeing even a single part through which a state is inferred,
one should recognize that as *prāpti*, a characteristic based on drama.
Having impulsively done what should not be done, or having failed to do what ought to be done,
that distress of the mind which follows is proclaimed as *paścāttāpa* (remorse).
That following of another which is joined with purpose and characterized by humility—whether arising from affection or from a sense of courtesy—is designated as *anuvṛtti*. (BhN 16.35)
Where the pacification of faults already arisen is performed, that should be known as the "arising" (upapatti), which is a characteristic based on drama. BhN 16.36.
That connection of meanings which is established by great beings through their collective association, acting in mutual conformity with one another, is proclaimed as *yukti*. (BhN 16.37)
Where one sets aside a fault and connects a virtue with the purpose,
or conversely, where one emphasizes a fault while praising a virtue, the wise know that to be the characteristic of *kārya*.
When one wipes away an offense born of unprecedented anger and speaks sweet words for the sake of service, that is proclaimed as conciliation (*anunīti*). (BhN 16.39)
When one employs words with well-known meanings that have been designated by other names due to certain defects,
yet which are connected to a different meaning, that should be known as *paridevana* (lamentation).
Simile, metaphor, the lamp-ornament, and likewise the chiming-ornament—
these four ornaments should be known as based upon drama.
Whatever is compared through similarity within poetic compositions,
that should be known as *upamā* (simile), which rests upon the commonality of qualities and form.
That [work] should be performed by one person for one [person], or again by many;
likewise, by one for many, and by many for many. (BhN 16.43)
The comparison "Your face is equal to the moon," which relies on a single [subject] with a single [object], may be that [type] where "the stars shine like the moon. (BhN 16.44)
That [simile] which has a single subject and multiple objects is proclaimed as the "Equal Purpose" (tulyārtha), such as that which pertains to hawks, peacocks, and vultures. (BhN 16.45)
