When one thing is compared with many due to their similarity, it is an *upamā* based on drama (*nāṭaka*); when many things are compared with many, it is known as "the elephants are like clouds," for example. (BhN 16.46)
Praise and blame, as well as the "imagined" (kalpitā) and the "similar" (sadṛśī), and whatever else is similar—these are known by the wise as the fivefold simile (upamā). (BhN 16.47)
An example of praise is as follows:
"Upon seeing that large-eyed woman, the lord of men rejoiced,
as if she were the very embodiment of the perfection achieved by the sages through great hardship" (BhN 16.48).
As for censure:
She embraced him, who was destitute of all virtues and possessed a harsh complexion, like a thorny creeper in the forest embracing a tree scorched by a forest fire. (BhN 16.49)
An example of the imaginary (kalpita) is as follows:
"Exuding the water of their ichor and moving slowly with their trunks, the elephants shine like moving mountains. (BhN 16.50)
An example of the similar [type] is as follows:
"The deed which you have performed today, acting in accordance with the minds of others, is truly worthy of you, whose actions transcend those of ordinary men. (BhN 16.51)
An example of slight similarity is as follows:
"This friend of mine has arrived, with a face like the full moon, eyes like the petals of a blue lotus, and the gait of an elephant in rut. (BhN 16.52)
These varieties of simile should be understood by the wise in brief;
those others which have not been mentioned by their specific characteristics are to be grasped from the world of poetry.
That which illuminates words having various distinct meanings by being joined with a single sentence is called *dīpaka* (the illuminator).
O Brahmins, that which is pervasive, sweet, and adorned with all excellent qualities within a poem or a drama is known as *dīpaka*.
For example:
"In that place, the lakes were never empty of swans, the trees of flowers, the lotuses of intoxicated bees, and the garden groves of social gatherings. (BhN 16.56)
That form which is fashioned by one's own imagination, possessing symmetrical parts and endowed with some degree of similarity, is indeed *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification). BhN 16.57.
That which, through the blending of various substances and so forth, serves as the basis for qualities of comparison and is employed for the description of form,
is known as *rūpaka* (metaphor).
Just as:

"Those women of the ponds, with faces like lotuses, smiles like white water-lilies, and beautiful eyes like blooming blue lotuses, shone together with the swarms of warbling swans, as if calling out to one another. (BhN 16.59)
The repetition of sounds, however, is considered *yamaka* (chiasmus) when occurring at the beginning of words and so forth; listen as I explain its specific varieties. (BhN 16.60)
Furthermore, there is the *pādānta-yamaka*, the *kāñcī-yamaka*,
the *samudga-yamaka*, and likewise the *vikrānta-yamaka*.
The Yamaka (rhyme), the Cakravāla, the Sandaṣṭayamaka, as well as the Padādiyāmaka, and also the Āmreḍita.
Furthermore, the *caturvyavasita* and the *mālāyamaka*:
such types of *yamaka* should be known as those based on drama (*nāṭaka*). (BhN 16.63)
Where there is a matching syllable at the end of four quarters, that should be known by name as *pādāntayamaka* (end-of-quarter rhyme), as for example: [BhN 16.64].
At the end of the day, the solar disc in the sky, its circle of rays withdrawn,
shines copper-red like a sphere of refined gold fixed upon the heavens.
Just like the rounded mass of the breasts of a young woman.

Victorious is the Lord Viṣṇu, the sovereign of the worlds, who endured the blow of the mace of the lord of the Daityas; he is the conqueror of gods and demons alike, the one who performs the destruction of the foremost of the Asuras.
Where both at the end and at the beginning of a foot occur in an even (even-numbered) foot, that should be known by the wise as the *kāñcīyamaka*, as for example: [BhN 16.67].
In every watch of the nights— those moonlit, flowing, and clearly manifest nights that produce the essence of existence—
whether the blossoms are in full bloom with bees or without bees, [the world continues].
The beautiful women are both amazed and filled with pride.
When an entire verse is completed by means of a single half-verse, that should be known by the wise as *samudgayamaka*, as for example: [BhN 16.69].
The elephant of the excellent forest shines with tusks as white as *ketakī* flowers;
he shines with tusks as white as *ketakī* flowers.
He shines like an elephant in a magnificent forest.
If, having stepped over each single foot, two feet are identical, this should be known as *vikrānta-yamaka*, as for example: [BhN 16.71].
Having previously been an elephant like a two-peaked mountain,
he became like a mountain without peaks due to the loss of his tusks.
When the final syllable of the first quarter is identical to the initial syllable of the next, it should be known by name as *cakravāla*, like a circle; for example: [BhN 16.73].
When the first [foot] is equal to one of the last two feet, it should be understood by the wise as the *cakravāla* meter, occurring in all [four] places. (BhN 16.74)
Just as mountains struck by enemies— though already shattered and repeatedly pierced by arrows flying one after another—
are gathered together in battle by all manner of sky-faring beings, piled up, and laid down with palm against palm.
Where the first two feet have syllables that are equal, that should be known by the wise as *sandaṣṭayamaka*, as follows: [Example].
Look, look at the qualities of my lover, by which and by which he brings me under his sway;
for by whatever means he comes into my sight, by that very means he brings me under his sway.

Where there is an equal-syllable occurrence at the beginning of a quarter-verse, that should be recognized by the wise as *pādādi-yamaka* (the rhyme at the beginning of the quarter), as for example: [BhN 16.78].
Viṣṇu creates all beings; Viṣṇu withdraws all creatures;
Viṣṇu brings forth the three worlds; Viṣṇu is the presiding deity of the worlds. (BhN 16.79)
Where a single word is stated twice in succession at the end of a quarter-verse,
that is to be known by the wise as the *yamaka* named *āmreḍita*.
Your yawning and sighing recur again and again; how can your mindfulness be maintained at every step?
And as for this meditation of yours, it occurs repeatedly; surely your nights have passed without her, without her.
Where all four feet are equal and consist of a fixed number of syllables, that should be known by the wise as *caturvyavasitam*. (BhN 16.82)
This indeed is the time for elephants; this indeed is the time for elephants.
This indeed is the time for elephants; this indeed is the time for elephants.
Where a single consonant is joined with various forms and vowels, that should be recognized by the wise as *mālāyamaka*, as for example: [BhN 16.84].
May Lalī, Balī, Halī, Mālī, Khelī, Mālī, Salī, Jalī,
Khalo, Balo, Abalo, Mālī, and Musalī protect you.

For this beautiful woman, who delights in the physical union of love and is bold in privacy, would have gladdened her lover’s heart with supreme passion throughout the night— if only that formidable enemy, the rising young moon, were not about to appear.
With eyes like lotuses though drenched in blood, his wounds streaming and his blood difficult to behold,
his face covered with gashes as if by windows, he shone like the thousand-eyed Indra in person.
By these characteristics, which are concerned with purposeful action, poetry is to be defined;
hereafter, I shall explain the defects and the excellences in poetry.

Obscure meaning, ambiguity, lack of meaning, contradictory meaning, tautology, redundant meaning, deviation from logic, unevenness, faulty euphonic junction, and loss of word— these are indeed the ten defects of poetry.

When that which is designated as having a hidden meaning is expressed through synonymous terms, and what is not [ordinarily] described is described therein, that is considered "Arthāntara" (the Different). BhN 16.90.
One should recognize as defective speech that which is devoid of meaning, incoherent, leaving the sense incomplete, contradictory, vulgar, and even common. (BhN 16.91)
When the intended meaning is indeed something else, yet it is distinguished by another meaning,
the experts in poetry call that too "poetry with distinct meanings" (bhinnārtha).
That which is a non-specific designation is known as "having a single meaning" (ekārtha); it should be understood as having a cumulative sense when it is compounded with another word. (BhN 16.93)

That which deviates from logic and is devoid of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) should be understood as such; where there is a discordance in the structure of the verse, that is called "the Irregular" (viṣama). BhN 16.94.
That which lacks the prescribed phonetic sequence is known as *visandhi*;
that which is devoid of the word [itself] should be understood as resulting from the improper application of phonemes and accents. (BhN 16.95)
These defects based on drama are to be recognized by the wise;
the virtues, characterized by sweetness and loftiness, arise from the opposite of these.

Cohesion (śleṣa), clarity (prasāda), evenness (samatā), concentration (samādhi), sweetness (mādhurya), vigor (ojas), softness of words (padasaukumārya), explicitness of meaning (arthavyakti), loftiness (udāratā), and beauty (kānti)—these are the ten qualities (guṇas) of poetry. BhN 16.97.
The mutual cohesion of words that are connected with a desired set of meanings is indeed designated as *śleṣa* (punning conjunction).
That which is profound in its investigation, clear by its very nature, and naturally well-connected is proclaimed as "coherent" (śliṣṭa). (BhN 16.99)
Even where a word or its meaning is understood by the wise without being explicitly stated,
it is proclaimed as *prasāda* (clarity) due to the harmonious union of word and meaning.

That which is not composed of excessively fine words, nor of those that express the meaningless, and is not made difficult to understand due to unevenness—such is considered "evenness" (samatā) because of its evenness. (BhN 16.101)
Where ornaments and virtues are mutually similar and likewise serve as mutual adornments, they are considered equal, and this is regarded as the quality of evenness (samatā).
The specific excellence of an object that is perceived here by those who are diligent, and the meditative absorption (samādhi) endowed with that very object, is thus proclaimed. (BhN 16.103)

Because in this [treatise], there is a meditative concentration and a definitive determination of objects seen through analogies and those obtained with great effort, presented here in extreme brevity. (BhN 16.104)
That speech which, though heard many times or spoken again and again,
does not cause agitation, is indeed remembered as "sweetness" (mādhurya).
That which is joined with various compound words and diverse expressions, along with nasalized sounds (*anusvāra*) and noble [sounds], is proclaimed as *ojas* (vigorousness). BhN 16.106.
Even if it is censured or inferior, it may yet appear sublime;
where there is a perfection of word and meaning, that is proclaimed as *ojas* (vigor).
That which is joined with words that are easy to employ, possesses well-knit joints,
and is endowed with delicate meanings, is called *saukumārya* (delicacy).
But that action which, having a well-known designation established by worldly convention, is performed in poetry, is understood as "manifestation of meaning" (arthavyakti). (BhN 16.109)

That which is mentally conceptualized through the entry into its meaning, followed immediately by the application [of that conceptualization], is declared to be the manifestation of the object (arthavyakti). (BhN 16.110)
That which is permeated by a divine state, joined with the erotic and the marvelous, and endowed with manifold emotions, is proclaimed as "nobility" (udāratva). BhN 16.111.
That which is endowed with well-spoken words possessing multiple distinct meanings, joined with excellence, and containing exceedingly wonderful significations, is celebrated as *udātta*.
Poets know that splendor (*kānti*) to be that which, like the moon, delights the mind, the eyes, and the ears, or which is endowed with qualities such as playful charm (*līlā*). (BhN 16.113)
That bond of sound which is an object of the mind and ear and produces clarity, through its application, is called "the lovely" (kānta). BhN 16.114.
Thus have these ornaments, excellences, and defects been proclaimed;
furthermore, I shall explain their application as it pertains to the aesthetic sentiments (rasa).
However, those who know drama should compose poetry that consists mostly of short syllables, relies upon similes and metaphors, and is based on the heroic, the furious, and the marvelous sentiments.
It is composed mostly of heavy syllables in the *bībhatsa* (the loathsome) and *karuṇa* (the pathetic),
and occasionally in the *raudra* (the furious) and *vīra* (the heroic), when it arises from provocation.
A poem based on a drama should be composed in the heroic (*vīra*) and erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) sentiments, employing Āryā meters combined with *rūpaka* and *dīpaka* figures of speech. BhN 16.118.
That poetry which is composed in progressively more elevated meters may be in the Vīra meter, or in the Jagatī, Atijagatī, or even Saṃkṛti meters. (BhN 16.119)
In the same way, the *yuddhasaṃpheṭa* and *utkṛtyā* are proclaimed [in the *śāntika*];
in the *karuṇa*, the *śakvarī* is to be known, and likewise there should be *atidhṛti*.
Whatever meter is prescribed for the Heroic [rasa] should also be employed for the Furious;
for the remaining [rasas], the meters should be applied by practitioners according to the requirements of the meaning.
That *śloka* which was previously designated as *viṣama*, *ardhasama*, and *sama* should be composed with noble and sweet sounds, following the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). (BhN 16.122)
One should endeavor to compose sublime and sweet words denoting women within works based on drama;
for poetic compositions adorned by them shine greatly, like lotus ponds with blooming flowers when graced by royal swans.
For poets have established three kinds of syllables to be employed in drama: short, long, and protracted, which manifest the various sentiments (rasas) and emotional states (bhāvas). BhN 16.124.
A syllable consisting of one measure (mātrā) is short; two measures are intended as long;
and three measures constitute a protracted (pluta) syllable, through its conjunction with a vowel.
When there is recollection, when there is indignation, and likewise when there is lamentation, as well as among Brāhmaṇas who are reciting, the protracted vowel (pluta) is desired. BhN 16.126.
The syllable *akāra* is to be used when remembering; *ūkāra* when feeling resentment;
*hākāra* when lamenting; and likewise *oṃkāra* during Vedic study.
In all applications of poetry, one should employ syllables here—whether short, long, or protracted—in accordance with their inherent nature and their aesthetic flavor. (BhN 16.128)
The graceful performances of Bharata do not shine when joined with distorted sounds such as *cekrīḍita* and the like;
they are like a sacrificial rite performed by those smeared with the blood of wild animals, or like courtesans attended by Brahmins carrying water-pots and staffs in their hands.

A drama that possesses soft and graceful diction, avoids obscure words and meanings, is enjoyable for the wise, is endowed with logical reasoning, is fit for performance, follows the path composed of many sentiments, and is joined with proper junctures and transitions, becomes worthy of spectators in this world. (BhN 16.130)
The sequence [of topics] consists of: ornaments, clusters of syllables, beauty, examples, as well as reasons, doubt, illustrations, attainment, and intention. (BhN 16.131)
Illustration, etymological explanation, proof, and then qualification; the transcendence of qualities, excellence, equal reasoning, and the accumulation of words. BhN 16.132.
The seen and the taught, deliberation and its opposite, falling away and conciliation, the garland, courtesy, and likewise censure. (BhN 16.133)
Presumption, renown, inquiry, and similarity;
wishful thinking, a fragment, agitation, and the praise of virtues. (BhN 16.134)
One should point out thirty-six characteristics in poetic compositions: those already mentioned, implied accomplishments, and pleasant speech. BhN 16.135.
That which is adorned with many ornaments and qualities, like various meaningful decorations, is known as "ornament" (bhūṣaṇa). BhN 16.136.
Where something variegated is described by means of few, yet allusive, syllables—
one should know that collection of syllables as being designated by the term "lakṣaṇa."
When an unestablished meaning is employed by being made equivalent to established meanings,
wherein the various meanings are intertwined, that is called *śobhā* (beauty).
Where meanings are established by the skilled through the demonstration of a statement endowed with a similar meaning, that is remembered as an example (udāharaṇa). BhN 16.139.
That statement which, through the power of its purpose, accomplishes a desired object,
being concise and captivating to the mind, is designated as "the reason" (hetu).
Where a statement is concluded without its true meaning being fully understood due to the multiplicity of possible interpretations, that is traditionally known as doubt (*saṃśaya*). (BhN 16.141)
That which captivates the minds of all people and establishes the meaning of the thesis by means of the reason is known as the example (dṛṣṭānta).
When a state is inferred from the observation of certain parts,
one should recognize that as *prāpti*, a characteristic based on drama.
Even an object that has never existed before, which is imagined through similarity and captures the hearts of the world, is known as an "intentional meaning" (abhiprāya).
Where there is a full exposition of well-known objects for the purpose of setting aside dependence on others and so forth, that is called an illustration (nidarśana).
That statement which is uttered for the sake of establishing the meaning previously stated through faultless speech is cited as *nirukta*. (BhN 16.146)
When the names of many principal [deities] are proclaimed therein for the sake of accomplishing a desired object, that is designated as *siddhi*. (BhN 16.147)
Having stated many established primary meanings, that statement which is employed as something distinct should be understood as a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa). BhN 16.148.
Furthermore, through various descriptions of qualities that are applied with contrary meanings,
there may be a transgression of those very qualities by means of words that are sweet yet harsh in their import.
Having praised many virtues that arise among ordinary people,
that which is praised as a distinction should be understood by the wise as excellence (*atiśaya*).

When an object that is not directly perceived is brought into contact [with cognition] through metaphors, similes, or well-employed expressions of equivalent meaning, it is proclaimed as "analogical reasoning" (*tulyatarka*). BhN 16.151.
That which is a collection of many words employed with many other words, having a similar meaning, should be understood as *padoccaya*. (BhN 16.152)
It is described according to its location, its time, and its form—whether it be perceptible or imperceptible, or as it was seen even by way of its color. (BhN 16.153)
However, that statement which is expressed after having grasped the meaning of the treatise,
which captivates the minds of the learned and possesses a favorable conclusion, is called "taught" (upadiṣṭa).
Investigation is proclaimed as being joined with numerous conditions, having purposes consistent with prior intentions, and serving to establish objects that are not directly perceived. (BhN 16.155)
The alteration of deliberation, as well as that of what has been seen and what has been taught,
which is postulated due to doubt— that is to be known as error (viparyaya).

Having abandoned the intended meaning, falling into something else entirely through various means such as [misinterpreting] what is seen and so forth—this is considered "falling" (bhraṃśa) in this context. (BhN 16.157)
The wise should understand conciliation as that which generates pleasure for both parties who are fixed in opposition, and which indeed accomplishes the objective. (BhN 16.158)
That [work] in which various purposes are proclaimed by the wise for the sake of accomplishing desired goals is designated as a *mālā*. (BhN 16.159)
When one follows another with joyful and serene countenances through both speech and action, that is remembered as *dākṣiṇya* (courtesy).
Where, while mentioning a fault or a virtue, one demonstrates it through its underlying purpose—whether by the transgression of a virtue or by a fault—that is called *garhaṇā* (censure). BhN 16.161.
When another meaning is understood from the statement of a different matter, that is cited as *arthāpatti* (presumption), endowed with the sweetness of expression. (BhN 16.162)

When [an object] is expressed through many well-known sentences that are highly distinctive and which establish the meaning of the sentence, it is proclaimed as "established by renown" (prasiddhi). BhN 16.163.
That [speech] by which one asks about oneself or another through sentences arising from various forms,
or by which one expresses a meaning, is designated as *pṛcchā* (inquiry).
That which arises from the description of objects seen, heard, or experienced, and which produces agitation through similarity, is designated as *sārūpya*. (BhN 16.165)
The expression, by means of indirect references, of a thought residing in the heart whose meaning is hidden, is known as *manoratha*. (BhN 16.166)
That statement which is expressed by those skilled in speech through a skillful means for the purpose of bringing about a similar meaning is proclaimed as *leśa*.
Where the self—or even some other unseen entity—is proclaimed through various meanings that are actually defects, that is known as *kṣobha*. (BhN 16.168)
That in which even a single quality among those qualities that exceed all others in the world is expressed by its names, that should be known as "Praise of Qualities" (guṇakīrtana). (BhN 16.169)
When the entire remaining meaning is understood through the mere introduction,
such that what is not explicitly stated is established even without words, that is proclaimed as *anuktasiddhi*.
The speech uttered with a serene mind for the purpose of honoring that which is worthy of honor, yet intended to express one's joy, is called "affectionate speech" (priyokti). (BhN 16.171)
These thirty-six characteristics of poetry, which serve as illustrative examples, are like elixirs that experts should properly employ to bring beauty to their compositions. (BhN 16.172)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Poetry," in the section on Vocal Representation within Bharata’s *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter:
"O Brahmins, I shall now set forth the classification of the ten types of drama."
By way of name, by way of action, and likewise by way of application.
The Nāṭaka, along with the Prakaraṇa, the Aṅka, and the Vyāyoga; the Bhāṇa, the Samavakāra, the Vīthī, the Prahasana, and the Ḍima. (BhN 18.2)
And the *īhāmṛga* should also be known; these ten [types of drama] are defined in the science of dramaturgy.
I shall explain their characteristics in due order. (BhN 18.3)
The *vṛttis* (styles) are considered the mother of all poetic compositions;
for from these, the ten forms of drama (*daśarūpa*) have issued forth through their practical application.
Just as notes attain the state of scales through various birth-classes and shrutis,
so indeed do poetic compositions arise through the distinctions of their stylistic modes.
Just as the two scales, Ṣaḍja and Madhyama, possess complete tones,
so too these two poetic compositions are perfected through all modes of expression.
The *jñeyaprakaraṇa* (section on what is to be known), as well as the *nāṭaka* (drama),
is accomplished through all dramatic styles (*vṛtti*) and relies upon various poetic compositions (*bandha*).
The *vīthī*, the *samavakāra*, and likewise the *īhāmṛga*, the *utsṛṣṭikāṅka*, the *vyāyoga*, the *bhāṇa*, the *prahasana*, and the *ḍima*. (BhN 18.8)
One should have these forms fashioned as being devoid of the Kaiśikī style;
hereafter, I shall explain the various types of poetic compositions.
Its subject matter is a well-known event, its hero is a renowned and noble personage,
it concerns the life of one born in the lineage of royal seers, and likewise, it may involve divine beings.

Indeed, that which is endowed with various manifestations and qualities such as the play of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), and is enriched by *aṅka* acts and *praveśaka* interludes, is called a *nāṭaka*. (BhN 18.11)
The various deeds of kings, consisting of manifold sentiments, emotions, and gestures, and brought about by the arising of pleasure and pain— that indeed is what is called a drama.
Having carefully observed the action suited to this state [of the character], a mark (aṅka) should be made from the width of a drop;
moreover, that too must be endowed with excellence by those who know the principles of drama.

"Aṅka" is a conventional term; because it causes meanings to grow through both the emotional states (bhāvas) and the aesthetic sentiments (rasas), and because it is joined with various types of dramatic rules (anayas), it is therefore called an "act" (aṅka). (BhN 18.14)
The conclusion of an act (aṅka) should be made by means of a break in the narrative; there should be a withdrawal of the seed (bīja).
The "drop" (bindu), which pervades the entire subject matter and arises from the poetic work, must always be present here.
That in which the completion of the plot occurs and wherein the withdrawal of the seed takes place,
with some small portion of the bindu still lingering— that should always be understood as an *aṅka*.

The *aṅka* (act) should be composed as a direct encounter with the actions of those leaders who have been described, involving various situations, yet it must not be separated [from the main plot]. (BhN 18.17)
It should be understood that an *aṅka* (act) is indeed composed of no fewer than five varieties of sentiment, involving the hero, heroine, elders, priests, ministers, and caravan leaders. BhN 18.18.
An act (aṅka) in a drama or a playlet (prakaraṇa) should consist of five or ten scenes;
it is to be understood as that in which there is the exit of all characters.

Anger, favor, grief, the utterance of a curse, flight, marriage, and the witnessing of the occurrence of a marvel—these are the elements that should arise from direct perception within the *aṅka*. (BhN 18.20)

An act (*aṅka*) should be composed concerning the seed of the plot (*arthabīja*), occurring within the span of a single day, without contradicting the necessary requirements of the dramatic performances. (BhN 18.21)
Sometimes a wise person may undertake many tasks with a single effort, provided they do not conflict with what is essential; among those, poetic compositions should be performed.
For all those who have entered the stage, there must be an exit;
having composed a poem endowed with the logic of the seed-meaning, it should possess its appropriate rasa.
One should not perform many tasks while seated alone;
for in that way, there would be an obstruction to those duties that are essential. (BhN 18.24)
Having understood the state of the day, endowed with its characteristics of moments (kṣaṇa), watches (yāma), and muhūrtas,
one should divide everything without exception individually according to the poetic meters (kāvyāṅka).
If any business of the day's conclusion cannot be accomplished within the act,
it should all be carried out by means of *praveśakas* after breaking off the act.
But if one must go to a distant place due to the exigencies of business,
he should briefly indicate that [journey] by means of *praveśakas* through the marking of the script.
In a *nāṭaka* or a *prakaraṇa*, an act (*aṅka*) should be composed with the hero present;
that which is connected with the conversation of the attendants is to be known as a *praveśaka*.
Regarding the *prakaraṇa* and *nāṭaka*, there should be from five to ten acts;
and at the junctions between acts, there should be as many *praveśakas*.

Having observed the purposeful action [required] between these two, an interlude (praveśaka) should be arranged within the junctures (sandhi) for the sake of condensing the meaning of the plot elements. 18.30.
Having made a mark on the body, whether it be for a month or accumulated over a year, all of that must be performed; however, never after a year has passed.
If any man must travel a long distance for the sake of some business,
those who know the law should likewise mark his body with a brand there as well, just as before.

In the context of plays (*prakaraṇa*) and dramas (*nāṭaka*), a *praveśaka* (interlude) should be employed with reference to the summary of the meaning that follows from one act to another. (BhN 18.33)
It should be performed by resorting to the usage of the Prakrit language, a practice neither followed by superior or middling persons nor composed in elevated speech.
This *praveśaka* (interlude), occurring at the appropriate time, consists of the movement [of characters] toward the objects of the exposition, the undertaking, and the action;
joined with the expression of meaning, it may have multiple purposes. (BhN 18.35)
Even if an action has many bases, one should condense it through *praveśakas* or within the *saṃdhis*;
for that which is joined with many fragmentary words causes weariness in the performance.
Where the completion of the plot does not occur within an act due to the abundance of action, that [remainder] should be conveyed through *praveśakas* containing brief accounts of events. (BhN 18.37)
War, the loss of a kingdom, death, and the siege of a city—these should indeed be presented directly on stage through interludes (*praveśaka*). (BhN 18.38)
In the *Aṅka*, the *Praveśaka*, or in a *Prakaraṇa* or even a *Nāṭaka*, no killing should be performed involving a protagonist who is renowned and destined for prosperity. (BhN 18.39)
Withdrawal alone should be performed, or capture, or peace should be employed—according to the sentiment, by those who know the principles of drama through many poetic allusions. (BhN 18.40)
One should not perform a drama or a play with a large retinue;
there should be only four or five essential characters therein.
Having undertaken a poetic composition, the conclusion should be made like the tip of a cow's tail;
and all those sentiments that are exalted should be placed at the very end.
In the conclusion of all poems, which are endowed with the application of various sentiments (rasas) and emotional states (bhāvas),
those who know [the art] must always employ the marvelous sentiment (adbhuta-rasa).
I have thus duly proclaimed the characteristics of the drama in brief;
hereafter, I shall explain the *prakaraṇa* according to the principles of its defining characteristics.
Where a poet, by his own power, creates from the outset the subject matter, the plot, and the hero, that should be known by the wise as a *prakaraṇa* (drama of invented subject). BhN 18.45.

That which is not based on the words of a seer (anārṣa), yet is composed as poetry (kāvya) that is not derived from [prior sources] and is endowed with qualities not found elsewhere, having as its subject matter a story whose seed has already arisen—that too should be known as a *prakaraṇa*. (BhN 18.46)
Whatever has been stated by me regarding the subject matter, the body [of the plot], and the varieties of dramatic styles (vṛtti) in the case of the *nāṭaka*,
that should also be applied to the *prakaraṇa*, along with its defining characteristics, across all the junctures (*saṃdhi*).
The manifold conduct of Brahmins, merchants, and warriors, as well as of priests, ministers, and caravan leaders—that which is to be known is called *Prakaraṇa*. (BhN 18.48)
That which does not feature a noble hero, nor celestial exploits, nor royal enjoyments, and which is concerned with common folk, should be known by the experts as a *prakaraṇa*. (BhN 18.49)
In a *prakaraṇa*, however, a poem should be composed concerning the conduct of women from humble families, involving servants, parasites, and merchants, and featuring the attentions of courtesans.
In a place where there are excellent ministers, guild-leaders, Brahmins, domestic priests, counselors, and caravan leaders, a courtesan should not be established. (BhN 18.51)
If it is joined with a courtesan, there would be no union even with a woman of good family; likewise, if it is joined with a woman of good family, there would be no courtesan therein. (BhN 18.52)
Alternatively, if there should be an enactment of the conduct of women from various households based on the logic of the cause,
then the recitation (*pāṭhya*) should be performed there with unaltered speech and behavior.
In this [drama], the *viṣkambhaka* should always be employed by persons of middle status who know the truth;
it follows the conventions of Sanskrit speech and serves as a concise summary, like a *praveśaka*.
The *viṣkambhaka* (interlude) should also be performed in two ways: pure (*śuddha*) or mixed (*saṃkīrṇa*).
The pure type is performed by a middle-ranking character; the mixed type is performed by characters of low or middle rank.

A *praveśaka* (interlude), placed between acts (*aṅka*), should be composed in brief after considering the necessary functions, as well as the purposes of the junctures (*sandhi*) and the plot elements (*artha*).
Furthermore, a distinction between these two should be made by the practitioners through their application of the plot;
otherwise, the other [type] is well-known in the context of a *nāṭaka* or a *prakaraṇa*. (BhN 18.57)

Based on the distinction between the *prakaraṇa* and the *nāṭaka*, the plot should be invented, the hero should be a king, and the work should be composed concerning a maiden from the harem or a singing girl. (BhN 18.58)

It consists mostly of women, possesses four acts, is characterized by graceful acting, has well-arranged limbs, abounds in dance, song, and recitation, and is essentially devoted to the enjoyment of love.
Accompanied by royal etiquette, endowed with favor, anger, and guile, and possessing a retinue including a mistress, a queen, and a messenger—such is to be known as a *nāṭikā*. (BhN 18.60)
For this [consciousness] is indeed contained within both of these two states;
for this very reason, these ten are truly declared to be "forms" (rūpa). (BhN 18.61)
O Brahmins, I have thus briefly stated the characteristics of the *prakaraṇa* and the *nāṭaka*;
hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the *samavakāra* with logical precision.

It is composed from the seeds of gods and asuras, features a well-known and noble protagonist, and consists of three acts; it should likewise possess three disguises, three chases, and three elements of erotic sentiment.
For it consists largely of twelve leaders and measures eighteen channels;
I shall explain the method for its numerical calculation according to however many channels exist therein.
The *Aṅka*, however, should be composed with laughter, flight, deceit, and the *vīthī*;
it should consist of twelve *nāḍīs* and be endowed with dramatic action. BhN 18.65.
Likewise, the second [lagna] should be established as relying on four nāḍīs;
however, the third, prescribed for the completion of the matter, should consist of two nāḍīs.
The term "nāḍī" should be understood as the measure of time known as half a muhūrta;
that is the standard for a nāḍikā, which is to be added to the figures as previously stated.
That which is designated as a *nāḍikā* is established through action within the division of time;
it must be performed with effort according to the sequence prescribed in the scriptures.
Having undertaken the composition of a poetic work, one should arrange the acts so that each act serves a distinct purpose;
for in a *samavakāra*, they desire the plot to be composed of unconnected themes.
Flight is to be known as threefold: that arising from the waters of battle, that caused by the agitation of wind, fire, and great elephants, or that born from the siege of a city. (BhN 18.70)

In this context, deceit should be understood as threefold: that which is determined by the sequence of actual facts, that which arises through the power of destiny, or that which is employed by another, all of which result in the production of pleasure or pain.
And here, those who know the rules should separately apply the threefold erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) for the sake of the specific purposes ordained for dharma, artha, and kāma.
That in which there is a means for attaining Dharma that is beneficial to oneself, consisting of various practices joined with vows,
observances, and austerities— this should be known as the adornment of Dharma.

The erotic sentiment based on wealth (*arthāśṛṅgāra*) arises from the connection with the desire for wealth in many ways through its objects, or where there is pleasure motivated by wealth in the context of sexual union with women. (BhN 18.74)

Whether it be the charming encounter of a man and woman brought about by the seduction of a maiden, or that which is secret or full of excitement— for whomsoever such erotic passion (kāma-śṛṅgāra) may exist.
In the *samavakāra*, poets should employ the *uṣṇih*, *gāyatrī*, and other such meters that possess curved structures. (BhN 18.76)
Thus should the *samavakāra*, which rests upon various sentiments (*rasas*), be composed by those who know it.
Hereafter, I shall describe the characteristics of the *īhāmṛga* as well.
It is caused by relying on divine beings, involves a battle undertaken for the sake of a celestial woman,
is bound to well-arranged matters, and indeed produces disbelief.
It consists mostly of boastful men, with poetic compositions bound by the anger of women;
it likewise creates agitation and flight, and is characterized by quarreling. (BhN 18.79)

The *īhāmṛga* should be composed with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) arising from the separation of women, abduction, and crushing, and it should be constructed with a very well-composed poetic arrangement. (BhN 18.80)

Whatever action, persons, modes of conduct, and sentiments [are appropriate] for the Vyāyoga, those same should also be present in the Īhāmṛga; the only difference is its connection with celestial women.
But where the slaughter of those desired to be killed would be excessive for men,
one should pacify their battle by employing some pretext.
O brahmins, the characteristics of the *īhāmṛga* have been stated in brief;
now I shall further explain the characteristics of the *ḍima* according to the principles of dramatic definition.
The *ḍima* should be composed with a well-known subject matter and a celebrated, noble hero; it must possess the characteristics of the six rasas and consist of four acts. (BhN 18.84)
Excluding the erotic and the comic, it is endowed with all the remaining sentiments; it has its source in poetry of intense sentiment and is perfected by various emotional states.
It should be composed of thunderclaps and the falling of meteors, as well as eclipses of the moon and sun,
along with battles, wrestling matches, assaults, and tumultuous clashes.
It abounds in illusions and sorcery, is joined with the practice of raising many corpses,
and is crowded with gods, lords of serpents, rākṣasas, yakṣas, and piśācas.

The *ḍima* should be composed with diligent effort, featuring many principal characters, endowed with the *sāttvatī* and *ārabhaṭī* styles of dramatic representation, and filled with various supporting emotions.
I have thus briefly explained the characteristics of the *ḍima* in accordance with its defining traits;
hereafter, I shall fully set forth the characteristics of the *vyāyoga*.

The *vyāyoga*, however, should be composed by those who know the rules, having a well-known protagonist as its central figure, involving few female characters, and likewise performed in a single day. (BhN 18.90)
And many men exert themselves therein as in a *samavakāra*;
however, this [work] should not be joined with divine heroes, but should consist of only one act (*ekāṅka*).
Nor should it be composed with divine heroes as its protagonists, nor bound by royal sages as its heroes;
rather, it should be made featuring battles, wrestling matches, insults, and rivalries.
A *vyāyoga* of this kind should be composed as a source for brilliant poetic sentiment;
hereafter, I shall describe the characteristics of the *utsṛṣṭikāṅka*.
However, that which has a well-known subject matter may sometimes be "unfamiliar" [in its specific details];
it should be devoid of divine beings and consist of the remaining types of men. (BhN 18.94)
It is characterized primarily by the sentiment of compassion; it involves the cessation of combat and the laying aside of weapons;
it abounds in the lamentations of women and consists of speech full of world-weariness.

The *utsṛṣṭikāṅka* should always be composed by those who know the rules of poetic composition as characterized by various agitated gestures and devoid of the *sāttvatī*, *ārabhaṭī*, and *kaisikī* styles. (BhN 18.96)
In poetic compositions, that which is composed by divine leaders and involves battles, binding, and slaying should be set in the land of Bhārata. (BhN 18.97)
Why is Bhārata favored among the other god-ordained regions?
Because its entire ground is pleasant, auspiciously fragrant, and golden.
There would be pleasures consisting of strolling in groves, sporting, and the delights of dalliance with women;
for in those years, there is never any suffering or sorrow there.
Those mountains which are described in the ancient discourses as their abodes—
therein shall be enjoyment, and in this [land] shall be the commencement of action.
The *prahasana* (farce) should also be known as being of two kinds: pure (*śuddha*) and mixed (*saṅkīrṇa*).
This definition of the *aṅka* (act) has been explained in its entirety, including all its constituent elements. BhN_18.101 //
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the *prahasana* (farce) along with its characteristics;
I shall describe the specific characteristics of each of those two separately according to their proper method.
It consists of humorous talk associated with the Blessed One, ascetics, brahmins, or others; it is connected with base persons and consists primarily of joking speech. (BhN 18.103)

But *prahasana* (the comic) should be known as pure, characterized by unaltered speech and conduct, consisting of verses endowed with a particular emotional state (*bhāva*), and having as its object matters pertaining to a fixed destiny. BhN 18.104.

A place where courtesans, servants, eunuchs, parasites, rogues, and unchaste women reside, and which is characterized by unrestrained dress, equipment, gestures, and conduct, is called *saṃkīrṇa* (mixed). (BhN 18.105)
Whatever discourse is consistent with worldly convention, whatever is joined with hypocrisy, and whatever is characterized by the mutual debate of rogues— such should be employed in the *prahasana*.
A farce (prahasana) should be composed by employing the constituent elements of the plot as appropriate;
hereafter, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the monologue (bhāṇa).
The *bhāṇa*, however, is characterized by praising what has been personally experienced and by describing the specific qualities of others;
it should be understood as having various bases and being captivating to the audience. (BhN 18.108)
One should internalize another's speech through replies composed of the most excellent phrases,
as well as by means of gestures and dramatic representations that resemble the "Person in Space" (ākāśapuruṣa).
The *bhāṇa* should always be composed by the wise as a one-act play featuring rogues and libertines, consisting of various changing states of affairs and abounding in diverse actions. (BhN 18.110)
For indeed, the entire definition of *bhāṇa*, in accordance with the traditional scriptures, has already been stated;
now, O Brahmins, I shall describe the entirety of *vīthī* in its proper sequence.
Richly endowed with the characteristics of all sentiments and possessed of thirteen constituent parts,
the *vīthī* should consist of one act (*aṅka*) and have either one or two characters (*hārya*).
It may be composed with the three types of characters—low, high, and middle—and it may also include the *uddhātyaka*, *avalagita*, *avaspaṇḍita*, *nālikā*, and *satpralāpa*. (BhN 18.113)
Speech, verbal proliferation (*prapañca*), softness, obstruction, force, deception, the threefold [path], discourse, and the tumor—these thirteen members are declared to belong to it. (BhN 18.114)
Now, the *vīthī* has been fully explained; I shall proclaim its characteristics. As for those words whose meaning is not yet understood, men who possess devotion [should study them]. (BhN 18.115)
When one connects [verses] with other words, it is called *uddhātyaka*; wherein, having introduced another matter, a different task is accomplished. (BhN 18.116)
And that should be known as *āvalagita* by those who employ dramatic techniques, when some matter—whether auspicious or inauspicious—is introduced. (BhN 18.117)
When another meaning is expressed through skillfulness, that becomes its "vibration" (tadavaspandita).
A *prahelikā* (riddle) whose meaning is approached through jesting is to be known as a *nālikā*.
When a wise person speaks what is beneficial in the company of fools,
yet his words are not accepted, that should be understood as mere idle chatter.
In this practice, "verbal play" (*vākkelī*) consists of one or two exchanges;
it is that speech which is unreal yet characterized by mutual intimacy between the two. (BhN 18.120)
And for the sake of a single object, that proliferation would give rise to laughter, because it results in the attribution of faults to qualities through the act of dispute. (BhN 18.121)
Or, the transformation of faults into virtues should be understood as "gentleness" (mṛdutva).
That is where the speech of another and one's own [speech] arise in successive succession for both parties. (BhN 18.122)
The wise should understand that *adhibala* is that which qualifies the meaning of one another;
whereas a statement intended for a different purpose is *chala*, which causes deception, laughter, or anger. (BhN 18.123)

That in which many meanings are joined by logical arguments due to their similarity to the sacred scriptures (śruti), whether it be humorous or very humorous, should be known as *trigata*. (BhN 18.124)
Direct discourse is said to be for the purpose of a slight joke;
it is characterized by agitation and haste, as well as by dispute and the making of accusations. (BhN 18.125)
Those who know the truth declare that a *gaṇḍa* (interlude) is formed by the implication of the plural number.
Thus, the entire prescription for the ten types of drama has been declared by me according to their characteristics;
now I shall further describe the characteristics regarding the joints (*sandhi*) within its body.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ten Types of Drama," in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* of Bharata.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter:
"The plot (*itivṛtta*) is proclaimed to be the body of drama."
Its division is conceived through five joints.
A wise man should consider the plot (itivṛtta) to be of two kinds: one is the primary (ādhikarika), and the other is the incidental (prāsaṅgika). BhN 19.2.
That action which is inferred by its capacity through the attainment of its fruit should be known as *adhikārika* (primary); others know that which is otherwise to be *prāsaṅgika* (incidental).

The conduct of one who is fit for the fruit by virtue of the cause is termed "pertaining to authority" (ādhikārika); that which is proclaimed for the sake of its equipment is indeed the "incidental" (ānuṣaṅgika).
Know that the attainment of the fruit is brought about through the poet’s effort, the reliance upon disciplined guides, and the excellence of the fruit itself. BhN 19.5.
The worldly states known as pleasure and pain arise from the emergence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*);
the tenfold state of love (*manmatha*) is considered to be established in three ways.
Regarding the causal operation within the sacrificial ritual of worldly existence,
its five successive stages should be understood by practitioners in their proper order.
The undertaking, the effort, the possibility of attainment, the certainty of obtaining the fruit, and fifthly, the union with the fruit. (BhN 19.8)
When the mere bond of longing for the seed is established, that is intended as the commencement of the fruit, which leads to a great attainment of results. (BhN 19.9)
That activity directed toward a result by one who does not perceive the attainment of that result,
and which involves a supreme state of eagerness, is proclaimed as "effort" (prayatna).
When some slight attainment of the fruit is conceived, those who know the rules declare that the possibility of attainment exists by the mere fact of its being [the object]. BhN 19.11.
But when one perceives with one's being that the attainment of the fruit is certain,
they declare that certain attainment of the fruit to be endowed with qualities.
When there is a connection with the fruit in the narrative—that which is intended, complete, and appropriate—then it is proclaimed as the "Fruit-yoga" (phalayoga). BhN 19.13.
For indeed, all effects that have been commenced by those seeking their fruit necessarily undergo these five stages in this very sequence.
The arrangement of these [energies], which are distinct by nature, through their mutual union into a single state, is proclaimed as the cause of the fruit.
Thus has the narrative been fully related, pertaining specifically to the individual soul;
its commencement and so forth should be performed until its fruit is attained.
One should conclude a treaty that is complete, or alternatively, one that is inferior;
by rule, it should be a complete treaty, whereas an inferior treaty occurs for a specific reason.
When one [of the four] is elided, it is the fourth; when two are elided, the third and fourth;
and when three are elided, the second, third, and fourth—their elision is thus prescribed.
In the case of incidental [verses], because they are for the sake of another, this restriction would not apply;
whatever meter is possible there should be employed, provided it is not contradictory.

In the *itivṛtta* (historical narrative), the five *arthaprakṛtis* (plot elements) beginning with the *ārambha* (undertaking) are traditionally taught as they exist in their actual state; likewise, there are also the five beginning with the *bīja* (seed).
The seed (bīja), the drop (bindu), the banner (patākā), the small banner (prakarī), and the purpose (kārya)—
these five elements of the plot (arthaprakṛti) should be employed according to rule once they have been understood.
That which, when sown in a very small measure, spreads in many directions and culminates in fruit— that indeed is proclaimed to be a seed.
That which is the cause for the non-interruption of purposes when they have been interrupted,
persisting until the completion of the bond— that is proclaimed as a *bindu*.
But that which occurs for the sake of another and assists the principal [action] should be considered as if it were the principal itself; that is proclaimed as the *patākā* (the banner).
That [plot] for which a result is devised solely for the sake of another, and which is devoid of a further consequence (anubandha), one should designate as a *prakarī*. (BhN 19.25)
When a subject pertaining to a specific office is properly applied by the wise, that undertaking for its sake is proclaimed as "action" (kārya). (BhN 19.26)
Among these, whichever is required for a particular purpose and from which a specific quality is desired—that should be made the primary factor; the others are secondary to it.
Whether a juncture (sandhi) be single or multiple, that which occurs within a banner (patākā) is proclaimed an "extended juncture" (anusandhi) because it follows the primary subject matter.
The *patākā* (subsidiary plot) ceases either at the *āgarbha* or at the *āvimarśa*.
Why? Because its connection is proclaimed to be for the sake of another [the main plot]. (BhN 19.29)
When, while one matter is being considered, another matter of a similar character is introduced through an adventitious circumstance, that is the *patākāsthānaka* (the episode of the banner).
The sudden attainment of a virtuous object through a service rendered is proclaimed as this first *patākāsthānaka*.
Speech that is highly distinguished, yet afflicted, and based upon a poetic composition—
this is proclaimed as the second *patākāsthānaka*.
Where the presentation of a meaning is subtle yet refined, and is endowed with a clever reply, this is considered the third [type]. (BhN 19.33)
The arrangement of words that possesses a double meaning, is well-knit, composed as poetry, and properly joined with the introductory context—that is declared to be the fourth [type]. (BhN 19.34)

Where there is a speech of exceptional excellence that serves as an introduction to the subject matter, and which is seen to conclude with a destruction, that indeed is the *patākārdha* (half-banner). // BhN_19.35 //
In this drama, the supreme form with four banners shall be enacted;
it is joined by five junctures, which I shall describe hereafter.
The Mukha (opening), Pratimukha (development), Garbha (embryo), Vimarśa (dissolution), and likewise Nirvahaṇa (conclusion)— these are the five junctures (*sandhi*) in a drama.
"The primary joints are proclaimed as being endowed with five types; the remaining ones are the secondary joints that support the primary joints. (BhN 19.38)
Wherein there is the production of seeds from which various meanings and aesthetic flavors arise, following along with the body of the poem— that is proclaimed as the "Introduction" (mukha).
Where the unfolding of the seed-syllable (bīja) is, as it were, seen and then lost in some places,
yet is present everywhere when placed at the beginning— that indeed is known as the *pratimukha* (counter-opening).
The manifestation of that seed, whether it be its attainment or non-attainment, and where there is further investigation—that is designated as the "embryo" (garbha). (BhN 19.41)
The *vimarśa* (doubt) is said to arise from the meaning of a seed that has been split by the embryo, or from a lure, or even from the affliction of anger. (BhN 19.42)
The *nirvahaṇa* (conclusion) is that which brings together the matters introduced at the beginning along with their seeds, following various developments. (BhN 19.43)
These junctures (sandhis) should be understood by the performers of a drama;
likewise for the *prakaraṇa*, and learn now of the others as well. (BhN 19.44)
The *ḍima* and the *samavakāra* are proclaimed to have four junctures (*saṃdhi*);
poets should never include the *avamarśa* (crisis) juncture in these two.
The Vyāyoga and the Īhāmṛga should also always have three junctures;
they should not possess the *garbha* or *avamarśa* junctures, and their style (*vṛtti*) should be the Kaiśikī.
The *prahasana*, the *vīthī*, the *aṅka*, and the *bhāṇa* each have two junctures;
in these, the *mukha* (opening) and *nirvahana* (conclusion) must always be employed by poets.
For the *vīthī*, the *bhāṇa*, and likewise the *prahasana*—
these works should always be composed by poets as being devoid of the *kaiśikī* style.
Thus indeed should the junctures (sandhis) be composed by performers in the *Daśarūpaka*.
Now, furthermore, learn the arrangement of the constituent parts (aṅgakalpa) of these junctures.
One should understand those constituent parts which are the occurrences of the *sandhis* in their respective sections in due order, endowed with the qualities of their own perfection.
The composition of the desired subject matter, the non-omission of the narrative, the attainment of passion, and the concealment of secrets in the performance; BhN 19.51.
The marvelous presentation, and the illumination of things to be illuminated—this sixfold purpose of the [auxiliary] limbs is indeed observed in the scripture. (BhN 19.52)
Just as a man lacking a limb is not capable of undertaking any enterprise,
so too a poem that lacks its constituent parts is not fit for performance.
Even that poetry may be elevated, yet it would be devoid of its constituent parts;
for, due to the deficiency in its execution, it does not delight the minds of the wise.
Even a poem whose subject matter is inferior attains beauty through the excellence of its constituent parts, owing to the brilliance of its performance; of this there is no doubt.
"Therefore, at the junctures, the constituent parts should be composed by the poet according to their fitness and their aesthetic flavor; understand them correctly. (BhN 19.56)
Introduction, elaboration, transition, enticement, application, attainment, resolution, arrangement, and contemplation. (BhN 19.57)
Unfolding (udbheda), the means (karaṇa), and division (bheda)—these are indeed the constituent parts (aṅgas) in the Opening (mukha);
likewise, in the Sub-opening (pratimukha), hear the constituent parts by name.
Vilāsa (graceful movement), parisarpa (gliding), vidhūta (shaking off), tāpana (tormenting), narma (jesting), narmadyuti (the brilliance of jesting), and again pragayaṇa (advancing).
Cessation itself is to be understood, as well as service;
the flower, the vajra, the introduction, and the withdrawal of the colors.
Know these indeed to be the constituent parts in the womb, facing toward the front:
the introduction (*abhūtāharaṇa*), the path (*mārga*), the illustration of form (*rūpodāharaṇa*), and the sequence (*krama*). (BhN 19.61)

Gathering (*saṃgraha*), inference (*anumāna*), and that which is implied by a request (*prārthanākṣipta*); likewise, the *toṭaka*, the *adhibala*, agitation (*udvega*), and flight (*vidrava*). BhN 19.62.
Understand that these are indeed the components within the *garbha* (the womb/interlude), namely:
*apavāda*, *saṃpheṭa*, *vidrava*, and *śakti*. BhN 19.63.
Resolution, attachment, radiance, exhaustion, prohibition, opposition, then taking, concealment, and persuasion; BhN 19.64.
Furthermore, these are the limbs of deliberation: judicial procedure, reasoning, reconciliation, suppression, composition, adjudication, and discussion. (BhN 19.65)
Radiance, clarity, joy, agreement, embracing, speaking, the opening speech, and likewise the conclusion of the poem. BhN 19.66.

The *praśasti* (eulogy) is to be known as occurring in the conclusion (*saṃhāra*). These sixty-four limbs should be known by the wise according to their names within the junctures (*sandhi*). BhN 19.67.

"In order to achieve the fulfillment of the seed (bīja), these actions which bring about its perfect accomplishment should be distributed by poets according to their purposes within the drama. (BhN 19.68)
Furthermore, I shall explain their characteristics in due order:
the origin of the poetic subject matter is known as the "Introduction" (upakṣepa).
That which is an abundance of developed meanings should be known as the *parikara* (accessory);
its completion should always be recognized by poets as the *parinyāsa* (conclusion).
The description of qualities is known as "enticement" (vilobhana),
and the thorough deliberation of matters is designated as "reasoning" (yukti).
The approach for the sake of the object of happiness is designated as "attainment" (prāpti); the approach for the sake of the seed is known as "concentration" (samādhāna). BhN 19.72.
The determination of the matter concerning pleasure and pain is known as *vidhāna*;
*paribhāvanā* should be understood as an intense surge of curiosity. (BhN 19.73)
The sprouting of the meaning of the seed is known as "emergence" (udbheda); the undertaking of the subject matter at hand is that which is called "instrumentality" (karaṇa). BhN 19.74.
That which aims at the breaking up of the assembly is proclaimed as "the division" (bheda).
I shall now describe these primary components; furthermore, regarding the "counter-introduction" (pratimukha): // BhN 19.75 //
Striving for the sake of pleasure and enjoyment is designated as *vilāsa* (sportiveness);
the pursuit of what has been seen and lost is known as *parisarpa* (crawling).

At the outset, after the initial conciliation has been rejected and there is no acceptance [of the request], that which consists in showing the dangers [of hell] is what is called "tormenting" (tāpana). BhN 19.77.
That laughter which is intended for the sake of play is known as *narma*;
however, laughter intended for the purpose of concealing a fault is known as *narmadyuti*.
Furthermore, the progressive sequence of statements is called pragayaṇa;
whereas the occurrence of calamities is proclaimed as nirodha.
That which is a conciliatory gesture toward one who is angry is called *paryupāsana*;
that which is a statement of distinction is designated as *puṣpa*.
A statement that is direct and harsh is called a "thunderbolt" (vajra); that which is an argumentative point and a formal presentation is known as an "introduction" (upanyāsa). (BhN 19.81)
The merging of the four castes is considered the dissolution of the social orders;
they know that speech based on deceit is the fabrication of what is unreal.
The statement of the true meaning is designated as the *mārga* (path). When there is a convergence of various meanings, *vitarka* (investigation) is considered to be their form.
That speech which possesses excellence is known as *udāharaṇa* (illustration).
The realization of the true nature of existence is designated as "the sequence" (krama),
while being endowed with conciliation and the other [means] is proclaimed as "inclusion" (saṃgraha).
Movement that conforms to one's form is known as *anumāna* (inference);
the longing for the festivals of pleasure and joy is called *prārthanā* (longing). That which is the manifestation of the embryo is designated as *ākṣipti* (suggestion).
Speech characterized by vehemence is designated as *toṭaka*;
the wise call the deception practiced through guile *adhibala*.
Fear arising from kings, enemies, or robbers is proclaimed as agitation (udvega); trembling caused by fear and terror is declared to be flight (vidrava).
The public exposure of faults is known as *apavāda* (reproach),
while speech strung together with rage is proclaimed as *saṃpheṭa* (wrangling).
That which is the transgression against the guru is proclaimed as *drava*;
that which is the pacification of opposition is proclaimed as *śakti*. (BhN 19.90)
Determination should be understood as arising from the proposition and the reason;
likewise, the application [of the reason] and the citation of authorities should be understood. (BhN 19.91)
Speech accompanied by insolence is described as *dyuti* by those who know it;
exhaustion produced from mental activity is described as *kheda*.
The obstruction of a desired object is proclaimed as "refutation" (pratiṣedha);
the admission of the failure of one's own effect is known as "contradiction" (virodhana). (BhN 19.93)
The presentation of one's own seed and its effects is designated as such;
a statement made out of disrespect would be a concealment for the sake of one's purpose. (BhN 19.94)
That which demonstrates the purpose of the summary is to be known as *prarocanā* (incitement);
that which is a statement of direct perception is remembered as *vyāhāra* (utterance).
Where speech is interrupted, that is designated as "Yukti" (Reasoning);
it should be known by the experts as "Vicalanā" (wavering), being joined with the purpose of disparagement.
"Understand these limbs as they relate to the withdrawal (saṃhāra):
the convergence of the seed-syllable with the mouth is designated as the juncture (sandhi)."
The investigation of the task through reasoning is proclaimed as "suppression" (nirodha); however, the introduction of the tasks is celebrated as "connection" (grathana). BhN 19.98.
The narration of an experienced matter is declared to be *nirṇaya* (a definitive conclusion);
that which is produced by censure is called *paribhāṣaṇa* (reproach). BhN 19.99.
Furthermore, they declare that the pacification of wealth already acquired is *dyuti*;
likewise, the acquisition of further riches is proclaimed as *ānanda*.
The removal of suffering is declared to be the occasion;
serenity, endowed with qualities such as a desire to hear [the teaching], is called joy.
The attainment of the marvelous is intended as concealment; speech endowed with conciliation, generosity, and so forth is declared to be [the means for that]. (BhN 19.102)
The "prior statement" (pūrvavākya) should be understood as the demonstration of the meaning as it has been explained;
the attainment of the granting of the boon is considered the conclusion of the poem.
The pacification of the king's command is called *praśasti* (the benediction).
These constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the drama should be performed according to the junctures (*saṃdhi*). BhN 19.104.
However, poets skilled in poetry may, depending on the aesthetic flavor (rasa) and emotional state (bhāva),
sometimes combine them in pairs or even in groups of three.
Having understood the task, its state, and the constituent parts at their joints,
one should connect these very parts together according to the logic of the purpose.
The intermediate junctures (*sandhyantara*) are twenty-one specific types of alliances (*sandhi*):
conciliation (*sāma*), sowing dissension (*bheda*), force (*daṇḍa*), bribery (*pradāna*), and even execution (*vadha*). BhN 19.107.
Present-mindedness, stumbling over one's lineage, recklessness, fear, shamelessness, deceit, and anger; BhN 19.108.
Vitality, concealment, delusion, as well as the determination of causes, a messenger, a letter, a dream, a painting, and intoxication—these are recorded [as the means of communication]. (BhN 19.109)
The *viṣkambhaka*, the *cūlikā*, and likewise the *praveśaka*;
the *aṅkāvatāra* and the *aṅkamukha*—these are the five types of *arthopakṣepa*.

The *viṣkambhaka* (interlude) should be performed by the chaplain, the minister, and the chamberlain; it involves characters of middle status and serves only to connect the opening (*mukha*) juncture of the drama.
The *viṣkambhaka* (interlude) is to be known as being of two kinds: pure (*śuddha*) or mixed (*saṃkīrṇa*).
The pure is performed by middle-ranking characters; the mixed is composed by low and middle-ranking characters.
When a suggestion of the plot is made in various ways by the *sūta* and others stationed behind the inner curtain (*antaryavanikā*), that indeed is called a *cūlikā*.

Following the intervals between acts, with reference to the summarized meaning of the *bindus*, that which occurs in the context of a *prakaraṇa* or a *nāṭaka* is to be known as the *praveśaka*. (BhN 19.114)
When one act follows immediately after another act,
having reached its performance and being joined with the application of the purpose of the seed (bīja), that should be known as an *aṅkāvatāra*.
That which is first introduced by a woman or a man whose face is separated from the stage is called the *aṅkamukha*. (BhN 19.116)
Furthermore, other varieties of *lāsya* that are useful for drama have emerged from this; however, those intended for solo performance are like the *bhāṇa*.
The *lāsya* dance should be understood as being performed by a single actor or taken up by multiple actors;
it should be composed like a *prakaraṇa* (drama), endowed with praise and various emotional states (*bhāva*). // BhN 19.118 //
The Geyapada, the Sthitapāṭhya, the Āsīna, the Puṣpagaṇḍikā, the Pracchedaka, the Trimūḍha, and that called the Saindhava, which is the Dvimūḍhaka. BhN 19.119.
The *uttamottamaka*, as well as the *uktapratyukta*—these ten types constitute the definition of the description of the limbs (*aṅga*) in *lāsya*. (BhN 19.120)
That which is sung by singers seated upon seats, accompanied by stringed instruments, and consisting of dry (unemotional) verses, is called *geyapada*.

When a woman dances upon her seat while singing a song endowed with the qualities of the beloved according to the rules of the primary and secondary limbs, that is called the *geyapada*. BhN_19.122 //
When she, though naturally detached,
recites with intense passion while her limbs are tormented by the fire of love, that is called *sthitapāṭhya*.
"Accompanied by *bahucārī*, followed by the five hand-gestures (*pañcapāṇikalā*),
or joined with *cañcatpuṭa*, this is prescribed as *sthitapāṭhya* (recitation while standing)."
Where one sits seated, devoid of all musical instruments,
with limbs not stretched out, and possessed by anxiety and grief.
Where there are various dances, singing based on vocal music,
and where men provide support through their gestures, that is the *puṣpagaṇḍikā*.
Where a woman, dressed in male attire, recites elegant Sanskrit for the amusement of her female companions, that should be known as *puṣpagaṇḍikā*. (BhN 19.127)
Where there is various dancing accompanied by song and instrumental music,
and where women behave like men, that should be known as *puṣpagaṇḍikā*.
That should be known as a period of separation when women, struck by the moonlight, become attached even to those who act unpleasantly toward their beloveds. (BhN 19.129)

A drama characterized by words that are neither harsh nor overly soft, adorned with balanced meters, rich in masculine sentiments, and featuring the three types of fools (mūḍhas), is known as *trimūḍhaka*.
The wise know that which has lost its conventional signs, yet possesses clearly manifest gestures and is accompanied by vernacular speech, as being *saindhavaka*. BhN 19.131.
"That which is joined with color, voice, and so forth, yet devoid of recitation, should indeed be known as *saindhava* dance by those skilled in drama. (BhN 19.132)

In the *dvimūḍhaka* [dance], it should be endowed with the *mukha* and *pratimukha* [junctures], proceed in a square formation, be possessed of the aesthetic emotions (*rasa*) of the *śliṣṭa-bhāva*, and exhibit variety for the sake of its meaning.
One should know that the *uttamottamaka* (the most excellent) is based on many sentiments (*rasa*),
characterized by various worldly compositions, and embellished with playful gestures (*helā*) and expressions (*bhāva*).
Arising from anger or favor, based on words of reproach, consisting of speech and counter-speech, and thus joined with the meaning of various songs—such would be [the *citragīta*]. (BhN 19.135)
That place where one whose limbs are tormented by the fire of love sees the form of her beloved and finds diversion for the mind is called *citrapada*.
When one who is tormented by the fire of passion sees a beloved in a dream and manifests various emotional states, that indeed is called *bhāvika*.
The characteristics of these [movements] in the performance of *lāsya* should be understood by those skilled in practice;
however, that which has not been stated here is for the purpose of avoiding prolixity. (BhN 19.138)
It has five joints, four modes of operation, and is endowed with sixty-four limbs;
it is possessed of thirty-six characteristics and adorned with qualities and ornaments.
It possesses great flavor and great enjoyment, is endowed with noble speech,
is frequented by great beings, and is dear to people of virtuous conduct.
A poet should compose a drama with well-knit joints and connections, employing skillful techniques, providing a source of pleasure, and characterized by the use of soft-sounding words. (BhN 19.141)
That state of the world which arises from pleasure and pain, involving the movement of various characters, is enacted here in the drama. (BhN 19.142)
There is no knowledge, no craft, no science, no art,
no action, nor even yoga, that is not seen in the sword-play of this actor.
This very nature of the world, consisting of various internal states,
when joined with the gestures of the limbs and other elements, is designated as "drama" (nāṭya).
That which consists of the past deeds and histories of deities, sages, and kings of superior intellect shall be known as a *nāṭaka*.
Because it is practiced and understood by completely setting aside one's own nature through the sequential stages of the limbs and sub-limbs, it is therefore known as *nāṭaka* (drama).
A drama is composed with all states of being, all sentiments, and the engagement in all types of actions, endowed with various internal conditions.
[The practitioners] should produce all those forms without exception—those consisting of various types of crafts and various types of actions. // BhN 19.148 //
Having thoroughly observed the nature of the world, the strength and weakness of men,
as well as their enjoyment and the proper method, one should then compose a drama.
In the future age, for the most part, men will be ignorant;
and even those who do exist will possess understanding only through effort and study.
When the world perishes, all these— occupations, crafts, scriptures, and the powers of discernment— all perish.
Thus, having carefully considered the strengths and weaknesses of worldly languages, a poet should compose a drama using soft-sounding words that convey pleasant meanings. (BhN 19.152)
Those poetic compositions which exist through words such as *caikrīḍita* and others do not shine when held by twice-born men carrying water-pots, any more than courtesans do.
O best of the twice-born, I have thus declared the rules for the ten forms [of drama];
hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the dramatic styles (vṛtti).
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Junctures," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
Now begins the twentieth chapter: "I shall explain the emergence of the dramatic styles (*vṛtti*) in their proper sequence."
Just as there is the arising of objects and the conceptualization of poetic works.
When the Blessed One Acyuta, having withdrawn the worlds through his illusory power (māyā), made the universe a single ocean, he lay upon the serpent-couch.
Then the two asuras, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, who were intoxicated by the power of their own vigor, swiftly threatened the god out of a desire for battle.
Wringing their own arms, they fought the Lord, the imperishable creator of beings, with their knees and fists.
With many harsh words, they rushed at one another with various insults, as if making the ocean tremble.
Then, hearing the various kinds of words spoken by those two as they conversed, Druhiṇa, his mind deeply struck, spoke these words.
What is this? Is it the Bharatī style of speech that proceeds through words alone?
Indeed, these two [arguments] lead to a conclusion that is mutually contradictory.
Having heard the words of his grandfather, Madhusūdana said: "O Brahmin, for the sake of a specific purpose, I have composed this *Bhārata*."
"The speech of those who speak shall abound in words;
therefore, I shall slay these two today," thus spoke Hari.
Skilled in the ways of combat, the two Daityas fought intensely with their limbs pure and unaltered, employing various graceful maneuvers.
At that time, due to the footprints of Hari—marked by their connection to the earth and their specific formations—the burden of the earth became excessive; thus, Bhāratī was manifested there.
Then, by means of the vigorous leaps of the Śārṅga bow, its intense and blazing movements,
and through those actions characterized by supreme courage and composure, the Sāttvatī [mudrā] was manifested there.
As the Lord bound his mass of hair with various graceful and playful movements of the limbs, the Kaiśikī style was manifested therein.
Then, from various movements arising with an abundance of impetuous force,
and from diverse techniques of wrestling, the *ārabhaṭī* [style of action] was produced.
Whatever ritual action established among the modes of life the Lord prescribed, Brahmā honored each of them with recitations that corresponded to their respective purposes.
When those two asuras, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, had been slain by Hari,
the Lotus-born One then spoke to Nārāyaṇa, the subduer of enemies.
"Oh, O Lord, the destruction of the Dānavas has been accomplished by you through bodily movements that are diverse, formidable, manifest, and yet graceful! (BhN 20.17)
Therefore, this sequence of rules for the occasion of wrestling shall indeed be known as the "Righteous" (nyāya) among all discharges of weapons in the world.
Because battles proceed by means of maneuvers that rely on logic and arise from logic itself, they are therefore proclaimed as "logics" (nyāyas).
"Furthermore, this designation 'Nyāya' was established by the high-souled Druhiṇa for those who have arisen among various practices and rely upon diverse modes of conduct."
Then, by the high-souled Druhiṇa, it was deposited within the Vedas and again within the various collections of missiles and weapons, which are filled with diverse modes of conduct.
Furthermore, in the performance of dramas, these things known as *vṛttis*— which are endowed with various emotional states (*bhāva*) and based upon poetic compositions— are indeed established.
Whatever kind of recitation was performed by the sages according to the conduct of that deity, such was the mode of life they adopted, including the manner of their recitation and so forth.
"Born from the Nāṭya-veda and consisting of vocal and physical expression,
this [work] has been composed by me at the command of Brahmā for the purpose of creating poetry."
Bhāratī was projected from the Ṛgveda, Sāttvatī from the Yajurveda, Kaiśikī from the Sāmaveda, and the remaining [Vaidarbhī] from the Atharvaveda as well. (BhN 20.25)
That mode of performance which is dominated by speech, employed by men, devoid of women, characterized by refined recitation,
and performed by the Bharatas according to their own names, shall be known as the Bhāratī style.
Its four divisions, which have attained the status of constituent parts (*aṅga*), should be known as:
*prarocanāmukha*, *vīthī*, and likewise *prahasana*. (BhN 20.27)
It brings victory and prosperity, is auspicious, and confers triumph;
it pacifies all evils and serves as the prologue that excites interest.

The invitation that occurs through the introduction of a poetic work, based on reasons and logical arguments, and which employs established facts, is to be understood as *prarocanā* (persuasion). // BhN_20.29 //
When the actress, the buffoon, or even the assistant engage in conversation together with the director, [it is called the prologue].

That should be known by the wise as the *āmukha* (prologue), or even as the *prastāvanā* (introduction), when it consists of various speeches arising from the poet's own purpose, through the limbs of dramatic action (*vīthyaṅga*), or otherwise. BhN 20.31.
The characteristics of the *vīthī* and the *prahasana* have already been stated;
therefore, I shall now describe the components of the *āmukha* in their proper order and according to tradition.
The *uddhātyaka*, the *kathoddhāta*, the *prayogātiśaya*,
the *pravṛttaka*, and the *avalagita*— these are the five components of the *āmukha*.
I have described the characteristics of the *uddhātyaka* and the *avalagita*;
