O Brahmins, I shall now explain the characteristics of the remaining [gestures] in their proper sequence.
When an actor enters having grasped either the words of the *sūtradhāra* or the very meaning of those words, that is proclaimed as *kathoddhāta*.
In the *prayoga*, however, the director (*sūtradhāra*) should employ the *prayoga*;
thereafter the actor (*pātra*) shall enter, for that is indeed the *prayogātiśaya*.
The description that is employed by relying on the progression of time,
and the entrance of a character based upon that [description], is called *pravṛttaka*.
Having applied one or another of these [reasons] in a connected manner through logical arguments for the purpose,
the possibility of both [types of] members is therefore not precluded.
Then one should perform the *āmukha* without crowding it with too many *pātra-granthas*.
Thus should this *āmukha*, which has various bases, be understood by the wise. (BhN 20.39)
The characteristics of the *vīthī* and the *prahasana* have already been stated previously.
Thus, this fourfold division of the *bhāratī* style has been described by me;
now I shall explain the rules for the *sāttvatī* style according to its defining characteristics.
That mode of acting which is endowed here with the quality of sattva, accompanied by righteous conduct,
characterized by intense joy and the removal of all states of sorrow, shall be known as the *sāttvatī* style.

The *sāttvatī* style of performance is to be understood as that which possesses the expressive representation of speech and limbs, and is characterized by the exaltation of spirit and the delivery of words within their proper context. (BhN 20.42)

It consists of the heroic, the marvelous, and the furious sentiments; it casts aside the erotic, the pathetic, and the sentiment of world-weariness; it is dominated by haughty men and characterized by mutual insults.
The Utthāpaka, the Parivartaka, the Sallāpaka, and the Saṃghātya—these four varieties of it should be known by those skilled in drama. (BhN 20.44)
"I too shall rise; you, meanwhile, display your own power"—this [challenge] arising from rivalry is to be known by the wise as the "instigator" (utthāpaka). (BhN 20.45)
He who, having abandoned undertakings already commenced, pursues other matters for the sake of some gain,
he too should be known as a "shifter" (parivartaka).

The *parivartaka* (turning point) should be known as threefold: having a subject matter already indicated, bound by elaboration (*prapañca*), and joined with the three types of laughter; it is produced by a specific kind of rivalry. // BhN 20.47 //
Whether arising from provocation or not arising from provocation, speech joined with passion and accompanied by reproach should be known as "sallāpaka" (idle chatter). BhN 20.48.
Speech that arises from merit or demerit, which is joined with passion or hatred, and which is accompanied by abuse, should be known as "frivolous talk. (BhN 20.49)
One who, through the power of the meaning of mantras or sentences, by the force of destiny, or due to the influence of his own defects,
causes a schism within a community, should be known as a "schemer" (saṃghātyaka) by those who know him.
A "false assembly" (kūṭasaṃghātya) is to be understood as a collection of deceivers who rely on many stratagems and are motivated by the intent to harm others. // BhN 20.51 //
Thus, this Sāttvatī style, which has eight sub-varieties, has been described by me;
hereafter, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the Kaiśikī style.
That which is characterized by smooth and diverse costumes, accompanied by women, featuring much dancing and singing,
and consisting of refined conduct arising from the enjoyment of desires— that they call the Kaiśikī style.

[It is] accompanied by much speech, dancing, and singing; characterized by the graceful representation of amorous passion and wonderful costumes; adorned with garlands and ornaments; possessing a praiseworthy appearance and being lovely. (BhN 20.54)

The Kaiśikī vṛtti is to be known as that which is adorned with the composition of variegated words and sentences, characterized by laughter, weeping, anger, and the like, and associated with the amorous desires of women and men.
*Narma*, *narmasphuñja*, *narmasphoṭa*, and *narmagarbha*:
these are declared to be the four divisions of *kaiśikī*.

One should recognize that jesting (narma) is of three kinds: that which establishes erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), that which employs pure means (viśuddhakaraṇa), and that which has desisted from the heroic sentiment (vīrarasa) and abounds in humorous speech.
Humor (narma) is known as that which consists primarily of envy and anger, is permeated by reproachful speech, involves self-deprecation, and is accompanied by deception. (BhN 20.58)
The enjoyment arising from a new union, characterized by expressions of passion, dress, and speech,
should be known as *narmasphuñja*, which consists essentially of fear toward the conclusion.

A *narmasphoṭa* (comic burst) should be understood as that which is adorned with various fragments of different states of being through many specific qualities, wherein the emotional flavor is not fully developed.

Where the leader, possessing the splendor of consciousness and form, is surrounded by hosts of wealth and other such things, that [assembly] is for the sake of conducting affairs; it is characterized by jesting, yet it is for the purpose of action.
"In the dramatic performances, one should recognize that as being 'full of jest' (narmagarbha) wherein the leader might perish while another remains in his former position. // BhN 20.62 //
Thus have I described this Kaiśikī style, which has eight varieties of dramatic action;
hereafter, I shall fully explain the Ārabhaṭī style, which possesses intense sentiment.
That which consists primarily of boisterous qualities, is likewise endowed with much deceit and trickery, and contains hypocrisy and false speech, should be known as the *ārabhaṭī* style. (BhN 20.64)

They call that *ārabhaṭī* which consists of leaping from heights, jumping over obstacles, cutting through things, illusions, sorcery, and various wonderful battles occurring therein constantly. (BhN 20.65)

The *ārabhaṭī* style of performance is to be understood as that which is undertaken through the six political expedients (*ṣāḍguṇya*), characterized by forceful deception, flight, and the pursuit of gain or loss. (BhN 20.66)
The *saṃkṣiptaka*, the *avapāta*, the *vastūtthāpana*, and also the *saṃpheṭa*—these are indeed its varieties;
I shall now explain their definitions.

That which is endowed with meaningful craftsmanship, featuring many figures, elevated scenes, and variegated costumes, and whose subject matter is concise, should be known as the *saṃkṣiptaka*. (BhN 20.68)
One should recognize this as the state arising from fear and joy, characterized by fleeing, falling down, and agitated behavior, as well as rapid entering and exiting and tumbling over.

That drama which is composed by condensing all aesthetic flavors (rasas), and which, though possessing both the solid and the liquid, is clearly manifested, should be known as "the production of the substance" (vastūtthāpana).
That which is characterized by intense fury, the breaking of many deceptive stratagems in combat,
and an abundance of blows with weapons, is to be known as *sampheṭa* (the clash).
In this way, these modes based on drama are to be understood by the wise; now learn of their application to the aesthetic flavors (rasas) as it is being proclaimed.
The Kaiśikī style is described as abounding in humor and the erotic sentiment;
it should also be understood as possessing the quality of *sattva*, and the Vīra, Adbhuta, and Śānta sentiments as its foundations.
The *ārabhaṭī* style should be understood by the wise as applicable to the furious (*raudra*) and the terrifying (*bhayānaka*);
the *bhāratī* style is proclaimed for the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) and the pathetic (*karuṇa*).

For in practice, there is no poetic composition whatsoever that arises from a single flavor alone—be it a state of being (*bhāva*), a sentiment (*rasa*), an activity (*pravṛtti*), or even a mode of conduct (*vṛtti*). (BhN 20.75)

Among all those emotions combined together, whichever one possesses the greatest intensity should be considered the permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva); the rest are known as transitory emotions (sañcāribhāvas).
This acting, which arises from speech, body, and spirit, has been correctly described by me according to its divisions.
Now, I shall further explain the acting performed through costume (*āhārya-abhinaya*) in the context of performance.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter of the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*, titled "The Classification of the Styles" (*vṛttivikalpana*).
Now begins the twenty-first chapter:
"O Brahmins, I shall explain the representation through external ornaments (*āhāryābhinaya*) in due order."
For this entire application is established within the representation of the assumed [state].
Various dispositions, previously established through costumes,
manifest effortlessly through the limbs and other means.
The method arising from the costume is to be known as "artificial representation" (āhāryābhinaya);
one who desires the welfare of the drama should apply diligent effort toward it. (BhN 21.3)
"One who desires success in this regard must apply effort toward the costume (*naipathya*), for it is proclaimed here that the costume is the ornament of drama. (BhN 21.4)
Costume (nepathya), however, is of four kinds: the artificial form, ornamentation, the arrangement of limbs, and that which is endowed with life. BhN 21.5.
Manuscripts, moreover, should be known as being of three types according to their various forms and dimensions:
they are proclaimed as the stitched (sandhima), the sewn (vyājima), and the wrapped (veṣṭima).
That form which is fashioned by the wise out of materials such as straw, leather, and cloth,
known as *sandhi-mo*, should be understood as a model used for the purpose of drama.
That which is produced by means of a mechanical device is to be known as *vyājima*;
and that form which is wrapped around is designated as *veṣṭima*.
Mountains, vehicles, celestial chariots, shields, armor, banners, and trees—
whatever is fashioned for the purpose of drama is designated as *pusta* (modeling).

Furthermore, ornamentation (alaṅkāra) should be understood as the various combinations of garlands, jewelry, and garments; it is also traditionally defined as the arrangement of the primary and secondary limbs of the body.

Wreaths are traditionally said to be of five kinds: the wrapped (*veṣṭima*), the spread-out (*vitata*), the joined-together (*saṃghātya*), the knotted (*granthima*), and likewise the hanging (*prālambita*).
Indeed, ornaments in drama should be understood by the wise as being of four kinds:
those to be pierced, those to be bound, those to be inserted, and those to be placed upon.
Whatever here is to be pierced, such as earrings which are ornaments for the ears, or what is to be strung, such as golden threads and various necklaces, [should be fashioned]. (BhN 21.13)
One should always know that pearl ornaments for the waist-string and armlets, as well as anklets, are indeed types of clothing and jewelry to be worn. BhN 21.14.
I shall indeed describe the various types of ornaments for men and women, as well as those originating from different regions and castes.
The crest-jewel together with its crown is known as the ornament for the head;
the earring is called *mocaka* or *kīla*, and it is intended as an ear-ornament.

The pearl necklace (muktāvalī), the joy-bringer (harṣaka), the thread (sūtraka), and the neck ornament (kaṇṭhabhūṣaṇa); the wristlet (vetikā) and the finger-ring (aṅgulimudrā) shall be the ornaments for the fingers.
The *hastalī*, the *valaya*, and the *bāhunālī* are ornaments for the arm;
the *rucaka* and *cūlikā* are to be made as ornaments for the wrist.
Keyūras and aṅgadas are ornaments for above the elbows;
likewise, the trisara and the hāra are ornaments for the chest.
A long pearl necklace and a garland are ornaments for the limbs;
likewise, a *talaka* and a *sūtraka* serve as ornaments for the waist.
This application of ornaments for men, which rests upon their attire, has been explained;
now I shall speak again concerning that of gods, kings, and women.
The hair-tuft, the serpent-like hair, the cluster-leaf,
as well as the crest-jewel, the makara-shaped ornament, and the lattice-window of pearl nets.
An ornament for the head, a variegated turban, a crest,
a peacock-feather plume, and a braid with its end tied in a loop.
There was also a forehead mark (tilaka) fashioned with various artistic techniques,
as well as clusters of blossoms above the eyebrows, imitating the appearance of flowers.
The *karṇikā*, the *karṇavalaya*, as well as the *patrakarṇikā*, the *kuṇḍala*, the *karṇamudrā*, and the *karṇotkīlaka*. (BhN 21.25)
Indeed, ivory leaf-patterns variegated with various jewels serve as ornaments for the ears,
as well as ear-pendants.
Tilakas and patralekhas should serve as ornaments for the cheeks;
likewise, the trivaṇī should be known as an ornament for the chest.
One should know the application of collyrium to the eyes and the coloring of the lips;
there is also the various staining of the teeth, or else the whiteness of all four.
Furthermore, there is a variety of internal passion that is even more brilliant due to its beauty;
for the innocent and the beautiful women, these [ornaments] possess a splendor illuminated by pearls.
Or else, her teeth may be deep red, colored like the petals of a lotus;
her lower lip, glowing with the hue of a ruby, should possess the luster of a young sprout.
Their graceful charm consists of glances that are both wandering and steady;
they are like strings of pearls, rows of serpents, flower clusters, and garlands of jewels.
The *ratnāvalī* and the *sūtraka* are to be known as ornaments for the neck;
likewise, there are those with two strings, three strings, and four strings.
Likewise, there should be a chain as an ornament for the neck,
as well as armlets and bracelets as ornaments for the base of the arms.
Furthermore, necklaces fashioned from various crafts serve as ornaments for the chest,
and an ornament for the breasts should be composed of a network of jewels.
The *kharjūraka*, the *socchitika*, the arm-staff ornament (*bāhunālī-vibhūṣaṇa*),
the *kalāpī*, the bracelet (*kaṭaka*), the conch (*śaṅkha*), the hand-leaf (*hastapatra*), and the *sapūraka*.
A seal-ring, which is indeed an ornament for the fingers, as well as a palm enriched with a network of pearls, or a girdle, or even a golden waistband. BhN 21.36.
The *raśanā* and the *kalāpa* serve as ornaments for the hips;
the *kāñcī* consists of a single string, while the *mekhalā* consists of eight strings.
The girdle consists of two sets of eight strands, a bundle of twenty-five,
thirty-two, sixty-four, and likewise one hundred and eight.
These become pearl necklaces for the women of gods and kings; likewise, they become anklets, small bells, tinkling ornaments, and nets of jewels. (BhN 21.39)
On the *saghoṣa* and the *kaṭaka*, there should be ornaments for above the ankles;
on the shanks, leaf-patterned ornaments for the feet; and on the fingers, finger-rings.
There were also thumb-marks and tilakas, as well as ornaments on the feet,
and likewise the red dye of lac applied with various decorative patterns.
The shade of the *aśoka* and *palāśa* trees is indeed natural;
this is the ornament of a noble woman from her hair down to her very nails. (BhN 21.42)
O best of the twice-born, it should be understood according to its state as the essence of existence;
likewise, there is scripture, valid authority, and the description of form.
Even by those of keen intellect who apply themselves to the work according to the doctrine of Viśvakarman, it is not possible [to achieve perfection] merely with gold, pearls, and gems. (BhN 21.44)
Thinking "it is under my own control," one may indeed adorn a limb according to one's taste;
when applied with due proportion, it will bring beauty to that limb. (BhN 21.45)
Just as a jewel-encrusted ornament may be worn when one has gone to another place, so too,
heavy ornaments should not be used during dramatic performances.
For that indeed produces exhaustion due to strenuous exertion; from the state of being weighed down by heaviness, sweat and fainting arise.
For one burdened by heavy ornaments does not perform [proper] activity;
therefore, the ornament should be made of gold with a thin skin.
Or, bound with jewels and gold, it shall not cause fatigue;
the method of ornamentation for divine beings is taught according to their own desire.
That which is produced through effort is the ornament of human beings;
it is either woven, stretched out, sewn together, or likewise knotted.
Likewise, five kinds of garlands are prescribed that shine with long-lasting beauty;
and there are many varieties of garments produced in various cities.
That object of knowledge is of three kinds: pure, red, and variegated.
This is the method of divine ornamentation that has been proclaimed.
But for human beings, [the representation] should be based on various regions,
as well as on ornaments and costumes that reflect their diverse conditions.
The classification of divine women born in their respective realms—namely, the Vidyādharīs, Yakṣīs, Apsarases, and Nāga women—must be established. (BhN 21.54)
A diversity of dress is prescribed for the sages and the daughters of the gods,
as well as for the wives of the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, and Asuras.
Likewise, there were divine men and women with topknots,
their hair-buns and crests adorned primarily with pearls.
The dress and equipment of the Vidyādharīs should be made pure;
likewise, the Yakṣiṇīs and Apsarases should be adorned with jewels.
The attire of all the yakṣīs shall consist solely of a crest;
likewise, the ornamentation of the nāga women should be made to resemble that of the divine ones.
Their hoods consist merely of rows of pearl-jewels;
for the daughters of the sages, however, their duty is to bear their heads with a single braid of hair.
Nor was their mode of adornment or their dress suited to the forest; for the ornaments of perfected women consist primarily of pearls and emeralds.
Furthermore, for those Gandharva women, their attire should consist of yellow garments,
and their ornaments should be primarily made of rubies.
He should be depicted with a lute in his hand and likewise dressed in saffron-colored garments;
the ornaments of the rākṣasīs should be made of sapphire.
She should be depicted with white fangs and dressed in black garments;
the celestial women should be adorned with ornaments of beryl and pearls.
Their attire should be made of garments resembling the plumage of a parrot,
and in some places adorned with *puṣyarāga* gems and *vaiḍūrya* stones.
The attire for celestial women and monkeys should consist of blue garments;
thus, the costumes based on celestial damsels should be made to appear amorous.
Having reached the final stage, they should again be purified in that same manner;
however, for human [mudrās], those originating from various regions should be employed.
Listen as I describe the combinations of dress and ornaments [of various regions]:
the head of the young women of Avanti has hair adorned with *sālaka* flowers.
The women of Gauḍa generally wear their hair in a single braid with a topknot,
while the young women of the Ābhīras wear two braids.
One should perform the circumambulation of the head while wearing clothing that is predominantly blue;
likewise, the women of the eastern and northern regions should have their topknots tied up high.
For those women, the covering down to the hair is prescribed for the rite;
likewise, for the women of the South, the work should be based on painting.
The *kumbhībandhaka*, the *āvarta*, and the *lalāṭika*—
these should be employed as ornaments for courtesans to break the monotony of their desires.
According to the regulations for country, caste, and class, one should likewise arrange the dress, ornaments, shaving, and equipment for all others as well.
One should also employ the traditional sources (āgama) for the costume of the drama in this manner;
for a costume not suited to the setting will not produce beauty. (BhN 21.73)
But when tied around the waist or the chest, it produces laughter;
likewise, so does it when worn by women whose lovers are away or who are stricken by calamity.
Indeed, her dress should be soiled and her hair worn in a single braid; however, in the case of a woman's separation [from her husband], her attire here should be pure.
Neither excessively adorned with ornaments nor embellished by grooming—
such is the dress of women, arising from the customs of their particular region.
Furthermore, I shall describe the dress of men according to their true nature;
therein, the arrangement of limbs must first be performed by those who employ dramatic gesture.
Thereafter, the costumes originating from various regions should be employed:
white, blue, yellow, and the fourth indeed red. (BhN 21.78)
These are the primary vowels (*varṇa*) born of their own nature, by which the formation of the limbs [of the phonemes] is accomplished;
furthermore, there are other secondary vowels (*upavarṇa*) which are born of combination.
I shall fully explain those [colors] as they are to be employed by practitioners:
when white and blue are combined, it is known as *kāraṇḍava*.
From the combination of white and yellow, the pale-white (pāṇḍu) color is proclaimed;
from the combination of white and red, the lotus-color (padmavarṇa) is proclaimed. (BhN 21.81)
From the combination of yellow and blue, that which is called green is produced;
from the combination of blue and red, that which is called brown is produced.
From the union of red and yellow, the fair (gaura) complexion is said to arise;
these are the colors born of combination, as well as other secondary (upavarṇa) colors.
Many [syllables] are proclaimed to be joined with three or four letters;
therefore, the portion belonging to whichever letter possesses strength shall be [the dominant one].
For the weak [pigment], one should cause two parts to be given, excluding the blue;
there should be one part of blue, while the other four parts are for the coloring agent.
The powerful [color] among all the castes is proclaimed to be Nīla alone;
having thus understood the rule of colors based on various combinations.
Then the wise one should appropriately fashion the limbs;
the form consists of the shaping and covering [of the body], while being devoid of personal attire.
However, that which pertains to the practice of dramatic art should be understood as remaining within its own natural state;
one's own true complexion must be concealed by means of colors applied through the adoption of various costumes.
The form of that [body] must be fashioned according to the nature it has assumed,
just as a living being, having abandoned its own innate nature, assumes another bodily one.
For one who has taken refuge in another body partakes of its very nature;
likewise, a person is concealed by dress and pigments. (BhN 21.90)
He assumes the nature of whichever form he takes on,
whether it be that of a god, a dānava, a gandharva, a yakṣa, a rākṣasa, or a pannaga.
For these are known as the perceptions of living beings, as well as those other bonds of the soul:
the states of womanhood, mountains, rivers, oceans, and vehicles.
Likewise, various weapons, as well as mountains, palaces, and machines, as well as shields, armor, and banners, should be understood by the designation "living beings."
Furthermore, various weapons and the like are traditionally considered to be non-living;
or else, when endowed with their causes, they become embodied beings.

Having observed the dramatic conventions (nāṭyadharma), and having understood the rules for the castes (varṇa) as well as their age and temperament, one should employ [the appropriate] dress, speech, and physical bearing.
One should fashion the arrangement of the limbs according to the requirements of the region, caste, and age;
the gods, yakṣas, and apsarases are to be known as fair-complexioned. (BhN 21.96)
Rudra, Arka, Druhiṇa, and Skanda are remembered as having the luster of refined gold;
so too are Soma, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Varuṇa, and the hosts of stars.
The ocean, Himavat, and the Gaṅgā are indeed white, as is Bala;
one should know that Aṅgāraka is red, while Budha and Hutāśana are yellow.
Nārāyaṇa and Nara, Śyāma and the nāga Vāsuki,
as well as the Daityas, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, Guhyakas, and mountain-dwellers.
In the six continents, the Piśācas are black in color, as are the waters and the sky; and the human beings there are likewise black in color.
Through the application of dramatic art, they should be made to possess the luster of refined gold;
however, in the region of Jambudvīpa, men take on various complexions.
But having excluded the people of Uttarakuru, those men of Bhadrāśva should also be depicted with a golden luster and white in color.
In Ketumāla, the men are blue; in the remaining regions, they are said to be fair-complexioned.
Beings such as Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Pannagas are recorded as being of various colors.
Likewise, the Vidyādharas and the Pitṛs are equal to human beings;
furthermore, learn of those various castes that exist in the land of Bhārata.
Kings may be lotus-colored, fair, or even dark; likewise, those mortals who are happy should be depicted as fair by the wise.

Those of evil deeds, those seized by planets, those afflicted by disease, those engaged in ascetic penance, those whose actions are strenuous, those who are dark-complexioned, and those of low birth; BhN 21.106.
The sages should always be made to resemble jujube fruits;
and the sages established in austerity should always be depicted as dark-complexioned by the wise.
Furthermore, under the pretext of a specific reason or by one's own will,
the caste therein should be assigned in accordance with the requirements of the region and the lineage.
Having understood the country, the occupation, the caste, and the dependence on the region of the earth, one should conduct the affairs of men through appropriate application.
The Kirātas, Barbaras, Andhras, Draviḍas, Kāśikas, Kosalas,
Pulindas, and Southerners are generally considered to be dark-complexioned.
The Śakas, Yavanas, Pahlavas, and those who are Vāhlikas—
those who generally dwell in the northern direction should be depicted as fair-complexioned.
The Pāñcālas, Śūrasenas, Māhiṣas, Auḍras, Māgadhas,
Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, and Śyāmas should be depicted according to their respective complexions.
The Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas should indeed be made fair-complexioned;
likewise, the Vaiśyas and Śūdras should be made dark-complexioned according to their respective castes.
Having thus performed the arrangement of the face and its primary and secondary features according to the rule,
one should apply the shaving of the beard in accordance with the place, time, and age.
The beard may be of four kinds— pure, variegated, dark, and likewise hairy— consisting of various internal conditions.

But the duty of those bearing sectarian marks, as well as that of ministers and domestic priests, and of those persons who are neutral and those who have taken up initiation, must be performed purely.
Whosoever are the divine persons, such as the Siddhas and Vidyādharas,
as well as the princes of the earth and those who live in service to the king.
And for those mortals who are amorous and those who are intoxicated by youth,
the performers of drama should fashion their beards in various wonderful ways.
One should employ a dark beard for those ascetics who have not fulfilled their vows, who are suffering, and who are struck by calamity.
Among the seers, ascetics, and those men who observe long-term vows, as well as among those bound in bark garments, a hairy beard is prescribed. (BhN 21.120)
In this manner, the various types of facial hair should be applied by those who practice it;
hereafter, I shall describe the diverse applications of dress arising from various practices.
Attire is said to be of three kinds: pure, variegated, and soiled;
I shall describe their application correctly and in due order.

And likewise during the approach of the gods, at auspicious times, while established in religious observances, and during the conjunction of lunar days and constellations for the performance of marriage.
Whatever action is performed according to the Dharma by women or men,
their dress shall be pure, as shall that of those men who are diligent in their efforts.
The diverse attire of gods, dānavas, yakṣas, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas, as well as that of harsh kings, has been described.
And [he should consult] the elders, the brahmins, the chief ministers, the domestic chaplains,
the merchants, the chamberlains, and likewise the ascetics.
For Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and those men who are local residents,
a pure costume arrangement should be employed, based on their respective roles in the drama.
For those who are insane, for those who are intoxicated, for travelers, and likewise for those afflicted by calamity, a soiled dress is prescribed. (BhN 21.128)
One who knows the principles of dance should employ pure, red, and variegated garments as upper cloths for the two types of dress: the pure and the variegated.
A wise person should, however, respond with impurity toward those who are impure— namely,
among the Munis, Nirgranthas, Śākyas, Yatis, and Pāśupatas.
One should adopt an outward appearance consistent with one's vows according to the customs of the world;
however, one should employ rags, bark garments, and skins for ascetics.
For those who have renounced the world and become sages, saffron-colored robes are prescribed;
however, among the Pāśupatas, one may wear garments of various colors and patterns.
And those who are declared to be of low birth, as well as those men who are appointed for entry into the inner apartments, [should be treated] according to their respective merit.
They too should be made with saffron-colored tunics and garments according to the prescribed rule; furthermore, the dress of men should correspond to their respective social stations.
The attire of heroes is proclaimed to be martial:
wearing various weapons and armor, with a quiver fastened and a bow in hand.
A king’s attire must always be variegated;
however, it should be purely white on the occasion of a lunar mansion, an omen, or an auspicious ceremony.
In this way, this dress may be appropriate for women and men of the highest, lowest, and middle classes, according to their country, caste, and age. (BhN 21.137)
In this manner, the rules for clothing should be applied in the performance of a drama,
having assumed various states according to the performer's role as a doer of good or evil.
Likewise, one should also compose prologues based on dramas, relying upon the divine and human characters according to their region, caste, and age. (BhN 21.139)
Those with side-locks, those with hair reaching the crown of the head,
and those wearing crowns— these three types of headdresses are to be known as belonging to the divine and the earthly.
For gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, pannagas, and rākṣasas,
crowns with various designs should be fashioned, featuring crests on the sides.
Those who are the best among the divine should be made to wear crowns;
those of middle rank should wear turbans, and the lowest should wear simple head-cloths.
Wise men should place crowns upon the heads of sovereigns,
as well as those of the Vidyādharas, the Siddhas, and likewise the Cāraṇas.
The performers should fashion crowns of knotted hair for the Rākṣasas,
Dānavas, and Daityas, for their hair and eyes are indeed tawny.
One should likewise have them with golden beards and faces adorned with crowns;
furthermore, those who are the most excellent among them should be depicted with their crests turned toward the sides.
But for what reason were crowns created for use in divine and royal rites? Why is the cutting of hair observed in the Vedic injunctions according to the sacred tradition? BhN 21.146.
Or, for one who has been consecrated in a sacrifice, the wearing of a crown is prescribed because of the desire to cover the head and because the hair is not long.
Furthermore, one should place the half-crested crown upon the general and likewise upon the crown prince, as well as upon those men who are high ministers.
He should cause turbans bound with cloth bands to be made for the ministers, chamberlains, guild-leaders, and family priests.
The heads of Piśācas, those driven mad by spirits, practitioners who have failed in their austerities,
and those who have not fulfilled their vows, shall have long, hanging hair.
In the case of Śākyas, śrotriyas, Nirgranthas, and wandering mendicants who have been initiated,
as well as those who have undergone initiation for a sacrifice, the shaving of the head must be performed.
Likewise, the heads of the remaining ascetics (liṅgins) follow their respective vows;
they may be shaven, curled, or even long-haired. BhN 21.152.
For rogues, those who live by night,
and men whose minds are set on amorous passion, the hair should be curled.
The heads of even children should be adorned with three tufts of hair,
while the heads of sages should be bound with a crown of matted locks.
For servants, the hair should be made into three tufts or shaved clean;
for a jester, it should be bald or marked with a "crow's foot" (kākapaṭa).
For the remaining [metaphors], the user should employ the "head" (śiras) according to the connection with the meaning, based on place and genus, and depending on various different states.
With ornaments, pigments, garments, and garlands, according to the prescribed rule—
one should thus fashion various kinds of costumes through the power of the imagination.
But first, having established the natural disposition arising from the qualities of practice, and having reached such a state as that of women or even of men; BhN 21.158.
All the divine attributes should be made dependent upon human beings;
furthermore, their lack of blinking and other such traits need not be employed by the creators.
In this context, the aesthetic flavors (rasas) and the mental states (bhāvas) are established by means of the dramatic determinants (dṛṣṭis);
for the object is indeed established by the determinant alone, and subsequently it is developed by the constituent parts (aṅgas).
Thus, the arrangement of the limbs of the object of knowledge arises from various constituent elements;
I shall now describe the characteristics of that which is called "the living being" (sajīva).
That which is the entry into living beings is indeed designated as "jīva" (the vital principle);
it is known to belong to those with four feet, those with two feet, and likewise those without feet.
One should know bipeds as snakes, birds, and humans;
quadrupeds are to be understood as domestic and wild animals.
Those [fights] involving laughter, as well as scuffles and likewise obstructions,
equipped with various weapons, should be employed by the wise in a drama.
And the weapons must be fashioned according to the proportions of men;
I shall describe them according to the measurements found in the manuals.
The *bhiṇḍi* should be twelve *tālas* long; the *kunta* should be ten [tālas];
and the *śataghnī*, the *śūla*, the *tomara*, or the *śakti* should be eight [tālas]. (BhN 21.166)
The bow should be known as eight *tālas* in length, and its span is two cubits;
the arrow, the mace, and the thunderbolt are prescribed to be four *tālas*.
The sword should be made with a measurement of forty finger-breadths;
the discus is twelve finger-breadths, and the javelin is desired to be half of that.
One should know that the *prāsavat* cloth is twenty finger-breadths in measure, and the staff (*daṇḍa*) is likewise twenty;
the *kaṇaya* is also twenty finger-breadths according to its standard measurement.
The wise should fashion a mouthpiece (kheṭaka) thirty finger-breadths in length, sixteen finger-breadths in width, provided with a handle and a small bell.
A broken staff and wooden rod, as well as a headrest, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, a banner, and even an ornament; BhN 21.171.
Whatever object in the world of men serves as a means for men,
and whatever accessory there may be— all that is proclaimed in drama.
Whatever object is appropriate for a particular [staff], by that its characteristics should be inferred;
and I shall now fully explain the characteristics of the wooden staff when it is worn out.
The banners have indeed been described by Viśvakarman according to their characteristics as belonging to Mahendra;
one should construct one of these from wood in a manner that is somewhat worn.
Alternatively, it may be of tree origin, or even a sprout or a withered one;
a bamboo flute is indeed the best, and I shall describe its characteristics.
Furthermore, a bamboo that has grown on white ground and under the Puṣya asterism should indeed be carefully selected for the purpose of making a jarjara.
The measure [of the staff] shall be one hundred and eight finger-breadths;
it should likewise have five joints, four knots, and be the size of a palm tree trunk.
One should not use bamboo that has a thick knot, nor one with branches, nor one infested by insects;
nor one whose joints are damaged by worms, nor one inferior to other bamboos.

Having honored the bamboo flute according to the prescribed rite— with offerings of honey, clarified butter, and mustard seeds, and preceded by garlands and incense— one should take hold of it, even if it is worn out.
Whatever ritual procedure and whatever sequence are prescribed for the *māhebdra* banner,
those should be performed for the *jarjara*, relying upon the same bamboo of the *puṣya* asterism.
That bamboo which has long joints, thin leaves,
and grains at the tips of its joints is celebrated as *puṣyaveṇu*.
This rule has been declared by me according to the measurement of a worn-out staff;
hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the staff-wood.
Furthermore, the wooden staff should be made from *kapittha*, *bilva*, or bamboo;
it must be curved at one-third [of its length] and endowed with the proper characteristics.
That staff-wood which is not infested by insects, nor afflicted by disease, and whose branches are sparse, should be used. (BhN 21.184)
But he who should have a wooden staff made that is devoid of these characteristics and is worn out will certainly incur great misfortune. (BhN 21.185)
Now, for the purpose of dividing the head, a circle (ghaṭī) should be carefully constructed according to its own measurement, which is indeed thirty-two finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
The *ghaṭī* should be made from the pulp of the *bilva* fruit, shaped like a head, and combined with steamed *bilva* paste and liquid. (BhN 21.187)
One should fashion a head-covering either with ashes or with husks;
then, having covered it with cloths, one should apply bilva-milk contained within jars.
Having smeared a cloth with a paste of *bilva* fruit, one should join it to the jar;
one should not make it too thick, nor crooked, nor too thin, nor too long.
When that [skin] has been dried by the sun, or even when it is thoroughly dried,
the wise perform the excision according to the procedure prescribed by rule.
Having divided [the forehead] into equal halves with a very sharp instrument,
one should mark the corners according to its own specified measurements on the forehead.
The forehead should be made half an aṅgula [in height], and it should be cut away six aṅgulas;
the portion to be cut away at each of the two sides should be half of a half-an-aṅgula, and the width of the hips should be two aṅgulas.
At the edge of the ear-lobe, the portion of the ear-stalk to be excised shall be two fingers' breadth;
likewise, the ear-cavity itself shall be three fingers' breadth and must indeed be excised.
And from that, an *avaṭu* (a hollow or notch) should be made, perfectly even and twelve finger-breadths long;
for this is the rule always prescribed by me for cutting the vessel.
Above that, crowns fashioned from many artistic elements should be made,
covered with various jewels and adorned with many forms.
Likewise, one should indeed prepare various kinds of accessories for the application of drama here, according to the specific nature [of each character].
Whatever action or craft is prescribed in this world, which is endowed with both the moving and the unmoving, that is remembered as an instrument (upakaraṇa).
Whatever object comes within its range, that alone it pursues;
for it does not enter into the interior of men who are merely supports for theatrical equipment.
Whatever action, craft, application, or activity has been produced by someone,
by that very thing its creation, its measure, and likewise its characteristic are established.
That creation which was fashioned by the Great-Souled One as consisting mostly of wooden machinery is not ours; why indeed should it cause distress in the practice of dance?
Whatever substance exists in the world of living beings, characterized by various features,
its imitation in form shall constitute the equipment for drama.
Palaces, houses, vehicles, and various weapons—
these cannot indeed be produced here according to the characteristics as they have been described.
One thing is the nature of worldly phenomena (*lokadharmin*), while another is the nature of dramatic performance (*nāṭyadharmin*);
indeed, the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) belongs to worldly phenomena, whereas manifestation (*vibhāva*) is drama itself.
Theatrical equipment should not be made of iron, nor likewise of lead; for those who know the art, such materials would cause excessive strain.
One should have light-weight theatrical props made here from wood, leather, cloth, lac, bamboo, and leaves. (BhN 21.205)
Shields, armor, banners, mountains, palaces, temples, chariots, elephants, vehicles, celestial mansions, and houses; BhN 21.206.
First, having fashioned implements from bamboo leaves based on the intended purpose,
one should then cover them with cloths and bring them into conformity [with the desired form].
Alternatively, if a lack of cloth should occur here,
the making of garments may be done with palm leaves or with smooth pieces of kiliñja grass.
Likewise, in the drama, there should be weapons made of grass, bamboo, leaves, and so forth,
as well as various forms fashioned from animal skins and other materials.
One should fashion replicas according to their form, using grass, bamboo, or earthenware, for every foot, every head, every hand, and every limb. BhN 21.210.
Whatever form is similar to this, arising from the quality of resemblance,
one should have that entire [image] made of clay, yet fashioned in various forms.
Those various serpents should be fashioned from vessel-materials, cloth, beeswax, lac, mica, and from linseed, hemp, and bilva.
One may also have various kinds of flowers, diverse fruits, vessels, garments, beeswax, or even lac prepared [as offerings]. (BhN 21.213)
Indeed, [the signs are seen] through vessels, clothing, beeswax, and likewise copper plates;
also properly through indigo dye, and even through mica plates.
One should fashion the jewels with a colored mica-leaf,
and likewise, one should have the shelter constructed from copper and tin.
The various crowns that were previously described by me should be made radiant with cloud-like petals and adorned with the brilliance of jewels.
For it is taught that their ritual action does not originate from the scriptures;
rather, it should be performed with the mindset of a teacher, employing reasoning and refutation.
This application of mortal activity has been devised by me for the future;
why indeed will there be such weakness of strength among human beings?
Even for mortals, manifestations consisting entirely of gold cannot be desired, whether as crowns or as other ornaments made of gold and jewels. (BhN 21.219)
In battle, wrestling, dancing, or during activities involving exposure to rain,
sweat and fainting arise in one who is exhausted by the burden of exertion.
For one afflicted by perspiration, fainting, and exhaustion, the practice will fail;
moreover, there may even be loss of life due to excessive exertion. (BhN 21.221)
Therefore, ornaments should be fashioned from copper leaves, or even from abhraka minerals, or from bheṇḍa wood, or from beeswax.
Thus, by means of worldly convention and through the power of his own intellect,
the wise man should properly employ the instruments of drama here.
It is not to be pierced, nor indeed to be cut, nor even to be struck;
one should perform actions with weapons on the stage merely as a symbolic representation.
Alternatively, the discharge of weapons should be performed by the actors in the midst of the stage through yogic training or by means of what is created through magic and illusion.
In this way, various kinds of weapons and ornaments have been described; furthermore, those which have not been mentioned by me should also be taken from the world.
This "artificial" (āhārya) representation has indeed been declared by me in brief;
hereafter, I shall speak concerning the "general" (sāmānya) representation.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter of the *Bhāratīya Nāṭyaśāstra*, titled "The Representation by Means of Costumes and Make-up" (*Āhāryābhinaya*).
Now begins the twenty-second chapter, titled "General Representation" (*Sāmānyābhinaya*), which is to be understood as arising from speech, the limbs, and the inner being (*sattva*).
In this regard, one must exert effort; for drama is established upon inner being (*sattva*).

An abhinaya that exceeds the [actor's] inner being (sattva) is called "superior" (jyeṣṭha); one with equal inner being is "middling" (madhya); and one deficient in inner being is known as "inferior" (adhama). BhN 22.2.
For the unmanifest form of being (sattva) is to be understood as that which rests upon the state [of emotion],
endowed with its appropriate flavor and qualities such as horripilation, tears, and so forth.
The ornaments, which are based on the emotions (*bhāva*) and sentiments (*rasa*), should be understood by those knowledgeable in drama;
they are the transformations arising from the face and limbs of women that increase in youth.
At the beginning, there are three born of the limbs (aṅgaja); ten others are innate (svābhāvika);
furthermore, seven are effortless (ayatnaja), being augmented by rasa and bhāva.
The essence (sattva) consists of the body; from the essence, emotion (bhāva) arises;
from emotion, gesture (hāva) arises; and from gesture, playful grace (helā) arises.
Playfulness, gesture, and emotion arise from one another;
these exist within the body, established in its fundamental nature according to the distinctions of the constituent elements.
One who brings to life the inner state of the poet through speech, gestures, facial expressions, spirit, and dramatic representation is called a *bhāva*.
The existence of an entity, which is distinct from its own sources, is not produced by a single state; one should describe that entity here as being produced by various states.
In that context, *hāva*— rich with movements of the eyes and eyebrows, indicative of amorous form,
and accompanied by the graceful movement of the neck— is to be understood as occurring while standing or rising.
That which is indeed *hāva* is what is called by the wise *helā*, arising from the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), consisting of graceful gestures (*lalita-abhinaya*). (BhN 22.11)
Līlā, vilāsa, vicchitti, vibhrama, kilikiñcita, moṭṭāyita, kuṭṭimita, bibboka, and likewise lalita; BhN_22.12 //
And "dalliance" (vihṛtam) should be known as the tenth; these are the ten qualities born of the nature of women.
Furthermore, I shall describe their specific characteristics individually.

Līlā (coquetry) is to be understood by those skilled in performance as the imitation of a beloved person through refined ornaments of speech and body, which are sweet and motivated by affection. (BhN 22.14)

That specific excellence which arises in one's standing, sitting, and walking, as well as in the actions of the hands, eyebrows, and eyes, when it is closely knit together, is called *vilāsa* (coquetry).
For even a very slight arrangement of garlands, coverings, ornaments, and ointments, when applied with disregard for ostentation,
produces supreme beauty because of its elegance.
Vibhrama (bewilderment) should be understood as a confusion arising from intoxication, passion, or joy, involving various objects such as speech, limbs, attire, and demeanor. (BhN 22.17)
The mingling of smiles, weeping, laughter, fear, joy, pride, sorrow, fatigue, and longing, occurring repeatedly out of delight, should be known as *kilakiñcita*. (BhN 22.18)

When, during conversation with a beloved person or even upon witnessing their playful gestures and the like, one manifests an imitation of that person's state of being, it is called *moṭṭāyita*. (BhN 22.19)

*Kuṭṭamita* should be understood as that which arises from excessive joy and agitation due to the grasping for hair, breasts, lips, and so forth; it is pleasure expressed through the pretense of pain. (BhN 22.20)
The state known as *bibboka* should be understood as arising from pride and conceit upon obtaining desired objects, characterized by a display of disregard toward women.
The graceful arrangement of hands, feet, and limbs, executed through the movements of the eyebrows, eyes, and lips,
which arises from delicacy, is proclaimed as *lalita* (the playful).
"The placement of hands, feet, and limbs, joined with the eyebrows, eyes, and lips, performed according to a delicate method by women—this is known as *lalita*. // BhN 22.23 //
The failure to speak words that are full of affection when they have been obtained—whether by means of a pretext or by one's own nature—that is called *vihṛtam*. (BhN 22.24)
When women, out of modesty, refrain from speaking words they have already acquired—
whether by pretext or by their very nature— this is described as *vihṛtam*.
Beauty, loveliness, brilliance, as well as sweetness,
fortitude, boldness, and magnanimity— these are qualities that arise effortlessly.
The adornment of the limbs by means of form, youth, and beauty, augmented by objects of enjoyment, is proclaimed as "splendor" (śobhā). (BhN 22.27)
Likewise, *kānti* (loveliness) is to be understood as beauty itself when the passion of love is not yet fully developed;
and *kānti* when it is exceedingly expansive is designated as *dīpti* (brilliance).
In all specific states, whether intense or graceful,
the absence of excess in physical movement is designated as *mādhurya* (sweetness).
The natural state of the mind, unassailed by fickleness and free from boastfulness regarding all objects, is designated as fortitude.
Confidence is defined as the absence of timidity in practice;
and nobility, which accompanies all circumstances, is declared by the wise to be humility.
These [ornaments] occur in a delicate application characterized by grace;
however, when applied to a brilliant [style], they indeed occur even while abandoning their playful grace.
Beauty, grace, sweetness, steadfastness, profundity, as well as charm,
magnanimity, and splendor— these are the varieties of the quality of goodness (sattva) pertaining to manhood.
Dexterity, heroism, energy, revulsion toward base matters,
and rivalry with those of superior qualities— because of these, it is known as *śobhā* (splendor).
A steady, wandering glance and a gait as graceful as that of a bull,
followed by speech preceded by a smile— this is celebrated as *vilāsa* (coquetry).
When a state of cohesion arises from the repeated practice of the constituent elements,
even amidst great transformations, that is known as *mādhurya* (sweetness).
Steadfastness (sthairya) is defined as the non-deviation from a resolve that is connected with virtue, wealth, and pleasure, and which arises from what is wholesome or unwholesome.
That power by virtue of which facial expressions are not observed in states such as joy, anger, or fear is known as "depth" (gāmbhīrya). BhN 22.38.
That which is not preceded by conscious intent, which possesses a changeless nature,
and consists of gestures in the form of the erotic sentiment, is declared to be *lalita* (the playful).
Generosity, assistance, and likewise pleasant speech—
whether toward one's own kin or others— that is proclaimed as magnanimity.
The refusal to tolerate insults, contempt, and the like when employed by another, even at the cost of one's life— that is declared to be *tejas* (vitality).
O best of the twice-born, I have previously explained the *abhinaya* born of emotion;
now I shall explain the bodily *abhinaya* in its proper sequence.

The bodily [gesture] consists of six components: the sentence (vākya), the sprout of the cue (sūcāṅkura), the branch (śākhā), the enacted performance (nāṭyāyita), and the sprout of withdrawal (nivṛttyaṅkura). BhN 22.43.

The recitation of both Prakrit and Sanskrit, composed of metrical compositions endowed with various sentiments and meanings, and accompanied by explanatory glosses (*cūrṇa*) and words, should be understood by the wise as the dramatic representation of speech (*vākyābhinaya*).

When the meaning of a sentence or the sentence itself is indicated first by means of the limbs of the body, and the subsequent enactment of the sentence is designated as *sūcī*, that is indeed so called. (BhN 22.45)
The anga-abhinaya (limb-gesture) performed with words residing in the heart is to be accomplished with skill;
however, the aṅkura-abhinaya (sprout-gesture) is to be understood as that which is produced by a mere hint.
That which is performed by means of the head, mouth, shanks, thighs, hands, and feet, respectively,
is to be understood as the *śākhābhinaya*, the path of the branch-gesture.
That which is performed in drama through the indication of gestures by means of formal conventions is called *nāṭyāyita*;
it continues until the reunion [of characters] occurs through *praveśakas* due to the necessity of extending the duration of the plot.

That which is performed as an expression (*abhinaya*) in a fixed place (*sthāna*) through joy, sorrow, anger, and so forth, conjoined with the emotions (*bhāva*) and aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), should also be known as *nāṭyāyita*. (BhN 22.49)
When another person joins a statement spoken by someone else through a suggestive gesture (*sūcābhinaya*), that which expresses a meaning connected to it is the *nivṛttyaṅkura*. (BhN 22.50)

The path for these [works], however, consists of twelve types of dramatic representation (abhinaya) as prescribed in poetic subjects, endowed with the flavors (rasa) according to their nature. (BhN 22.51)
Discourse, idle chatter, and likewise lamentation;
as well as repetitive talk, conversation, and slander. (BhN 22.52)
Sandeśa, atideśa, and likewise another, nirdeśa, as well as upadeśa, apadeśa, and vyapadeśa are proclaimed [as types of indication]. (BhN 22.53)
Speech that consists of addressing someone is known as *ālāpa* (conversation);
whereas speech that is devoid of meaning is proclaimed to be *pralāpa* (incoherent chatter).
That lamentation which arises from compassion is proclaimed as such;
a statement uttered repeatedly is remembered as *anulāpa*. (BhN 22.55)
A discourse joined with statement and reply is celebrated as *saṃlāpa*;
indeed, speaking otherwise than what was previously stated is recorded as *apalāpa* (denial).
"Speak these words"—this is called an *saṃdeśa* (message). That which was spoken by you has been spoken by me; this is known as an *atideśa* (extended application). (BhN 22.57)
"This very one, I say" is proclaimed as *nirdeśa* (direct designation);
speaking by means of another pretext is here called *vyapadeśa* (indirect designation).
"Perform this! Take this!"—this indeed is proclaimed as *upadeśa* (instruction);
whereas that which consists of speaking for another purpose is proclaimed as *apadeśa* (pretext).
These paths should be understood as that which joins all modes of dramatic representation;
furthermore, I shall describe their characteristics in seven ways.
Direct perception and indirect perception, as well as the three types produced by time;
those residing in oneself and those residing in another—these indeed are the seven modes. (BhN 22.61)
When I say, "O sir, I am not speaking," that speech itself would be both perceptible and imperceptible, as well as present. (BhN 22.62)
"I act, I go, I speak your words;
being established in the self and present, it is indeed considered to be directly perceived. (BhN 22.63)
The speech "I shall do," "I shall go," or "I shall speak"—whether referring to oneself or another, and whether situated in the present or the future—is indeed [mere] time. (BhN 22.64)
All the hosts of enemies have been slain, conquered, and broken by me;
that time is remembered as being established within oneself, beyond perception, and having already passed.

"If one says in the performance of a drama, 'They were killed by you' or 'They were conquered by you,' while being out of sight, standing at a distance, or likewise referring to a past time; [he commits an offense]."
When one says such words as "he speaks," "he acts," or "he goes," that [agent] would likewise be situated elsewhere,
yet present and perceptible.
The statement that "he goes" or "he acts," as it has been cited, would refer to something situated elsewhere, something present, and indeed something imperceptible. (BhN 22.68)
That speech which says "they will do," "they will go," or "they will speak," refers to what exists in another person and pertains to a future time as well as something imperceptible.
Just as one might speak while placing a hand inside during a performance of drama,
that which is situated within oneself, within the heart, and even beyond perception is considered such.
Through the specific distinctions of others, of oneself, and of time,
the divisions of these very seven types should be understood as manifold.
These applications should be understood as being joined with the performance of the Path;
when one has mastered these here, manifold dramatic representation (abhinaya) arises.
However, that division of action which is equal across the head, hands, waist, breasts, shanks, and thighs is indeed general gesture (*sāmānyābhinaya*).

It should be performed by those skilled in drama, who are endowed with aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) and emotional states (*bhāva*), through graceful movements of the hands as well as gentle gestures of the limbs.
It is undisturbed, unconfused, and characterized by movements of the limbs that are not exaggerated;
its nature is regulated by the measures of tempo, rhythm, and the proportions of the musical arts.
When a dramatic performance consists of well-articulated phrasing and speech that is neither harsh nor cacophonous, it should be known as internal (ābhyantara).
This very same [performance], when inverted, characterized by movements according to one's own whim,
and consisting of unrestrained song and instrumental music, is known as external drama (bāhya-nāṭya).
For that which is within the characteristics [of the treatise] is accepted as being internal;
whereas that which is outside the treatise is said to be external. (BhN 22.78)
Since both the performance and the action are characterized by this,
it is for this reason that this definition has been applied to this drama.
Those who have not lived with a teacher and those who are excluded from the scriptures employ the external [rituals],
for they do not understand the activity pertaining to the teacher.
The wise practitioner should represent sound, touch, form, taste, and likewise smell, as well as the sense organs and the objects of the senses, through their respective states of being.
Having cast a sidelong glance and likewise inclining the head to the side,
the wise man should indicate sound by placing the index finger at the region of the ear.
Having slightly contracted the eyes and likewise raised the eyebrows, as well as by touching the shoulders and cheeks— one should thus indicate the act of touching.
Having placed the two flags (patākās) upon the head and with the face slightly moved,
the wise performer should represent your form with a gaze that scrutinizes you.
Having slightly contracted the eyes and expanded the nostrils,
one should indicate taste and smell by means of a single exhalation.
For these five objects of the senses are indeed the experienced entities, belonging respectively to the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and likewise to the nose. BhN 22.86.
For the sense objects, together with the mind, become perceivers;
indeed, one who is without the mind does not know anything of the fivefold range of objects.
The wise should understand that there are three types of mental states to be expressed in dramatic performance:
the desired, the undesired, and likewise the neutral.
One should provide an indication of the desired [result] by means of the gladdening of the limbs, as well as by horripilation and the expansion of the face.
When a desirable sound, form, touch, smell, or taste is encountered by the senses or the mind, one should manifest a cheerful countenance. (BhN 22.90)
By turning the head away, by pulling at the eyes and nose,
and by not allowing the gaze to meet, one should indicate that which is undesirable.
Neither with a mind of excessive joy nor with extreme loathing,
but with a perfectly neutral disposition, one should point out that which is neutral.
"This belongs to him," "this is his pond," or "he does this"—
when there is such a representation of something out of sight, that is known as the neutral (madhyastha) dramatic gesture.
That object which is experienced by oneself is known as "situated in oneself" (ātmastha);
whereas that which consists in the description of another's experience is designated as "situated in another" (parastha). (BhN 22.94)
Generally, the accomplishment of all things is held to arise from desire;
and that [desire], endowed with the quality of wishing, is conceptualized in many ways.
The desire for dharma, the desire for wealth, and likewise the desire for liberation—yet that union of man and woman is traditionally known as *kāma*. (BhN 22.96)
For indeed, in the world as a whole, desire is seen to be the primary means for removing both pleasure and pain; it provides happiness even in the midst of calamities.
That union of man and woman which brings about sexual pleasure and enjoyment should be known as *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment); it is auspicious when performed through refined courtesy.
This world almost always desires happiness above all else;
yet women are the root of happiness, and they, moreover, possess diverse characters.
Of gods, dānavas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, nāgas, and birds;
of piśācas, yakṣas, and serpents; and of humans, monkeys, and elephants.
Women are said to possess characteristics similar to those of deer, fish, camels, crocodiles, donkeys, pigs, horses, buffaloes, goats, gavayas, and other such animals.
With smooth limbs and graceful secondary features, steady and with slow blinking,
free from disease, endowed with luster, and possessed of generosity, courage, and uprightness.

One who perspires little, is moderate in passion, eats sparingly, and is fond of sexual union; who delights in perfumes and flowers, is charming, and possesses the character of a goddess—such a woman is known as Devaśīlā. (BhN 22.103)
Delighting in unrighteousness and deceit, she is stubbornly angry and exceedingly cruel;
always fond of liquor and meat, she is prone to wrath and excessively proud.
Fickle, excessively greedy, harsh, fond of quarreling,
prone to envy, unstable in affection, and possessing a demonic nature— such is her character.
Devoted to play, with beautiful eyes, her nails and teeth like well-blossomed flowers, she possesses excellent limbs, speaks with composure, has few children, and is fond of sexual pleasure.
Delighting in song, instrumental music, and dance, joyful, and well-groomed;
one with smooth skin, hair, and eyes should be known as having the nature of a Gandharva. (BhN 22.107)
One whose every limb is large and elongated, whose eyes are red and wide, who has coarse hair, who is devoted to sleeping during the day, and who speaks in an excessively loud voice; BhN 22.108.
Inflicting wounds with her nails and teeth, fond of anger, envy, and quarreling,
and habitually roaming at night— she has adopted the nature of a rākṣasī.
She has a sharp nose-tip and teeth, is slender-limbed with copper-colored eyes,
possesses the hue of a blue lotus, is habitually inclined toward sleep, and is exceedingly prone to anger.
The animal realm is characterized by unstable undertakings, heavy breathing, and excessive pride;
its female beings are known to delight in perfumes, garlands, and liquor, and to lack self-control.
She is extremely distinct, possessing a sharp character, fond of rivers,
devoted to wine, spirits, milk, and ghee, having many offspring, and fond of fruit.
She is constantly breathing heavily, fond of gardens and groves, fickle, talkative, and quick; she has resorted to the nature of a bird.
One with hands having too few or too many fingers, who wanders in the garden at night,
who is habitually terrifying to children, who is slanderous, and who speaks with malice.
Those women who have foul conduct, hairy limbs, and a loud voice, and who delight in liquor, meat, and offerings, should be known as having the nature of a *piśāca*. (BhN 22.115)
Her body perspires during sleep, she is fond of a steady bed and seat,
she is wise and intelligent, and she has a taste for the scent of wine and meat.
She experiences joy upon seeing those who have been long absent because of her gratitude;
she does not sleep for long periods, and thus the woman of the Yakṣas is described.

She who regards honor and dishonor as equal, whose skin is rough and whose voice is harsh, who engages in deceitful, false, and arrogant speech, who possesses a predatory nature, and whose eyes are tawny— BhN 22.118.
With well-proportioned limbs, grateful, and fond of her gurus, gods, and brahmins;
devoted to dharma, pleasure, and wealth, and indeed free from egoism;
dear to her friends, virtuous, and possessing a human nature—BhN 22.120.
She has a compact and slender body, is joyful, possesses reddish-brown hair, and is fond of deceit;
she is bold, fickle, sharp-tongued, and delights in trees, gardens, and forests.
She who always regards even the slightest benefit as great,
and who is characterized by impetuous passion, is one who has taken refuge in the nature of a monkey.
She has large jaws and a broad forehead, possesses a well-developed body,
has tawny eyes, hairy limbs, and is fond of perfumes, garlands, and wine.
Those of elephant-like nature are proclaimed to be irascible yet steady-minded, fond of water, gardens, and forests, and delighting in sweet things.
With a very small belly, a broken nose, and slender shanks, she is like a cuckoo;
with moving, wide eyes, she is fickle and swift of foot.

One who is constantly afraid during the day, who delights in songs and instrumental music, and whose mind is unsettled regarding her dwelling, is proclaimed to be of the deer-nature (*mṛgasattva*). (BhN 22.126)
She has a long, full, and elevated chest; she is restless and does not blink excessively;
she has many servants and many children; she possesses the nature of a fish and is fond of water.
She has long lips, perspires profusely, and walks with a somewhat awkward gait;
she has a slender waist and is fond of flowers, fruits, salt, sour, and pungent flavors. BhN 22.128.
With her sides and waist hanging loose, speaking harshly and cruelly, with an excessively high waist and neck, she has the nature of a camel and is fond of the wilderness. (BhN 22.129)
With a thick head, a curved neck, a gaping mouth, and a loud sound, she should be known as the Makara-natured; she is cruel and endowed with the qualities of a fish.
She has a thick tongue, lips, and teeth; her skin is rough and she speaks harshly;
she engages in amorous combat, is audacious, and delights in the wounds of nails and teeth. (BhN 22.131)

One who hates her co-wife, is clever, fickle, and quick-moving; one who is diseased, has many children, and possesses a harsh nature—such a woman is proclaimed [to be of the donkey temperament]. (BhN 22.132)
She has a long back, belly, and face; she is hairy, strong, and has a very narrow forehead; she is fond of bulbs, roots, and fruits. (BhN 22.133)
Dark-complexioned, with a mouth fierce with tusks, having a short belly and hair,
of low conduct and many offspring— such a woman has resorted to the nature of a sow.
She is firm, with well-proportioned sides, thighs, hips, back, head, and neck;
she is fortunate, generous by nature, upright, and possesses thick hair.
Lean, with a flickering mind, speaking softly yet moving swiftly, and devoted to passion and anger— such is the female horse characterized by the nature of a horse.
With a thick back, eyes, and teeth; with thin sides and belly; firm;
covered with tawny body hair; fierce; hated by the world; yet fond of pleasure. (BhN 22.137)
With her face slightly upturned, fond of water-sports and forest groves,
possessing a broad forehead and shapely hips, she has taken on the nature of a buffalo.
She is emaciated, with thin arms and chest; her eyes are fixed and steady;
her hands and feet are contracted, and she is covered with fine body hair.
A woman with the nature of a forest bird is known to be fearful in character, anxious about water, having many children, fickle, swift-moving, and lacking in steadfastness.
With her limbs and eyes hanging down, she is intent on yawning;
she has a long and small face, and is adorned with very small hands and feet.
Loud-voiced, having little sleep, prone to anger, fond of good deeds, of low conduct, yet grateful—she is proclaimed to have the character of a dog. (BhN 22.142)
She has broad, fleshy, and elevated hips, slender shanks, and is beloved by her friends;
she has well-proportioned hands and feet, is firm in her undertakings, and is devoted to the welfare of her subjects.
Devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, truthful, pure, and fond of her teachers, she is steadfast, enduring of hardships, and possesses the nature of cows.
Women should be known to have diverse characters, each depending upon her own innate nature;
having discerned their nature accordingly, one should then attend to them.
For women, even a slight act of courtesy according to their disposition brings joy;
however, even a great one, if performed otherwise than appropriate, does not produce satisfaction at all.
Just as joy arises from obtaining what was earnestly desired,
so too is ritual practice prescribed for the sake of the pleasure between a man and a woman.
For ascetic practice is for the sake of Dharma, while Dharma is desired for the sake of happiness;
women are the root of happiness, and enjoyment with them is desired.
In the dramatic theory (nāṭyadharma), the enjoyment of desire is said to be twofold:
external and internal, pertaining respectively to women and men.
That which concerns the inner circle of kings should be employed in a *nāṭaka*, while that which concerns the outer circle, such as matters involving courtesans, should belong to a *prakaraṇa*.
In this regard, I shall explain in due order the royal enjoyments,
as well as the correct procedures for ritual service arising from the Kāma-tantra.
The nature of women is threefold, arising from various types of beings:
the external, the internal, and another which is both external and internal.
Women of noble birth are to be known as internal; courtesans are considered external;
but that woman who has performed purification is considered both external and internal. (BhN 22.153)
In the service within the inner apartments, however, there may be women of noble birth or even maidens;
for in the royal service, the enjoyment of external women is not desired.
One should be an insider to the king and an outsider to the common folk;
for kings have union with celestial women.
That which is desired by a woman of noble birth should be understood to apply to maidens as well;
and even a courtesan here is just like a woman of noble birth.
In this world, the arising of desire in women or men— whether superior, inferior, or middling— is produced from various states of being.
From hearing, from seeing his form, from the movements of his limbs and playful gestures,
and from his sweet conversations, desire is fully aroused.
Having seen a distinguished man endowed with physical beauty, virtues, and the like, possessed of artistic skills and knowledge, and in the prime of youth, a woman becomes afflicted by passion.
Thereafter, one who knows [the signs] should observe here the gestures of men and women who desire one another, even when their passion is not manifest.
In this context, the desirable gaze is one where the eyelashes move gracefully, the eyes are half-closed like buds, and the upper lids are slightly drooping.
When the corners of the eyes are turned slightly and revealed with graceful and measured gestures during a woman's side-long glance, that gaze is called *lalitā*.
In this case, the color of the face becomes slightly reddened at the cheeks, variegated with drops of perspiration, and the hair stands on end while quivering. BhN 22.163.
By means of intentional distortions of the limbs, side-long glances, as well as by the touch of ornaments and even by scratching the ears; BhN 22.164.
By scratching with the tips of the thumbs, by exposing the breasts and the navel, by pricking with the fingernails, and even by tying up the hair; BhN 22.165.
One should recognize a courtesan afflicted by passion through such signs as these; now I shall likewise describe the gestures of a woman of noble birth.
She seems to laugh with her eyes and gazes steadily;
she smiles secretly and speaks with her face cast downwards.
A woman of good family smiles gently, speaks softly, conceals her signs of perspiration, bites her lower lip, and remains startled.
Not having yet attained the festival of sexual union, she should display the ten stages of love through various states by means of such signs of desire.
In the first stage there is longing; in the second, reflection occurs;
in the third, there is recollection; and in the fourth, the praise of qualities.
Agitation is declared in the fifth [house], lamentation is said to be in the sixth;
insanity is to be known in the seventh, and likewise disease occurs in the eighth.
In the ninth [month] there is indeed dullness, and in the tenth death shall occur;
this is the rule for both women and men—now learn the characteristics as well.
That which has been initiated through resolve, arising from intention and desire,
and accomplished by means of union, is proclaimed as *abhilāṣa*.
She repeatedly emerges and enters, and assumes the very form of Love;
she stands within the range of vision, established in the foremost place of desire.
"By what means is attainment reached, and how might it come to me?"—
thus she should demonstrate her reflection upon the states of being communicated by the female messenger.
In the second [watch], however, she should perform side-long glances with half-closed eyes, the touching of bracelets and girdles,
and the contact with the knot of her lower garment and the navel.
The recollection [of the object] is said to arise from frequent sighs, from reflections on one's desires, and from aversion toward other activities. (BhN 22.177)
Neither on a seat nor on a bed does one find composure, being distracted from one's own task by the pursuit of those thoughts; therefore, one should employ the third [meditation] alone.
"By the grace of his limbs and minor members, by his speech, gestures, smiles, and glances, there is no other equal to him"—this would be the praise of his qualities. (BhN 22.179)

But in the fourth [act], there is the employment of dramatic representation through the chanting of virtues, the raising up [of the body], the wiping away of tears and sweat, and the confidential conversations during the separation caused by the messenger.
Neither on a seat nor even on a bed does she find contentment, nor does she remain still;
she is constantly restless, having taken her resort in a state of agitation.
One should act in this way through the exhaustion of anxious sighs, the simulation of a burning heart,
and likewise through the simulation of extreme agitation.
"Standing here, sitting here, and having approached here by me"—with such various lamentations, one should employ wailing. (BhN 22.183)
Exceedingly agitated by longing and lack of composure,
lamenting and resorting to places for wailing, she wanders here and there.
For one who engages in talk concerning that [object], even when in all other circumstances, and who feels aversion toward others, is proclaimed to have the insanity of *anya*. BhN 22.185.
He stands with unblinking eyes, sighs deeply, and sinks into meditation;
he weeps during the time for recreation—this performance may belong either to one who is intoxicated or one who is insane.
When conciliation, gifts, sharing of wealth, and even desirable commands have all been rejected, illness subsequently arises.
The heart becomes bewildered, a sharp pain arises somewhere in the head, and one finds no steadiness; thus one should employ the eighth [stage].
When questioned, she does not say anything; she neither hears nor sees.
Uttering cries of "Alas! Woe!", she remains silent, having become dull-witted and lost her memory.
In the representation of stupor, one should emit a "huṃ" sound unexpectedly, likewise have the limbs become slack,
and have the face seized by labored breathing.
If, despite all remedies employed, there is no reunion,
then death occurs for one who is consumed by the fire of desire.
Thus, having carefully examined the system of love, one should prepare the appropriate positions,
excluding those that fail to achieve sexual union, except for the final position.
In this way, a person may also employ these various forms of desire through diverse emotional states arising from deception.
Thus, for women or even for men who are desiring in this way,
the wise man should employ dramatic representation through the application of common qualities.
By means of anxiety, sighing, and exhaustion; by the manifestation of a burning heart;
by following after [the object] in that manner; and likewise by gazing at the path.
Also from gazing at the sky, as well as from speaking dejectedly,
from touching and crushing, and likewise from taking refuge in that which provides a basis for misfortune.
One should extensively employ all the various objects of desire that arise from these diverse sources and originate from deception. (BhN 22.197)
Burning with the fire of desire, he resorts to garlands, ornaments, perfumes, houses, and groves as cooling remedies.
Burning with desire, afflicted by many circumstances, and tormented in various ways,
he should, out of passion, dispatch a female messenger who can demonstrate his own condition.
And she should deliver the message of the messenger concerning love; with modesty, she should say, "Such is her condition. (BhN 22.200)
Then, having made his intentions known, he should consider the means for sexual union;
this procedure should be performed by those who know the rules when the desire is concealed.
