I shall again explain, according to the truth, the procedure for royal service that has entered into the inner circle and arises from the science of love.
Whatever various states produced by pleasure and pain, arising from diverse moral conducts,
the king brings about, those very things the world follows.
Qualities that carry out the commands of kings for the sake of women are not difficult to find;
however, desire arising from courtesy is what truly produces pleasure.
Out of great respect for the queens, out of affection for his favorites, and out of fear,
the king must maintain his secret desires toward his attendants.
Although kings possess many systems of love,
that which is practiced in secret and with desire is indeed what brings true pleasure.
That which consists of attachment to what is undesirable, that from which one is turned away, and the difficulty in finding noble women— that is the supreme pleasure of desire.
For the people of the royal harem, enjoyment during the day is prescribed;
as for their practice of staying overnight, that is proclaimed to take place at night.
In succession, for the sake of fruit, at the birth of a child, or even at the onset of new growth;
in times of suffering and likewise in times of joy—these six are known as the [proper] occasions for dwelling.
Kings should approach women in their designated quarters, or even during their fertile period; likewise, they should approach female servants or beloved women for the sake of their purpose.
In that regard, there is the woman adorned for her lover's arrival (*vāsakasajjā*), or the one longing in separation (*virahotkaṇṭhitā*),
or the one whose husband is under her control (*svādhīnabhartṛkā*), or the one separated by a quarrel (*kalahāntaritā*).
The abandoned woman, the deceived woman, likewise the woman whose husband is away, and the woman going to meet her lover— these eight are to be known as the heroines (nāyikās).
She who, longing for sexual enjoyment, joyfully adorns herself while staying in her own quarters is indeed called *vāsakasajjikā*.

But she whose beloved does not come due to being occupied with various affairs, and who is afflicted by the suffering of his non-arrival, is one "longing for separation" (virahotkaṇṭhitā). (BhN 22.214)
She by whose side the hero is bound with the excesses of love,
having attained the quality of intense joy, is one who has her husband under her own control.
When a woman's beloved has departed due to jealousy or a quarrel and does not return,
she, having fallen under the sway of resentment, becomes one separated by a quarrel (*kalahāntaritā*).
She whose beloved has not come to the appointed dwelling due to some distraction is proclaimed as a *khaṇḍitā*, afflicted by the pain of his non-arrival. (BhN 22.217)
If a lover, having sent a messenger for her or having given her a rendezvous,
does not come here for some reason, she would be deceived.
A woman whose beloved husband has gone abroad for various tasks should have her forehead-marks and the ends of her hair smeared with ashes while he is away. (BhN 22.219)
But she who, casting aside shame, embraces [her lover] through intoxication and passion,
and goes to meet her beloved, she shall be known as an *abhisārikā*.
In these states, the heroine based on drama is to be understood;
and I shall describe for her the various methods of the Kāmatantra in many ways.
Through sighs of anxiety and weariness, through the simulation of a burning heart, through conversations with her friends, and by observing her own physical state; BhN 22.222.
By means of exhaustion, dejection, and the shedding of tears; by the onset of anger, by being unadorned and having a plain appearance, and by weeping out of sorrow. (BhN 22.223)
One who has been rejected, one who has been deceived, one separated by a quarrel,
and likewise one whose lover is away— these women should employ these emotional states.
But she who has her husband under her control should be depicted with variegated and radiant attire, her face illuminated by joy, and possessing exalted beauty.
The rendezvous should be arranged by the suitors according to these specific dispositions: for a courtesan, for a woman of noble birth, and for a servant girl. BhN 22.226.
Restrained, with gentle movements, and likewise surrounded by her attendants,
the courtesan should walk slowly, her limbs adorned with various colorful ornaments.
With her limbs withdrawn, terrified, and her face cast down,
a woman of noble birth covers herself with her garment as if to hide her heart.
With speech faltering from intoxication, eyes wide with amorous confusion,
and her movements and gait agitated, the female messenger should proceed with boldness.
When she has gone there and sees her beloved asleep,
she should then awaken him with this following procedure.
A woman of noble birth should awaken [her husband] with ornaments; a courtesan with cool fragrances; and a servant girl with garments and fans. (BhN 22.231)
This rule concerning the basis of desire has not been stated solely for noble women, because a drama must be experienced by all persons in every situation. (BhN 22.232)
When she is engaged in new amorous pursuits or is angry during their union,
he should bring her to the bedchamber by means of pretexts and various stratagems.
Filled with joy, one should enjoy various ornaments, garments, perfumes, and garlands, as well as food and drink provided by one's beloved.
A man under the sway of passion does not become so distressed when failing to obtain a beloved woman as he becomes when,
having attained union with his dear one, his joy increases twofold.
Endowed with the qualities of grace, emotional expression, gestures, speech, playfulness, and sweetness,
a union brought about by desire should be accomplished through mutual glances of love.
Then, when passion has been aroused by the various attentions,
she should prepare her chamber in anticipation of the hero's arrival.
Having taken perfumes and garlands, as well as powdered incense and garments,
one should hold up a mirror playfully, or again and again according to one's desire.
In the practice of dressing, there should not be an excessive taking up of ornaments;
rather, those consisting primarily of waist-bands and anklets, which are resonant with sound, are praised.
There is no taking up of garments on the stage, nor bathing, nor anointing;
there is no collyrium, nor body-paste, nor likewise the binding of hair.
Neither when she is unclothed, nor wearing only a single garment, nor when the lower part of her body is not covered with red dye,
should a woman— whether of high or middle rank— ever perform [the ritual] anywhere.
This entire rule always applies to those of inferior status;
however, having encountered another cause, one should not have [the work] performed even by them.
In a drama, female servants and others, as well as women or men,
should perform the taking up of ornaments and the taking up of flowers.
Having applied her ornaments, she should await the arrival of her beloved;
she should assume a playful, adorned attire that is not inconsistent with propriety.
When the hero arrives, the heroine should properly prepare the bed;
then, while waiting for him, she should give the signal by clapping her hands.
But having heard the sound of the *nālikā*, she, distressed by the arrival of the leader,
dejected and trembling, should go to the gateway itself.
Holding the gateway with her left hand and the door-panel with her right,
she should stand leaning against the gateway and await the Leader.
Resorting to the archway, the woman, not seeing her lover, would feel doubt, anxiety, and fear; she would become despondent for a moment.
Sighing deeply and shedding tears from his eyes,
and making his heart despondent, he should release that limb upon the seat.
Furthermore, due to distraction, she should deliberate regarding the arrival of the hero by means of various methods of inquiry arising from both auspicious and inauspicious signs.
Was he perhaps occupied with duties for his guru, or by friends, or with the counsel of ministers and the affairs of state; or was he chosen by his beloved for some pleasant diversion? BhN 22.251.
One should also predict portents arising from both auspicious and inauspicious causes,
by means of signs located upon one's own body, such as throbbing and twitching.
In auspicious matters, an omen on the left side of a woman is favorable;
however, in all undesirable matters, the omen on the right side should be so.
If the left eye, the forehead, the eyebrows, the nose, the lips, as well as the thighs,
the arms, and the breasts throb, there will be a meeting.
If these appear otherwise than they should, one should declare it an ill omen;
upon seeing such an ill omen, one should then fall into a momentary state of confusion.
In the absence of a leader, one should employ the hand in a gesture of grasping the throat;
furthermore, one should display contempt for ornaments and perform lamentation.
Now, if that omen should be auspicious regarding the arrival of the hero, the heroine should indicate his proximity by smelling a fragrance. (BhN 22.257)
Having seen him, she should rise up with joy and go out to meet him according to the prescribed rite;
then, her eyes wide with great delight, she should gaze upon her beloved.
Placing her hand upon her friend’s shoulder and assuming a wide stance,
she should then show her beloved with his identifying marks and fresh wounds.
If, however, he should have committed an offense,
the hero should be reproached with various approaches or with words of censure.
The utterance of words by women arises from honor and dishonor, from delusions, from dissimulation, fear, and stratagems, and is produced by jealousy.
In matters of confidence, affection, and passion; likewise in doubt, intimacy, and satisfaction; and in cases of rivalry, courtesy, censure, and amorous playfulness.
In matters of dharma, artha, and kāma; in secret communications;
in jest, in curiosity, in agitation, and likewise in times of calamity; BhN 22.263.
Whether the anger between a man and a woman was caused by one or the other, or whether it was mutual, even if he is normally not to be spoken to, he should be conciliated by these pleasing means.
Wherever there is affection, there arises jealousy born of passion;
understand now as they are being described its four origins.
Dejection, offense, unpleasantness, and resentment—
of these, I shall explain the characteristics in their proper order.
Seeing her beloved in such a state— with a gait sluggish from the exhaustion of sleep, bearing visible marks, and covered in fresh wounds— a woman will experience despondency.
One should act out the performance in this manner: with eyes glancing with envy at sleep, with limbs trembling with rage, and with words such as "Excellent! and "Well done!", she shines forth.
Even when restrained in many ways, he is seen by her to be intent on that very [object];
through rivalry and envy, falsehood arises there in the woman.
Placing the left hand upon the chest and likewise shaking the right hand,
while pressing down with the feet, the gesture should be performed for the expression of offense.
"As long as you live, I live; I am your slave and you are dear to me.
If one speaks thus and then acts otherwise, doing what is disagreeable, an offense is committed therein.
Through the mediation of female messengers, letters, and replies, as well as by means of anger, laughter, and weeping,
one should employ gestures of displeasure accompanied by the shaking of the head.
But when one who boasts of his own good fortune approaches an adversary with signs of arrogance, resentment arises therein.
Then, by turning her bracelets and loosening her girdle with a lifting motion,
she should express her indignation with eyes full of tears and filled with apprehension.
Seeing her beloved standing there, apprehensive, guilty, and deeply ashamed,
she should indeed distress him with reproaches arising from words of jealousy.
One should not speak harshly, nor should one engage in excessive joking;
rather, one should address them with words mixed with tears and joined with self-revelation.
By moving the tips of the middle fingers and thumbs while placing the hands upon the chest, and by rolling the eyes upward with continuous, wide-ranging glances; BhN 22.277.
Through the turning of the hands at the waist, through their separation, as well as by the joining of the palms,
and also by the whirling of the head, the striking down, the falling, and the clashing together.
Whether through a glance of feigned indifference, the bending of fingers, or playful threats,
one should perform the appropriate gestures during acts of conciliation by means of these specific emotional expressions.
"You shine; you are seen well. Go, why do you delay?
Do not touch me—go where your beloved dwells in your heart."
Having said, "Go," and having turned away, she should, by means of some pretext, withdraw from his presence and then again instill joy in him with some word or purpose.
Furthermore, having considered the woman's transgression, one should appease her by seizing her roughly by the hand, the garment, or the hair. (BhN 22.282)
When a woman has been seized by the hand, by the garment, or by the hair,
she should slowly effect her release while approaching her beloved.
Then, when her hair is grasped at the end or again on her hand or garment, the lover should say "Huṃ! Release! to her as she approaches him with limbs sluggish from touch.
A woman standing on the tips of her toes, with a slightly exaggerated and haughty coquettish movement,
should slowly loosen her hair in the *aśvakrānta* (horse-step) manner.
When her hair-tuft is not being released, she, with a slight perspiration breaking out and her limbs languid from his touch, should say: "Ha! Ha! Release me! Move away! (BhN 22.286).
With the angry words "Go!", and having gone and then returned,
one should say, for some purposeful reason, "You shall not go."
One should employ the syllable *huṃ* with a shaking hand;
it should be used for shaking off [an opponent], as well as for oaths and even for deception.
One should cover one's eyes and embrace from behind;
furthermore, when a woman's garment has been removed, one should even extinguish the lamp.
He should be exhausted until he has reached her feet;
then, once he has arrived at her feet, she should fix her gaze upon the messenger.
Then the heroine, having raised the hero and embraced him,
being delighted by the enjoyment of love, should proceed toward the bed.
One should employ this according to the gentle method of singing when it is associated with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and serves as the cause for sexual enjoyment.
And when the poetry is based on words situated beyond the person in the sky, then this performance must indeed be carried out by a woman.
Whatever action related to the inner apartments occurs in a drama,
even when it is connected with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), this same rule shall apply there as well.
One who understands the rules of dramatic performance should not sleep on the stage during a scene;
however, for a specific purpose, the interruption of an act may be prescribed.
Alternatively, he may sleep alone or even together with her, according to the requirements of the situation;
likewise, there may be kissing, embracing, and whatever else is secret.
One should not perform biting with the teeth, scratching with the nails, loosening the waist-knot, or the pressing of the space between the breasts in the midst of the arena.
Eating, playing in water, and whatever else may cause shame— whatever is of such a nature, one should not perform it on the stage.
Since a drama depicts a father, a son, a daughter-in-law, and a mother-in-law,
all of these should therefore be avoided with great effort.
An expert in that art should compose a drama with sentences that are exceptional, pleasant to hear, sweet, not overly harsh, and endowed with beneficial instruction. (BhN 22.300)
Thus, a wise man should employ this dramatic representation performed within the inner apartments;
furthermore, when in the company of women, he should utter words centered on the god of love.
Understand here those words concerning beloved ones:
"beloved," "dear," "humble," "protector," "master," and "life. (BhN 22.302)
For indeed, there are words such as "delighting" (*nandana*) used for one who is beloved;
yet [there are others] such as "of bad character," "of evil conduct," "deceitful," "contrary," or "boastful. (BhN 22.303)
One who is shameless and cruel is said to be "dear" only in his anger;
he who does nothing unpleasant and speaks nothing improper is truly dear.
Likewise, one whose conduct is upright is called "dear" (priya), provided that no mark arising from another woman is seen upon him. (BhN 22.305)
Whether it be toward his inferior or his body, he is called a "beloved" who, even when provoked to anger by a woman, does not offer a retort.
One who does not speak harshly is called disciplined;
such a person seeks the welfare of others, is capable of protecting them, and is neither arrogant nor envious.
He who is undeluded in all affairs is designated as a "Lord" (nātha),
through conciliation, gifts, and the enjoyment of wealth, as well as through nurturing and protection.
He who attends upon a woman is called her master; he skillfully performs the act of lying with her according to her desired intentions.
He who acts for the sake of communal enjoyment is known as "Life";
he is of noble birth, steadfast, skillful, dexterous, and eloquent in speech.
"He is called Nandana, praiseworthy among his friends.
These arrangements of speech are remembered as those that produce pleasure and delight.
Likewise, listen to these words of displeasure as I speak them:
he is cruel, intolerant, arrogant, impudent, and boastful.
And he whose mind is unstable is considered to be of immoral conduct;
likewise, he who inflicts beating or imprisonment after having reflected [upon it]. BhN 22.313.
Likewise, he who is harsh in speech and of evil conduct is stretched out [in suffering];
whereas he who is sweet in speech but not consistent in his actions is likewise extended.
That rogue is rebuked by women for even the slightest matter;
yet, wherever he is restrained regarding a particular object, he does exactly that very thing.
One who has perverse inclinations is designated as "left-handed" (vāma);
he is marked by scars from wounds caused by love-play and boasts of his own fortune with women.
One who is excessively proud, as well as stubborn and boastful, is so described;
he who, even when being restrained, approaches a woman with even greater persistence.
He who, having committed an offense, desires to pursue a woman impulsively, is known as one who is marked with signs of transgression and is devoid of shame. (BhN 22.318)
And one whose mind is not serene is called harsh;
these are the arrangements of speech, spoken as either pleasant or unpleasant.
Many other [roles] as well should be assigned to female dancers in the drama;
this, however, is the rule for a delicate arrangement of song.

That which arises from the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), causing exhaustion from the enjoyment of sexual passion, and that which pertains to the "space-person" (ākāśapuruṣa) based on the speech of another; BhN 22.321.
Thus, the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) should be expressed; even there, this same sequence should apply, or else the action involving a male character should take place in the drama.
In that case as well, this same sequence should apply when it is joined with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa);
thus should the performance be employed when one has entered the inner apartments.
I shall now explain, in due order, the rule for celestial women:
their attire is eternally radiant, and their minds are eternally joyful.
For the gods, time is eternally pleasant, providing a basis for their graceful play;
there is neither envy nor anger, neither malice nor the need for conciliation.
Among divine men and women, whatever human emotions there may be in the context of love, as well as whatever limbs and gestures they possess, are likewise seen [in them]. (BhN 22.326)
All that which is appropriate for the union of gods and humans must be performed when the enjoyment of divine women occurs among men. (BhN 22.327)
At that time, all those states of being that depend upon human beings must be brought about;
likewise, divine states are attained through the removal of a curse or through the desire for offspring.
An association with men, centered on the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), should be cultivated;
even if she is invisible, she should entice him with flowers, ornaments, and suggestive words.
Having granted another vision, she may vanish in an instant,
even while [the practitioner] offers garments, ornaments, garlands, and the like, or sends written messages.
When the hero is driven to madness by such attentions,
the passion arising from that intoxication becomes the source of sexual delight.
But that which has attained its own nature is not something that exists in an ultimate sense;
in this way, the royal service should be performed based on internal reliance.
"Now I shall also explain the external figurative representation according to the Vaiśika school.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "General Representation," in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* composed by Bharata.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
He is called *vaiśika* because he distinguishes all the arts (*kalā*); or rather, he is proclaimed as *vaiśika* because he is skilled (*sādhu*) in the conduct of the brothel (*veśa*). (BhN 23.1)
For he who is endowed with all arts, skilled in every craft,
and proficient in capturing the hearts of women— he is a man who is truly a courtesan.
Furthermore, his qualities arising from his own body should be known as being, in brief, thirty-three: those that are innate and those that are acquired.
He was accomplished in the sciences and the arts, handsome and pleasing to behold, valiant and resolute, and endowed with youth, a graceful appearance, and noble lineage.
Fragrant, sweet, generous, patient, free from boastfulness, fearless, speaking kindly, clever, auspicious, and pure.
Skilled in the arts of love, dexterous, knowing the proper place and time,
free from harsh speech, smiling, eloquent, capable, and sweet-spoken.
One who is fond of women, shares his wealth, is full of faith, possesses firm memory,
does not place undue trust even in those women with whom he may go, and is dignified— such indeed is the professional courtesan’s lover.
One who is devoted, pure, skillful, upright, and possessed of right conduct,
who is eloquent and shares those same qualities, should be his companion.

One endowed with the qualities of discernment, one who is firm, as well as one who bears the marks [of initiation], a neighbor, a female friend, a female slave, a maiden, and one who is a crafts-woman or artisan. BhN 23.9.

A nurse, a heretic woman, one who lives by the stage, one skilled at incitement, one of sweet speech, one who is clever, and one who knows the proper time—these are the [qualities required]. BhN 23.10.
A messenger should be charming and one whose secret counsel is well-guarded; she should be appointed for these qualities.
By her, too, encouragement should be given through various demonstrated reasons.
Speaking exactly as one has been told and likewise demonstrating one's inner disposition;
one who is not dull-witted, who possesses physical beauty, who is not lacking in purpose, and who is not afflicted by illness.
A wise man should never employ a male or female messenger who boasts excessively of his or her family, enjoyments, and wealth.
The messenger should announce his desire and describe the matters at hand;
however, there should be no union with one who has not approached out of desire or who is angry.
One should not employ improper means, for the messenger's role depends upon the man;
[these opportunities include] at festivals, wandering at night, in gardens, or in the house of a friend.
In the houses of nurses, or likewise at the invitation of a female friend, or under the pretext of illness, or by staying in an empty house; BhN 23.16.
At the first encounter with women, men should arrange a meeting;
having thus arranged the meeting with skillful means and according to the prescribed rules, [one should proceed].

Whether she is attached or detached, one should discern her by means of her physical signs and forms; for a woman who is the abode of passion reveals herself through the excellence of her natural disposition and state.
Constantly afflicted by love, she performs her amorous play in secret;
in the midst of her friends, she speaks of his virtues and bestows her own wealth upon him.
Her friends honor her, and she always hates her circle of enemies;
she becomes exceedingly joyful during the coming and going of her companions. (BhN 23.20)
She is pleased by his words and gazes at him with affection;
when he sleeps, she sleeps after him, and being kissed, she kisses him in return.
She rises before him, and likewise endures his afflictions;
she is joyful in his prosperity and sorrowful in his adversity.
A woman endowed with such qualities is considered to be "attached" (anuraktā).
As for the signs of one who is "disaffected" (viraktā): when kissed, she does not kiss back on the navel.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
In brief, however, *prakṛti* (nature) is proclaimed to be of three kinds.
Now, for both men and women, [the types] are superior, inferior, and middling.
She had conquered her senses, was possessed of wisdom, and was skilled in various arts;
she was as auspicious as the great Lakṣmī and was a consoler of those who were afraid.
Endowed with the meaning of various scriptures, characterized by profundity and magnanimity,
and possessed of the qualities of steadfastness and renunciation— this should be known as the supreme nature.
Skilled in worldly conventions, proficient in the treatises on the arts,
and endowed with the sweetness of discernment— such is remembered as the middling nature.
Furthermore, those base beings are harsh of speech, immoral, dull-witted,
prone to anger and malice, treacherous toward friends, and preoccupied with finding faults.
They are slanderers, arrogant in speech, ungrateful, and likewise indolent;
they distinguish between those worthy and unworthy of honor, are lustful for women, and fond of quarreling.
Informers, evildoers, and stealers of others' property—endowed with these faults, men become base in this world. (BhN 24.7)
Thus, the threefold nature of men according to their conduct has been described;
now, however, I shall explain the nature of women in due order.
Gentle in nature, not fickle, speaking with smiles, and free from harshness;
she is skillful in following the words of her elders, modest, and endowed with humility.
Endowed with natural qualities such as beauty, noble birth, and sweetness,
and possessed of profundity and fortitude— she should be known as the best of women.
That which is endowed with all these very qualities except for those that are most excellent,
and is permeated by slight defects, is known as the middling nature.
That which is proclaimed as the lowest nature among men should,
in brief, be understood as the very same that characterizes the lowest of women.
The neuter should be known as mixed and indeed inferior;
likewise, those such as servants and the like should be known as mixed castes, O twice-born ones.
The Śakāra, the Viṭa, and whoever else is of similar kind— these should also be understood by the wise as mixed characters and the lowest in a drama.
These natures are to be known through men, women, and neuter beings;
I shall now fully explain their application based upon their character.
In this regard, exactly four types of heroes are proclaimed,
distinguished by various characteristics according to their middling or superior natures.

The heroes are proclaimed to be of four types: the haughty-resolute (dhīroddhata), the playful-resolute (dhīralalita), the noble-resolute (dhīrodātta), and likewise the tranquil-resolute (dhīrapraśānta).
Gods are to be known as *dhīroddhata* (bold and haughty), while kings are *dhīralalita* (bold and playful);
the commander-in-chief and the minister are proclaimed to be *dhīrodātta* (bold and noble).
The wise and the peaceful should be known as Brāhmaṇas, and likewise the merchants;
furthermore, among these, four should be known as jesters.
One who bears the sectarian mark (liṅgin), a twice-born man, one who lives off the king, and a disciple— these, in that order,
he should employ for the gods, the sovereign, the ministers, and the brahmins respectively.
These friends, who are skilled in pleasant conversation during times of separation,
are fit for one who has encountered misfortune or suffering, or for one who is destined for prosperity.
Likewise, the wise call that Puruṣa the Pradhāna and the Leader,
wherein the misfortunes and successes of many beings repeatedly occur.
Where those two [the *puṣṭi* and *vipralambha*] exist together with nourishment (*sapuṣṭi*), there the hero (*nāyaka*) does not appear;
likewise, [the heroines are] a celestial woman, a king’s wife, a woman of good family, and a courtesan.
These heroines are to be known by their various characteristics of nature:
they may be firm (dhīrā), graceful (lalitā), noble (udāttā), or modest (nibhṛtā).
Indeed, divine royal women are endowed with excellent qualities;
a woman born of noble lineage should be both dignified and modest.
In the Lalita and Abhyudatta [styles], the female courtesans and artisans are employed;
indeed, for all the [other] natural types, they are traditionally held to be used in two ways through their application.
There is both the external and the internal; I shall describe their characteristics.
Among them, that which constitutes the royal service is indeed the internal.
Then, that which is external is called the "conduct of speech";
furthermore, the conduct toward kings refers to that which pertains to the royal harem.
I shall explain the classification of women according to their respective functions;
indeed, I shall describe the royal service pertaining to the inner apartments.
Likewise, the great queens, the goddesses, and the mistresses were established there,
as well as courtesans, artisans, actresses, and dancers.
And the female attendants (anucārikās) are to be known, as well as the female servants (paricārikās),
likewise the female messengers (saṃcārikās), and those who carry out errands (preṣaṇakārikās).
The high-ranking female attendants, the doorkeepers, the maidens, the elderly women,
and the royal officials— this is the retinue of the king's inner apartments.
In this regard, she who has been consecrated as queen, who is endowed with noble lineage and virtue, possessed of good qualities, of middle age, and likewise moderate yet capable of anger; BhN 24.33.
Free from envy, knowing the character of her husband, enduring both happiness and sorrow,
she was equanimous and constantly sought her husband's welfare through rites of peace and auspicious blessings.
Peaceful, devoted to her husband, steadfast, and intent on the welfare of the inner apartments—
one endowed with these qualities is designated as a "Great Queen" (mahādevī).
Endowed with these very same qualities, yet devoid of their refinement,
they are arrogant, exceedingly beautiful, and intent upon the enjoyment of their husbands.
Those women who possess a pure, eternal, and radiant form, who are hostile toward their husband's rivals and envious of them, and who are rich in youth, beauty, and virtue, are said to be goddesses.
Furthermore, those daughters who may belong to a general, ministers, or servants, yet are devoid of proper respect; BhN_24.38 //
Those women who are endowed with virtue, beauty, and good qualities, who are beneficial to the king,
and who have received honor on account of their own merits, are known as *svāminīs*.
Possessing beauty and youth, they are harsh yet full of coquettish gestures; skilled in the enjoyment of sexual pleasure, they are envious of their rivals.
They were skillful and knew the minds of their husbands; they were always radiant with perfumes and garlands; they followed the will of the king and were free from envy, pride, and arrogance.

Those who are diligent, free from negligence, having abandoned laziness, and not harsh; who know the distinction between those worthy of honor and those not; they are known as the "established" (sthāpitā). BhN 24.42.
Those who have received honor due to their noble lineage and good character, who are gentle, not overly haughty,
impartial, composed, and patient, are known as *bhoginīs*.
They were experts in various specialized arts, skilled in diverse crafts,
knowledgeable in the classification of perfumes and flowers, and discerning in the distinction between what is worthy and unworthy of being depicted in painting.
They are knowledgeable regarding beds and seats, clever, sweet-spoken, dexterous, gentle, articulate, adept at social graces, discreet, and skilled in the arts.

Those who know the release and dissolution of the planetary influences, who discern the various sentiments and emotional states, who are skilled in the four types of dramatic dance, and who are adept at the processes of reasoning and refutation; BhN 24.46.

Those actresses, endowed with beauty and youth, are known for being rich in the particularities of graceful gestures (*hela*), emotional states (*bhāva*), and through their character and performance (*abhinaya*).
She was endowed with sweetness and likewise skilled in musical instruments;
she possessed all major and minor limbs and was proficient in the sixty-four arts.
She should be clever, endowed with the ability to answer questions, and free from the faults of women;
she should always be bold, likewise free from laziness, and have overcome fatigue.
She was skilled in the application of various arts, proficient in dance and song,
and endowed with beauty, virtues, magnanimity, fortitude, good fortune, and moral conduct.
And her throat was melodious, sweet, smooth, resonant, and variegated;
she stood among the assembled women who were distinguished by their beauty, youth, and splendor.
She who has no equal in her qualities is known as a *nartakī* (dancer), for she does not abandon the king in any situation or during any service.
Those skilled in dramatic arts should be known as the clever attendants;
likewise, there should be a bed-guardian, a parasol-bearer, and a fan-bearer.
The female masseuse, the preparer of perfumes, likewise the female decorator, as well as the female jeweler and the female florist; BhN 24.54.
Those who are of such a kind should be known as attendants;
they move through various courtyards and likewise wander through the groves.
The deities who sport in their abodes, the attendants of the palaces,
the yāminīs, and likewise those women who possess such characteristics.

Those described by experts in drama as "intermediaries" (saṃcārikās) are to be understood as occurring when a message is sent that is not connected with desire, arising from matters both secret and non-secret.
Those women who are appointed by kings should be known as attendants;
they are employed for the protection of the entire inner apartment, as well as for offering praise and benedictions.
Those who rejoice in prosperity should be known as the most eminent; they are those from whom arise various conducts connected with peace and war. (BhN 24.59)
Those who announce the business [of the king] are known as the *pratihārīs*;
they have not experienced the enjoyment of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), nor are they agitated or arrogant.
Young girls who have not yet known a husband and who have been honored by former kings are considered to be modest and bashful. (BhN 24.61)
Those who have served previous kings are well known as "the elders";
they are appointed as overseers of the treasuries and likewise as overseers of the armaments.
She was likewise the overseer of fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs,
and the one who attended to perfumes, ornaments, garments, and garlands.
Likewise, those women who are attached to many men should be known as unrighteous; thus have the women who frequent the inner apartments been described in brief.
O twice-born ones, I shall indeed describe them according to their specific distinctions:
they are devoted and faithful, arising from various sides.
Those appointed to official duties and various tasks who are neither arrogant nor distracted, and who are neither greedy nor cruel; BhN 24.66.
They are self-controlled, patient, serene, having conquered anger and subdued their senses;
free from desire, devoid of greed, and entirely rid of the faults associated with women.
She, however, should be employed in moving within the inner apartments of the royal palace;
likewise, artisans, chamberlains, and eunuchs [should attend to her].
A female attendant who has had her head shaved should be employed for the task of sending messages among women,
as well as for the protection of young girls and infants.
In matters concerning the inner apartments, he should appoint those who follow the king’s conduct as transmitters of all news within the royal residence.
Those who are disciplined, of little strength, indeed impotent, possessing the nature of women,
and not at fault by birth— they are known as *varṣavara*s.
Brahmins who are skilled, elderly, and free from the defects of desire should always be employed by kings for the rites of the goddesses.
Thus have I described this eighteenfold inner harem;
hereafter, I shall explain the outer [harem] arising from men.
The king, the commander-in-chief, the domestic priest, as well as the ministers, the counselors, the judges, and the officials overseeing the princes; BhN 24.74.
There are many other honorable persons who should be known by a king;
I shall describe their specific distinctions according to their characteristics—listen! (BhN 24.75)
Strong, endowed with intelligence, truthful, with senses conquered,
skillful, bold, steadfast, courageous, wise, and pure.
Far-sighted, possessed of great energy, grateful, pleasant-spoken, and gentle;
upholding the vows of the world-protectors and proficient in the path of action.
He should be industrious and vigilant, devoted to serving his elders, knowledgeable in the treatises on statecraft,
skilled in discerning the intentions and gestures of others, brave, and provided with a guard.
He should be capable of critical inquiry through reasoning and refutation, skilled in the application of various arts,
proficient in the meaning of the treatises on ethics and statecraft, and likewise possessed of affection.
A king should be knowledgeable in the Dharma and free from vices through these qualities;
he should be of noble birth, endowed with intelligence, and learned in various treatises.
The people of that land are affectionate, cannot be led astray by others, and are not negligent;
they are free from greed, disciplined, pure, and likewise righteous.
Indeed, domestic priests and ministers should be endowed with these qualities:
they must be intelligent, accomplished in statecraft, free from laziness, and pleasant of speech. (BhN 24.82)
One who knows the methods for discovering the vulnerabilities of others, understands the specific times for military expeditions,
is skilled in the meaning of the treatises on statecraft, is loyal, and is of noble birth.
Those who know the principles of legal procedure, who are intelligent and highly learned, must always be appointed by kings as experts in both place and time.
Impartial, righteous, and steadfast, they distinguish between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done;
patient, self-controlled, and having conquered anger, they look upon all things with equanimity.
Such twice-born men as these should be appointed as judges upon the seat of justice:
those who are upright, vigilant, free from indolence, and have conquered fatigue.
They are affectionate, peaceful, disciplined, impartial, and likewise skillful;
they understand policy, they understand discipline, and they are adept at reasoning and refutation.
Likewise, those appointed as princes who are endowed with the meaning of all the śāstras should desire their qualities according to the opinion of Bṛhaspati.
That which is to be known, that which is to be presented, and the deliberation of the court members—thus has this decision of the judge been declared by me to you. (BhN 24.89)
Henceforth, I shall again expound upon the various modes of dramatic representation (*abhinaya*).
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Conduct of Men and Women," in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* composed by Bharata;
now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.

That particular variety of bodily gesture (aṅgābhinaya) which, in various instances, is not explicitly mentioned [in the rules] but is nevertheless expressed, is called "variegated" (citra); it is known as variegated gesturing (citrābhinaya). (BhN 25.1)
Having placed the two hands palm-upward and positioned them in the svastika gesture at the sides, with the head tilted upward and likewise gazing upwards; BhN 25.2.
He saw the dawn, the sky, the night, the twilight, and likewise the day;
the seasons, the clouds, the forest edges, and vast reservoirs of water.
One should perform the mimetic representation (abhinaya) of the quarters, the planets together with the stars, and whatever else may be stable, employing various types of glances (dṛṣṭi).
Again with these same hands and that same head,
one should then indicate those situated on the ground by looking downward.
By the very perception of touch, as well as by its grasping and its upward movement, one should indicate the moonlight, pleasure, wind, taste, and smell. (BhN 25.6)
By concealing oneself with clothing, one may ward off the sun, as well as dust, smoke, and wind;
furthermore, by desiring shade, one can counteract the heat of the earth and the warmth [of the air].
With an upward and squinting gaze, one should indicate the sun at midday;
likewise, with expressions of wonder, one should point to the sun at its rising and setting.
Those [sentiments] which are associated with gentle objects and produced by a good disposition should be enacted through touches of the limbs accompanied by horripilation.
The wise person should also act out those forms that are harsh through non-contact, through agitation, and through the contortion of the face.
A wise person should represent matters that are profound and sublime with limbs that are full of dignity, pride, and graceful poise.
One should indicate laughter by placing the hand at the region of the sacred thread;
the two hands in the svastika gesture, when moved away from the body, indicate necklaces, garlands, and strings of pearls.
Through the rotation of the revolving instrument and the complete turning of the vision,
there occurs the grasping of all objects, free from the affliction of the *alapa* and *padmaka* [visual defects].
That which is to be heard should be indicated by means of hearing, and that which is to be seen by means of visual observations;
one should point it out as abiding in oneself, in another, or in between.
Likewise, lightning, meteors, thunderous roars, sparks,
and flames should be represented by the performers through trembling limbs and the blinking of eyes.
Having crossed the arms and turned them away, with the head bowed,
one should cause [the person] to act with a sidelong glance when there is no contact or when it is undesirable.
One should ward off wind, heat, darkness, and fire by covering the face, and one should also keep away dust, water, insects, and bees.
Having formed them into the shape of a svastika, with the palms closed like lotus buds and facing downwards,
one should visualize lions, bears, monkeys, tigers, and other beasts of prey.
The *svastika* and *tripatāka* gestures are prescribed for saluting the feet of teachers;
the *khaṭaka* and *svastika* are likewise remembered for grasping the goad.
One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eightfold; or it may be nine or even ten—this is the counting that occurs by means of the fingers. (BhN 25.20)
Those called the "ten," the "hundred," and likewise the "thousand," should be employed by performers with their two hands as banners.
That which occurs here beyond the enumeration known as the "ten" must be accomplished through the meaning of the sentence itself and by means of indirect representation (parokṣābhinaya).
The parasol, banner, and flag are to be indicated by means of holding a staff;
furthermore, various weapons are to be indicated based on their mode of grasping.

For when recollecting the meditative absorption that has been reflected upon, one should have a single-pointed mind, avoid downward glances, keep the head slightly inclined, and form a pincer-like gesture with the left hand.
Having raised the head and made the two swan-wings move clockwise,
they should be held high and employed by the performers in the imitation of offspring.
Having raised the head so that it faces like a swan’s beak and points upward,
one should pacify whatever pride there may be and indicate a long-term commitment.
Having raised the left hand in a curved position at the level of the head,
one should employ it when [the opponent] has moved away, is exhausted, is defeated, or when his speech is faltering from fatigue.
One should designate it as autumn when the face is serene due to the well-being of all the sense faculties, and when there are various sightings of the ground.
Furthermore, the winter season should be represented by men of middling and inferior status through the contraction of their limbs and their exposure to the sun and fire.
One should indicate that it is cold by the trembling of the head, teeth, and lips; by the contraction of the limbs; and by moans accompanied by hissing sounds. (BhN 25.30)
Having reached another state, even at times when she is with superior men,
she may perform a gesture of coldness due to a calamity arising from fate.
Likewise, by smelling the fragrance of flowers blooming in their proper season,
and from the touch of a dry wind, the wise man should discern the presence of cold.
The spring season is to be enacted through various kinds of enjoyments that produce delight,
and by displaying diverse flowers.
A wise person should represent the summer through the wiping away of sweat, by means of heating the ground along with its inhabitants, and by the touch of warm winds.
One should indicate the rainy season by means of groves of Kadamba and Nīpa trees, grassy meadows filled with Indragopaka insects, and clouds accompanied by winds pleasant to the touch.
Then, one should predict a rainy night by means of the deep sounds of massed clouds, the falling of torrents, and the noise of lightning and thunderclaps.
If a person's mark, dress, action, or even physical form is indicative of a particular season, that season is to be identified by it through the perception of desired or undesired objects.
One should indeed represent these seasons according to their purpose, following the nature of their flavors:
those [seasons] associated with pleasure as endowed with happiness, and those associated with suffering as joined with pain.
Whosoever is permeated by whatever state— whether it be one that bestows happiness or its opposite— that person,
having formed a latent impression (saṃskāra) based on that, perceives everything as being composed of that very thing.
One should perform the representation of emotions through the illustration of determinants (*vibhāva*);
in that very way, the accomplishment of the emotions (*bhāva*) is set in motion by means of the consequents (*anubhāva*).
The effect brought forth by the *vibhāva* is led forward by the *anubhāva*;
*bhāva* is the self-experience, while *vibhāva* is the perception of another.
Whether he be a teacher, a friend, a companion, an affectionate one, a relative, or even a kinsman—
whoever is presented as having arrived is traditionally known as the "vibhāva" (the excitant).
But that worship which is performed with devotion through respectful offerings, water for the feet, seats, and so forth, along with rising in haste to greet him— that is proclaimed as *anubhāva*.

In this way, it should be understood that even in other cases, whether it be non-existence (*vibhāva*) or existence (*bhāva*), the wise should discern it according to the requirements of the meaning, by demonstrating various effects. (BhN 25.44)
Furthermore, whatever counter-message is delivered here to the messenger should be understood as "anubhāva" (the response), as it is manifested through that counter-message.
Thus, emotion (*bhāva*), its cessation (*vibhāva*), and the consequent emotion (*anubhāva*) have been described;
these should be enacted by men or even by women.
In the representation of natural disposition (*svabhāva-abhinaya*), men should adopt the Vaiṣṇava stance;
for women, however, it should naturally be either the *āyata* or the *avahittha* stance.
Indeed, the remaining [limbs] also exist by virtue of their specific purposes,
through the various enactments of diverse births and through manifold applications.
The activity of men is characterized by movements of the limbs performed with fortitude,
whereas the activity of women is to be carried out with soft, playful gestures of the limbs.
The graceful movements of the hands, feet, and limbs of women are prescribed [for them],
whereas those of men should be performed by practitioners as either very firm or haughty.

Just as there is the manifestation of emotion according to the sentiment and the state of women, so too is there the distinct representation of emotion through dramatic gesture for both men and women. (BhN 25.51)
I shall explain, in due order,
the appropriate cultivation of emotional states through the embracing of limbs and with a smiling gaze.
Likewise, a man should display joy even at the sight of an owl;
with his hair standing on end and his eyes clouded with tears, he should manifest delight. (BhN 25.53)
The dancer should manifest joy through affectionate words accompanied by smiles;
meanwhile, [the lover] should have his eyes wide and red, and his lower lip bitten.
A man should act out anger with his limbs trembling from sighs, his eyes filled with tears, and by the quivering of his chin and lips. (BhN 25.55)
By shaking the head, by knitting the brows, by silence, by the contraction of the fingers, and by the avoidance of garlands and ornaments; BhN 25.56.
In a woman whose armpits remain spread wide, jealousy and anger arise,
indicated by frequent sighs and gasps and by her downward-looking reflections.
Furthermore, one should infer the suffering of men from their speech about the sky, as well as from their weeping, sighing, and striking their heads. (BhN 25.58)
One should cause suffering in women through the impact of falling from a height;
whether that suffering arises from joy, from affliction, or indeed from jealousy.
That which was previously described as weeping should be employed for women and low-born persons,
along with gestures of agitation and distress, and by the falling of weapons.
One should inspire fear in men by means of courage, impetuosity, strength, and so forth,
through the rolling of the eyes and by means of limbs that are quivering and trembling.
And because her heart was terrified, she looked about from both sides;
and likewise, because she was searching for her husband, she cried out loudly.
A woman should even fear the embrace of her beloved;
she should apply those intoxications previously described to low-class women.
By constant faltering with soft steps due to leaning upon the sky, by the rolling of the eyes, and likewise by speech uttered with lassitude; BhN 25.64.
A woman should manifest intoxication through the trembling of her limbs;
by this method, the applications arising from specific causes should be performed.
Whether they be masculine or feminine states of being, all emotions in relation to dramatic representation should be performed with great effort by women in a graceful manner.
Manly sentiments endowed with firmness and sweetness should be performed;
one should employ them with the fingers formed into the *tripatāka* gesture and turned inward.
Parrots and mynas, as well as those birds that are minute, and peacocks, cranes, swans, and others, even those that are large by their very nature; BhN 25.68.
Their performance should be executed through exhalations (*recaka*) and bodily movements (*aṅgahāra*);
[the subjects include] donkeys, camels, mules, lions, tigers, cows, buffaloes, and so forth.
Performers should represent spirits, piśācas, yakṣas, dānavas, and rākṣasas through their movements and bodily gestures.
Those who cannot be identified even by the mention of their names,
yet can be identified by their bodily movements (*aṅgahāra*), become invisible through those very movements.

The gods, however, should be represented visibly through gestures of fear and agitation, along with expressions of wonder, by means of their characteristic marks, acts of salutation, internal dispositions, and physical movements.

For in dramatic performance, those things that are not perceptible to the senses must be conveyed by those skilled in the application [of gestures] according to the requirements of the subject matter.
Indeed, with the left hand raised and curved, one should touch the head.
For this salutation is prescribed for a man when he is not directly perceived,
either by means of a *khaṭakā*, a *vardhamāna*, or again by what is called a *kapota*.
One should salute the deities, the gurus, and women;
as well as those celestial beings who are worthy of worship and those who appear in person.
One should engage them with authoritative means, displays of power, and profound meanings—
namely, the great public, the circle of female companions, and likewise the company of libertines and rogues.
With his hand held in a circular position and raised high,
a man [should represent] mountains and lofty trees through this gesture.
One should employ the *samūhasāgara* formation with both arms extended and raised, even when the army is very extensive.
With both hands in the *patākā* (flag) gesture raised,
one should display heroism, fortitude, pride, arrogance, generosity, and loftiness.
One should display the *tvarāla* [mudrā] by means of its position at the forehead;
the two hands, however, are the *mṛgaśīrṣaka*, cast down from the region of the chest.
The *vistīrṇa* (extended) and *pradruta* (flowing) *utkṣepa* (upward throws) should be employed when [the face] is uncovered;
the hands, with palms facing downward and then turned upward, are slightly extended.
Having performed [the ritual], one should enact the time [of the eclipse] at the mouth of a cave, a house, or a mountain cavern;
[one may represent those] who are seized by desire, by curses, or by malevolent planets, and whose minds are afflicted by fever.
A wise man should perform their gestures with corresponding limbs and other parts;
he should execute the mimetic representation of a swing by means of glances directed toward a swing.
When the swing, Aṅgavatī, made of cloth, becomes visible through the friction of the limbs and the absence of seizing with ropes and reins; BhN 25.84.
For those who have entered upon their seats, swinging [the body] there should be performed;
here I shall speak of the words of the void and those directed toward the self. (BhN 25.85)
The *apavāritaka* and likewise the *janāntika*, as well as that which is speech from a distance and the communication of the bodiless (*aśarīra*). BhN 25.86.
A statement that is indirect or interrupted is called "speech like the sky" (ākāśavacana);
in such a case, one should engage in conversation by means of responses provided by others. (BhN 25.87)
That speech of the heart which arises from the nature of poetry and is joined with various causes is considered to be "internal" (ātmagata). (BhN 25.88)
That [dialogue] should generally be applied with *vitarka* (reflection) in dramas and similar works;
when it is joined with a concealed meaning, it is known as *apavāritaka*.
That which is not heard by those standing nearby due to the exigencies of the action is *janāntika*.
That which resides in the heart, accompanied by mental construction (*savikalpa*), and that which resides in the inner disposition (*bhāvastha*) belongs exclusively to oneself (*ātmagata*).
Thus, these words containing hidden meanings in this drama should be employed by the speakers in the ear as *janāntika*s. (BhN 25.91)
However, whatever matter was previously related should be told again for a specific reason; it should be spoken in the ear so that it does not become a mere repetition.

One should recite without deviation the *ākāśabhāṣita*, *janāntika*, *ātmagata*, and those passages arising from oneself or others, whether they concern things perceived directly or indirectly. (BhN 25.93)
Having concealed the hand by using the *tripatāka* gesture,
performers should employ the *janāntika* and likewise the *apavāritaka*.
Indeed, the meaning of a sentence spoken in sleep should not be represented by the movements of the hands;
rather, that meaning should be represented by the very words uttered while asleep.

In a state characterized by dreams, the recitation should be performed with a slow movement of the voice, making the meaning of the words— whether clear or obscure— seem as if repeated, and based upon the recollection of what occurred previously.

At the time of death, one should produce a faltering, plaintive cry accompanied by hiccupping and gasping, arising from words that echo like the sound of a bell with loose and heavy syllables of compassion.

One should describe as being like death a state accompanied by hiccups and labored breathing when fainting occurs; likewise, even in cases of extreme intoxication or when one is dreaming, the treatment should be as prescribed for that condition.
One should employ for the elderly a recitation with faltering and stumbling syllables, as well as one with unfinished syllables; but for children, it should have a sweet, melodic sound.
Having assumed various states, it is highly proclaimed that one should act out the simulation of death with hands and feet cast about, yet remaining still and collapsed.
And for one overwhelmed by disease, death should be associated with a body that is slumped;
likewise, it is accompanied by hiccups and labored breathing, as well as a loss of independent movement of the limbs.
Even when poison has been drunk, death must be depicted with the limbs, hands, and feet distorted,
joined with the onset of the poison's force, and accompanied by the twitching of the body's movements.
In the first impulse, emaciation is to be represented; in the second, trembling;
likewise, in the third, a burning sensation; and in the fourth, a parched throat.
If the Moon is in the fifth house, there is swelling; in the sixth, the neck is broken;
in the seventh, there will be stupor; and in the eighth, death shall occur.
In that regard, during the first stage [of emaciation], one should employ the representation of sunken and curved cheeks; as for thinness, there should be little speaking of words.
One should also act out trembling of all the limbs, scratching of the body parts,
the tossing about of hands and limbs, and burning sensations.
One should thus represent *vilallikā* through wide-open eyes, through belching and vomiting, through convulsive movements, and through the utterance of indistinct syllables. (BhN 25.107)
Phlegm should be represented through the acts of belching and vomiting, by various kinds of shaking the head,
and by means of being unconscious and blinking the eyes.

Touching the shoulders and cheeks, then bowing the head and casting the gaze toward the outer corners of the eyes— one should thus represent stupefaction through the total delusion of all the sense faculties.
Due to the closing of the eyes, or from the increase of a disease, or from the bite of a serpent—
in this manner, indeed, deaths should be enacted by the wise according to the rules of drama.
Furthermore, in cases of agitation, anger, or those utterances produced by an onset of grief,
there is no fault of tautology here regarding such words.
"Excellent! O day! And 'He-he!'—what do you say to me?
One should cause such actions to be performed two or three times.
When a poem is performed that is deficient in its constituent parts or is distorted,
the wise should not apply the technical definitions of abhinaya (acting) therein.
One should not apply that disposition which belongs to the superior among people to those who are middling;
nor should one apply that disposition which belongs to the middling to those who are inferior. (BhN 25.114)
Indeed, through the various aesthetic sentiments arising from one's own movements,
drama attains passion among the superior, middling, and inferior [audiences].
These specific modes of dramatic representation (abhinaya) should be performed in conjunction with the internal states of being (sattva-bhāva);
however, those others which are worldly should all be executed in accordance with worldly custom.
Just as a garland-maker weaves a wreath from various kinds of flowers,
so should one employ the limbs, the subsidiary limbs, the sentiments, and the emotional states in the performance of drama.
Whatever performance and movement is prescribed for one who has entered the stage, provided with the necessary equipment, he— remaining focused on his being—
should perform that very thing until he has withdrawn from the stage.
Thus have these modes of representation in drama been explained by me in due order; however, those others which are worldly should always be adopted by the wise from common life.
The world, the Veda, and likewise the inner self (adhyātma) are known as the threefold authority.
Drama is for the most part established upon the subjects of the Veda and the inner self.

But drama, which is endowed with the Vedas and the inner self (adhyātma), and possessed of grammar and prosody, becomes perfected as it is established in the world; for drama is essentially of the nature of the world.
Furthermore, it is not possible for a treatise to provide a definitive determination regarding the nature and conduct of all beings, both stationary and moving, in this world.
"Beings possess diverse dispositions, yet drama is established upon character;
therefore, those who speak of drama must understand that the world itself is the authority. (BhN 25.123)

Having correctly understood these rules of dramatic gesture, the person who applies them on the stage—that performer of the principles and gestures of dance—indeed receives the highest honor in the world. (BhN 25.124)
Thus, these modes of representation— arising from speech, costume, and the limbs—
must be employed by one who knows the performance technique and desires success in the drama.
Chapter Twenty-Six:
The threefold nature of recipients has been clearly explained here as being the conformable, the discordant, and likewise the one who conforms to the form. BhN 26.1.

The stage setting, endowed with various states and actions, as well as the natural disposition, should intensely illuminate the drama, which rests upon the foundation of innate character and performance.
Some had many arms and many faces, and others had deformed countenances;
some had the faces of beasts and wild animals, while others had the faces of donkeys, camels, and elephants.
These and many others of various forms exist;
these, however, should be fashioned by the teacher from clay, wood, lac, and leather.
One should enter the ritual circle (*raṅgamaṇḍala*) in one's natural form,
having concealed one's own appearance with pigments and ornaments.
Whatever form belongs to anyone by nature, that very same form should be employed in the performance of drama, in accordance with age and dress.
For just as [a being], having abandoned its own living nature, assumes another bodily state,
it brings about that other state by relying upon that other state.
Thus the wise one, mentally recollecting the supreme state as "I am that," should perform his activities through the movements of speech, limbs, and gestures.
That application which is delicate and produces delight for kings,
having attained the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), one should employ it among women.
Those [gestures] characterized by martial exuberance, piercing movements, and intense, forceful displays should not be employed by women; they are to be used among men.
It should be performed without ostentation and without agitation, with bodily movements that are not overstrained,
and with syllables regulated by the measures of tempo, rhythm, and the divisions of time.
One should employ women in such a drama as this, where the speech consists of well-divided words, and which is neither harsh nor cacophonous.
Thus should the arrangement of the stage be performed by those skilled in dramatic technique:
for women there is the feminine disposition, and for men the masculine.
That mindfulness is considered appropriate when it conforms to age and condition;
however, that man who transforms his state into that of a woman does so through form.
O wise one, that natural disposition (*prakṛti*) should be known as corresponding to one's form during practice;
according to her own desire, a woman may assume a masculine state in accordance with her nature. (BhN 26.15)
The elderly and the childish should not be employed in mutual interactions;
for in the performance of recitation, men refined in the Sanskrit language should be engaged.
The throats of women are naturally sweet, while those of men are powerful;
even if a man should know the rules of singing along with their defining characteristics. (BhN 26.17)
That song which is devoid of the quality of sweetness (mādhurya) does not produce beauty,
wherein the sweetness of men's voices is surpassed by the qualities of women's recitation.
These two ornaments, produced by the reversal of nature,
should be understood as occurring generally in the dwellings of gods, kings, generals, and eminent men.
The performances created by women come to possess a masculine nature;
thus, in heaven, the art of drama is established through figures such as Rambhā and Urvaśī.
In the same way, in this world of men, teachers should diligently provide instruction to the women within the harems of kings. BhN 26.21.
The wise should not personally practice the various roles in a drama;
rather, the performance should be applied with effort by women, while the roles themselves should be based on men.
Since grace that is inherent in their very nature exists in women,
therefore their limbs are naturally sweet and easily attainable in their beauty.
That which is graceful and elegant is considered the supreme ornament;
furthermore, the application based on drama should be understood as being of two kinds.
The *sukumāra*, the *tathāviddha*, which are the substrata for the flavors of various emotions;
the *nāṭaka* along with the *prakaraṇa*, the *bhāṇa*, the *vīthī*, and the *aṅka*. (BhN 26.25)
These [objects] are to be known as delicate and are resorted to by human beings;
this application of delicacy brings delight to kings.

Having attained the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), one should employ that [style] for women; as for those who are fierce in battle, impetuous, violent, and full of martial fury, they are the *ārabhaṭa* [sentiment].

Those [arts] should not be performed by women; rather, they should be performed by men, consisting of combat that involves piercing and being pierced, as well as the execution of bodily movements according to the prescribed rules.
Abounding in illusions and sorcery, illuminated by books and theatrical costumes,
with a population consisting mostly of men and few women, it was moreover arrogant.
The dramatic form known as Āviddha is characterized by the Sātvatī and Ārabhaṭī styles;
likewise, there are the Ḍima, the Samavakāra, the Vyāyoga, and the Īhāmṛga.
These should be known as "pierced" (āviddha) by practitioners;
their application should be performed by gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas.
Even those men who are haughty and endowed with valor and heroism must apply themselves with constant effort and vigilance.
For without skill, there can be no excellence whatsoever in the aesthetic essence of an emotion; rather, the constant labor involved in musical performance is itself a virtue for women.
Through the practice of drama, women attain sweetness and softness; through dramatic charms, they acquire a variegated beauty like that of flowers;
and being skilled in the arts of love, they become especially desirable.
Singing, versification, instrumental music, the practice of rhythmic expansion (*prastāra*), and the training of disciples are recorded as the six qualities of a master.
He who knows these five is proclaimed an Ācārya: namely, the capacity for reasoning and refutation, intelligence, memory, and likewise retentive power.
Intelligence, memory, praise of virtues, passion, emulation, and enthusiasm—these six are known to be the qualities of a disciple as well. (BhN 26.37)
In this way, those skilled in application should perform the conceptualization of the various levels.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the accomplishments as well.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Classification of Vikṛtis," in the Indian *Nāṭyaśāstra*.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter:
"I shall now proclaim the characteristics of the supernatural attainments (*siddhis*) as they relate to drama."
For this entire application has been demonstrated for the sake of accomplishment.
Success should be known as twofold, arising from speech, mind, and body;
it is both divine and human, originating from various states of being.
Human success is said to consist of ten limbs, while divine success is twofold:
that produced by relying on various sentient beings, and that arising from speech, gestures, and the body.
Smitāpahāsinī, Hāsā, Sādhvaho, Kaṣṭameva, Prabaddhanādā, and likewise Siddhi—these are to be known as the [deities] consisting of speech. (BhN 27.4)
Physical accomplishment is desired through horripilation, bristling of the hair, rising from one's seat, the giving of garments, and the gesture of beckoning with the fingers. (BhN 27.5)
When a slight residue of rasa is joined with dancing, it is called *hāsya* (the comic);
that should always be received by the spectators with a smile. BhN 27.6.
Whatever is slightly humorous, as well as speech that is likewise [humorous], should always be understood by the spectators through its underlying meaning. (BhN 27.7)
Whatever is performed by a jester or by means of a craft,
and whatever is done through excessive laughter, should always be appreciated by the spectators.
Likewise, pride should be understood as arising from the nature of men,
which is connected to the state of dharma and occurs according to its specific excellence.
In that regard, practitioners should indeed employ the word "sādhu" when there is a state of being overcome by wonder, and for the purpose of expressing great joy. (BhN 27.10)
In the case of *karuṇa* (compassion), however, it should be employed with difficulty as produced by the treatise;
likewise, it is always used for purposes of wonder (*vismaya*) with a continuous sound.
When words are accompanied by reproach, one should win them over with great respect, while their hair stands on end and their eyes are filled with curiosity and wonder.
Whatever task involves a blazing region—consisting of cutting, piercing, or combat;
or involving flight, or likewise expansion—as well as that arising from wrestling and boxing.
With trembling shoulders and head, with tears, and even while rising up—
this [state] must be treated by skilled observers according to the prescribed method.
In this way, this human accomplishment (siddhi) is to be achieved by those who know it;
now, furthermore, I shall explain the divine accomplishment according to its true nature.
That which is endowed with excellence of being and likewise possessed of essence should be performed by the spectators through the application of divine accomplishment.
Where there is no sound, no agitation, and no appearance of portents,
and the assembly is complete— this is remembered as divine accomplishment (daivī siddhi).
This accomplishment, both divine and human, has been declared by me;
hereafter I shall explain the calamities arising from fate.
The wise should understand that afflictions are of three kinds—arising from fate, from oneself, or from others;
occasionally, a fourth type, arising from portents, may occur among these.
The collapse of pavilions due to wind, fire, rain, elephants, or serpents,
as well as the entry of insects, venomous snakes, ants, or wild animals, are caused by fate.
Next, I shall fully describe those who are joined with the supreme [state] through the act of slaying:
discoloration, lack of movement, bewilderment, and loss of memory.

Furthermore, speaking irrelevantly, poetic composition, physical deformity, and lack of manual dexterity—these self-originated defects should be recognized by those skilled in performance. (BhN 27.22)
Whether out of stinginess, hatred, partiality for that side, or due to a difference in purpose—these harms arising from others should always be understood by the wise as such. (BhN 27.23)
Excessive laughing, weeping, bursting, and likewise the dragging away and falling of measuring rods,
as well as the scattering of cow dung, clods of earth, and ants— these are produced by enemies.
There are also sudden calamities caused by the entry of those intoxicated or insane, as well as those produced by signs;
furthermore, I shall describe those various calamities that arise from oneself.
There is a change in appearance, a lack of movement in the faculties, and a loss of memory;
there is speaking of something else, as well as poetic speech, crying out in distress, and agitation. (BhN 27.26)
Excessive laughter, weeping, and discordant cries; the chirping of ants, insects, and beasts;
the falling of crowns and ornaments; and the faults of poetry—all these arise from the lotus-born [Brahmā].
Excessive laughing, weeping, and laughter cause the destruction of the spiritual state (*bhāva*) by the perfected ones (*siddhas*);
the falling of insects and ants destroys success (*siddhi*) with their entire being.

One should avoid singing in such a manner: lacking resonance, lacking the proper rhythmic beats (*tāla*), deficient in the perfection of vocal color and tone, and failing to know the correct placement of notes and tempo. BhN 27.29.
The falling off of a crown or ornament and the breaking out of loud cries bring about destruction;
likewise, the slaughter of animals in ritual applications leads to the loss of many words.
An uneven, deficient in measure, poorly cleaned, and struck by a clumsy blow;
one with an improperly divided grip and release—such a sword, when it reaches the pommel, brings destruction.

For the faults are: tautology, lack of compounding, variation in case endings, absence of euphonic combination (*visandhi*), meaninglessness, the fault arising from the three genders, and confusion regarding the direct and the indirect. (BhN 27.32)
The abandonment of meter and prosody, and the confusion of heavy and light syllables, constitute the defects of a *yati*; these are, in brief, the points of destruction for poetry. (BhN 27.33)
In the classification of poetry, two types of decline that are incurable should always be known:
that which arises from one's innate nature or from calamities, and the state of being like a water-channel with its remaining water [evaporated].
Lack of eloquence, stumbling, and the mispronunciation of poetry; misplaced ornamentation, the falling of the crown, and its slipping off. (BhN 27.35)
There is a lack of skill and confusion regarding the mounting and dismounting of horses, chariots, elephants, donkeys, camels, palanquins, celestial vehicles, and other modes of transport.
There is also the improper grasping or the failure to maintain even one's weapons and armor;
or perhaps the wearing of a crown and ornaments, or entering the arena after a long delay.
By these specific signs, the wise and skillful should recognize those destined for death,
with the exception of the taking up of sacrificial posts, fire-altars, darbha-grass garlands, and ritual vessels.
Success mixed with obstruction may be all-pervasive or localized; for those skilled in drama, there may be success or there may be failure, as if depicted in a painting. (BhN 27.39)
One born many days ago, who has traveled everywhere and whose specific characteristics are unmanifest, should not be drawn;
however, one born on the very same day, even if inferior, may be drawn.

At the conclusion of the *jarjara*, liberation from the performance is achieved; however, for the *nālikā*, liberation must be performed here constantly by those knowledgeable in drama according to the prescribed rule.
In times of misery they fall into a state of wretchedness; such are remembered as spectators in a drama who experience joy when there is joy, and go into sorrow when there is sorrow. (BhN 27.42)
If one recites the *nāndī* verse for another deity at the head of the performance,
there will be a failure of the success of the ritual application due to one's own lack of control over the preliminary stage (*pūrvaraṅga*).
If one should employ poetic composition in a language devoid of regional characteristics through mere intellectual effort,
those skilled in the application [of such arts] should likewise record the destruction of that region.
Who is capable of correctly performing the execution of a dramatic production in the art of dance-drama, whether with a distracted mind or even when it has been properly understood as it was taught?
Therefore, those words of profound meaning that are established in common worldly usage and in the Vedas should be grasped by all people and employed according to rule in a drama.
Nothing is devoid of qualities, nor is anything entirely free from defects;
therefore, in the nature of drama, defects should be understood according to their dramatic purpose.
Furthermore, the actor must never fail to pay due attention to speech, physical gestures, inner disposition, and costume;
likewise, he must attend to the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) and emotions (*bhāva*), the songs, the musical instruments, and worldly propriety.
Thus should this characteristic of the supernatural powers (siddhis) be understood by the wise;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the characteristics of the judges (prāśnikas).
Endowed with good conduct and noble birth, peaceful in their behavior and diligent in their efforts, devoted to fame and dharma, and possessed of middle age; BhN 27.50.
Skilled in the six-limbed dance, awakened, pure, and equanimous; proficient in the four types of musical instruments, knowing the meters, and perceiving reality.
They were knowledgeable in the rules of regional dialects, practitioners of the arts and crafts,
endowed with the four types of dramatic representation, and capable of discerning the aesthetic flavors (rasas) and emotional states (bhāvas).
Those who know the rules of grammar and prosody, and are experts in various sciences—
such persons should be appointed as judges for the ten types of dramatic compositions.
