O Lord, how did this drama fall from heaven onto the surface of the earth?
How was this lineage of yours established under the name 'Naṭa'?
O Great Sage, tell me everything exactly as it truly is.
Having heard those words of the sages, the sage Bharata replied again with a statement concerning the symbolic representation of the secret meaning.
O you of excellent vows, since you ask me, I shall tell you this secret narrative;
listen closely to my account of the preliminary ritual arrangements.
I have previously proclaimed that auspicious rite which destroys obstacles;
by way of its continuation, I have now described the preliminary ritual (pūrvaraṅga).
Just as armor is worn to counteract weapons,
so indeed is evil pacified by the oblation alone.
Thus, by means of recitations, burnt offerings, and the worship of deities, as well as by the performance of all kinds of musical instruments and the sound of singing; BhN 36.19.
When the removal of obstacles has been performed by me through peaceful hymns of praise, words of benediction, and recitations of past deeds that take away sin; BhN 36.20.
"I have been addressed by the gods who were engaged in hymns of praise and song;
we are exceedingly gratified by this performance of yours."
"Since it brings joy to the gods, the asuras, and the humans,
this performance shall therefore be known by the name 'Nāndī'."
For in that place where there is the resonance of song and instrumental music, and where there is an auspicious modulation of voice, there shall be freedom from evil and prosperity.
As far as the sound based on the dance fills that space,
neither demons nor obstructing spirits (vināyakas) shall remain in that place.
At the time of a son's arrival, at a wedding, at a sacrifice, or during the auspicious rites for a king,
upon hearing the sound of the *nāndī*, predatory beasts indeed perish.
Recitation, drama, song, and instrumental music—
these shall indeed become equal to the words and meanings of the Vedic mantras.
I have heard from Śaṅkara, the God of gods, the truth regarding what is beneficial:
that singing and instrumental music are more purifying than thousands of ritual baths and recitations.
In whatever region the auspicious sound of instrumental music, dance, song, and recitation shall exist, there shall never be anything inauspicious.
Thus, for the purpose of the section on worship, I have performed the preliminary rite through various words of praise and the veneration of the deities. (BhN 36.29)
O best of the twice-born, since salutation is defiled [in that context], it is prescribed that the purification for it occurs on the stage of that performance.
Since the purification, the recitation of mantras, and the worship of the jarjara are said to take place in this preliminary stage (pūrvaraṅga), therefore it is proclaimed as "śauca" (purification).
And this very drama, exactly as it was brought down to the surface of the earth—
all of this must indeed be told, for it is not possible to conceal it.
"All these sons of mine are proficient in the science of drama;
through their performances based on dramatic art, they trouble the entire world with their comedies."
Then, after some time, certain [beings] practiced a vulgar art of craftsmanship that mocked the sages by making them the objects of ridicule, while relying upon their virtues.
That poetry, when employed in an assembly, is unfit to be heard: it is characterized by bad conduct, promotes vulgar customs, is harsh, and is irrelevant to the occasion. (BhN 36.35)
Having heard that, all the sages, trembling with fierce rage,
spoke to those descendants of Bharata like fires about to consume them.
"O twice-born ones, do not say that this mockery of us is improper;
for what kind of insult is this, and what is there among us that is not approved? (BhN 36.37)
Because you are intoxicated by the pride of knowledge and do not understand, being grounded in lack of discipline,
therefore this false knowledge of yours shall surely come to destruction.
Having assembled in the company of sages and brahmins,
you shall become those who have abandoned the sacrificial offerings, who perform no oblations, and whose conduct is that of śūdras.
"You shall become excluded from the company at meals, contemptible, and indeed lowly;
and whatever lineage you shall have will be entirely impure."
And those born of your lineage will also become dancers,
attendants upon others, and those who subsist by the trade of weapons.
Having learned that the curse had been given by my sons,
all the gods then became despondent and approached those sages.
Then, having made their request, the gods led by Śakra said:
"Now that suffering has arisen, this dance will perish."
Then the sages declared: "Indeed, this shall not perish;
whatever else was proclaimed elsewhere, all of that shall come to pass."
Having heard these words of the sages of fierce splendor, they were all then distressed;
having heard me, they approached me.
And my sons said to me: "Alas, we have been ruined by you! For by this fault in dramatic performance, you have indeed made us follow the conduct of Śūdras. (BhN 36.46)
I too, having consoled them, said: "O sinless ones, do not give way to anger;
surely, O children, this is the destiny ordained for us by Kṛtānta."
"For the word of sages can never be false; they have consoled you so that your minds might not be set on death. (BhN 36.48)
Know that drama was thus originated by Brahmā;
we transmit it to other disciples through practical performance.

"Let this drama, which has been set forth for the alleviation of suffering, which possesses a great foundation and great merit, and which originates from the Vedas and their auxiliary and secondary branches, not perish! (BhN 36.50)
Having given this dance to the Apsarases exactly as it truly is and according to what you have heard, you shall all then perform penance.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Curse on Drama," in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* of Bharata.
Now begins the thirty-seventh chapter:
Then, after some time, there was a king named Nahuṣa.
For he, endowed with statesmanship, wisdom, and prowess, indeed attained the sovereignty of the gods.
He then ruled the kingdom, attaining prosperity through the grace of the gods;
yet, upon seeing both the Gandharva music and the dance, he fell into deep reflection.
Having reflected in his mind, "How might this performance of dance take place in my house? he remained full of respect.
With palms joined in reverence for the sake of its performance, the king said to the gods:
"Let this dance take place in my palace together with the Apsarases."
Then he was answered by the gods, led by Bṛhaspati:
"There is no union here with celestial women for those who are human."
"You must speak what is beneficial and wholesome, for you are indeed the lord of heaven;
let the teachers go there, and having gone, let them do what is pleasing to you."
Then that king, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to me:
"O Blessed One, I desire that this art of drama (nāṭya) be established upon the earth."
O best of the twice-born, that which was previously spoken by you as the state of being a teacher has been heard; indeed, through your manifest presence, this has been obtained from you.
In our grandfather’s palace, among the people of his inner apartments,
a rite for the grandfather was performed by Urvaśī.
When the king’s madness had ceased due to the grief over her loss,
and the women of the inner apartments had perished, he himself met his end once more.
We desire this to be further explained by you,
so that it may be employed in the performance of sacrifices on lunar days along with auspicious rites.
In that house of mine, he shall be bound, taking refuge in various forms,
so that through the graceful gestures of women, he will be made to manifest himself to us.
When I said, "So be it," King Nahuṣa was then addressed by me,
and his daughters were summoned and spoken to by me along with the gods in conciliatory terms.
For this King Nahuṣa entreats us with palms joined in reverence:
"Please go together to the earth to perform a dramatic dance."
"And when this [rite] is properly performed, we shall bring about the end of the curse;
you shall no longer be objects of contempt among brahmins and kings."
Having gone there, let them apply their stratagems upon the surface of the earth;
for it is not possible to act otherwise than according to the word of the king.
"For all of us, as well as for the high-souled Nahuṣa, drama has been declared by the Self-born One to be perfected through instruction on the self. (BhN 37.17)
The remainder—namely the practical applications, the verses, and likewise the etymological explanations—Kohala shall provide by means of the subsequent tantra. (BhN 37.18)
This place, intended for sport together with the Apsarases,
was consecrated by me in heaven, as well as by Svāti and Nārada.
Then, having gone to the earth and into the house of Nahuṣa, O twice-born ones,
they employed various stratagems among the women in due order.
O best of the twice-born, because of that enjoyment there, those sons of mine conceived an excessive affection for human women. BhN 37.21.
Having fathered sons and performed the ritual application with their wives in due order,
the sons, authorized by Brahmā, attained heaven once again.
Thus was the art of drama brought down to the surface of the earth by his disciples;
and this lineage of the Bharatas, as well as its future development, has been set in motion.
Thus, for some time, Kohala and others remained, deceiving Vatsa and Śāṇḍilya with their displays, while remaining intent on practices contrary to the Dharma.
Indeed, this treatise has been composed for the increase of the intellect of men;
it is endowed with the activities of the three worlds and serves as an illustration of all scriptures;
it is auspicious, elegant, and born from the mouth of Brahmā.
The man who would constantly hear this which was spoken by the Self-Existent One, or who would perform the practice accordingly, or even one who has studied it; BhN 37.26.
Whatever destination belongs to those who know the Vedas, whatever destination belongs to those who perform sacrifices,
and whatever destination belongs to those whose nature is generosity— verily, he shall attain that very destination.
Among all the dharmas of giving, it is proclaimed that there is great fruit;
indeed, the gift of things to be beheld is praised above all other gifts.
The gods, when honored, are not so pleased by perfumes and garlands as they are always pleased by the auspicious performances of dramatic arts.
He who properly preserves both the science of music and the art of dance here attains the supreme, auspicious state of the lords and Gaṇeśas.
Thus, in the practice of drama, the treatise on action has been composed with many prescribed rules; however,
that which is not explicitly stated here should be inferred by experts through imitation of the ways of the world.
Furthermore: May the earth be completely filled, with famine and disease destroyed;
may there be peace for cows and brahmins, and may the king protect the entire world.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Secret Principles," in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* of Bharata;
the *Nāṭyaśāstra* is complete.
